    The Constitutional Development of India

    155 facts · 3 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Government of India Act 1935 provided dyarchy at the centre and abolished dyarchy in the provinces.×3

    Quick quiz: 10 of 21 UPPSC questions

    Regulating Act 1773

    • Acts for East India Company rule were passed during 1773–1853.
    • Regulating Act 1773 made the Governor of Bengal, Warren Hastings, the Governor General of Bengal.
    • It put the Presidencies of Madras and Bombay under Bengal's control.
    • Governor General got an executive council of four; military and non-military decisions were taken by majority of the council.
    • Governor General could vote only in a tie = he had a casting vote.
    • Regulating Act 1773 provided for a Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta; it was set up in 1774.UPPSC
    • The Supreme Court had a Chief Justice and three other judges.
    • Sir Elijah Impey was the first Chief Justice of the Calcutta Supreme Court; Lemaister was not.UPPSC
    • The Act barred Company servants from private trade and from taking gifts or bribes from Indians.
    • British Government tightened control: the Court of Directors (governing body of the Company) had to report on revenue, civil and military affairs in India.

    Pitt's India Act 1784 and Act of 1786

    • Pitt's India Act 1784 separated the commercial and political functions of the Company.
    • It created the Board of Control for political matters; the Court of Directors kept commercial affairs.
    • The Board of Control had 6 members.
    • Act of 1786: Governor General could overrule his council in important matters of safety, peace or interest of the Empire in India.
    • Act of 1786 gave the Governor General the powers of Commander-in-Chief.
    • Lord Cornwallis was the first Governor General to enjoy these powers.

    Charter Acts 1793 and 1813

    1. 1793Charter Act 1793 extended the Company's commercial monopoly for another 20 years.
    2. 1813Charter Act 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly in India, except trade in tea and trade with China.UPPSC
    3. 1813Charter Act 1813 asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over Indian territories held by the Company.
    4. 1813Charter Act 1813 left territory and revenue with the Company for the next 20 years; it did not give revenue control to British Parliament.
    5. 1813Charter Act 1813 empowered local governments to impose taxes and punish those who did not pay.
    6. 1813Charter Act 1813 permitted English missionaries to work in India.
    7. 1813Charter Act 1813 first provided at least Rs 1 lakh per year for education, revival and improvement of literature of Indians.
    8. 1813English education in India came through three things: Charter Act 1813, General Committee of Public Instruction 1823, and the Orientalist–Anglicist controversy.
    9. 1823General Committee of Public Instruction was formed in 1823; it had the job of granting the 1 lakh rupees.
    10. 1835On 7 March 1835, under Governor General Lord William Bentinck (1828–35), Lord Macaulay's proposal was accepted: English became the medium of higher education.
    11. 1858Indian revenue came under direct control of British Parliament by the Act of 1858 (Secretary of State, a British Cabinet Minister, helped by the Council of India).
    • Charter Act 1793 extended the Company's commercial monopoly for another 20 years.
    • Charter Act 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly in India, except trade in tea and trade with China.UPPSC

    • Charter Act 1813 left territory and revenue with the Company for the next 20 years; it did not give revenue control to British Parliament.
    • Indian revenue came under direct control of British Parliament by the Act of 1858 (Secretary of State, a British Cabinet Minister, helped by the Council of India).
    • Charter Act 1813 empowered local governments to impose taxes and punish those who did not pay.
    • Charter Act 1813 permitted English missionaries to work in India.
    • Charter Act 1813 first provided at least Rs 1 lakh per year for education, revival and improvement of literature of Indians.
    • English education in India came through three things: Charter Act 1813, General Committee of Public Instruction 1823, and the Orientalist–Anglicist controversy.
    • General Committee of Public Instruction was formed in 1823; it had the job of granting the 1 lakh rupees.
    • East India Company discouraged orientalist education and promoted western education.
    • Orientalist–Anglicist controversy = dispute on the kind of education the Company should give to local people.
    • H.T. Prinsep and Dr. H.H. Wilson supported orientalist education.
    • Anglicists were led by Charles Trevelyan; they wanted western education through English medium.
    • On 7 March 1835, under Governor General Lord William Bentinck (1828–35), Lord Macaulay's proposal was accepted: English became the medium of higher education.

    Charter Acts 1833 and 1853

    1. 1833Charter Act 1833 made the Governor General of Bengal the Governor General of India, with all civil and military powers.
    2. 1833Charter Act 1833 ended the Company's commercial activities; it became a purely administrative (political) body.
    3. 1833Charter Act 1833 added a law member (fourth member) to the Governor General's executive council.
    4. 1833Charter Act 1833 first made it possible for Indians to share in the administration of their country.UPPSC
    5. 1833Section 87 of Charter Act 1833: no person of India or the Crown to be barred from any Company post on grounds of religion, place of birth, descent or colour.
    6. 1853Charter Act 1853 first separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor General's council.
    7. 1853Charter Act 1853 set up a separate Indian (Central) Legislative Council for law-making.
    8. 1853Charter Act 1853 introduced open competition for selection and recruitment of civil servants.
    • Charter Act 1833 made the Governor General of Bengal the Governor General of India, with all civil and military powers.
    • Lord William Bentinck became the first Governor General of India.
    • Charter Act 1833 ended the Company's commercial activities; it became a purely administrative (political) body.
    • Charter Act 1833 added a law member (fourth member) to the Governor General's executive council.
    • Macaulay was the first law member; the law member could act only for legislative purposes.

    Government of India Act 1858

    • Acts under the British Crown were passed during 1858–1947.
    • By the Government of India Act 1858, the British Crown took sovereignty over India from the East India Company.
    • The Governor General also came to be called the Viceroy, the direct representative of the British Crown.
    • Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India.
    • The Board of Control and the Court of Directors were ended.
    • A new post, Secretary of State for India, was created; he got the powers of the Court of Directors and Board of Control.
    • He was assisted by a council of 15 members (Council of India).
    • The Council of India was advisory; initiative and final decision mostly stayed with the Secretary of State.

    Indian Councils Act 1861

    • Indian Councils Act 1861 began the participation of Indian representatives in law-making.
    • It restored law-making powers to Madras and Bombay provinces = start of decentralization.
    • It empowered the Viceroy to issue ordinances in an emergency, without the Legislative Council's permission; valid for not more than six months.
    • It turned the Viceroy's Executive Council into a miniature cabinet on the portfolio system.
    • All five members got one department each: Revenue, Finance, Law, Home, Military.
    • In 1874, a sixth member was added to the executive council for the Public Works Department.
    • For legislative work, additional members = minimum 6, maximum 12; nominated by the Viceroy for 2 years.
    • At least half of the additional members were to be non-official.
    • Indian Councils Act 1861 made no difference between Central and Provincial subjects.

    Indian Councils Act 1892

    • Indian Councils Act 1892 got royal assent on 20 June 1892 and commenced on 3 February 1893.
    • It increased non-official members in Central and Provincial Legislative Councils but kept the official majority.
    • Additional members of the Governor General's Council were raised to minimum 10, maximum 16.
    • At least half of these had to be non-official; as per rule, 6 official and 10 non-official.
    • Non-official members included both Indians and Europeans.
    • Indian Councils Act 1892 gave the Legislative Council the power to discuss the budget, but not to vote on it.UPPSC
    • Members could ask questions to the executive with 6 days' prior notice; supplementary questions were not allowed.
    • It introduced the principle of election in a limited sense; the word "election" was carefully avoided.

    Indian Councils Act 1909

    • Indian Councils Act 1909 is also called the Morley-Minto Reforms.
    • It gave separate electorates to Muslims = communal representation.
    • Lord Minto came to be known as the father of the communal electorate.
    • It sowed the seeds of separatism that later led to the partition of the country.
    • It first provided for association of Indians with the executive councils of the Viceroy and Governors.
    • Satyendra Prasad (Prasanna) Sinha was the first Indian to join the Viceroy's Executive Council, as law member.
    • Functions and size of legislatures at the centre and in provinces were enlarged.
    • Council members got the right to discussion and to ask supplementary questions.

    Government of India Act 1919

    1. 1854Merit-based civil services were introduced in 1854, after Lord Macaulay's Report of the select committee of British Parliament.
    2. 1855A Civil Services Commission was set up in London; competitive examinations began in 1855 in London.
    3. 1909Separate electorates for Muslims came from the 1909 Act; the 1919 Act continued them.
    4. 1918In 1918 Britain gave limited suffrage to women property holders; this did not apply to other parts of the Empire.
    5. 1919Government of India Act 1919 is known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms; passed by the British Parliament.
    6. 1919Government of India Act 1919 introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
    7. 1919Principal features of the 1919 Act: dyarchy in the provincial executive and devolution of legislative authority from centre to provinces.
    8. 1919The 1919 Act extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Europeans and Anglo-Indians.
    9. 1919The 1919 Act separated subjects into Central (Federal) and Provincial subjects.
    10. 1919The 1919 Act first introduced provincial autonomy by relaxing central control through this separation of subjects.
    11. 1919The 1919 Act adopted direct elections for the first time.
    12. 1919Government of India Act 1919 made the central legislature bicameral for the first time.UPPSC

    14. 1919Under the Rules of the 1919 Act, Council of State = 60 members: 33 elected and 27 nominated.
    15. 1919The 1919 Act gave women no right to vote or to stand in elections.
    16. 1919The 1919 Act let Provincial Councils decide if women could vote, subject to strict property, income or education levels.

    19. 1919Chamber of Princes was set up by King-Emperor George V's Proclamation on 23 December 1919, after royal assent to the 1919 Act.
    20. 1919The last election of the Indian legislature under the 1919 Act was held in 1945.
    21. 1919The 1919 Act provided for a commission after 10 years to review its working and report.
    22. 1922The ICS examination in India started in 1922, first in Allahabad and later in Delhi.
    23. 1926Central Legislative Assembly elections of 1926 and 1945 were held under the 1919 Act; 1937 was not.
    24. 1927In November 1927 (2 years before schedule) the British Government announced a seven-member statutory commission under Simon = Simon Commission.
    • Government of India Act 1919 is known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms; passed by the British Parliament.
    • It embodied reforms recommended by Secretary of State Edwin Montagu and Viceroy Lord Chelmsford.
    • Its objective was to gradually introduce responsible government in India; the term was used for the first time.
    • Government of India Act 1919 introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
    • Principal features of the 1919 Act: dyarchy in the provincial executive and devolution of legislative authority from centre to provinces.
    • Separate electorates for Muslims came from the 1909 Act; the 1919 Act continued them.
    • The 1919 Act extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Europeans and Anglo-Indians.
    • Dyarchy comes from Greek "di-arche" = double rule.
    • Dyarchy = division of provincial subjects into two categories: reserved and transferred.
    • Reserved subjects: governor and his executive council, not responsible to the legislative council.
    • Transferred subjects: governor with the aid of ministers responsible to the provincial legislature.
    • Reserved subjects: judicial administration (justice), police, prisons (jail), land revenue, finance, irrigation, law and order, press, forests, water, labour disputes settlement, agriculture loans.
    • Transferred subjects: local self-government, public works, health and sanitation, industrial research, education, agriculture.
    • The 1919 Act separated subjects into Central (Federal) and Provincial subjects.
    • The 1919 Act first introduced provincial autonomy by relaxing central control through this separation of subjects.
    • It separated provincial budgets from the central budget and let provincial legislatures enact their budgets.
    • The 1919 Act adopted direct elections for the first time.
    • Government of India Act 1919 made the central legislature bicameral for the first time.UPPSC
    • The bicameral Central Legislature could make laws for the whole of British India.
    • Upper House = Council of State; Lower House = (Central) Legislative Assembly.
    • Council of State: 60 members, maximum 20 official (section 18 of the 1919 Act).
    • Central Legislative Assembly: originally 140 members, 100 elected and 40 nominated (section 19).
    • Under the Rules of the 1919 Act, Council of State = 60 members: 33 elected and 27 nominated.
    • Under the Rules, the Assembly was raised first to 143 (102 elected, 41 nominated), then to 145 (104 elected, 41 nominated).
    • One member in each house was elected from Berar out of the nominated members; so many sources count him as elected.
    • In 1918 Britain gave limited suffrage to women property holders; this did not apply to other parts of the Empire.
    • The All India Women's Deputation led by Sarojini Naidu met Secretary of State Edwin Samuel Montagu; women's demands were ignored in the reforms.
    • The 1919 Act gave women no right to vote or to stand in elections.
    • The 1919 Act let Provincial Councils decide if women could vote, subject to strict property, income or education levels.
    • Merit-based civil services were introduced in 1854, after Lord Macaulay's Report of the select committee of British Parliament.
    • A Civil Services Commission was set up in London; competitive examinations began in 1855 in London.
    • Government of India Act 1919 provided a separate Indian Civil Service examination to be held in India; in 1941 Indians were a higher percentage than Europeans in the ICS.UPPSC
    • The ICS examination in India started in 1922, first in Allahabad and later in Delhi.
    • The Act of 1919 created the Chamber of Princes with 120 members.UPPSC
    • Chamber of Princes was set up by King-Emperor George V's Proclamation on 23 December 1919, after royal assent to the 1919 Act.
    • It was a forum for rulers of princely states to voice needs and aspirations to the colonial government.
    • The Viceroy presided over its annual meeting; it was an advisory body.
    • First chancellor of the Chamber of Princes: Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner.
    • Central Legislative Assembly elections of 1926 and 1945 were held under the 1919 Act; 1937 was not.
    • The last election of the Indian legislature under the 1919 Act was held in 1945.
    • The 1919 Act provided for a commission after 10 years to review its working and report.
    • In November 1927 (2 years before schedule) the British Government announced a seven-member statutory commission under Simon = Simon Commission.

    • Government of India Act 1935 provided for an All India Federation of provinces and princely states = federal polity.UPPSC ×2
    • The federation was named the Federation of India.
    • Its units: British Indian Provinces (Governor's Provinces and Chief Commissioners' Provinces) and Princely States.
    • The federation never came into existence.
    • Government of India Act 1935 provided dyarchy at the centre and abolished dyarchy in the provinces.UPPSC ×3
    • Dyarchy at the centre never came into force; central subjects were divided into reserved and transferred.
    • Section 11(1): Defence, Ecclesiastical Affairs, External Affairs and Tribal Areas were handled by the Governor-General in his discretion, not by the federal legislature.

    Note from the book The book notes: in Union-State terms, Defence and External Affairs were in the Federal List and the Governor-General was part of the federal legislature; on that view both statements are correct.

    • The 1935 Act further extended and established Provincial Autonomy.

    • The 1935 Act divided legislative powers between central and provincial legislatures; the Constitution's Centre–State distribution of power is based on it.
    • Under the 1935 Act, residuary powers were vested in the Viceroy (Governor-General), not in the central or provincial legislature.UPPSC
    • The 1935 Act introduced the Principle of Constitutional Autocracy.

    Indian Independence Act 1947

    • Indian Independence Act 1947 declared India an independent dominion on 15 August 1947.
    • It abolished the office of Viceroy; a Governor General was appointed for each dominion.
    • It dropped the title "Emperor of India" from the royal titles of the King of the United Kingdom.

    Demand for a Constituent Assembly

    1. 1932Third and last Round Table Conference: November–December 1932, London; Congress did not take part.
    2. 1934First formal demand for a Constituent Assembly: Swaraj Party, at its Ranchi conference, May 1934; first time Indians demanded it.
    3. 1934The idea of a Constituent Assembly was first put forward by M.N. Roy in 1934.UPPSC
    4. 1934Indian National Congress first officially demanded a Constituent Assembly (after the Swaraj Party) in May 1934, at Patna.
    5. 1935Third Round Table Conference discussions led to the Government of India Act 1935, which provided an All India Federation of British Indian provinces and princely states.
    6. 1938In 1938, Jawaharlal Nehru, for the INC, declared: free India's constitution must be framed without outside interference by a Constituent Assembly elected on adult franchise.
    7. 1939Gandhi wrote this in his article "The Only Way" in the Harijan of 19 November 1939.
    8. 1940The demand was finally accepted in principle in the August Offer of 1940.
    9. 1942Cripps Mission (1942) proposed that an elected Constituent Assembly frame India's Constitution after the Second World War.UPPSC
    10. 1942Cripps Mission was sent by the British government to India in March 1942.
    • First formal demand for a Constituent Assembly: Swaraj Party, at its Ranchi conference, May 1934; first time Indians demanded it.
    • The Swaraj Party wanted it composed of Indian representatives elected on adult suffrage.
    • The idea of a Constituent Assembly was first put forward by M.N. Roy in 1934.UPPSC
    • Indian National Congress first officially demanded a Constituent Assembly (after the Swaraj Party) in May 1934, at Patna.
    • In 1938, Jawaharlal Nehru, for the INC, declared: free India's constitution must be framed without outside interference by a Constituent Assembly elected on adult franchise.
    • Mahatma Gandhi: "Constituent Assembly alone can produce a Constitution indigenous to the country and truly and fully representing the will of the people".
    • Gandhi wrote this in his article "The Only Way" in the Harijan of 19 November 1939.
    • The demand was finally accepted in principle in the August Offer of 1940.
    • Cripps Mission (1942) proposed that an elected Constituent Assembly frame India's Constitution after the Second World War.UPPSC
    • Cripps Mission was sent by the British government to India in March 1942.
    • Cripps proposal: setting up Dominion status.
    • Cripps proposal: any province unwilling to join the Indian dominion could form a separate union with a separate constitution.
    • Cripps proposal: the Constituent Assembly would have members elected by provincial assemblies and nominated by princely states.
    • Third Round Table Conference discussions led to the Government of India Act 1935, which provided an All India Federation of British Indian provinces and princely states.
    • Third and last Round Table Conference: November–December 1932, London; Congress did not take part.

    Wavell Plan

    • Lord Wavell succeeded Lord Linlithgow as Viceroy in October 1943 and tried to end the deadlock in India.
    • He went to England for consultation in March 1945; his proposals were made public in June 1945 as the Wavell Plan.
    • Wavell Plan proposed equal Hindu and Muslim members in the Executive Council; it was not meant to avoid partition.
    • Wavell Plan: restructure the Governor-General's Executive Council with balanced representation of main communities.
    • All members except the Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief were to be Indian.
    • All portfolios except Defence, including the foreign department, were to be held by Indian members.
    • A conference at Shimla was to be called at the earliest.
    • It proposed that after the Second World War, Indians would make a Constitution for India.
    • Aim of the Wavell Plan: remove the deadlock on constitutional and political issues and promote self-governance for Indians.

    Cabinet Mission and composition

    • The Constituent Assembly was constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan 1946.UPPSC
    • Cabinet Mission arrived in India on 24 March 1946.
    • Cabinet Mission members: Sir Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary for India), Stafford Cripps (Chairman, Board of Trade), A.V. Alexander (Navy Minister); William Wood was not a member.UPPSC
    • Provinces' seats were based on population: about one representative per 10 lakh (a million) people.UPPSC
    • Seats: 296 to British India and 93 to Princely States (a minimum of 93).
    • Of 296: 292 from the eleven Governor's provinces and 4 from the four Chief Commissioners' provinces (one each).
    • Princely states' representatives were to be nominated by the heads of the princely states.
    • The Assembly was partly elected and partly nominated.
    • Members from provinces were elected by the Provincial Legislative Assemblies, which acted as the electoral college.UPPSC
    • The Assembly came from indirect election, not adult franchise; it was a multi-party body and worked through committees.
    • Provincial legislature members were themselves elected on limited franchise based on tax, education and property (Government of India Act 1935, sixth schedule).
    • Universal adult franchise lets all citizens join in governance on the basis of adult suffrage.
    • Congress, Muslim League and some independent members got representation in the Assembly.
    • Minority communities like Christians, Anglo-Indians and Parsis were adequately represented.
    • The Assembly had many committees: 8 major committees, others minor; the Drafting Committee was the most important.
    • Elections for the 296 seats were held in July–August 1946.
    • Results: Indian National Congress 208 seats, Muslim League 73, small groups and independents 15.
    • Princely states did not take part at first; their representatives joined gradually from the third session starting 28 April 1947.
    • Members of the Assembly: H.C. Mukherjee = first Vice-President; K.M. Munshi = originally the only Congress member of the Drafting Committee; V.T. Krishnamachari = representative of Rajasthan's princely state; Jawaharlal Nehru = Chairman, Union Constitution Committee.
    • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was elected to the Constituent Assembly from the Pune seat of Bombay Presidency.
    • In the 1946 preliminary election Ambedkar was first elected from the eastern part of undivided Bengal (East Bengal), which later went to Pakistan.
    • The Pune seat had been vacated by the resignation of M.R. Jaikar (of Congress).
    • Ambedkar was born on 14 April 1891 at Dr. Ambedkar Nagar (then Mhow), Madhya Pradesh; died on 6 December 1956 at Delhi.
    • Women members in the Constituent Assembly = 15.UPPSC
    • The 15 women: Vijayalakshmi Pandit, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, Sarojini Naidu, Sucheta Kripalani, Purnima Banerjee, Leela Roy, G. Durgabai (Deshmukh), Hansa Mehta, Kamala Choudhry, Renuka Ray, Malati Choudhury, Dakshayani Velayudhan, Begum Aizaz Rasul, Annie Mascarene, Ammu Swaminathan.

    Interim Government 1946

    • The first Interim National Government was announced on 24 August 1946, to take charge by 2 September 1946.UPPSC
    • Interim Government was formed on 2 September 1946 from the newly elected Constituent Assembly, as per the Cabinet Mission's declaration.
    • At first it had no Muslim League member; on 26 October 1946, 5 Muslim League members joined the Cabinet.
    • The Viceroy was ex-officio President of the Executive Council.
    • Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was not a member of the Interim Government.UPPSC

    Sardar Vallabhbhai PatelHome, Information & Broadcasting

    First meeting and office bearers

    • The Constituent Assembly was established with its first meeting on 9 December 1946; the Viceroy invited the elected members.UPPSC ×3
    • First session: 9 December 1946 to 23 December 1946; 207 members attended (Rajya Sabha website).
    • It met in Constitution Hall, New Delhi, now the Central Hall of old Parliament House.
    • Nehru was a member of the Assembly from the very first day of its proceedings.
    • The Muslim League boycotted the first meeting; Dr. Sachchidanand Sinha was not its first permanent President.
    • Dr. Sachchidanand Sinha, the oldest member, chaired the first meeting as temporary (provisional) President.UPPSC ×2
    • Dr. Rajendra Prasad was unanimously elected permanent President (Chairman) of the Assembly on 11 December 1946.
    • Dr. Rajendra Prasad's name was proposed by J.B. Kripalani.
    • Frank Anthony was the first nominated (temporary) Deputy Chairman, nominated on 9 December 1946 by Dr. Sachchidanand Sinha.
    • Frank Anthony founded the All India Anglo-Indian Association in 1942.
    • Frank Anthony was a nominated Lok Sabha member for seven terms between 1950 and 1992.
    • H.C. Mukherjee was the first permanent Vice-President of the Constituent Assembly.
    • B.N. Rau (Sir Benegal Narsing Rau) was the Constitutional Advisor to the Assembly.UPPSC ×2
    • The first draft of the Constitution was prepared by B.N. Rau and put before the Drafting Committee for opinion, discussion and changes.UPPSC
    • Rau's original draft had 243 Articles and 13 Schedules.

    Objectives Resolution

    • Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946, in the fifth meeting of the first session.UPPSC
    • The Assembly unanimously adopted the Objectives Resolution on 22 January 1947.UPPSC
    • It gave the philosophy and guiding principles for constitution-making and shaped all later stages.
    • Its amended form became the Preamble of the Constitution.
    • Nehru's Objectives Resolution affected constitution-making; the Preamble fulfils important aims; the people of India ordained the Constitution; the President is not directly elected.UPPSC
    • The President is elected by elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of State Legislative Assemblies of all States including Union Territories.

    Making and adoption of the Constitution

    1. 1929The Purna Swaraj declaration was made at the Lahore Session of Congress (December 1929); it asked people to observe 26 January as Independence Day.
    2. 193026 January was chosen because Congress had observed it as Independence Day since 1930.
    3. 1946Order of events: Assembly first met 9 December 1946 → Drafting Committee appointed 29 August 1947 → Constitution adopted 26 November 1949 → commenced 26 January 1950.UPPSC
    4. 1947The Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947: seven members, chairman Dr. B.R. Ambedkar; task = prepare the draft Constitution.
    5. 1949Third reading of the Constitution began on 17 November 1949 and ended on 26 November 1949.
    6. 1949The Constituent Assembly adopted and enacted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, the last day of its 11th session.UPPSC ×6
    7. 1949The Preamble itself says: "We the People of India enact, adopt and give to ourselves this Constitution on 26 November 1949".
    8. 194926 November 1949 = date of adoption, completion and passing; the Constitution was signed by President Rajendra Prasad.
    9. 1949Provisions on Citizenship, Interim Parliament, and Temporary, Transitional and special provisions came into force on 26 November 1949 itself.
    10. 195011 sessions covering 165 days were held; one more meeting on 24 January 1950 makes 12 the nearest exam answer.UPPSC
    11. 1950The Constitution came fully into force on 26 January 1950 = its commencement (enforcement) date.UPPSC
    12. 1950The last (final) meeting of the Assembly was on 24 January 1950, when members signed the Constitution.UPPSC
    13. 1950On 24 January 1950 the Assembly adopted the national anthem and national song and elected Dr. Rajendra Prasad the first President of India.
    14. 2015Constitution Day was announced by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment on 19 November 2015.
    • The Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947: seven members, chairman Dr. B.R. Ambedkar; task = prepare the draft Constitution.
    • Constitution-making took 2 years, 11 months and 17 days (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha websites); exam answers accept 2 years, 11 months, 18 days.UPPSC
    • 11 sessions covering 165 days were held; one more meeting on 24 January 1950 makes 12 the nearest exam answer.UPPSC
    • Third reading of the Constitution began on 17 November 1949 and ended on 26 November 1949.
    • The Constituent Assembly adopted and enacted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, the last day of its 11th session.UPPSC ×6
    • The Preamble itself says: "We the People of India enact, adopt and give to ourselves this Constitution on 26 November 1949".
    • 26 November 1949 = date of adoption, completion and passing; the Constitution was signed by President Rajendra Prasad.
    • Provisions on Citizenship, Interim Parliament, and Temporary, Transitional and special provisions came into force on 26 November 1949 itself.
    • The Constitution came fully into force on 26 January 1950 = its commencement (enforcement) date.UPPSC
    • 26 January was chosen because Congress had observed it as Independence Day since 1930.
    • The Purna Swaraj declaration was made at the Lahore Session of Congress (December 1929); it asked people to observe 26 January as Independence Day.
    • Order of events: Assembly first met 9 December 1946 → Drafting Committee appointed 29 August 1947 → Constitution adopted 26 November 1949 → commenced 26 January 1950.UPPSC
    • The last (final) meeting of the Assembly was on 24 January 1950, when members signed the Constitution.UPPSC
    • On 24 January 1950 the Assembly adopted the national anthem and national song and elected Dr. Rajendra Prasad the first President of India.
    • Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas) = 26 November every year, to promote constitutional values among citizens.
    • Constitution Day was announced by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment on 19 November 2015.
    • The Constitution provides a parliamentary form of government, federal in structure with a certain unitary leaning.
    • The Constitution provides for all necessities of the country and has amendment provisions for the future.
    • It is called an "Adopted Constitution" because it takes views and principles from other countries' constitutions; this does not explain why it meets all needs.UPPSC

    Views and sayings

    • Maulana Azad pleaded in the Assembly to defer adult franchise for 15 years.
    • Dr. Rajendra Prasad and Jawaharlal Nehru strongly supported adoption of adult franchise.
    • Mahatma Gandhi advised that the Indian National Congress, formed only to win independence, be disbanded as a political party after independence.UPPSC
    • Dr. Rajendra Prasad: "A Constitution, like a machine, is a lifeless thing… India needs today nothing more than a set of honest men"; said on 26 November 1949.
    • Sir Ivor Jennings: the Founding Fathers "tended to minimize the importance of minority interests and emotions" (on minority protection provisions).UPPSC
    • Granville Austin: "Constituent Assembly was Congress and Congress was India", in his book "The Indian Constitution".UPPSC
    • Granville Austin was a famous historian and Padma Shri award holder.

    Drafting Committee

    • The Drafting Committee was formed by a resolution on 29 August 1947 under Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.UPPSC
    • Its task: discuss and decide the form and structure of the Constitution.
    • It had 7 members including the chairman = 6 other members.UPPSC
    • Original other members: Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, K.M. Munshi, Mohammad Saadullah, B.L. Mitter, D.P. Khaitan; Nehru and Sardar Patel were not members.UPPSC ×2
    • N. Madhav Rao later replaced B.L. Mitter.
    • T.T. Krishnamachari was included after the death of D.P. Khaitan in 1948.
    • K.M. Munshi's full name: Kanhaiyalal Maneklal Munshi.

    National Flag committees

    • The Constituent Assembly appointed the Ad hoc Committee on the National Flag on 23 June 1947; chairman Dr. Rajendra Prasad.UPPSC
    • Its members: Dr. Rajendra Prasad (Chairman), Abul Kalam Azad, Sarojini Naidu, C. Rajagopalachari, K.M. Munshi, Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar.
    • An earlier Flag Committee was formed on 2 April 1931 at the Karachi Session under Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
    • J.B. Kripalani was neither chairman nor member of any Flag Committee.

    Chapter 4 · Making and basics of the Constitution

    Sources of the Constitution

    54 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The Concurrent List is borrowed from the Constitution of Australia.×5
    2. Fundamental Rights are borrowed from the Constitution of the USA (U.S. Bill of Rights).×4
    3. The system of judicial review exists in both India and the USA.×2
    4. Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are inspired by the Constitution of Ireland.×2
    5. Federation with a strong centre (Union of States with greater powers to the Union; Union–State relations) = from Canada.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 19 UPPSC questions

    Supremacy and the 1935 Act

    • The Constitution is supreme in the Indian political system; it is the supreme law of India.UPPSC
    • It lays down fundamental political principles; structure, procedures, powers and duties of government institutions; fundamental rights, directive principles and citizens' duties.
    • A major portion of the Constitution is borrowed from the Government of India Act 1935 = "Blue Print of the Indian Constitution".
    • The Constitution's framers took inspiration for many aspects from other countries' constitutions.

    Britain

    • From Britain: rule of law, parliamentary form of government, single citizenship, bicameral legislature, law-making procedures, parliamentary privileges, prerogative writs.
    • Cabinet system (Cabinet Government) = from the British Constitution.
    • Rule of Law = England.

    USA

    • From the USA: Preamble, judicial review, independence of judiciary, Fundamental Rights, post of Vice-President, impeachment of President, removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges.
    • Fundamental Rights are borrowed from the Constitution of the USA (U.S. Bill of Rights).UPPSC ×4
    • Fundamental Rights = essential rights everyone needs to live with honour and integrity; in Part III, Articles 12–35.
    Fundamental RightArticles
    Right to Equality14–18
    Right to Freedom19–22
    Right against Exploitation23–24
    Right to Freedom of Religion25–28
    Cultural and Educational Rights29–30
    Right to Constitutional Remedies32
    • Judicial review in India is adopted from the Constitution of the USA.UPPSC
    • The system of judicial review exists in both India and the USA.UPPSC ×2
    • Judicial review = power of courts to examine actions of the legislative, executive and administrative arms for consistency with the Constitution.
    • Actions found inconsistent are declared unconstitutional, so null and void.
    • The Judiciary has the upper hand in interpreting the Constitution; it can overturn a legislative or executive order that conflicts with the Constitution.
    • Common to Indian and American federal systems: a federal Supreme Court to interpret the Constitution.
    • USA has one judicial system at Union level and another at State level (dual judiciary); it has no three lists.
    • India gives single citizenship; the US Constitution gives dual citizenship.
    • The US Constitution is the world's first written Constitution; the tradition of written constitutions began in America.
    • The US Constitution is the world's shortest written Constitution, with only 7 Articles.
    • The Indian Constitution is the longest written Constitution in the world; originally 22 Parts, 395 Articles, 8 Schedules.
    • Fundamental Rights are borrowed from the US model, but this is not the only reason for the Constitution's length.UPPSC

    Ireland

    • Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are inspired by the Constitution of Ireland.UPPSC ×2
    • DPSP are in Part IV, Articles 36–51.
    • DPSP are not enforceable in court, but are fundamental in governance; the State has a duty to apply them in making laws for a just society.
    • Within its economic capacity and development, the State shall secure adequate means of subsistence for all men and women and equitable wages for equal work.
    • The State shall also secure the right to employment, education, and public assistance in unemployment, old age, illness, disablement or other justifiable needs.
    • Method of election of the President = inspired by Ireland.
    • Nomination of Rajya Sabha members for talent, qualification, experience and service = influenced by the Irish Republic.UPPSC

    Canada

    • Federation with a strong centre (Union of States with greater powers to the Union; Union–State relations) = from Canada.UPPSC ×2
    • Residuary powers vested in the centre = from Canada, not Australia.UPPSC
    • Appointment of Governors by the centre and advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court = from Canada.
    • Reserving of a bill by the Governor for the President's consideration = from Canada.UPPSC
    • The concept of "a Union of States" comes from the British North America Act 1867 (the Constitution of Canada).UPPSC
    • Article 1(1): "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States".
    • Constituent Assembly Debates vol. VII: the Drafting Committee followed the language of the British North America Act 1867 in describing India as a Union, though the constitution may be federal in structure.

    Australia

    • The Concurrent List is borrowed from the Constitution of Australia.UPPSC ×5
    • Concurrent List = items on which both Union and States can make law; it is in the Seventh Schedule.
    • Concurrent List originally had 47 items; now 52 (items 11A, 17A, 17B, 20A, 33A added by amendments).
    • Also from Australia: joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament, language of the Preamble, freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse.

    Other countries

    • Emergency provisions (except financial emergency) = from Germany (Weimar Constitution).
    • Procedure established by law = from Japan.
    • Procedure of constitutional amendment and election of Rajya Sabha members = from South Africa.
    • Fundamental Duties = from the USSR (Russian / former Soviet Union) Constitution.UPPSC
    • Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment Act 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.
    • Ideals of justice (social, economic and political) in the Preamble = from the USSR.
    • Republican system and the principles of liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble = from France.
    • The Election Commission in the Indian Constitution is not inspired by any other constitution of the world.

    Parts of Indian Constitution

    Number of Parts

    • The Constitution was originally divided into 22 Parts, with 395 Articles and 8 Schedules.UPPSC ×2
    • At present there are a total of 25 Parts.
    • Part IV-A and Part XIV-A were added by the 42nd Amendment Act 1976.
    • Part IX-A was added by the 74th Amendment Act 1992 (with effect from 1-6-1993).
    • Part IX-B was added by the 97th Amendment Act 2011.

    • Order in the Constitution: Union and its territory (I) → Citizenship (II) → Directive Principles (IV) → Fundamental Duties (IV-A).UPPSC

    Details of some Parts

    • Part IV-A (Fundamental Duties) was inserted in 1976.
    • Attorney General of India is in Part V (Article 76), not Part XIII.UPPSC
    • Part VI covers the Governor, Council of Ministers, State Legislature, High Court.
    • Part XI, Chapter I = distribution of legislative powers between Union and States; Chapter II = administrative relations.UPPSC
    • Subject → Part: abolition of titles = Fundamental Rights; village panchayats = Directive Principles; education for child 6–14 years = Fundamental Duties; "India, that is Bharat, is the Union of States" = Union and its Territories.
    • Tribunals were inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act 1976: Article 323-A = Administrative Tribunals; Article 323-B = tribunals for other matters.
    • Part XV covers the Election Commission's establishment and powers, electoral rolls, and elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and offices of President and Vice-President.
    • Article 243-W (Part IX-A) = powers, authority and responsibilities of Municipalities.
    • Article 243-X = power of Municipalities to impose taxes.

    Panchayats and the 73rd and 74th Amendments

    • The 73rd and 74th Amendments were passed by Parliament in 1992.
    • 73rd Amendment = rural local government (Panchayati Raj Institutions); 74th Amendment = urban local government (Nagarpalikas).
    • The 73rd Amendment put the three-tier Panchayat system in Part IX.
    • Base level: Gram Panchayat, covering a village or group of villages.
    • Intermediate level: Block, Mandal or Taluka Panchayat.
    • The intermediate level need not be set up in smaller states with population below 20 lakhs.
    • Apex level: Zila Panchayat, covering the whole rural area of the district.

    Chapter 7 · Making and basics of the Constitution

    Schedules

    94 facts · 9 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Seventh · Division of powers between Union and States: Union, State and Concurrent Lists · Original×4
    2. Fourth · Allocation of seats in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) to States and Union Territories · Original×3
    3. The Sixth Schedule applies to tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; not to Manipur, Nagaland, Sikkim or Arunachal Pradesh.×3
    4. First · States and Union Territories with their territories · Original×2
    5. Tenth · Disqualification of members of Parliament and State Legislatures for defection (Anti-Defection Law) · 52nd Amendment Act 1985×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 32 UPPSC questions

    Number of Schedules

    • The Constitution had 8 Schedules at adoption; there are 12 Schedules at present.
    • The Ninth, Tenth, Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules were added by Constitution Amendment Acts.
    • The Constitution has 22 Parts and 395 Articles (not 20 Parts or 390 Articles).
    ScheduleSubjectAdded by
    FirstStates and Union Territories with their territoriesOriginalUPPSC ×2
    SecondSalary, emoluments and allowances of Union office bearers (public officials, Judges, CAG)Original
    ThirdForms of oaths and affirmationsOriginalUPPSC
    FourthAllocation of seats in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) to States and Union TerritoriesOriginalUPPSC ×3
    FifthAdministration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled TribesOriginal
    SixthAdministration of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and MizoramOriginal
    SeventhDivision of powers between Union and States: Union, State and Concurrent ListsOriginalUPPSC ×4
    EighthLanguages recognised by the ConstitutionOriginalUPPSC
    NinthValidation of certain Acts and Regulations (land reforms)1st Amendment Act 1951
    TenthDisqualification of members of Parliament and State Legislatures for defection (Anti-Defection Law)52nd Amendment Act 1985UPPSC ×2
    EleventhPowers, authority and responsibilities of Panchayats (Panchayati Raj)73rd Amendment Act 1992UPPSC ×2
    TwelfthPowers, authority and responsibilities of Municipalities74th Amendment Act 1992

    First to Fourth Schedules

    • The First Schedule must be amended if a new State or Union Territory is created.
    • Third Schedule oaths cover: Union Minister, candidate for Parliament, Member of Parliament, Supreme Court Judges, Comptroller and Auditor-General.
    • Third Schedule also covers: State Ministers, candidate for State Legislature, member of State Legislature, High Court Judges.
    • The President's oath is in Article 60, not in the Third Schedule.UPPSC

    Fifth Schedule

    • The Fifth Schedule covers Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in any State other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
    • The Fifth and Sixth Schedules are made to protect the interests of Scheduled Tribes.
    • Scheduled Areas = areas the President declares so by order (Article 244(1); Part C of the Fifth Schedule).
    • Para 4 of the Fifth Schedule: a Tribal Advisory Council in any State having Scheduled Areas.UPPSC
    • Largest administrative unit of a Scheduled Area = district; lowest = cluster of villages in the block.
    • At present 10 States have Scheduled Areas: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan.
    • The Governor (not the Chief Minister) reports to the President on administration of Scheduled Areas, annually or whenever the President requires.
    • The President, in consultation with the Governor, can alter, add to or diminish the boundary of a Scheduled Area.
    • The Governor can repeal or amend regulations for a State having Scheduled Areas, only with the President's assent.
    • Para 5 of the Fifth Schedule gives the Governor special power to prevent transfer of land from tribal people to non-tribal people.
    • Samatha vs State of Andhra Pradesh (1997): Supreme Court held transfer of tribal land to private parties for mining unconstitutional, void and inoperative, under the Fifth Schedule.
    • The State's executive power continues in Scheduled Areas, subject to the Fifth Schedule; the Union cannot take over their total administration on the Governor's recommendation.
    • Neither the Fifth Schedule nor Article 339 has any such take-over provision.
    • Part X, Article 244 gives a special administrative structure for "scheduled areas" and "tribal areas".

    Sixth Schedule

    • The Sixth Schedule applies to tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; not to Manipur, Nagaland, Sikkim or Arunachal Pradesh.UPPSC ×3
    • Its main objective is to save and maintain tribal culture.
    • Sixth Schedule provisions come under Articles 244(2) and 275(1).
    • Tribal areas are administered as Autonomous Districts and Autonomous Regions.
    • Each autonomous district has a District Council of not more than 30 members: not more than 4 nominated by the Governor, the rest elected by adult suffrage.
    • The Governor has the right to direct how Acts of Parliament apply in the Autonomous Districts of Assam.

    Seventh Schedule: three lists

    ListOriginal subjectsPresent subjectsWho makes laws
    Union List (List I)9798Only the Centre
    State List (List II)6659Primarily the States
    Concurrent List (List III)4752Both Centre and States
    • If Union and State laws conflict on a Concurrent subject, the law made by Parliament prevails.
    • Article 246 distributes legislative powers, including taxation, between Parliament and State Legislatures.
    • The right of Union and States to impose taxes and fees is given in the Seventh Schedule.
    • The 52 Concurrent subjects are the joint domain of State Governments, Union Territories and the Central Government.

    Union List subjects

    • Union List: Radio and Television, stock exchanges and futures market, share market, Post Office, Banking, Census, Insurance, Defence, Railways, corporation taxes, Foreign Affairs.
    • Stock Exchange and Post Office Savings Bank are Union List subjects; Stock Exchange is not Concurrent.UPPSC
    • Inter-State trade and commerce = Union List, Entry 42.
    • Inter-State migration and inter-State quarantine = Union List, Entry 81.
    • Corporation tax = Union List, Entry 85.
    • Union List Entry 72: elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and offices of President and Vice-President.
    • State List Entry 37: elections to the State Legislature, subject to any law made by Parliament.

    Note from the book The book notes: for the list and entry on State legislature elections, both List I Entry 72 and List II Entry 37 are correct; MPPSC's official key accepted both.

    • Space Research = residuary subject, vested in the Centre.UPPSC

    State List subjects

    • State List: Police, public order, public health and sanitation, gas, agriculture, railway police, prisons, Panchayati Raj or local government, land reforms.
    • Gas is a State List subject; Banking, Insurance and Census are Union List.UPPSC
    • Agriculture is a State List subject; Defence, Foreign Affairs and Railways are Union List.
    • Railway Police is in the State List, though Railways is in the Union List.UPPSC ×2
    • Panchayati Raj (Local Government) = State List, Entry 5.
    • Land Reforms = State List.
    • Public Health and Sanitation = State List Entry 6; Treasure Trove = State List Entry 44; per-person tax = State List.
    • Tax on agricultural income = State List Entry 46; tax on consumption or sale of electricity = State List Entry 53.
    • Trade and commerce within the State = State List Entry 26, subject to Entry 33 of the Concurrent List.

    Concurrent List subjects

    • Concurrent List: economic and social planning, criminal procedure, population control and family planning, education, forests, marriage, divorce, adoption, electricity.
    • Economic and Social Planning = Concurrent List, Entry 20; the Planning Commission was set up under this entry.UPPSC
    • Prevention of cruelty to animals = Concurrent List, Entry 17.
    • Criminal law, including all matters in the Indian Penal Code (at present BNS 2023) = Concurrent List.UPPSC
    • Criminal Procedure = Concurrent List; public order, prisons and police = State List.UPPSC ×2
    • Population control and family planning = Concurrent List, Entry 20-A, added by the 42nd Amendment Act 1976.
    • Marriage, divorce and adoption = Concurrent List, Entry 5.UPPSC
    • Adulteration of foodstuffs and other goods (Entry 18) and Succession (Entry 5) are in the Concurrent List.UPPSC
    • Concurrent Entry 33: trade, commerce, production, supply and distribution of products of Union-controlled industries and like imported goods; foodstuffs including edible oilseeds and oils; cattle fodder including oilcakes and other concentrates; raw cotton (ginned or unginned) and cotton seeds; raw jute.

    Note from the book The book notes: trade and commerce in Entry 33 goods is also in the Concurrent List, but UPPSC's key left "Trade and Commerce" out because inter-State and intra-State trade are in the Union and State Lists.

    • Protection of wild animals and birds (Entry 17B) and price control (Entry 34) are in the Concurrent List.
    • Education was first in the State List (Entry 11); the 42nd Amendment 1976 moved it to the Concurrent List.UPPSC ×2
    • The 42nd Amendment Act 1976 moved Forests, Education, and Protection of Wild Animals and Birds from the State List to the Concurrent List.
    • Provisions bearing on education: Directive Principles, rural and urban local bodies, and the Fifth, Sixth and Seventh Schedules.
    • Article 45 (after the 86th Amendment Act 2002): early childhood care and education for all children till age six.
    • Articles 243G (Panchayats) and 243W (Municipalities) give powers that include management of education; the Fifth Schedule covers education indirectly.

    Eighth Schedule

    • The Eighth Schedule originally had 14 languages; at present 22 languages.
    • Sindhi was added by the 21st Constitutional Amendment Act 1967.
    • Konkani, Nepali and Manipuri were added by the 71st Amendment Act 1992.
    • Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali were added by the 92nd Amendment Act 2003.
    • Oriya was renamed Odia by the 96th Amendment Act 2011.

    Ninth Schedule

    • The Ninth Schedule was introduced during the prime ministership of Jawaharlal Nehru, by the First Amendment Act 1951 (June 1951).
    • State land reform and Zamindari abolition laws are placed in the Ninth Schedule for constitutional protection.UPPSC
    • It holds Acts and Regulations: originally 13, presently 284; State laws on land reforms and Zamindari abolition, and Parliament's laws on other matters.
    • It was added to protect its laws from judicial scrutiny on the ground of violation of Fundamental Rights.
    • Main aim of the First Amendment: fully secure the constitutional validity of Zamindari abolition laws in general and certain specified State Acts.
    • Parliament can place a law in the Ninth Schedule; but in 2007 the Supreme Court ruled laws added after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review.
    • The Coelho case (Ninth Schedule case) upheld judicial review of laws, including Ninth Schedule laws, against violation of the basic structure.UPPSC

    Tenth, Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules

    • The Tenth Schedule lays down the process by which legislators may be disqualified on grounds of defection.
    • The Eleventh Schedule has 29 subjects (entries); it is mentioned in Article 243G.UPPSC
    • The Twelfth Schedule has 18 subjects.
    • The Eleventh Schedule gives Panchayats administrative control; the Twelfth gives Municipalities administrative control.
