    Chapter 8 · Making and basics of the Constitution

    The Preamble

    57 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1976 added three words to the Preamble: Socialist, Secular and Integrity; they were absent in 1950.×8
    2. The Preamble is called the "Soul of the Constitution".×4
    3. Justice in the Preamble is of three types: social, economic and political.×2
    4. The ideals and objectives of the Preamble are elaborated in the chapters on Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties.×2
    5. On 26 January 1950, India's exact constitutional status was "A Sovereign Democratic Republic".×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 25 UPPSC questions

    Origin of the Preamble

    • The Objectives Resolution was moved in the Constituent Assembly by Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946.
    • The Assembly unanimously adopted it on 22 January 1947; it later became the foundation of the Preamble.
    • The idea of the Preamble was adopted from the Constitution of the USA.
    • A preamble = an introductory statement that makes clear the objectives and philosophy of a document.
    • The Constitution starts with the Preamble, which describes the nature, objectives and ideals of the Indian political system.
    • The Preamble reflects the mind of the makers of the Constitution.
    • The objectives of the Constitution are reflected in the Preamble.UPPSC
    • The Preamble holds the basic philosophy and fundamental values on which the Constitution is based.

    Text of the Preamble

    • The Preamble begins with "We, the People of India"; these words show the sovereignty of the people.
    • People's sovereignty means Indians are not governed by any external power but are directed by the Constitution.
    • The Preamble declares India a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic, in that order.UPPSC
    • It secures to all citizens: Justice, Liberty, Equality; and promotes Fraternity assuring dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the Nation.UPPSC
    • Justice in the Preamble is of three types: social, economic and political.UPPSC ×2
    • "Religious justice" is not mentioned in the Preamble.UPPSC
    • Liberty in the Preamble: of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; economic liberty is not included.UPPSC
    • Equality in the Preamble: of status and of opportunity.
    • The Preamble mentions 3 types of justice, 5 types of liberty, 2 types of equality and 1 kind of fraternity.UPPSC
    • The Preamble gives the date of adoption: "this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution".
    • The word "Federal" is not mentioned in the Preamble.UPPSC
    • The words "Public Welfare" are not in the Preamble.
    • The word "People's" is not in the Indian Preamble; it is in the Constitution of China.
    • The ideals and objectives of the Preamble are elaborated in the chapters on Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties.UPPSC ×2
    • The people's advancement should not hinder the nation's advancement, so the Constitution also aims at promoting fraternity.
    • Economic Justice as an objective is provided in the Preamble and the Directive Principles of State Policy.
    • Article 38(1): the State shall promote people's welfare by securing a social order in which justice, social, economic and political, informs all institutions of national life.
    • Social equality is guaranteed in the Constitution under Right to Equality, Articles 14 to 18; the Preamble also aims at it.UPPSC

    42nd Amendment and the Preamble

    • On 26 January 1950, India's exact constitutional status was "A Sovereign Democratic Republic".UPPSC ×2
    • The Preamble adopted on 26 November 1949 had the words Sovereign, Democratic and Republic; "Reliable" and "Non-religious" were never part of it.
    • The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1976 added three words to the Preamble: Socialist, Secular and Integrity; they were absent in 1950.UPPSC ×8
    • "Sovereign Democratic Republic" became "Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic"; "Unity of the Nation" became "Unity and Integrity of the Nation".
    • The Preamble has been amended only once so far, in 1976; this amendment was held valid.
    • The 42nd Amendment was based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
    • "Sovereign" and "Republic" were already in the original Preamble, not added by the 42nd Amendment; "Gram Swarajya" was not added either.
    • The Preamble describes India as a Secular State, through the word "Secular".UPPSC
    • Secular in India = there is no official religion of the State; the State treats all religions equally.UPPSC
    • The Indian Constitution embodies the positive concept of secularism.
    • Universalism = the principle that "all individuals are fully and equally human".
    • Under universalism every person is entitled to human rights without any discrimination.

    Legal status and cases

    • The Preamble is non-justiciable: its provisions cannot be enforced in a court of law.UPPSC
    • The Preamble is a part of the Constitution but has no legal effect independently of other parts.
    • The Preamble can be amended; it cannot override the specific provisions of the Constitution.UPPSC
    • The Preamble is very helpful in legal interpretation of the Constitution; it has utility, describes the aims of governance and helps give judicial meaning.
    • Berubari case (1960): Supreme Court first held the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution.UPPSC
    • In the Berubari case the Supreme Court also called the Preamble the key to the minds of the Constitution makers.
    • Golaknath vs State of Punjab (1967): the Preamble was considered the core soul of the Constitution.
    • Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala (1973): Supreme Court accepted the Preamble as part of the Constitution and of its basic structure.UPPSC
    • In Kesavananda Bharati a 13-judge bench outlined the Basic Structure doctrine.
    • In Kesavananda Bharati the Court said the Preamble can be used to explain ambiguous areas of the Constitution.
    • S.R. Bommai vs Union of India (1994): Supreme Court again held the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.UPPSC

    Sayings about the Preamble and Constitution

    • The Preamble is called the "Soul of the Constitution".UPPSC ×4
    • Pt. Thakur Das Bhargav said the Preamble is the soul of the Constitution.
    • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) the heart and soul of the Constitution.

    Note from the book The book notes: if the "soul of the Constitution" is asked with respect to Dr. Ambedkar, the answer is the Right to Constitutional Remedies.

    • K.M. Munshi, a Drafting Committee member, called the Preamble the political horoscope: "horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic".
    • Subhash Kashyap: if the Constitution is the body, the Preamble is the soul; if the Constitution is the building, the Preamble is the foundation stone.
    • Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar: "The Preamble to our Constitution expresses what we had thought or dreamt so long".
    • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called the Constitution a pious paper, a basic and sacred document.
    • Ambedkar became Chairman of the Drafting Committee in 1947; he was a staunch constitutionalist who held that government must be constitutional.
    ← SchedulesThe Governance System →

    Chapter 9 · Making and basics of the Constitution

    The Governance System

    170 facts · 3 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. K.C. Wheare · Quasi-Federal×3
    2. India is a Democratic Republic with a Parliamentary form of government; supreme power is vested in the people of India.×2
    3. Republic = supreme power held by the people and the Head of the state is elected; there is no hereditary ruler.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 39 UPPSC questions

    Government and its forms

    • Government = institution or system made of a group of people that takes care of or manages a country or a State.
    • Every Government has its own Constitution or set of fundamental principles to ensure effective governance.
    • Autocracy = supreme power or rule in the hands of one individual or entity.
    • Autocracy includes absolute monarchy, where a family or a group of families rule a country; now it also includes dictatorship.
    • In an absolute monarchy the post of monarch is inherited.
    • Monarchy is one of the oldest forms of Government.
    • Dictatorship = an individual possesses absolute power without any effective limitations.
    • Democracy = most widely adopted system of governance at present; final power resides with the people.
    • Democracy: a state where people are supreme, power vests in an elected head, government formed by elected representatives; supreme power vested solely in one person like a king is not democracy.UPPSC
    • Democratic governments are classified into two categories: Unitary and Federal.

    State and sovereignty

    • State (Garner) = community of persons, more or less numerous, permanently occupying a definite territory, independent or nearly so of external control, with an organized government to which the great body of inhabitants render habitual obedience.
    • The term 'State' is central to the study of Political Science.
    • State has four essential elements: Population, Territory, Government and Sovereignty; Sovereignty is the most important element.UPPSC
    • People = the community of persons permanently living there.
    • Territory = demarcated boundary that separates one state from another.
    • Sovereignty = independent say in all domestic and external decision-making.
    • India before 1947 was not a State: it had population, territory and government, but sovereignty was missing because of British control.
    • 'Sovereign' means India is neither a dependency nor a dominion of any other nation, but an independent state.
    • In 1947 India declared continuation of full membership of the Commonwealth of Nations and accepted the British crown as head of the Commonwealth; this extra-constitutional declaration does not affect India's sovereignty in any manner.UPPSC
    • Idea of the Preamble borrowed from the Constitution of the USA; language of the Preamble borrowed from the Constitution of Australia.UPPSC

    Parliamentary system

    • Mainly two types of systems of governance: Parliamentary and Presidential.
    • India follows the Parliamentary form of government, influenced by the Parliamentary system of the United Kingdom.UPPSC
    • India is a Parliamentary Democracy; it is not Presidential, not a titular monarchy, not an aristocracy.UPPSC
    • Presidential form of Government is not a feature of the Indian Constitution; Parliamentary Government, Independent Judiciary and Federal Government are its features.UPPSC
    • In India the President is only the formal (nominal) head of the executive; the real executive is the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister; India also adopted a secular State and a federal system.UPPSC
    • Modern concept of Parliamentary government emerged in the Kingdom of Great Britain; Prof. Pushpesh Pant in his book 'Vishwa ka Itihas' calls the UK its birth-place.UPPSC
    • In a Parliamentary system the Executive is controlled by the Legislature.UPPSC
    • In a Parliamentary system, members of the executive are taken from the legislature and are accountable to it; the Government is responsible to Parliament and can be removed by it.
    • In a Parliamentary system the executive derives its democratic legitimacy from the Legislature.
    • Main advantage of the parliamentary form: the executive remains responsible to the Legislature, which gives a responsible Government.
    • India has a parliamentary system because the Council of Ministers (executive) is responsible to the Lok Sabha (House of the People).
    • Article 75(3) (Union): Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People (Lok Sabha).UPPSC
    • Article 164(2) (States): Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
    • Collective responsibility of the executive to the Lower House is the central characteristic of parliamentary government.
    • Parliamentary system is also called the Cabinet form of government, responsible government, or the Westminster model of government.
    • The government is responsible to the popular House of the legislature and remains in power as long as it has majority support in that House.
    • Cabinet form of Government = a mechanism of parliamentary democracy to ensure collective responsibility of the Government to the people (House of the People).
    • In the Parliamentary system the Union Council of Ministers exercises executive authority.
    • Article 75(5): a Minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament for six consecutive months ceases to be a Minister at the end of that period.
    • Implied in India's Parliamentary Government: Cabinet members are Members of Parliament; Ministers hold office while they enjoy the confidence of Parliament.
    • In India the Cabinet is headed by the Head of the Government, the Prime Minister; the Head of the State is the President.
    • Features of the parliamentary form: Executive responsible to legislature, majority party rule, collective responsibility, nominal and real executives, political homogeneity, double membership, leadership of Prime Minister, dissolution of lower House, secrecy of procedure.
    • The Constitution sets up the Parliamentary system at the Centre and in the States; the Constitution is the source of authority for both Central and State governments.UPPSC
    • Parliamentary System in India shifted from Centralism to Federalism in the 1970s (1971-80), when the Congress Party lost power in many Indian States.UPPSC

    India and Britain compared

    • Judicial Review was adopted from the U.S. Constitution; it does not apply in the British Parliamentary System, so it differentiates the Indian system from the British one.UPPSC
    • Real and nominal executive, collective responsibility and bicameral legislature are common to both the Indian and British Parliamentary systems.
    • Parliamentary sovereignty is a principle of the UK constitution: Parliament is the supreme legal authority and can create or end any law.
    • In the UK, courts generally cannot overrule Parliament's legislation, and no Parliament can pass laws that future Parliaments cannot change.
    • With no written Constitution, the British Parliament is a sovereign body; the Indian Parliament is subject to the Constitution and its powers are not absolute.
    • India follows a constitutional government: Parliament's power to legislate is limited by the Constitution, and constitutionality matters are referred to a Constitution Bench.
    • Basic Structure principle lets the Judiciary curb any action of the Legislature and the Executive found contradictory to it.
    • Supreme Court has the power of judicial review: it can declare any legislative action inconsistent with the Basic Structure null and void.
    • Constitution bench is provided under Article 143 and Article 145(3).
    • The Chief Justice of India is constitutionally authorized to constitute a constitution bench and refer cases to it.
    • A constitution bench has at least five judges; it decides substantial questions of law on interpretation of the Constitution.
    • The Constitution explicitly establishes Judicial Review in Articles 13, 32, 136, 137, 226 and 227.

    Presidential system

    • In the Presidential form the President is the head of the executive branch; the best example is the Government of the USA.
    • In a Presidential Government all executive powers are vested in the President, who is both head of the State and head of the Government.UPPSC
    • Basic feature of Presidential Government = single Executive; power is centralized.UPPSC
    • Presidential form: President is Head of the state and the executive, appoints his Council of Ministers, and cannot dissolve the Legislature.UPPSC
    • Presidential form of Government first emerged in America; the American Presidency is regarded as the oldest and purest form of Presidential Government.
    • In the American system the President is elected indirectly by the people for a fixed period.

    India and the USA compared

    • Pocket Veto = indirect veto of a legislative Bill by an Executive, by keeping the Bill unsigned until adjournment of the legislature.
    • Both the President of India and the American President possess a pocket veto; this is the feature common to India and the USA.UPPSC
    • American President must return a Bill within 10 days if he refuses assent; the Indian Constitution sets no such time limit for the President of India.
    • Residuary powers: vested in the Centre in India, in the States in the USA.
    • All members of the upper House of the USA are directly elected; in the upper house of the Indian Parliament 12 members are nominated by the President.
    • The government system of America is federal: the USA is a federal republic of 50 States.

    Democracy, republic and Indian polity

    • India is a Democratic Republic with a Parliamentary form of government; supreme power is vested in the people of India.UPPSC ×2
    • The Indian political system does not provide for a unified authority; it divides powers between the Union and the States.
    • According to the Constitution, India is a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular and Democratic Republic.
    • The Constitution provides for a welfare State through the Directive Principles of State Policy; India is a democratic polity, sovereign state, democratic society and welfare state.UPPSC
    • India has the Rule of Law and a democratic Government, which is the opposite of an authoritarian Government.UPPSC
    • Every five years the people of India elect representatives who form a Government following the Constitution.
    • India is a democratic country: important decisions of governance are made by the elected representatives of the people.
    • India has a written constitution, but that does not explain its democracy: the United Kingdom is democratic without a written constitution, and non-democratic countries also have some form of constitution.UPPSC
    • The Constitution begins with "We the People of India"; the people are the source of political power in India.
    • Democratic republic = a state in which supreme power is held by the people and their elected representatives.
    • India's democracy rests on the people's right to elect representatives who form the Government; people are supreme and free to choose and change the government at elections.
    • Democracy's virtue: it builds on the wisdom (intelligence) and character of common people.
    • Democracy needs people's participation; participation develops awareness, and democracy's success depends on the quality of decisions made by the people.
    • Republic = supreme power held by the people and the Head of the state is elected; there is no hereditary ruler.UPPSC ×2
    • In India the Head of the State is elected by indirect election, through elected representatives.
    • President of India is elected indirectly because the Parliamentary system in India is combined with republicanism (Head of State = President).
    • In a Republic all representatives and some other authorities are elected by direct or indirect election by the people.
    • Political parties are the life-blood of democracy: they help form government, bring people together to gain control of Government and develop policies in people's interest; people usually blame them for bad governance.UPPSC
    • Both Mahatma Gandhi and Jay Prakash Narayan supported party-less democracy in India.
    • Democracy protects individual rights and raises the self-respect and dignity of women, poor, Dalits and minority groups; they are the biggest stakeholders of democracy in India.
    • From the Mauryan period to the modern era, specific elements of the Indian political system still exist; it shows continuity and change, with elements of modern style, traditional style and saintly style.UPPSC
    • The Indian Constitution is the longest written Constitution in the world.

    Note from the book Question on why the Indian Constitution is the bulkiest: no single option is the reason; all four reasons given are true, so no answer is keyed.

    • Reasons the Constitution is bulky: it uses the experience of many Constitutions, has detailed administrative provisions, governs a large country, and contains the Constitution of both Union and State Governments.

    Welfare state and philosophy of the Constitution

    • Welfare State = State plays a key role in protecting and promoting the social and economic well-being of its citizens; it aims at management of welfare of weaker sections.
    • Welfare State rests on equality of opportunity, equitable distribution of wealth, and public responsibility for those unable to get the minimum necessities for a good life.
    • "The State is everywhere: it leaves hardly a gap" explains the concept of a welfare state.
    • Philosophy and ideals of the Constitution are reflected in the Preamble.
    • India is a democratic republic committed to equality of opportunity and status.
    • The Preamble describes a socialist state as an ideal to be realised by India.
    • For political equality India adopted the principle of 'Adult Franchise'.
    • A Communist state is not the philosophy of the Constitution of India; welfare state, socialist state and political equality are.UPPSC

    Federal and unitary features

    • In a Unitary Constitution all powers are concentrated in a Central authority and the States are subordinate to it.
    • In a federal Constitution power is distributed between the Centre and the States; States are not subordinates of the Centre.
    • Federal government = powers divided between central and state governments by the constitution itself; both operate independently in their own jurisdictions.
    • The Indian Constitution is called Federal because the 7th Schedule distributes powers between the Union and the States.
    • The Constitution introduces a federal system as the basic structure of Government, with a strong admixture of unitary bias; distribution of legislative powers is in the Seventh Schedule and Articles 245-255.UPPSC
    • Only the Union is sovereign, not the States: State legislatures have no power over Foreign and Defence matters, which lie with the Union Parliament.
    • Judicial power is not divided between the Union and the States; there is only a hierarchy in the judicial system.
    • The Indian Constitution has both Federal and Unitary features.
    • Federal features: two (dual) governments, written Constitution, rigid Constitution, supremacy of the Constitution, division of powers between Centre and States, independent judiciary, bicameral legislature.
    • Unitary features: strong Centre, single Constitution, single citizenship, flexibility of the Constitution, integrated judiciary, appointment of Governors by the President, All India Services, Emergency provisions, Parliament's power to implement international agreements.UPPSC
    • Unitary elements also include President's approval on state bills and constitutional crisis (emergency) provisions, along with appointment of Governor.
    • Unitary elements also include unequal representation of States in the Rajya Sabha, along with appointment of Governors and All India Services.
    • Article 250: Parliament can legislate on any State List matter during an Emergency.
    • Article 249: Parliament can legislate on a State matter in the national interest.
    • Independence of the judiciary is an essential condition of a federal system, because the judiciary has the power to interpret the constitution.
    • Characteristics of a unitary form of government: strong Centre, single Constitution, flexible Constitution, Emergency provisions, single citizenship, integrated judiciary, All-India Services, integrated audit machinery, Parliament's authority over State List, appointment of Governor, integrated election machinery, veto over State Bills.
    • It cannot be said outright that unitary government is ideal for large countries; that depends on a country's will.
    • Article 1 declares India a Union of States; India has 28 States and 8 Union Territories.
    • India's federal design aims to weave a nation out of its many diverse parts and protect national integration; accommodating diversities has built a stronger nationhood; more powers are given to the Union.
    • Features of Indian federalism: written Constitution, distribution of powers, supremacy of the Constitution, independent judiciary, unequal representation of states in Rajya Sabha, dual governments.
    • Indian federalism is not the result of an agreement among the federating units.
    • Dr. Ambedkar on the word 'Union': the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement by the units, and the units have no freedom to secede from it.
    • Framers adopted the federal system for two main reasons: the large size of the country and its socio-cultural diversity.
    • Institutions needed for 'unity among diversity' in Indian federalism: Inter-State Council, National Development Council, Finance Commission, Regional Council, Unitary Judicial System, All India Services.
    • Inter-State Council: formed under Article 263; discusses or investigates policies, subjects of common interest and disputes among states.
    • National Development Council: apex body for decision-making and deliberations on development matters; presided over by the Prime Minister.
    • Finance Commission: established under Article 280; defines financial relations between the Central Government and the State Governments.
    • India has a Unitary Judicial system with the Supreme Court at the top.
    • Article 312 provides for the constitution of All India Services.

    Nature of the Constitution: views of scholars

    • Constitutional experts have no unanimous view on the nature of the Constitution.
    ScholarDescription of Indian federalism / Constitution
    Granville AustinCooperative Federalism
    K.C. WheareQuasi-FederalUPPSC ×3
    Morris-JonesBargaining FederalismUPPSC
    Ivor JenningsFederalism with Centralising Tendency
    D.D. BasuNeither purely federal nor unitary, but a combination of bothUPPSC
    Dr. B.R. AmbedkarConstitution has not been set in a tight mould of federalism; it has both federal and unitary featuresUPPSC
    • K.C. Wheare in his book 'Federal Government' called the Indian system "a quasi-federal state – a unitary state with subsidiary federal features"; he is cited as originator of the concept of Quasi-federalism.
    • Quasi-federal = constitution with both federal and unitary features, but with comparatively greater powers vested in the Centre.
    • Quasi-federal also means the government is generally federal, but the Constitution lets the Federation turn into a unitary state, generally during an emergency.
    • Indian federalism is called quasi-federal; an independent judiciary with Judicial Review is a crucial feature of the Constitution, but it is not the reason for the quasi-federal label.UPPSC
    • K.C. Wheare: the Indian Constitution strikes a good balance between rigidity and flexibility, because the amending process has variety (some provisions by simple majority, some by special majority).UPPSC
    • Ambedkar: the Constitution can be both unitary and federal as time and circumstances require; in normal times it works as a federal system, in war or Emergency as a unitary system.UPPSC
    • India is not a complete Federal State because some provisions give it a unitary character; many experts still accept it as a federal state because powers are divided between Union and States.UPPSC
    • The Indian Constitution is federal in nature but unitary in spirit.
    • Some experts call the Indian Constitution unitary because it gives a strong centre in emergency; in reality it is federal in nature with some unitary features.
    • The Indian Constitution is partly rigid and partly flexible: some provisions amended by simple majority, some by two-thirds majority under Article 368, and some also need ratification by at least 50% of State Legislatures.UPPSC

    Constitutional government, rule of law, liberty and equality

    • A Constitution establishes the structure and nature of the government and the roles and duties of the legislature, the executive and the judiciary.
    • The chief purpose of a Constitution is to define and limit the power of government.
    • The Constitution is the source of power of a Constitutional Government; it imposes limitations on the Government in the interest of the people (individual liberty).
    • A constitutional government is, by definition, a limited government.
    • Constitutional government or Constitutionalism = a government's authority is determined by a body of laws or constitution; a government limited by the terms of the Constitution.
    • Constitutionalism is sometimes regarded as a synonym for limited government, but that is only one interpretation and not the most prominent one.
    • Constitutionalism evolved to protect public interest and liberty from autocratic power of Government; constitutional governments have institutional mechanisms to protect citizens' liberties.
    • Rule of Law was propounded by A.V. Dicey, a British jurist, with three elements: limitation of powers, equality before law, liberty and civil rights.
    • Limitation of powers = absence of arbitrary power; no man can be punished except for a breach of law.
    • Equality before law = equal subjection of all citizens to the ordinary law of the land, administered by ordinary law courts.
    • Liberty and civil rights = primacy of the rights of individuals; the Constitution is the result of individual rights as defined and enforced by courts.
    • Law and liberty complement each other; liberty comes only from established laws: if there are no laws, there is no liberty.
    • Liberty = absence of restraints on individuals' activities and, at the same time, opportunities to develop individual personality; the positive definition is the opportunity to develop oneself fully.
    • Protection against tyranny of rulers and absence of restraint are negative views of liberty; doing whatever one likes relates to anarchy and lawlessness.
    • The Constitution's liberty provisions (reservation, protection of minority rights, no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth) create an enabling atmosphere for full self-development.
    • Equality in society implies the absence of privileges; the principle of equality is largely about removing special privileges.
    • Calls for formal equality were first made to break the hierarchy of ranks and orders surviving from feudal times.
    • Privileges given to one class on grounds of gender, colour, creed or religion are seen as irrational prejudices against the principle of equality.

    Good governance and administration thinkers

    • Features of good governance: accountability, transparency, rule of law; Red Tapism (excessive regulation that hinders action or decision-making) is not one.
    • Second Administrative Reforms Commission Report 12, 'Citizen-Centric Administration: The Heart of Governance', identifies barriers to good governance in India and describes pre-conditions for good governance.
    • Herbert A. Simon rejected the 'principles of administration' as myths and proverbs; Dwight Waldo, Frank Marini and F.W. Riggs accepted them.
    • Fred W. Riggs gave the concept of Development Administration: organised efforts by large-scale organisations, notably governments, to carry out policies and plans to meet development objectives.
    • Development administration is a dynamic concept that brings socio-economic and political-economic changes in society.
    • Henri Fayol = father of modern management theory; gave 14 universal principles of management; favoured similarities in public and private administration.
    • B. Donham: "If our civilization fails, it will be mainly because of a breakdown of administration."

    Chapter 10 · Making and basics of the Constitution

    National Symbols

    47 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Present design of the National Flag was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 July, 1947, during its fourth session.×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 5 UPPSC questions

    National Flag

    • National Flag (Tricolour) is rectangular and has three colours; ratio of length to width (height) = 3:2 (width to length = 2:3).
    • Top band = Indian saffron (Kesariya): symbol of strength and courage.
    • Middle band = white: symbol of peace and truth.
    • Bottom band = Indian green: symbol of fertility, growth and auspiciousness of the land.
    • Centre of the white band has a navy blue wheel representing the Ashoka Chakra, with 24 spokes.
    • Wheel design is that of the wheel on the abacus of the Sarnath lion capital of Ashoka.
    • The wheel is a depiction of the Dharma Chakra (Wheel of the Law); it symbolizes Justice.
    • National flag was designed by Pingali Venkayya.
    • Present design of the National Flag was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 July, 1947, during its fourth session.UPPSC ×3
    • Dr. S. Radhakrishnan's description of the importance of the three colours and the wheel is reproduced in the Flag Code of India.

    Flag Code of India, 2002

    • Flag Code of India 2002 allowed unrestricted display of the Tricolour as long as the honour and dignity of the flag are respected.
    • Flag Code of India 2002 took effect from 26 January, 2002.
    • The Code has three parts: (1) general description of the tricolour, (2) rules on display by public and private bodies and educational institutions, (3) rules on display by governments and government bodies.
    • Code: the National Flag shall be rectangular and the ratio of length to height (width) shall be 3:2.
    • 600 mm × 400 mm is not one of the nine standard sizes of the National Flag.

    State Emblem

    • State Emblem is an adaptation of the Sarnath lion capital of Ashoka (Ashoka pillar at Sarnath, Varanasi).
    • State Emblem was adopted by the Government of India on 26 January, 1950.
    • 'Satyameva Jayate' (national motto) from the Mundaka Upanishad is inscribed at the base of the emblem in Devanagari script.

    National Anthem and National Song

    • National Anthem 'Jana Gana Mana' was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 24 January, 1950.
    • 'Jana Gana Mana' was composed originally in Bengali by Rabindranath Tagore; its Hindi version was adopted as the National Anthem on 24 January, 1950.
    • 'Jana Gana Mana' was first sung on 27 December, 1911 at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress (President: Pt. Bishan Narayan Dar).
    • Playing time of the full (formal) version of the anthem is approximately 52 seconds.
    • Shortened version of the anthem (first and last lines) takes 20 seconds.
    • 'Vande Mataram' was adopted as the National Song by the Constituent Assembly on 24 January, 1950.
    • 'Vande Mataram' is taken from the novel 'Anand Math' by Bankimchandra Chatterjee.
    • 'Vande Mataram' was first sung at the 1896 session of the Indian National Congress (President: Rahimatullah Sayani).

    National Calendar

    • National Calendar is based on the Saka era (first month Chaitra, last month Falgun); adopted on 22 March, 1957 along with the Gregorian Calendar.UPPSC
    • Chaitra generally begins on 22 March; in leap years it begins on 21 March.

    Chapter 11 · States, citizens and rights

    States and Union Territories

    116 facts · 7 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Article 2: Parliament may by law admit into the Union or establish new States; admission of new States is not under Article 3.×4
    2. 36th Amendment Act, 1975 made Sikkim a full-fledged State, the 22nd State, and included it in the First Schedule; Sikkim became an integral part of India in 1975.×3
    3. Meghalaya · 21 January, 1972×3
    4. At present India has 28 States and 8 Union Territories.×2
    5. States have no right to secede from the Union; as per Dr. Ambedkar, that is why the term 'Union of States' is used.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 32 UPPSC questions

    Integration of princely states and the 1950 classification

    • Indian Independence Act of 1947 created two independent and separate Dominions: India and Pakistan.
    • Princely States had three options: join India, join Pakistan, or remain independent.
    • More than 560 princely States lay within Indian territory; most joined India; three refused: Hyderabad, Junagadh and Kashmir.
    • Hyderabad was included through military action, Junagadh through a referendum.
    • Kashmir was included through the Instrument of Accession (a legal document) executed by Maharaja Hari Singh, ruler of Jammu & Kashmir.
    • The Constitution in force from 1950 recognised four categories of States and territories in the First Schedule.
    CategoryMade up ofGoverned by
    Part AFormer British India provincesGovernor and a Legislature
    Part BFormer Princely States'Raj pramukh'
    Part CPrincely States and chief commissioner's provincesChief commissioner
    Part DAndaman and Nicobar Islands onlyPresident, through a Chief Commissioner or other authority appointed by him
    • Part C states and Part D territories became the basis for the creation of Union Territories.

    Union and its territory: Article 1

    • Article 1(1): "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States"; the Constitution names the country India and Bharat.
    • India is a Union of States, not a Federation of States.UPPSC
    • States and their territories are as specified in the First Schedule; it lists the names of States and Union Territories.
    • Territory of India comprises: (1) States, (2) Union Territories, (3) such other territories as may be acquired.
    • India, a Union of States, is a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic with a Parliamentary system of Government.
    • The President is the constitutional head of the executive of the Union.
    • At present India has 28 States and 8 Union Territories.UPPSC ×2
    • In 2002 there were 28 States and 7 Union Territories.
    • Telangana became the 29th State on 2 June, 2014.
    • With the formation of the UTs of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, the count became 28 States and 9 UTs.
    • With the merger of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, the count became 28 States and 8 UTs.
    • States have no right to secede from the Union; as per Dr. Ambedkar, that is why the term 'Union of States' is used.UPPSC ×2
    • States in India have no right to territorial integrity; Parliament can by unilateral action change the area, boundaries or name of any state by simple majority.
    • Article 19(1) guarantees six rights to all citizens: speech and expression; assemble peaceably without arms; form associations, unions or co-operative societies; move freely throughout India; reside and settle in any part of India; practise any profession, occupation, trade or business.
    • The State can impose 'reasonable' restrictions on these six rights only on grounds mentioned in Article 19(2) itself; even mere advocacy of secession is subject to reasonable restriction.

    Articles 2, 3 and 4: new states and alteration

    • Article 2: Parliament may by law admit into the Union or establish new States; admission of new States is not under Article 3.UPPSC ×4
    • Article 3: Parliament may form a new State by separating territory from any State, by uniting two or more States or parts of States, or by uniting any territory to a part of any State.UPPSC
    • Article 3 also lets Parliament increase the area, diminish the area, alter the boundaries and alter the name of any State.UPPSC
    • Altering the name of a State is a power of Parliament, not of a State Legislature.UPPSC
    • No State has the authority to include any territory by itself; "a State may include a Union territory" is not a provision.UPPSC
    • Explanation 1 of Article 3: in clauses (a) to (e) "State" includes a Union Territory, but in the proviso "State" does not include a Union Territory.
    • Parliament forms new States or alters them by a simple majority and the ordinary legislative process; no special procedure is needed.UPPSC
    • Article 4(2): such a law is not deemed an amendment of the Constitution for the purpose of Article 368; changes under Articles 2 and 3 are outside Article 368.UPPSC
    • Such a law contains provisions for amending the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule.
    • Parliament can alter the area, boundaries or name of a State without the State's consent.UPPSC
    • A Bill for these changes can be introduced in Parliament only with the prior recommendation of the President.
    • Before recommending, the President must refer the Bill to the concerned State Legislature for its views within a specified period; the President (or Parliament) is not bound by those views.UPPSC
    • If the State Legislature gives no views within the period fixed by the President, the Bill can still be presented in Parliament.
    • Article 14: equality before law for all persons, citizens and non-citizens.
    • Article 16: equality of opportunity in public employment for Indian citizens only.

    Reorganisation of states on linguistic basis

    1. 1920In 1920 the Congress session was held at Nagpur under C. Vijayaraghavachariar; after it, provincial Congress committees were formed on a linguistic basis.
    2. 1948S.K. Dhar Commission, 1948: examined feasibility of linguistic states; rejected it and recommended reorganisation on administrative convenience (viability), not language.
    3. 1948JVP Committee: formed by Congress in December 1948 to scrutinize the Dhar Commission's recommendations; members Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
    4. 1949JVP Committee report, presented in April 1949, officially rejected reorganisation of States on a linguistic basis.
    5. 1953Andhra Pradesh = first State formed on a linguistic basis, on 1 October, 1953, by separating Telugu-speaking areas from Madras state.UPPSC ×2
    6. 1953The Commission was set up on 29 December, 1953 and submitted its report on 30 September, 1955.
    7. 1956The Government accepted the recommendations with some changes and enacted the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 and the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956.
    8. 195614 States and 6 Union Territories were created on 1 November, 1956.
    9. 1956Large-scale reorganisation of States on a linguistic basis took place in 1956.
    • In 1920 the Congress session was held at Nagpur under C. Vijayaraghavachariar; after it, provincial Congress committees were formed on a linguistic basis.
    • S.K. Dhar Commission, 1948: examined feasibility of linguistic states; rejected it and recommended reorganisation on administrative convenience (viability), not language.
    • JVP Committee: formed by Congress in December 1948 to scrutinize the Dhar Commission's recommendations; members Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
    • JVP Committee report, presented in April 1949, officially rejected reorganisation of States on a linguistic basis.
    • Death of Potti Sriramulu after a 56-day hunger strike forced the Government to form Andhra Pradesh on a linguistic basis.
    • Andhra Pradesh = first State formed on a linguistic basis, on 1 October, 1953, by separating Telugu-speaking areas from Madras state.UPPSC ×2
    • States Reorganisation Commission: chairman Justice Fazal Ali; members K.M. Panikkar and H.N. (Hridaynath) Kunzru; K.T. Shah and Pattabhi Sitaramayya were not members.UPPSC
    • The Commission was set up on 29 December, 1953 and submitted its report on 30 September, 1955.

    Note from the book Question asking when the Commission for linguistic reorganisation was established (options 1856, 1956, 1957, 1960): no option is correct, since it was established on 29 December, 1953.

    • The Commission broadly accepted language as the basis of reorganisation but rejected the theory of 'one language-one state'.
    • The Commission suggested abolishing the four-fold classification of states and territories.
    • The Commission did not support the splitting of Bombay and Punjab.
    • The Government accepted the recommendations with some changes and enacted the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 and the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956.
    • The Act abolished the distinctions among Part A, Part B and Part C states.
    • 14 States and 6 Union Territories were created on 1 November, 1956.
    • Large-scale reorganisation of States on a linguistic basis took place in 1956.

    Union Territories

    • Delhi is a Union Territory under the First Schedule; officially also called the National Capital Region.
    • 69th Amendment Act, 1991 gave Delhi special status among the Union Territories.UPPSC
    • Goa is a State, not a Union Territory; Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Daman and Diu, and Puducherry are Union Territories.UPPSC

    • Diu is an island in the Gulf of Khambhat.

    Sikkim, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura, Arunachal Pradesh

    1. 1956Tripura was a Part 'C' State after its initial merger, and became a Union Territory after the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
    2. 1962Nagaland came into existence by an ordinary Act of Parliament, the State of Nagaland Act, 1962, not by a Constitution Amendment Act.
    3. 1972Tripura got full statehood from 21 January, 1972 under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971.
    4. 1974In 1974 the Sikkim Assembly passed the Government of Sikkim Act, 1974: paved the way for the first responsible Government in Sikkim and sought its representation in India's political institutions.
    5. 197435th Amendment Act, 1974 inserted new Article 2A making Sikkim an Associate State; it set the terms and conditions of Sikkim's association with the Union.
    6. 197436th Amendment Act: Legislative Assembly of Sikkim shall have not less than 32 members; the Assembly formed by the April 1974 elections with 32 members is deemed the Legislative Assembly of the State.
    7. 197536th Amendment Act, 1975 made Sikkim a full-fledged State, the 22nd State, and included it in the First Schedule; Sikkim became an integral part of India in 1975.UPPSC ×3
    8. 1975Sikkim became a State on 16 May, 1975 (State Foundation Day), after a referendum; the 36th Amendment came into force on 26 April, 1975.
    9. 1986Memorandum of Settlement on Mizoram was signed by the Government of India and the Government of Mizoram on 30 June, 1986.
    10. 1987Mizoram got statehood by the 53rd Amendment Act; the State was formed on 20 February, 1987.
    • In 1974 the Sikkim Assembly passed the Government of Sikkim Act, 1974: paved the way for the first responsible Government in Sikkim and sought its representation in India's political institutions.
    • 35th Amendment Act, 1974 inserted new Article 2A making Sikkim an Associate State; it set the terms and conditions of Sikkim's association with the Union.

    Note from the book Question "Sikkim became a state under": the 36th Amendment is not among the options, so the 35th Amendment is taken as the answer.

    • 36th Amendment Act, 1975 made Sikkim a full-fledged State, the 22nd State, and included it in the First Schedule; Sikkim became an integral part of India in 1975.UPPSC ×3
    • Sikkim became a State on 16 May, 1975 (State Foundation Day), after a referendum; the 36th Amendment came into force on 26 April, 1975.
    • 36th Amendment Act: Legislative Assembly of Sikkim shall have not less than 32 members; the Assembly formed by the April 1974 elections with 32 members is deemed the Legislative Assembly of the State.
    • Sikkim is called the Paradise of Botanists because of its biodiversity; it falls under the Himalayan hotspot.
    • Natives of Sikkim are Lepchas, Bhutias and Nepalis.
    • Memorandum of Settlement on Mizoram was signed by the Government of India and the Government of Mizoram on 30 June, 1986.
    • Mizoram got statehood by the 53rd Amendment Act; the State was formed on 20 February, 1987.
    • Capital of Arunachal Pradesh, Itanagar, is named after Ita Fort, a historic fort whose name means "fort of bricks".
    • By the latest official data, Arunachal Pradesh has only two national parks: Namdapha National Park and Mouling National Park.
    • Nagaland came into existence by an ordinary Act of Parliament, the State of Nagaland Act, 1962, not by a Constitution Amendment Act.
    • Tripura was a Part 'C' State after its initial merger, and became a Union Territory after the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
    • Tripura got full statehood from 21 January, 1972 under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971.

    Chapter 12 · States, citizens and rights

    The Citizenship

    43 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Citizenship is dealt with in Part II of the Constitution.×2
    2. India, like Britain, adopted single citizenship for the whole country; every citizen has citizenship of India only.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 9 UPPSC questions

    Constitutional provisions

    • Citizenship is dealt with in Part II of the Constitution.UPPSC ×2
    • Citizenship Articles = Articles 5 to 11.UPPSC
    ArticleSubject
    6Rights of citizenship of certain persons who migrated to India from Pakistan
    7Rights of citizenship of certain migrants to Pakistan
    8Rights of citizenship of certain persons of Indian origin residing outside India
    9Persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State are not to be citizens
    11Parliament has power to regulate the right of citizenship by lawUPPSC
    • Only Parliament has the exclusive power of determining the issue of citizenship in India (Article 11: acquisition and termination of citizenship).

    Note from the book Question on who has exclusive power to determine citizenship (options: Court, President, Lok Sabha, Central Government, State Government): none of the options is correct, since the answer is Parliament.

    Single citizenship

    • India, like Britain, adopted single citizenship for the whole country; every citizen has citizenship of India only.UPPSC ×2
    • Single citizenship concept was adopted from the British Constitution of the United Kingdom.
    • In India a person can have only one citizenship and, at a particular time, only one domicile.
    • Any citizen (by birth or naturalised) can become the Head of State, i.e. the President, in India.
    • The USA has dual citizenship: one of the U.S.A. (federation) and one of the state where the citizen resides.
    • Articles 371-A to 371-I were inserted to meet regional demands of Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa.

    Citizenship Act, 1955: acquiring and losing citizenship

    • Using Article 11, Parliament passed the Indian Citizenship Act in 1955; it provides for acquisition and termination of citizenship.
    • Five ways of acquiring citizenship: Birth, Descent, Registration, Naturalisation, Incorporation of territory; depositing money in Indian banks is a commercial action, not a way.
    • Three ways of losing citizenship (whether acquired under the Act or earlier under the Constitution): Renunciation, Termination, Deprivation; a citizen loses it by renouncing it or by voluntarily acquiring another country's citizenship; marrying a foreigner or criticizing the government is not a way.UPPSC
    • Citizenship by Registration = Section 5; Citizenship by Naturalization = Section 6.
    • Section 5(1)(a): a person of Indian origin can get citizenship by registration after being ordinarily resident in India for 7 years before applying.
    • A naturalized citizen may be deprived of citizenship under Section 10 of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
    • Registration or naturalization can be cancelled if obtained by fraud, false representation or concealment of a material fact.
    • It can also be cancelled if the citizen shows disloyalty or disaffection to the Constitution by act or speech.
    • It can also be cancelled if the citizen unlawfully traded or communicated with an enemy during a war India is engaged in.
    • It can also be cancelled if the citizen has been ordinarily resident out of India for a continuous period of seven years.
    • Central Government made the Citizenship Rules, 2009 under Section 18 of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
    • The Citizenship Act was amended in 1957, 1985, 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015 and 2019.

    Overseas Citizen of India cardholder

    • Section 7A of the Citizenship Act, 1955 (inserted by the Citizenship Amendment Act, 2015): Central Government may register a person as an Overseas Citizen of India cardholder on application, subject to prescribed conditions.
    • Eligible: person of full age and capacity who is a citizen of another country but was a citizen of India at or any time after the commencement of the Constitution.
    • Eligible: citizen of another country who was eligible to become a citizen of India at the commencement of the Constitution.
    • Eligible: citizen of another country who belonged to a territory that became part of India after 15 August, 1947.
    • Eligible: a child, grandchild or great-grandchild of such a citizen; also a minor child of any such person.
    • Eligible: a minor child whose both parents are citizens of India or one parent is a citizen of India.
    • Eligible: spouse of foreign origin of a citizen of India or of an OCI cardholder, whose marriage is registered and has subsisted for at least two continuous years before the application.
    • Such a spouse must get prior security clearance from a competent authority in India.
    • Not eligible: a person who, or whose parent, grandparent or great-grandparent, is or has been a citizen of Pakistan, Bangladesh or any other country notified by the Central Government; so Indians who migrated to Pakistan after partition are not eligible.UPPSC

    Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019

    • Citizenship (Amendment) Bill 2019: passed by Lok Sabha on 9 December 2019, by Rajya Sabha (Parliament) on 11 December 2019; President's assent on 12 December 2019.UPPSC
    • The Act inserted Section 6B in the Citizenship Act, 1955; it came into force on 10 January, 2020.
    • It grants citizenship to Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Parsi, Buddhist and Christian minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan who came due to religious persecution on or before 31 December, 2014; they are not treated as illegal migrants.
    • Citizenship is granted through certificates of registration or naturalisation, subject to conditions; Muslims are not included in this Act.
    • For the first time it provides citizenship based on religion, to non-Muslim communities from the three countries.
    • Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, 2024 were notified on 11 March 2024 to implement Section 6B.
    • The Act does not apply to tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura included in the Sixth Schedule.
    • The Act does not apply to areas under the inner line under the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873.
