    Chapter 13 · States, citizens and rights

    Fundamental Rights

    217 facts · 21 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 deleted the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights: it omitted Article 19(1)(f) and inserted Article 300-A.×8
    2. Article 24: no child below 14 years shall be employed in any factory or mine or any other hazardous employment; it relates to exploitation of children.×6
    3. Article 17: untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden; enforcing any disability arising from it is an offence punishable by law.×5
    4. 'Equal pay for equal work' was deduced as a Fundamental Right from Articles 14 and 16 read with the word 'Socialist' in the Preamble and Article 39(d) (Randhir Singh Vs. Union of India).×4
    5. Article 30(1): all minorities, whether based on religion or language, have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice; this is not Article 29 or Article 31.×4
    Quick quiz: 10 of 91 UPPSC questions

    History and nature of Fundamental Rights

    • First explicit demand for Fundamental Rights (FR) = "Constitution of India Bill, 1895", inspired by Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
    • Motilal Nehru Report (1928) demanded inalienable Fundamental Rights and favoured including them in the Constitution of India.UPPSC
    • Congress adopted the resolution on Fundamental Rights at the Karachi Session, 1931, presided over by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
    • Karachi session was held on 26 to 31 March, 1931, after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and the execution of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru.
    • At Karachi the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (Delhi Pact) was endorsed, the goal of Purna Swaraj was reiterated, and resolutions on Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme were adopted.
    • Fundamental Rights are in Part III, Articles 12 to 35; Part III lists 6 Fundamental Rights.UPPSC
    • Part III is regarded as the Magna Carta of India.
    • Fundamental Rights are compared with, and are like, the Bill of Rights in the U.S. Constitution; in philosophical and conceptual sense they are similar to it.
    • Fundamental Rights are defended and guaranteed by the Constitution; they are a guarantee against arbitrary State action and are listed in Part III.UPPSC
    • Socio-economic justice is found mostly in the Directive Principles (Part IV) and to a little extent in the chapter on Fundamental Rights and certain other provisions.
    • Fundamental Rights are justiciable: enforceable by the Courts, subject to certain restrictions.
    • Fundamental Rights are natural and non-transferable rights.
    • They are called Fundamental Rights because they are written in the Constitution, are essential for personality development, and Parliament cannot make laws against them (they are part of the basic structure).
    • Fundamental Rights can be suspended only during an emergency, under Articles 358 and 359: enforcement is suspended by an order of the President during a national emergency; rights under Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended.UPPSC
    • Article 358: suspension of provisions of Article 19 during emergencies.
    • Article 359: suspension of enforcement of Fundamental Rights except Articles 20 and 21 during emergencies (after the 44th Amendment Act).
    • If National Emergency is declared on grounds of war or external aggression, rights under Article 19 are automatically suspended.
    • After the 44th Amendment (1978), the right to life and personal liberty (Article 21) cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency.UPPSC
    • Jawaharlal Nehru: "A fundamental right should be looked upon, not from the point of view of any particular difficulty of the moment, but as something that you want to make permanent in the Constitution."
    • Dr. S. Radhakrishnan ('philosopher king'): Fundamental Rights are "a pledge to our people and a pact with the civilized world".UPPSC
    • Patanjali Sastry (former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court): the whole object of Part III is to protect the freedoms and rights in it against arbitrary invasion by the state.
    • In a liberal democracy, separation of powers is the best safeguard of liberty; it works as a vehicle for restraint of powers.
    • Liberal approach: all power is rooted in the will of the people; rule of law is a basic foundation of democracy; individual rights and freedoms are a prerequisite of dignity.
    • A committed judiciary will never go against the government's policies.
    • Centralization of power concentrates decisions in a few leaders at the top and may lead to authoritarian tendencies.
    • An elected government is expected to ensure liberty but is not its best safeguard.
    • Article 13: pre-constitutional and post-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights (Part III) are void to the extent of the inconsistency; it secures paramountcy of the Constitution regarding Fundamental Rights.UPPSC
    • Article 13 gives the power of Judicial Review to the Supreme Court and High Courts when Fundamental Rights are violated.
    • Article 245 = extent of laws made by Parliament and State Legislatures.
    • Article 326 = elections to Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies on the basis of adult suffrage.

    List of Fundamental Rights

    • Originally the Constitution gave seven Fundamental Rights: Equality, Freedom, against Exploitation, Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational, Property, Constitutional Remedies.
    Fundamental RightArticles
    Right to Equality14–18UPPSC ×3
    Right to Freedom19–22UPPSC
    Right against Exploitation23–24UPPSC
    Right to Freedom of Religion25–28UPPSC
    Cultural and Educational Rights29–30
    Right to Constitutional Remedies32
    • Articles 14, 15 and 16 give the Right to Equality; Article 13 does not.
    • 'Right to protest' is not among the six Fundamental Rights.UPPSC
    • The Constitution gives Right to Equality (Art. 14-18), Right to Freedom of Religion (Art. 25-28) and Right to Liberty/Freedom (Art. 19-22), but no 'Right of Equal Shelter'.

    Right to Equality: Articles 14 to 18

    • Article 14: the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.UPPSC
    • Article 14 puts a limitation on the legislative power.UPPSC
    • Article 14 rights belong to every person, citizen or foreigner.
    • Concept of 'Equal Protection of the law' is taken from the American Constitution.
    • Equal protection means: equal treatment in equal circumstances, in privileges conferred and liabilities imposed; same laws applied alike to all similarly situated; likes treated alike without discrimination.
    • A law giving vague, wide (unguided, uncontrolled) discretionary power to an administrative authority may be declared ultra vires Article 14, Article 19 and other provisions.
    • Courts control delegation of discretionary powers by testing the constitutionality of the delegating law against Part III rights.
    • Article 14 guarantees equality but courts permit reasonable classification; even under a valid law, a discriminatory action still violates the equality clause.
    • The State can treat unequals differently to create a level playing field in social, economic and political spheres; among equals the law should be equal and equally administered.UPPSC
    • Equal protection under Article 14 does not mean all laws must be general in character.
    • Rule of Law: creation and enforcement of laws are legally regulated, so no one, even the highest official, is above the law; one act and one judiciary for all.
    • Under Rule of Law the government is subject to existing laws as much as citizens are.
    • Equality before law: no legal person enjoys privileges not extended to all, and no person is immune from legal sanctions.
    • Article 15: prohibition of discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; it falls under the Right to Equality.
    • Article 15(4) was added by the First Amendment (1951) after State of Madras Vs. Champakam Dorairajan; it amended the right against discrimination.UPPSC
    • Article 15(4): nothing in Article 15 or Article 29(2) prevents the State from making special provision for socially and educationally backward classes or for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
    • Article 15(5): State may make special provisions for reservation in admission to educational institutions, including private ones, aided or unaided, other than minority institutions under Article 30(1).
    • 93rd Amendment Act, 2005 enabled 27% reservation for Other Backward Classes in Government and private educational institutions.
    • OBC reservation rests on Article 15(4) and Article 16(4).
    • Article 16: equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.
    • Article 16(1) and 16(2) ensure equal opportunity for all citizens in employment or appointment to any office under the State.UPPSC
    • Article 16(2): no citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for or discriminated against in any employment or office under the State.UPPSC
    • Article 16(4): State may reserve appointments or posts for any backward class of citizens which, in its opinion, is not adequately represented in State services.
    • Supreme Court (Indra Sawhney Vs Union of India 1993; M Nagaraj Vs Union of India 2006): reservation under Article 16(4) must be read with Article 335, which provides for "maintenance of efficiency of administration".
    • Article 335: claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to be considered, consistently with efficiency of administration, in appointments under the Union or a State; it does not define 'efficiency of administration'.
    • 77th Amendment Act, 1995 inserted clause (4A) in Article 16: reservation in promotion for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
    • Right to equality includes equality before law (Art. 14), social equality (Art. 15) and equal opportunity (Art. 16); it does not include economic equality.UPPSC
    • 'Equal pay for equal work' was deduced as a Fundamental Right from Articles 14 and 16 read with the word 'Socialist' in the Preamble and Article 39(d) (Randhir Singh Vs. Union of India).UPPSC ×4
    • Randhir Singh: the principle applies to unequal pay scales based on no classification or irrational classification, for identical work under the same employer.
    • Article 17: untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden; enforcing any disability arising from it is an offence punishable by law.UPPSC ×5
    • Article 17 is classified under the Right to Equality.
    • Article 17 is a "statement of principle" to remove humiliation and harassment of Dalits and ensure their fundamental, socio-economic, political and cultural rights.
    • Untouchability can be abolished by making laws, improving education and public awareness; giving jobs/services is not a proper solution.UPPSC
    • Parliament declared the practice of untouchability a punishable offence by the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.
    • Structural violence = preventable harm where no actor commits the violence; it arises from unequal distribution of power and resources, built into the structure; forms include racism and untouchability.
    • Untouchability is an extremely harsh social punishment on the lowest castes on the purity-impurity scale and has religious approval, so it is the worst form of structural violence.UPPSC
    • Article 18: abolition of titles, except military and academic.UPPSC

    Right to Freedom: Article 19

    • Article 19(1) guarantees all citizens six rights.
    ClauseFreedom
    19(1)(a)Speech and expression
    19(1)(b)Assemble peaceably and without arms
    19(1)(c)Form associations or unions or co-operative societies
    19(1)(d)Move freely throughout the territory of India
    19(1)(e)Reside and settle in any part of the territory of India
    19(1)(g)Practise any profession, or carry on any occupation, trade or business
    • Freedom to own, acquire and dispose of property was Article 19(1)(f) in the original Constitution; the 44th Amendment, 1978 removed it.UPPSC
    • Equality of opportunity in public employment (Article 16) is under the Right to Equality, not under Article 19(1).
    • Freedom of the Press is not given directly; it is included in freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) (Sakal Papers Ltd. Vs. Union of India, 1961).UPPSC ×2
    • Supreme Court: hoisting the National Flag atop private buildings is a fundamental right of every citizen under Article 19(1)(a).
    • Supreme Court: Right to Information lies in freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a), though it is not mentioned in the Constitution.
    • Bijoe Emmanuel vs. State of Kerala: Supreme Court overruled the High Court; expelling children for their conscientiously held religious faith violated Articles 19(1)(a) and 25(1); no provision of law obliges anyone to sing the National Anthem.
    • Article 19(2) grounds to restrict speech and expression: sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence.
    • 'Unbecoming criticism' and 'sedition' are not grounds listed in Article 19(2).
    • Under Article 19(3) the State can impose reasonable restrictions on the freedom to assemble (Article 19(1)(b)) in the interest of public order; gherao of officials is not part of this freedom.
    • Articles 19(2) to 19(6) allow reasonable restrictions by law only for specified objectives: sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, public order, decency or morality, protection of interests of Scheduled Tribes, professional/technical regulations.
    • Reasonableness of restrictions must safeguard the interest of the general public and take account of prevailing social values and social needs.

    Articles 20 and 22: protection of accused and arrested persons

    • Article 20: protection in respect of conviction for offences; it covers ex-post facto law, double jeopardy and self-incrimination.
    • Article 20(1): no conviction except for violation of a law in force at the time of the act, and no penalty greater than that under the law then in force.
    • Article 20(2): no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once = Doctrine of Double Jeopardy.UPPSC
    • Double jeopardy aims to avoid harassment by successive criminal proceedings for one crime; maxim: Nemo Debet Bis Vexari (no man shall be put twice in peril for the same offence).
    • Article 20(3): no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself (self-incrimination).UPPSC
    • Article 20(3) rests on the presumption that the accused is innocent till guilt is proved; the prosecutor must establish guilt.
    • Prohibition against torture is not part of Article 20; protection from torture is a fundamental right under Article 21.UPPSC
    • Article 22: protection against arrest and detention in certain cases; safeguards the rights of an arrested person.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 22(1): no arrested person shall be detained without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds of arrest, nor denied the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice.
    • Article 22(2): every arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding journey time to the magistrate's court.
    • Article 22(4): no preventive detention law shall authorise detention for longer than three months.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 22(5): the authority must tell a preventive detainee the grounds of the order as soon as possible and give the earliest opportunity to make a representation; so the detainee gets a legal opportunity.
    • Article 355: duty of the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and to ensure State government runs according to the Constitution.
    • Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2002 (repealed in 2004): a confession made before a police officer and recorded in writing or on a mechanical or electronic device was admissible in trial under the Act.
    • Parole = release of a prisoner, temporarily for a special purpose or completely before the sentence ends, on promise of good behaviour (word of honour in the parole order).
    • Parole is not recognized as a right in India; a prisoner's claim is not absolute and prison authorities have considerable discretion; State governments have their own parole rules and guidelines.
    • Several international accords and organizations consider parole a right for prisoners.
    • Grant of parole is governed by rules made under the Prison Act, 1894 and the Prison Act, 1900.
    • Prisons (Bombay Furlough and Parole) Rules, 1959 were made under section 59(5) of the Prisons Act, 1984.

    Article 21 and Article 21A

    1. 1975Govind vs. State of M.P. (1975) and Malak Singh vs. State of Punjab and Haryana (1980): right to privacy is implicit in Article 21; it is the right to be let alone.
    2. 1978Maneka Gandhi Vs. Union of India, 1978: right to travel abroad is a fundamental right secured by Article 21; Satwant Singh Vs. Union of India also held it a fundamental right.UPPSC
    3. 1978Maneka Gandhi judgment: delivered on 25 January 1978, unanimously by a 7-Judge bench; it widened the scope of Article 21.
    4. 1989Parmananda Katara Vs. Union of India 1989: medical aid to the injured by a doctor falls under Article 21.
    5. 1991Subhash Kumar Vs. State of Bihar 1991: pollution of the quality of air or water falls under Article 21.
    6. 1993Unnikrishnan vs. State of Andhra Pradesh, 1993: citizens have a fundamental right to education flowing from Article 21; free education for children up to 14 years.
    7. 1995Chameli Singh Vs. State of U.P. 1995: 'Right to Livelihood' under Article 21 includes 'Right to Shelter'; shelter means all infrastructure needed to live, not a mere roof.UPPSC
    8. 1997Vishakha Vs. State of Rajasthan 1997: sexual harassment of women at the workplace falls under Article 21.
    9. 200286th Amendment Act, 2002 added Article 21A: free and compulsory education for all children aged 6 to 14 years is a fundamental right, in such manner as the State may by law determine.UPPSC
    10. 2006Lata Singh v/s State of U.P. 2006: right to marry is a component of the right to life under Article 21; Hadiya case: right to convert and choose a partner is implicit in Article 21.
    11. 2009Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 is the law envisaged under Article 21-A; it came into effect on 1 April, 2010.
    12. 2017Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) vs. Union of India: nine-Judge Constitution Bench on 24 August, 2017 unanimously ruled privacy a fundamental right, an intrinsic part of life and personal liberty under Article 21 and of the freedoms of Part III.
    • Article 21: protection of life and personal liberty.
    • Article 21 text: no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law; the due process doctrine is read in this Article.UPPSC
    • Maneka Gandhi Vs. Union of India, 1978: right to travel abroad is a fundamental right secured by Article 21; Satwant Singh Vs. Union of India also held it a fundamental right.UPPSC
    • Maneka Gandhi judgment: delivered on 25 January 1978, unanimously by a 7-Judge bench; it widened the scope of Article 21.
    • Maneka Gandhi: Article 21 cannot allow an arbitrary or irrational process; 'procedure established by law' is by and large the same as procedural due process in the U.S.A.
    • Maneka Gandhi: Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not mutually exclusive; 'Right to life' includes the right to live with dignity.
    • The statement that the petitioner bears the burden of proving the procedure arbitrary is not part of the Maneka Gandhi interpretation.
    • Rights brought within Article 21: clean water, clean air, freedom from noise pollution, livelihood, speedy and fair trial, food, clean environment.
    • Chameli Singh Vs. State of U.P. 1995: 'Right to Livelihood' under Article 21 includes 'Right to Shelter'; shelter means all infrastructure needed to live, not a mere roof.UPPSC
    • Govind vs. State of M.P. (1975) and Malak Singh vs. State of Punjab and Haryana (1980): right to privacy is implicit in Article 21; it is the right to be let alone.
    • Intrusive surveillance that seriously encroaches on privacy can infringe freedom of movement under Article 19(1)(d) and Article 21; privacy is thus available under Article 19(1)(d) read with Article 21.UPPSC ×3
    • Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) vs. Union of India: nine-Judge Constitution Bench on 24 August, 2017 unanimously ruled privacy a fundamental right, an intrinsic part of life and personal liberty under Article 21 and of the freedoms of Part III.
    • Lata Singh v/s State of U.P. 2006: right to marry is a component of the right to life under Article 21; Hadiya case: right to convert and choose a partner is implicit in Article 21.
    • Bachan Singh Vs. State of Punjab: capital punishment (sentencing discretion in section 302 IPC) does not violate Articles 14, 19 and 21, as it is given only for serious crimes; so it is outside the purview of Article 21.UPPSC
    • Parmananda Katara Vs. Union of India 1989: medical aid to the injured by a doctor falls under Article 21.
    • Vishakha Vs. State of Rajasthan 1997: sexual harassment of women at the workplace falls under Article 21.
    • Subhash Kumar Vs. State of Bihar 1991: pollution of the quality of air or water falls under Article 21.
    • 'Right to Die' is not a Fundamental Right under Article 21.UPPSC
    • Unnikrishnan vs. State of Andhra Pradesh, 1993: citizens have a fundamental right to education flowing from Article 21; free education for children up to 14 years.
    • Unnikrishnan: the right to education is not absolute; its content must be determined in light of Articles 41 and 45.
    • 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added Article 21A: free and compulsory education for all children aged 6 to 14 years is a fundamental right, in such manner as the State may by law determine.UPPSC
    • Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 is the law envisaged under Article 21-A; it came into effect on 1 April, 2010.
    • Education is a fundamental human right, indispensable to the right to development as a human right; it promotes individual freedom and empowerment of children.UPPSC

    Right against Exploitation: Articles 23 and 24

    • Article 23: prohibits traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour; contravention is an offence punishable by law.
    • Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Ordinance, 1975 was promulgated by the President on 25 October, 1975; the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Bill was passed by both Houses and became an Act in 1976.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 24: no child below 14 years shall be employed in any factory or mine or any other hazardous employment; it relates to exploitation of children.UPPSC ×6
    • The prohibition in Article 24 is an absolute prohibition.
    • Article 24 of the ICCPR (International Convention on Civil and Political Rights) protects child rights; Article 24 of the Indian Constitution also does.UPPSC
    • M.C. Mehta Vs. State of Tamil Nadu, 10 December 1996: Supreme Court held employing children below 14 in hazardous work unconstitutional and prohibited it; child labour in hazardous work is barred by the Constitution, this judgment and the UN Charter.UPPSC ×2
    • United Nations Charter: childhood is entitled to special assistance for full and harmonious development; a child should grow up in a healthy environment.

    Freedom of Religion: Articles 25 to 28

    • Article 25: all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion; the State may make laws for social reform.UPPSC ×2
    • Wearing and carrying of 'Kirpans' by Sikhs is deemed part of freedom of religion by Explanation I of Article 25.
    • Right of religious bodies to convert people is not given under Article 25.
    • In Article 25, 'Hindus' includes persons professing the Sikh, Jain or Buddhist religion, but not Parsis.UPPSC
    • Article 25 rights are limited on grounds of public order, morality and health; humanism is not a limitation.
    • Article 26: every religious denomination or section may establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes, manage its own affairs in religion, own and acquire movable and immovable property, and administer it according to law.
    • Article 26 (freedom to manage religious affairs) is subject to public order, morality and health, but not to the other Fundamental Rights restrictions.

    Cultural and Educational Rights: Articles 29 and 30

    • Article 29: protection of interests of minorities; citizens with a distinct language, script or culture have the right to conserve it.
    • Article 29(2): no citizen shall be denied admission to any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving State aid on grounds of religion, race, caste, language or any of them.
    • Article 30(1): all minorities, whether based on religion or language, have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice; this is not Article 29 or Article 31.UPPSC ×4
    • Article 30(2): in granting aid, the State shall not discriminate against an educational institution because it is managed by a religious or linguistic minority.
    • Article 30 does not define 'minority'.UPPSC
    • The Constitution recognizes both religious and linguistic minorities.
    • A community given national minority status can establish and administer exclusive educational institutions and benefit from the Prime Minister's 15-Point Programme; the Constitution gives minorities no special representation.
    • Article 31 was for compulsory acquisition of property; it was repealed by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
    • Article 31(1) (former): no person shall be deprived of his property save by the authority of law.

    Constitutional Remedies: Article 32 and writs

    • Article 32 gives constitutional remedies against violation of Fundamental Rights; the Supreme Court issues writs under it only to enforce Fundamental Rights.UPPSC
    • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it", because it gives an effective remedy against violation of Fundamental Rights.UPPSC ×4
    • Ambedkar: Article 32 is the most important Article, "without which the Constitution would be a nullity".
    • Article 32 lets individuals approach the Supreme Court directly and makes protection of Fundamental Rights itself a fundamental right.
    • The Preamble is also at times called the Soul of the Constitution, but per Ambedkar it is Article 32.
    • Article 32(2): Supreme Court has extensive original jurisdiction to issue directions, orders or writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari) to enforce Fundamental Rights.
    • Article 32(3): Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise, within the local limits of its jurisdiction, all or any of the Supreme Court's powers under clause (2).UPPSC
    • High Courts under Article 226 issue the five writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose (legal rights also).
    • Supreme Court (Art. 32) and High Courts (Art. 226) enforce Fundamental Rights and may declare any law void or unconstitutional for contravening them.
    • The Judiciary (Supreme Court and High Courts) is the guardian of Fundamental Rights, not the President.UPPSC ×4
    • The most significant Fundamental Right is the right to constitutional remedies under Article 32 (High Courts' jurisdiction is under Article 226).
    • The Supreme Court is the protector of Fundamental Rights (through Article 32) and Guardian of the Constitution; it interprets and enforces the Constitution.UPPSC ×3
    • K.M. Munshi was a member of the Drafting Committee; the Constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly; Panchayati Raj was recommended by the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee Report, 1957.
    • Habeas Corpus ('to have the body of' / 'let us have the body'): detained person is produced before the court and set free if detention is illegal; greatest safeguard of personal liberty and bulwark of individual liberty against arbitrary detention.UPPSC ×2
    • Habeas Corpus can be issued against both public authorities and private individuals.
    • Mandamus ('we command'): command by the court to a public official, public body, corporation, inferior court, tribunal or government to perform official duties it has failed or refused to perform.UPPSC ×2
    • Mandamus ('we command' in Latin) is one of the prerogative writs in the common law, sometimes called mandate; a superior court uses it to compel a lower court or Government officer to perform mandatory or purely ministerial duties correctly.
    • Prohibition ('to forbid'; writ to subordinate courts): issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to stop it exceeding its jurisdiction or usurping a jurisdiction it does not have.
    • Certiorari ('to be certified' / 'be more fully informed'): issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to transfer a pending case to itself or to quash its order.UPPSC
    • Certiorari is issued on grounds of excess of jurisdiction, lack of jurisdiction or error of law.
    • Certiorari is known as 'postmortem': the Supreme Court and High Courts re-examine the decision given by subordinate courts.

    Note from the book 'Postmortem' writ: the Bihar commission keyed Certiorari, but the book says both Certiorari and Quo Warranto have a sense of postmortem, so "more than one of the above" would be the appropriate answer.

    • Quo-Warranto ('by what authority or warrant'): court enquires into the legality of a person's claim to a public office; prevents illegal assumption of public office.

    Amendability of Fundamental Rights and basic structure

    1. 1950Order of judgments: A.K. Gopalan v/s State of Madras (1950) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda Bharati (1973) → Minerva Mills (1980).
    2. 1951State of Madras Vs Champakam Dorairajan (1951): in a conflict, Fundamental Rights prevail over the Directive Principles of State Policy.
    3. 1951Shankari Prasad Vs. Union of India (1951) and Sajjan Singh Vs. State of Rajasthan (1965): Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights.UPPSC
    4. 1967Golaknath Vs. State of Punjab (1967): reversed the earlier view; Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights.
    5. 1973Kesavananda Bharati Vs. State of Kerala (1973): Parliament's amending power is wide but not unlimited; it may amend Fundamental Rights but not destroy the Basic Structure; this case propounded the Basic Structure doctrine.UPPSC ×2
    6. 1980The Basic Structure doctrine was approved in Minerva Mills Vs. Union of India (1980).
    • State of Madras Vs Champakam Dorairajan (1951): in a conflict, Fundamental Rights prevail over the Directive Principles of State Policy.
    • In Champakam, Madras ordered community-based reservation of Medical College seats in furtherance of Article 46; it was challenged under Articles 15(1) and 29(2) and cancelled by the Supreme Court.
    • Shankari Prasad Vs. Union of India (1951) and Sajjan Singh Vs. State of Rajasthan (1965): Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights.UPPSC
    • Golaknath Vs. State of Punjab (1967): reversed the earlier view; Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights.
    • Kesavananda Bharati Vs. State of Kerala (1973): Parliament's amending power is wide but not unlimited; it may amend Fundamental Rights but not destroy the Basic Structure; this case propounded the Basic Structure doctrine.UPPSC ×2
    • The Basic Structure doctrine was approved in Minerva Mills Vs. Union of India (1980).
    • Order of judgments: A.K. Gopalan v/s State of Madras (1950) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda Bharati (1973) → Minerva Mills (1980).
    • Fundamental Rights can be amended but not removed, because they come under the basic structure.
    • Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment.UPPSC
    • The Indian Constitution is not a complete federal constitution but a quasi-federal one.

    Right to Property

    • The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 deleted the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights: it omitted Article 19(1)(f) and inserted Article 300-A.UPPSC ×8
    • Right to Property is now a legal (statutory) right under Article 300-A in Part XII, available to any person; it is not a Fundamental Right.UPPSC ×4
    • Article 300-A: no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
    • The 44th Amendment was made during the Janata Party Government, not a Congress Government.
    • Article 301 relates to freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse, not to the right to property.

    Rights of citizens and of all persons

    • Fundamental Rights available only to citizens: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30; all others are available to citizens and non-citizens.
    • Freedom of speech and expression (Art. 19) and cultural and educational rights of minorities (Art. 29) are available only to Indian citizens, not to aliens.UPPSC ×2
    • Rights given to both citizens and non-citizens: Art. 14 (equality before law), Art. 20, Art. 21, Art. 21-A, Art. 23 and 24, Art. 25, 26, 27 and 28.
    • Equality before law or equal protection of the laws (Article 14) is available to all persons.UPPSC
    • Right against discrimination (Art. 15, 16, 17), right to move freely throughout India [Art. 19(1)(d)] and right to contest elections are available only to citizens.UPPSC
    • Right to constitutional remedies is available to non-citizens too; freedom of speech, free movement and acquiring property are only for citizens.
    • A British citizen (foreigner) in India cannot claim freedom of trade and profession under Article 19(1)(g); equality before law, life and liberty, and freedom of religion are available to him.

    Note from the book Question on which Article belongs to a different category (14, 15, 16, 19): two answers are possible, so no single key is given.

    • Article 19 is under Right to Freedom while 14, 15, 16 are under Right to Equality; or Article 14 is for all persons while 15, 16, 19 are only for citizens.

    Rights, duties and Right to Service

    • Sir Ernest Barker: "Rights without duties are like men without shadow".
    • In India, Rights and Duties are correlative; they are two faces of the same thing and give effect to each other.
    • Holland: every right implies active or passive forbearance by others; that forbearance is called a duty.
    • Supreme Court: a rule may impose an obligation yet not be enforceable in court; it is still a legal rule as it prescribes a norm of conduct.
    • Rights are claims of the citizens against the State; they restrict State power and are essential for complete human development.UPPSC
    • Concept of 'Right to Service' originated in Great Britain (U.K.).
    • Right to service = laws guaranteeing time-bound delivery of public services by Government to citizens.
    • Right of Citizens for Time-bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal of their Grievances Bill, 2011 tried to bring such a law in India but could not be passed.
    • Madhya Pradesh was the first state to implement the Right to Services Act, on 25 September, 2010; Bihar was second, on 15 August, 2011.
    • Order of enactment of Right to Service Act (by Official Gazette dates): Punjab → Assam → Gujarat → Maharashtra.
    • Citizen's Charter aims: quality and time-frame service delivery, citizen-friendly governance, accountable government; creating an effective hearing system of public demands is not its aim.
    • Citizen's Charter = document stating commitments of a government or public service organization to give efficient, transparent and accountable services; its basic objective is to empower citizens in public service delivery, such as better quality and standard services with the taxpayer's money.

    Chapter 14 · States, citizens and rights

    Directive Principles of State Policy

    97 facts · 12 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Article 39(d): equal pay for equal work for both men and women; it is a Directive Principle, not a Fundamental Right.×5
    2. Idea of DPSP was borrowed from the Irish Constitution (Ireland).×4
    3. 40 · Organisation of Village Panchayats×4
    4. DPSP embody the concept of a Welfare State; the welfare state concept is in Part IV (Articles 36 to 51).×3
    5. Article 43A: State shall take steps to secure participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations engaged in any industry; added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 38 UPPSC questions

    Basics and nature

    • Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are in Part IV, Articles 36 to 51.
    • Idea of DPSP was borrowed from the Irish Constitution (Ireland).UPPSC ×4
    • Article 37 deals with the application of the principles in Part IV.
    • Article 37: DPSP are non-justiciable (not enforceable by any court), yet fundamental in the governance of the country; it is the State's duty to apply them in making laws.UPPSC ×2
    • Purpose of DPSP = to establish social and economic democracy; this helps India grow as a welfare state.UPPSC
    • A religious State is not an objective of DPSP; the Constitution makers aimed at a secular and democratic state ensuring socio-economic justice.UPPSC ×2
    • DPSP embody the concept of a Welfare State; the welfare state concept is in Part IV (Articles 36 to 51).UPPSC ×3
    • The idea of India as a welfare State is found in both the Preamble and the DPSP.UPPSC
    • Preamble gives importance to constituting India into a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic; DPSP guide both the Centre and the states to establish a welfare State.
    • Article 38(1): State shall promote people's welfare by securing a social order in which social, economic and political justice informs all institutions of national life.
    • DPSP also include clear political and institutional objectives: Panchayati Raj, Uniform Civil Code, separation of judiciary from executive, international peace.
    • DPSP are important for economic, social and political functions in a modern democratic State.
    • DPSP are directions to the Legislature and the Executive showing how the State should use its legislative and executive power.
    • DPSP are in nature an instrument of instruction to the Government to do certain things and achieve certain ends.
    • DPSP create no justiciable rights for the individual and are not a limitation on the legislative or executive function of the Government.
    • DPSP, being non-enforceable, impose no legal duty on the State; they lay down moral ideals, are merely instructions to guide the legislature and executive, and are not binding on the State.
    • The Constitution has no classification of DPSP; by content and direction they fall in three categories: socialistic, Gandhian, liberal-intellectual.UPPSC
    • K.T. Shah: DPSP is "a cheque which is paid at the Bank's convenience".UPPSC

    Fundamental Rights versus Directive Principles

    PointFundamental RightsDirective Principles
    EnforcementJusticiable: legally enforceable by courts on violationNon-justiciable: not legally enforceable by courts
    NatureMostly negativePositive
    SanctionLegal sanctionsMoral and political sanctions
    AimPolitical democracySocial and economic democracy
    WelfareWelfare of the individualCommunity welfare
    ImplementationAutomatically enforcedNeed legislation for implementation

    Article-wise Directive Principles

    ArticleDirective Principle
    38State to secure a social order for the promotion of the welfare of the people
    39Certain principles of policy to be followed by the State
    39AEqual justice and free legal aid, so that no citizen is denied justice by reason of economic or other disabilities
    40Organisation of Village PanchayatsUPPSC ×4
    41Right to work, to education and to public assistance in certain cases
    42Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief

    43BPromotion of cooperative societiesUPPSC
    44Uniform Civil Code for the citizensUPPSC ×2

    48Organisation of Agriculture and Animal HusbandryUPPSC

    Article 39 and equal pay

    • Article 39(a): citizens, men and women equally, have the right to an adequate means of livelihood.
    • Article 39(b): ownership and control of the community's material resources distributed so as best to subserve the common good.
    • Article 39(c): the economic system must not result in concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment; so concentration of wealth violates DPSP.
    • Article 39(d): equal pay for equal work for both men and women; it is a Directive Principle, not a Fundamental Right.UPPSC ×5
    • Article 39(e): health and strength of workers and the tender age of children not abused; citizens not forced by economic necessity into avocations unsuited to their age or strength.
    • Article 39(f): children get opportunities to develop in a healthy manner, in freedom and dignity; childhood and youth protected against exploitation and moral and material abandonment.
    • Randhir Singh vs Union of India, 1982: Supreme Court deduced Equal Pay for Equal Work as a fundamental right from Articles 14, 16 and 39(d) with the Preamble.
    • Parliament passed the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 with respect to Article 39(d).
    • Protection in respect of conviction for offences, protection of life and personal liberty, and protection of interests of minorities are not Directive Principles.

    Free legal aid and Legal Services Authorities

    • Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid) was added later, by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (w.e.f. 3/1/1977).UPPSC
    • Article 39A gives equal justice and free legal aid to the poor and weaker sections and ensures justice for all.
    • National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) was constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
    • NALSA gives free legal services to weaker sections and organises Lok Adalats for amicable settlement of disputes.
    • NALSA's objective: free and competent legal services to weaker sections on the basis of equal opportunity; it also instructs State Legal Services Authorities and gives them financial grants.
    • State Legal Services Authority is headed by the Chief Justice of the respective High Court, who is its Patron-in-Chief.
    • Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act: entitled to free legal service = member of SC or ST; victim of human trafficking or begar (Article 23); woman or child; person with disability (Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995); person with annual income below the prescribed amount; industrial workman.
    • The income limit may be any higher amount prescribed by the State government.
    • Income ceiling under Section 12(h): Andhra Pradesh 3 lakh; Arunachal Pradesh 1 lakh; Gujarat 1 lakh; Karnataka 1 lakh; Madhya Pradesh 1 lakh.
    • Delhi income ceiling: General 1 lakh; Senior Citizen 2 lakh; Transgender 2 lakh.
    • Free legal services go to a person with annual income below Rs. 1,00,000 and a transgender below Rs. 2,00,000 (Delhi); not to OBCs as a class, and not to all senior citizens.
    • Senior citizens' eligibility for free legal aid depends on rules of the respective state government; in Delhi it is subject to an annual income ceiling.

    Panchayats, work and workers

    • Panchayati Raj System is laid down under DPSP (Part IV), Article 40.
    • Article 40: State shall organise village Panchayats and give them powers and authority needed to function as units of self-government.
    • Article 33 = power of Parliament to modify Part III rights in their application to forces.
    • MGNREGA (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act) = Indian labour law and social security measure that aims to guarantee the "Right to Work".
    • MGNREGA gives at least 100 days of employment in a financial year to every household whose adult member volunteers for unskilled manual work, for livelihood security in rural areas.
    • MGNREGA aims to follow DPSP; right to employment is not enumerated in Part III.UPPSC
    • Article 43: State shall secure to all workers (agricultural, industrial or otherwise) a living wage, decent conditions of work, full enjoyment of leisure, and social and cultural opportunities.
    • MGNREGA is a flagship programme to achieve the goal of Article 43.UPPSC
    • Article 43A: State shall take steps to secure participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations engaged in any industry; added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.UPPSC ×3
    • Article 43B: State shall promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies.
    • 42nd Amendment added Article 39(f) (protection of children and youth from exploitation), Article 39A and Article 43A; Uniform Civil Code (Article 44) was not added by it.UPPSC
    • Article 44: State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India.
    • National Social Assistance Programme was launched on 15 August, 1995 to fulfil DPSP on right to work, education and public assistance in certain cases.
    • NSAP included from the beginning: National Old Age Pension Scheme (NOAPS), National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS), National Maternity Benefit Scheme (NMBS).
    • On 1 April 2001, NMBS was made a part of the population control scheme.

    Gandhian principles

    • Organisation of Village Panchayats and promotion of cottage industries in rural areas follow Gandhian principles; Uniform Civil Code (Liberal-Intellectual) and Right to work (Socialist) do not.
    • Securing reasonable leisure and cultural opportunities for all workers is a Directive Principle but not a Gandhian one.
    • Articles 40, 47 and 48 are based on Gandhian principles.
    • Article 48: prevention of slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle and improvement of their breeds.

    Health, education, environment

    • Article 47: State shall endeavour to prohibit consumption, except for medicinal purposes, of intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health.UPPSC
    • Prohibition of trafficking in human beings and forced labour (begar) = Article 23(1), a Fundamental Right.
    • Prohibition of employment of children in factories or mines = Article 24; abolition of untouchability = Article 17; both are Fundamental Rights, not DPSP.UPPSC
    • The Constitution grants the right against exploitation to children, women and tribals; the word 'Dalit' is not mentioned in the Constitution.UPPSC
    • Free and compulsory education for all children up to age 14 was in Article 45; in 2002 the 86th Amendment made it a Fundamental Right under Article 21-A.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 45 now: early childhood care and education to children below the age of six years.
    • Adult education is not mentioned in the DPSP.UPPSC
    • Article 48A: State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wild life; the same subject is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(g).UPPSC ×3
    • Article 51A(g) (Part IVA): duty of every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures.
    • Right to Information is not a Directive Principle; it is a legal right under the Right to Information Act, 2005.UPPSC ×2
    • Small family norm and education through mother tongue at primary level are not Directive Principles.
    • Article 350A directs every State and local authority to provide instruction in the mother-tongue at the primary stage to children of linguistic minority groups.

    Judiciary and international peace

    • Article 50: State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State; so it is a Directive Principle.
    • Article 51 deals with promotion of international peace and security; it is a Directive Principle and the Article related to Indian foreign policy.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 51: State shall endeavour to promote international peace and security; maintain just and honourable relations between nations; foster respect for international law and treaty obligations; encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

    Fundamental Duties

    44 facts · 7 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The 42nd Amendment added a new part, Part IV-A, where Fundamental Duties are enumerated.×4
    2. They were added on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, which recommended them in 1976.×2
    3. They were added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (in force 3 January 1977), as ten duties, in a new chapter.×2
    4. Present number of Fundamental Duties = 11; originally 10; the 11th, Article 51A(k), was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 (in force 1 April 2010); so duties came by the 42nd and 86th Amendment Acts.×2
    5. Fundamental Duties cannot be enforced by writs.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 21 UPPSC questions

    Origin and place in the Constitution

    • Fundamental Duties are inspired by the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.
    • Originally the Constitution of India did not contain Fundamental Duties.
    • They were added on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, which recommended them in 1976.UPPSC ×2
    • They were added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (in force 3 January 1977), as ten duties, in a new chapter.UPPSC ×2
    • The 42nd Amendment added a new part, Part IV-A, where Fundamental Duties are enumerated.UPPSC ×4
    • Part IV-A has only one Article: Article 51A, which lists the duties of every citizen of India.UPPSC
    • Present number of Fundamental Duties = 11; originally 10; the 11th, Article 51A(k), was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 (in force 1 April 2010); so duties came by the 42nd and 86th Amendment Acts.UPPSC ×2
    • Fundamental Duties are not a part of Fundamental Rights.UPPSC
    • Part V pertains to the Union Executive, not Fundamental Duties; Part II = Citizenship, Part III = Fundamental Rights, Part IV = Directive Principles.UPPSC

    Swaran Singh Committee

    • In 1976 the Congress Party set up the Sardar Swaran Singh Committee to make recommendations about fundamental duties.
    • The need for duties was felt during the internal emergency (1975-77).
    • The Committee stressed that citizens, besides enjoying rights, also have certain duties to perform.
    • The Government accepted the report and added Part IV-A through the 42nd Amendment.
    • The Committee had 12 members: Swaran Singh (Chairman), A.R. Antulay, S.S. Ray, Rajni Patel, H.R. Gokhale, V.S. Sayed Muhammed, V.N. Gadgil, C.M. Stephen, D.P. Singh, Dinesh Goswami, Vasanth Sathe, B.N. Banerjee.
    • Haridev Joshi was not a member; he was the 11th, 16th and 18th Chief Minister of Rajasthan.
    • Haridev Joshi fought 10 state assembly elections from 1952 until his death in 1995 and was undefeated in all.

    Nature of Fundamental Duties

    • Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable: no legal sanction behind them, not enforceable in court, no legislative process to enforce them; they are not correlative to legal duties.
    • Fundamental Duties cannot be enforced by writs.UPPSC ×2
    • Fundamental Duties can be promoted only by constitutional methods and can be used for interpreting ambiguous statutes.
    • Performance of any particular duty comes within the sphere of constitutional law, which the court has to decide.
    • They are moral obligations of all citizens to help promote a spirit of patriotism and uphold the unity of India.
    • Citizens are morally obligated by the Constitution to perform these duties.

    The eleven duties of Article 51A

    ClauseDuty of every citizen of India
    51A(a)To abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem
    51A(b)To cherish and follow the noble ideals which inspired our national struggle for freedom
    51A(c)To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India (number three)
    51A(d)To defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so
    51A(e)To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India; to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women
    51A(f)To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
    51A(g)To protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creaturesUPPSC ×2
    51A(h)To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reformUPPSC
    51A(i)To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
    51A(j)To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity
    51A(k)Parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the age of six and fourteen years (86th Amendment Act, 2002)

    What is not a Fundamental Duty

    • To vote in a general election or public elections is not a Fundamental Duty.UPPSC
    • To strive towards abolition of untouchability is not a Fundamental Duty; abolition of untouchability = Article 17 (Fundamental Rights, Part III).UPPSC
    • To help in organising Village Panchayats is not a Fundamental Duty; it is a Directive Principle (Article 40).UPPSC
    • Article 40: State shall organise village panchayats and give them powers and authority to function as units of self-government.
    • To pay income tax is not a Fundamental Duty.UPPSC
    • To protect the weaker sections from social injustice is not a Fundamental Duty.
    • To protect monuments and places of national (public) importance is not a Fundamental Duty; it is a Directive Principle under Article 49.UPPSC ×2
    • To respect our parents and teachers is not among the eleven Fundamental Duties.UPPSC
    • Separation of judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State = Article 50, Part IV (Directive Principle).
    • Prohibition of employment of children below 14 years in factories = Article 24, Part III (Fundamental Right).
    • To foster respect for international law = Article 51(c), a Directive Principle.

    The President

    178 facts · 15 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. If offices of both President and Vice-President are vacant, the Chief Justice of India acts as President: President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969.×6
    2. Article 53(1): executive power of the Union is vested in the President; exercised by him directly or through officers subordinate to him, in accordance with the Constitution.×5
    3. Article 62(2): a vacancy by death, resignation, removal or otherwise must be filled within six months of its occurrence; so the Vice-President can act for at most 6 months.×4
    4. Article 54: electoral college = elected members of both Houses of Parliament + elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry).×3
    5. Article 108: President summons a joint sitting of both Houses.×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 64 UPPSC questions

    Position of the President

    • President = head of the Indian State (Republic), the first citizen, and symbol of unity, integrity and solidarity of the nation.UPPSC
    • Article 52: there shall be a President of India.
    • Article 53(1): executive power of the Union is vested in the President; exercised by him directly or through officers subordinate to him, in accordance with the Constitution.UPPSC ×5
    • The President is the constitutional head of the Executive of the Union.
    • The President's power is not unlimited: he must exercise it in accordance with the Constitution.UPPSC
    • Article 53(2): supreme command of the Defence Forces is vested in the President, but its exercise is regulated by law (not independent of legislative control).UPPSC ×2
    • President is the supreme commander of the defence forces: Army, Navy and Air Force.
    • Article 77: all executive action (business) of the Government of India is expressed to be taken in the President's name.UPPSC
    • Executive power is concerned with carrying on the business of the Government.
    • "He represents the nation but does not lead the nation" applies to the President; real executive power is with the Prime Minister, who leads the nation.UPPSC
    • President of India is indirectly elected, British King is hereditary; U.S. President has more power than the Indian President, so the two offices are not similar.UPPSC
    • President has titular (formal) and de-jure authority; constitutional and nominal authority.UPPSC
    • 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 made the President bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.
    • 44th Amendment Act, 1978 (Janta Party Government): President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider advice, but must act on the advice given after reconsideration.
    • Article 74(1): President acts in accordance with the advice of the Union Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.

    Election: electoral college

    • President is elected by indirect election, not directly by the people, through an electoral college.UPPSC
    • Article 54: electoral college = elected members of both Houses of Parliament + elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry).UPPSC ×3
    • 70th Amendment Act, 1992 (effective 01-06-1995) included elected members of the assemblies of NCT of Delhi and UT of Puducherry in the electoral college.UPPSC
    • Elected members of the Legislative Assembly of UT of Jammu and Kashmir are not yet included in the electoral college.
    • Members of State Legislative Councils (elected and nominated) do not take part; a Chief Minister who is a member of the Legislative Council cannot vote.UPPSC
    • Nominated members of both Houses of Parliament and of State Legislative Assemblies do not participate in the election.
    • Article 55(3): election by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote; voting by secret ballot.
    • A dissolved Legislative Assembly cannot take part in the election.
    • Election cannot be challenged or postponed on the ground that the electoral college is incomplete (any vacancy among its members): Article 71(4).UPPSC
    • Election of the successor must be held before the term of the incumbent President expires.
    • On expiry of his term, the President continues to hold office until his successor enters upon office.

    Election: value of votes

    • Article 55: as far as practicable, uniformity in the scale of representation of different States, and parity between the States as a whole and the Union.
    • Value of an MLA's vote = State population ÷ total elected MLAs of the State, then ÷ 1000 (multiples of one thousand, not one hundred).
    • Value of an MP's vote = total value of votes of all elected MLAs ÷ total number of elected MPs.
    • Value of each MLA's vote varies from State to State because population and number of elected members differ.
    • Vote value of each Lok Sabha member and each Rajya Sabha member is the same.
    • More elective Assembly seats means lower value of each MLA's vote (seats are the denominator).
    • MLA vote values: Uttar Pradesh 208, Kerala 152, Madhya Pradesh 131, Puducherry 16, Arunachal Pradesh 8.
    • "Population" = 1971 census, until figures of the first census after 2026 are published (84th Amendment Act, 2001; Explanation to Article 55; Article 81(3)).
    • Article 81(3): "population" means the population at the last preceding census of which relevant figures have been published.
    • Presidential Election 2022: vote value of each Rajasthan MLA = 129 (1971 population 2,57,65,800 ÷ 200 MLAs = 1,28,829; ÷ 1000 = 128.82).
    • 2022 election: Droupadi Murmu (former Jharkhand Governor, NDA candidate) defeated opposition candidate Yashwant Sinha and became the 15th President.
    • Droupadi Murmu = first tribal woman President (Santhal tribe) and the youngest President.
    • Yashwant Sinha = former Union Finance Minister; the Murmu versus Sinha contest is also called the 16th Presidential election.
    • Meera Kumar was the candidate of the United Progressive Alliance (UPA) in the 15th Presidential election.

    Qualifications, nomination, conditions

    • Article 58(1): citizen of India; completed 35 years; qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha.UPPSC ×2
    • Citizenship by birth is not required; education is not a qualification.
    • Article 58(2): must not hold any office of profit.
    • Nomination must be subscribed by at least 50 electors as proposers and 50 electors as seconders.
    • Security deposit = Rs. 15000; forfeited if the candidate is not elected and gets valid votes not exceeding one-sixth of the votes needed to win.
    • Article 59(1): President cannot be a member of Parliament or a State Legislature; a member elected President is deemed to have vacated the seat on the date he enters office.UPPSC
    • Article 60: oath of office to the President is administered by the Chief Justice of India.
    • President's salary at present = Rs. 5 lakh per month, paid from the Consolidated Fund of India.
    • Article 361(2): no criminal proceedings can be instituted or continued against the President or a Governor in any court during his term.
    • Article 361(4): civil proceedings can be instituted against the President or a Governor during his term after two months' written notice.

    Election disputes

    • Article 71(1): all doubts and disputes about the election of President or Vice-President are inquired into and decided by the Supreme Court; its decision is final.
    • Article 71(2): if the election is declared void by the Supreme Court, acts done before the date of the decision are not invalidated.
    • V.V. Giri appeared in person before the Supreme Court as incumbent President in a petition challenging his election for corrupt practices.
    • The bench headed by Justice S.M. Sikri dismissed the petition and upheld Giri's election.
    • V.V. Giri had got the majority on counting of second preference votes.

    Term, re-election, resignation

    • Article 56(1): term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office.
    • Article 57: a person who holds or has held office as President is eligible for re-election, any number of times.
    • Article 56(1)(a): President resigns in writing addressed to the Vice-President.
    • Article 56(2): Vice-President immediately communicates the resignation to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

    Impeachment

    • Article 56(1)(b): President can be removed before his term by impeachment by Parliament; the only ground (Article 61(1)) is violation of the Constitution.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 61 lays down the procedure for impeachment of the President.UPPSC ×2
    • The Constitution does not define "violation of the Constitution".
    • The charge can be preferred (initiated) by either House of Parliament.UPPSC
    • At least 14 days' prior written notice is needed, signed by not less than one-fourth of the total members of the House: Article 61(2)(a).UPPSC
    • Article 61(2)(b): resolution must be passed by not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the House.
    • Article 61(3): the other House investigates the charge; President has the right to appear and be represented.
    • If the other House also passes the resolution by two-thirds of total membership, President stands removed from the date the resolution is passed.
    • Impeachment is a quasi-judicial procedure in Parliament.
    • State Legislative Assemblies are part of the electoral college but not of the impeachment process.
    • No President has so far been impeached.

    Vacancy

    • Article 62(2): a vacancy by death, resignation, removal or otherwise must be filled within six months of its occurrence; so the Vice-President can act for at most 6 months.UPPSC ×4
    • Article 65(1): on such vacancy the Vice-President acts as President until a new President enters office.
    • When the President cannot function due to absence, illness or other cause, Vice-President discharges his functions until he resumes.
    • If offices of both President and Vice-President are vacant, the Chief Justice of India acts as President: President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969.UPPSC ×6
    • In the absence of the CJI, the senior-most Supreme Court judge available performs the President's functions.

    Parliament: summoning, prorogation, dissolution

    • Article 79: Parliament = President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha; President is a constituent part of Parliament because a Bill cannot become law without his assent.UPPSC ×2
    • President addresses both Houses at a joint meeting every year but does not participate in Parliamentary discussions.UPPSC
    • The Union Cabinet prepares the President's address to Parliament, as real executive power vests in it.
    • Article 85: President summons and prorogues either House and can dissolve the Lok Sabha.
    • Article 85(2)(b): President may dissolve the Lok Sabha, on the recommendation of the Union Cabinet (Council of Ministers).
    • Prorogation = termination of a session by President's order under Article 85(2)(a); it needs the advice of the Council of Ministers.
    • Prorogation normally follows adjournment sine die, but the President can prorogue a House in session; dissolution is done on Council of Ministers' advice save in exceptional circumstances.
    • Time-lag between adjournment sine die and prorogation is generally two to four days; sometimes the same day.
    • Article 83(2): Lok Sabha continues five years from the date of its first meeting unless sooner dissolved; expiry operates as dissolution.
    • President may at his discretion look for an alternate government if the present government cannot prove majority in Lok Sabha.
    • Article 108: President summons a joint sitting of both Houses.UPPSC ×3
    • Article 118(4): the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over a joint sitting.
    • Joint sitting cases: Bill rejected by the other House; final disagreement on amendments; more than six months elapse without the other House passing it.
    • President notifies his intention to summon a joint sitting: by message if Houses are sitting, by public notification if not.
    • No joint sitting if the Bill has lapsed by dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
    • Article 86(2): President may send messages to either House, on a pending Bill or otherwise; the House must consider it with all convenient dispatch.
    • Sending messages to Parliament is literally a right of the President, not a power.

    Assent to Bills and veto

    • A Bill passed by Parliament becomes an Act only after the President's assent (Article 111).
    • Article 111: President declares that he assents to the Bill or withholds assent.UPPSC ×3
    • President may return a Bill (not a Money Bill) for reconsideration; if passed again, with or without amendments, he must give assent.
    • The Constitution prescribes no time-limit for the President to decide on a Bill presented for assent.
    • President cannot return a Money Bill or Finance Bill for reconsideration.UPPSC
    • Money Bill is introduced only in Lok Sabha and only with the President's prior recommendation; it cannot be introduced in the Council of States.
    • Returning an ordinary Bill, dissolving the Lok Sabha and appointing the Prime Minister are constitutional prerogatives of the President.
    • Pocket veto = President takes no action on a Bill; used only once, by Gyani Zail Singh in 1986 on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill.
    • Dr. Rajendra Prasad applied an absolute veto on the PEPSU Appropriation Bill 1954, on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
    • Pocket veto is used at the President's discretion; absolute veto is subject to the discretion of the Union Council of Ministers.
    • Discretionary powers of the President: to return a Bill with objections, to withhold a Bill, to send messages to Parliament.
    • Discretionary powers also: to detain a bill, to ask the Prime Minister for information, to ask the Council of Ministers to reconsider advice.
    • Not discretionary: appointing the majority party leader as Prime Minister, summoning Parliament, appointing ministers, assenting to a bill referred by a Governor.
    • Appointing judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts and the Council of Ministers = executive power; summoning a joint session = legislative power.
    • It is not essential for the President to take the Council of Ministers' advice when assenting to Bills (answer as per Chhattisgarh PSC).
    • Advice is essential for: appointing Ambassadors, assent to Bills referred by Governors, dissolving Lok Sabha, assent to a constitutional amendment bill.

    Ordinances

    • Article 123: President can promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session (except when both Houses are in session); a legislative power.UPPSC ×3
    • He must be satisfied that circumstances make immediate action necessary.
    • In 2002 the President assented under Article 123 to the Ordinance on electoral reforms when the Union Cabinet sent it back unchanged.
    • Article 123(2): an Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament.
    • Ordinance must be laid before both Houses and approved within six weeks of reassembly; otherwise it ceases to operate at the end of six weeks.
    • President can withdraw an ordinance at any time.
    • Scope of an ordinance = ordinary legislative powers of Parliament: it can amend any Central Act but not the Constitution.
    • An ordinance has the same constitutional limits as an Act; it cannot take away or abridge a Fundamental Right in violation of the basic structure.
    • Like any Act, an ordinance can be made effective retrospectively (from a back date).

    Note from the book For the 2025 question on ordinances, the printed answer is "I and II only", but the book's own explanation says only statements I and III are correct.

    Appointments

    • President appoints the Chairman of the Finance Commission (Article 280(1)) and the Chief Minister of a Union Territory (Article 239AA(5)).UPPSC
    • Article 239AA(5): other UT Ministers are appointed by the President on the Chief Minister's advice; Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure.
    • Vice-Chairman of the Planning Commission was appointed by the Prime Minister; Planning Commission is now replaced by NITI Aayog.
    • President appoints the Attorney General (Article 76), the Comptroller and Auditor General (Article 148) and the Governor of a State (Article 155).UPPSC
    • Vice-President is not appointed by the President; he is elected under Article 66.UPPSC
    • President appoints the Prime Minister, the Governor and the Chief Election Commissioner.
    • Article 160: President may make provisions for discharge of a Governor's duties in any contingency.UPPSC
    • Chief Minister of a State is appointed by the Governor (Article 164(1)), not by the President.
    • President cannot on his own remove a Supreme Court judge.
    • Article 124(4): SC judge removed by President's order after an address by each House, passed by majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting.
    • Such address is presented in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

    Judicial and other powers

    • Article 143: President can consult the Supreme Court on a question of law or fact.UPPSC
    • President is not bound to accept the Supreme Court's advice.UPPSC
    • Article 72: President can grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment, or suspend, remit or commute sentences.
    • Pardoning power is a judicial power of the President.UPPSC
    • Detention and continuation are not part of the pardoning power.
    • Article 72 applies to: offence against a Union law; punishment by a court-martial (military court); sentence of death.
    • President's clemency power is subject to limited judicial review; he cannot use it without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.
    • President must lay before Parliament: Finance Commission recommendations (Article 281), CAG report (Article 151(1)), report of National Commission for Scheduled Castes (Article 338(6)).
    • Public Accounts Committee is a committee of selected MPs constituted by Parliament; its chairman is appointed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
    • President can declare any area a Scheduled Area (Fifth Schedule); he has powers over administration of scheduled and tribal areas.UPPSC
    • President may order that the whole or part of a Scheduled Area ceases to be one.
    • President may increase the area of a Scheduled Area after consulting the Governor of that State.
    • President may alter a Scheduled Area only by way of rectification of boundaries.
    • On alteration of State boundary, admission or creation of a State, President may declare territory not earlier in any State as a Scheduled Area.
    • President has emergency powers and the power to extend President's Rule in States.

    4. 1950Dr. Rajendra Prasad completed two successive terms; he served three terms: 1950-1952, 1952-1957, 1957-1962.
    5. 1957Dr. Zakir Husain: Governor of Bihar 6 July 1957 – 11 May 1962; Vice-President 13 May 1962 – 12 May 1967; President 13 May 1967 – 3 May 1969 (till death).UPPSC
    6. 1962Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, second President (1962-1967), is known as the Philosopher King or Philosopher Ruler.UPPSC

    Chapter 17 · Union: executive, Parliament, Supreme Court

    The Vice-President

    48 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Article 67(b): removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of all its then members (absolute majority) and agreed to by the Lok Sabha; not by formal impeachment.×4
    2. Article 66(1): Vice-President is elected by an electoral college of all members (elected and nominated) of both Houses of Parliament.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 10 UPPSC questions

    Office and role

    • The post of Vice-President of India is modelled on the American Vice-President.
    • Vice-President is next to the President in the official order of precedence; second-highest constitutional office.
    • Article 63: there shall be a Vice-President of India.
    • Article 64: Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and shall not hold any other office of profit.
    • Rajya Sabha is presided over by the Vice-President, who is not its member.UPPSC
    • Vice-President: second highest dignitary; no formal function attached to the office; discharges President's functions in his absence; acts as President if President resigns, is removed or dies.UPPSC
    • Vice-President acts as President during casual vacancies caused by death, resignation, impeachment or other situations.
    • While acting as President or discharging his functions, Vice-President does not perform duties of Rajya Sabha Chairman (Article 64, proviso).
    • In that period he gets the President's salary and allowances (Article 65(3)), not the Chairman's.
    • If the Vice-President resigns while discharging President's duties, the Chief Justice of India performs them: President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969.
    • Vice-President draws salary (4 lakh per month) as ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha; the Constitution fixes no emoluments for him as Vice-President.

    Election and qualifications

    • Article 66(1): Vice-President is elected by an electoral college of all members (elected and nominated) of both Houses of Parliament.UPPSC ×2
    • Members of State Legislative Assemblies and Legislative Councils do not elect the Vice-President.
    • Election is by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote; voting by secret ballot.
    • Election of the Vice-President, like that of the President, is indirect; State Legislatures play no role in the Vice-President's election.UPPSC
    • Vice-President is elected, not appointed by the President.
    • 16th Vice-Presidential Election (2022): electoral college = 788 members: 233 elected Rajya Sabha + 12 nominated Rajya Sabha + 543 elected Lok Sabha.
    • Article 66(3): citizen of India; completed 35 years; qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha (not Lok Sabha), since he chairs it.UPPSC
    • A member of a State Legislature can be a candidate for Vice-President.
    • Minimum age to hold the office of President is 35 years; the first President was Dr. Rajendra Prasad.
    • Article 71(2): if the Vice-President's election is declared void by the Supreme Court, acts done on or before the date of the decision are not invalidated.

    Term, resignation, removal

    • Article 67: term of five years, the same as the President's.
    • Article 67(a): Vice-President resigns by writing addressed to the President.
    • Article 67(b): removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of all its then members (absolute majority) and agreed to by the Lok Sabha; not by formal impeachment.UPPSC ×4
    • The removal resolution can be moved only in Rajya Sabha, and only after at least 14 days' notice.

    Facts about Vice-Presidents

    • Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was the first Vice-President (1952 to 1962); Dr. Zakir Hussain was the second, from 13 May 1962 to 12 May 1967.UPPSC
    • Mohammad Hamid Ansari entered office in 2007 and was re-elected in July 2012.
    • Mohammad Hidayatullah (sixth, 1979-84) and Shankar Dayal Sharma (1987-92) were Vice-Presidents; Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed and Neelam Sanjiva Reddy were only Presidents.
    • Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (Ambassador to U.S.S.R., 1949-1952) and V.V. Giri (High Commissioner to Sri Lanka, 1947-1951) held diplomatic posts before becoming Vice-President.
    • K.R. Narayanan was ambassador to China from 1976 to 1978.

    Other facts in this chapter

    • A Constitutional Amendment Bill must be passed by both Houses of Parliament separately with special majority.
    • Constitutional cases in the Supreme Court are heard by a minimum of five judges.
    • Freedom of Press is included in the fundamental right of Freedom of Speech and Expression.
