    Chapter 18 · Union: executive, Parliament, Supreme Court

    The Council of Ministers

    142 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Article 75(3): Council of Ministers (including PM) is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha only, not Rajya Sabha or Parliament as a whole; a constitutional obligation.×5
    2. Article 75(5): a non-member of Parliament can be a minister (or Prime Minister) but ceases to be one unless he becomes a member of either House within six months, by election or nomination.×4
    3. At least 50 members are needed to table a No-Confidence Motion against the Council of Ministers.×3
    4. Article 75(1): Prime Minister is appointed by the President; other Ministers are appointed by the President on the Prime Minister's advice.×2
    5. The Council of Ministers can move a Confidence Motion, to prove majority support in Lok Sabha.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 31 UPPSC questions

    Council of Ministers and Prime Minister: basics

    • Article 300: the legal name of the Government of India is 'The Union of India'.UPPSC
    • Central Council of Ministers = Prime Minister, Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Ministers of State (Independent Charge).
    • Article 74(1): a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head aids and advises the President, who acts on such advice; so it is a constitutional body.
    • President may require the Council to reconsider advice, but must act on the advice given after reconsideration (added by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978).
    • Article 74(2): advice tendered by Ministers to the President cannot be inquired into in any court.
    • Prime Minister is the real head of the Council of Ministers; real executive power is exercised by the Prime Minister (Article 75).UPPSC
    • Prime Minister = Head of the (Central) Government; President = Head of the State.
    • Executive power of the Union is vested in the President (Article 53(1)), not the Prime Minister; President is the constitutional head of the Union executive.
    • Article 75(1): Prime Minister is appointed by the President; other Ministers are appointed by the President on the Prime Minister's advice.UPPSC ×2
    • Prime Minister has full discretion in choosing persons to serve as ministers in his Cabinet.
    • Article 75(2): Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President (not of the Prime Minister).
    • President administers the oath of office and secrecy to the Prime Minister and other ministers.
    • Prime Minister is the Chairman of Union Cabinet meetings; he submits his resignation to the President.
    • Minimum age to become Prime Minister = 25 years, same as for a Lok Sabha member.
    • Article 78: duties of the Prime Minister: communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers on Union administration and proposals for legislation.UPPSC
    • Article 78: PM furnishes information the President calls for; if President requires, submits to the Council a matter decided by a minister but not considered by the Council.

    Size and ranks of ministers

    • Article 75(1A): total Ministers including the Prime Minister cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha; added by the 91st Amendment Act, 2003.
    • 91st Amendment also added Article 164(1A): State ministers including the Chief Minister cannot exceed 15% of the Legislative Assembly's total members.
    • The Constitution has no classification of ministers; the ranking is based on British Parliamentary tradition.
    • Ranks in practice: Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State (Independent Charge), Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers.
    • Cabinet = Prime Minister and ministers of Cabinet rank only; it is the supreme decision-making body.UPPSC
    • Union Council of Ministers exercises executive authority; the Union Cabinet is its senior executive body.
    • The Council of Ministers seldom meets as a body; the Cabinet, an inner body, shapes government policy; Cabinet Ministers hold key portfolios.
    • The word 'Cabinet' appears only in Article 352(3), inserted by the 44th Amendment Act; it was not in the original Constitution.
    • Article 352(3): President shall not issue a Proclamation unless the Union Cabinet communicates in writing that it may be issued; 'Cabinet' appears twice in this Article.

    Membership of Parliament

    • Article 75(5): a non-member of Parliament can be a minister (or Prime Minister) but ceases to be one unless he becomes a member of either House within six months, by election or nomination.UPPSC ×4
    • The Constitution provides for a Parliamentary form of Government; Parliament provides a Cabinet; the Cabinet enjoys majority confidence in the popular chamber.
    • Cabinet membership is not restricted to the Lower House; ministers can be from either House.
    • Prime Minister is generally a member of Lok Sabha, but can be from Rajya Sabha.
    • Indira Gandhi was the first PM from Rajya Sabha at the time of appointment; later she became a Lok Sabha member.
    • A minister can speak in both Houses but vote only in the House of which he is a member; a Rajya Sabha PM cannot vote on a no-confidence motion.

    Collective responsibility and motions

    • Article 75(3): Council of Ministers (including PM) is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha only, not Rajya Sabha or Parliament as a whole; a constitutional obligation.UPPSC ×5
    • Article 74(3) does not exist in the Constitution.
    • Where Lok Sabha is not an option, the nearest answer for responsibility of the Council is Parliament.
    • Convention, not stated in the Constitution: Prime Minister resigns if he loses majority in the Lower House.
    • In Indian polity the executive is subordinate to the Legislature; Parliament is the supreme legislative body.
    • Ministerial responsibility: for every act of bureaucrats the concerned Minister is answerable to Parliament.
    • Ministers make policy and civil servants adhere to it; Parliamentary government works on 'Cabinet Collective Responsibility'; both are true, but the second does not explain the first.UPPSC
    • The Council of Ministers can move a Confidence Motion, to prove majority support in Lok Sabha.UPPSC ×2
    • No-Confidence Motion can be introduced only in Lok Sabha and is not mentioned in the Constitution; if passed, the Council must resign.UPPSC
    • Neither Confidence nor No-Confidence Motion is mentioned in the Constitution; procedure is in Rule 198 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business of Lok Sabha.
    • At least 50 members are needed to table a No-Confidence Motion against the Council of Ministers.UPPSC ×3
    • Rule 198(1)(b): written notice of the motion is given to the Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha.
    • First no-confidence motion: 1963, third Lok Sabha, moved by Acharya J.B. Kripalani against Jawaharlal Nehru's government.
    • Till 15 August 2023: 28 no-confidence motions (28th on the Manipur situation) and 11 confidence motions discussed.
    • 14 of the 28 motions (50%) were discussed between 1965 and 1975; 12 of these were against Indira Gandhi's governments.

    Note from the book The Commission deleted the 2023 Rajasthan question on wrong statements about the No-Confidence Motion.

    • On resignation of the Council of Ministers, President's Rule is not imposed.UPPSC
    • President asks the outgoing Council to continue till alternative arrangement, i.e. earliest General Election or formation of a new Government.
    • A minister who resigns can make a statement in the House when allowed by the Speaker; he cannot be compelled to do so.

    Ministries and allocation of business

    • Article 77(1): all executive action of the Government of India is expressed to be taken in the name of the President.
    • Article 77(3): President makes rules for convenient transaction of government business and its allocation among Ministers.
    • Ministries/departments are created by the President on the PM's advice under the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, which the President made under Article 77.
    • President assigns each Ministry to a Minister on the Prime Minister's advice; the PM does not create ministries on the Cabinet Secretary's advice.
    • Ministries at the Centre on 15 August 1947 = 18; at present = 53.
    • Ministry of Tribal Affairs was set up in 1999 by bifurcating the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, for focused, integrated socio-economic development of Scheduled Tribes (the most underprivileged section).
    • It is the nodal Ministry for policy planning and coordination of programmes for development of Scheduled Tribes.
    • Before it, tribal affairs were handled by different Ministries at different times.
    • Ministry of Minority Affairs was carved out of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment on 29 January, 2006.
    • Notified minority communities: Muslim, Christian, Buddhist, Sikhs, Parsis and Jain.
    • Smriti Zubin Irani was Minister for Minority Affairs and John Barla the Minister of State (at the question's time).
    • Minister for Minority Affairs at present (2025) = Kiren Rijiju.
    • After the 18th Lok Sabha elections, Giriraj Singh (MP from Begusarai, Bihar) became Union Minister of Textiles.
    • White Paper = official document of the Government of India or its Ministry explaining policy on a subject and collecting feedback before a bill.UPPSC

    Cabinet Secretariat and administration

    • Cabinet Secretariat is directly under the Prime Minister; its administrative head, the Cabinet Secretary, is ex-officio chairman of the Civil Services Board.
    • Union Cabinet Secretariat is supervised by the Prime Minister's Office, not the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs.
    • Cabinet Secretary is the highest civil services officer of the central government.
    • Cabinet Secretariat is in the 1st Schedule of the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961.
    • Its subjects: secretariat assistance to the Cabinet and Cabinet Committees; administration of the Rules of Business; inter-ministerial coordination.
    • Allocation of financial resources to Ministries is not a function of the Cabinet Secretariat.
    • Its assistance: convening Cabinet meetings on PM's orders; preparing and circulating agenda and papers; recording discussions; circulating record after PM's approval; watching implementation.
    • Inter-ministerial coordination: removing difficulties and differences, overcoming delays, coordinating administrative actions and policies.
    • Cabinet Committees are not in the Constitution (extra-constitutional); Rules of Business provide for them; the PM sets them up as needed.
    • Cabinet Committees are mostly chaired by the PM; sometimes by other Cabinet Ministers, the Finance Minister or Home Minister.
    • If the Prime Minister is a member of a Cabinet Committee, he is necessarily its Chairman.
    • Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs is chaired by the Minister of Defence.
    • Reorganisation of the Union Cabinet is based on the Report of N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar.UPPSC
    • Ayyangar's 1950 report 'Reorganization of the Machinery of Central Government' recommended grouping of ministries, better personnel capabilities and better O&M Division working.
    • It did not suggest a minister and secretary solely for administrative reform.
    • Department of Personnel was created under the Cabinet Secretariat on 1 August 1970.
    • 7 February 1973: Administrative Reforms work moved to it; renamed Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms.
    • April 1977: this Department shifted from the Cabinet Secretariat to the Ministry of Home Affairs.
    • March 1985: elevated to Ministry of Personnel and Training, Administrative Reforms, Public Grievances and Pensions.
    • 10 December 1985: renamed Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, under the Prime Minister assisted by a Minister of State.
    • Its three departments: Personnel and Training (DOPT); Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances; Pension and Pensioners Welfare.
    • Split system in Indian administration relates to policy/implementation; it ensures efficient policy-making and implementation; the Ex-Secretariat system is based on it.
    • Prime Minister is the President of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research.
    • National Defence Committee is headed by the Prime Minister.
    • Office of the Parliamentary Secretary was created in 1951.

    Note from the book The printed answer option for the Parliamentary Secretary question is 1952, but the book's explanation says 1951.

    Deputy Prime Minister

    • Office of Deputy Prime Minister is not in the Constitution: an extra-constitutional (non-constitutional) post created by political necessity.UPPSC
    • By convention a Cabinet Minister can be declared Deputy PM, a political decision; it confers no power of the Prime Minister.UPPSC
    • First Deputy Prime Minister = Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, 15 August 1947 to 15 December 1950; also Minister of Home Affairs.
    • Patel integrated over 500 princely states into the Indian Union.

    First Cabinet and ministers

    • R.K. Shanmukham Chetty was the first Finance Minister of independent India (1947-1948) in Nehru's Cabinet.
    • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the first Law Minister of post-independence India.
    • Jogendra Nath Mandal was Law Minister in the interim government of 1946.

    Chapter 19 · Union: executive, Parliament, Supreme Court

    The Attorney General and the C.A.G.

    100 facts · 7 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. AG = highest (first / top) law officer of the country and of the Government of India.×2
    2. Qualification: a person qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court [Article 76(1)].×2
    3. Every Minister and the AG can speak and take part in proceedings of either House, any joint sitting, and any Committee of Parliament of which he is named a member, but cannot vote.×2
    4. Solicitor General of India = a Legal Adviser; second law officer of the country.×2
    5. Advocate-General = legal adviser (first legal adviser) of the State Government; duty to advise the State Government on legal matters [Article 165(2)].×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 33 UPPSC questions

    Attorney-General: office, appointment, qualification

    • Article 76 provides for the office of the Attorney-General (AG) for India.
    • AG = highest (first / top) law officer of the country and of the Government of India.UPPSC ×2
    • AG is a part of the Union Executive.
    • AG is appointed by the President [Article 76(1)], on the advice of the government.
    • Qualification: a person qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court [Article 76(1)].UPPSC ×2
    • So (Article 124(3)) AG must be a citizen of India and: High Court judge for 5 years, or High Court advocate for 10 years, or an eminent jurist in the President's opinion.
    • AG need not be a member of either House of Parliament; appointed by President with SC-judge qualifications.UPPSC

    Attorney-General: duties and rights

    • Duty [Article 76(2)]: to advise the Government of India on legal matters referred to him by the President, and do other legal duties referred or assigned by the President.UPPSC
    • AG = chief legal adviser to the Government of India and the top law officer who represents the government in court (its primary lawyer in the Supreme Court); not the Solicitor General, CJI or CAG.UPPSC
    • AG has the right of audience in all courts in the territory of India in the performance of his duties [Article 76(3)].UPPSC
    • AG is not a full-time (whole-time) government servant/counsel; with permission he may do private legal practice.

    Attorney-General: tenure, removal, pay

    • AG holds office during the pleasure of the President [Article 76(4)]; not of the Prime Minister.UPPSC
    • AG has no security of tenure; the President can remove him at any time.
    • The Constitution does not state the procedure and grounds for removal of AG; he is not removed like a Supreme Court judge, nor by impeachment by Parliament.
    • AG gets such remuneration as the President may determine [Article 76(4)], not as Parliament may determine.
    • The Constitution does not say that AG resigns when the government that appointed him resigns.

    Attorney-General in Parliament (Article 88)

    • Article 88: rights of Ministers and the Attorney-General with respect to the Houses of Parliament.
    • Every Minister and the AG can speak and take part in proceedings of either House, any joint sitting, and any Committee of Parliament of which he is named a member, but cannot vote.UPPSC ×2
    • AG can take part in proceedings of both Houses of Parliament though not a member.UPPSC
    • AG enjoys all the privileges and immunities available to a Member of Parliament.UPPSC
    • The Vice-President is also not a member of Parliament, so he too can be an answer for "non-member who takes part in proceedings".
    • When a motion to remove the Vice-President is under consideration in Rajya Sabha, he does not remain ex-officio Chairman then; he can be part of the House and speak in it.
    • The Vice-President participates only in the Rajya Sabha; for proceedings of both Houses the answer is the Attorney-General.
    • Solicitor General is not given the right to participate in meetings of Parliament.

    Solicitor General of India

    • Solicitor General of India = a Legal Adviser; second law officer of the country.UPPSC ×2
    • Solicitor General is subordinate to the Attorney-General and assists him.
    • Solicitor General is himself assisted by several Additional Solicitor-Generals of India.

    Advocate-General of a State (Article 165)

    • Advocate-General = legal adviser (first legal adviser) of the State Government; duty to advise the State Government on legal matters [Article 165(2)].UPPSC ×2
    • Advocate-General also does other legal duties referred or assigned by the Governor, and functions conferred by the Constitution or any other law in force [Article 165(2)].
    • Advocate-General is appointed by the Governor of the State [Article 165(1)], not by the President.
    • Qualification: a person qualified to be appointed a Judge of a High Court [Article 165(1)].
    • Advocate-General holds office during the pleasure of the Governor [Article 165(3)], not of the Cabinet.
    • The post is created by the Constitution and corresponds to the Attorney-General at the Union level.
    • Article 177: Advocate-General can speak and take part in proceedings of the State Legislature, but has no right to vote.
    • Under the Civil Procedure Code, High Courts do not have original, appellate and advisory jurisdiction at State level.
    • Article 143: advisory jurisdiction belongs to the Supreme Court.

    CAG: office and appointment

    • The office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India (CAG) is created by the Constitution; Article 148 provides an independent office.UPPSC
    • Article 148(1): there shall be a CAG, appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.UPPSC ×2
    • CAG is a constitutional functionary, independent of Parliament/legislature and the executive.
    • CAG = head of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department.
    • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar: CAG is probably the most important officer under the Constitution of India.
    • Girish Chandra Murmu = 14th CAG of independent India.
    • Currently K. Sanjay Murthy = 15th CAG of India, appointed in 2024.

    CAG: Articles

    ArticleSubject
    148Appointment of CAG (office of CAG)
    148(1)Appointment by President; removal like a Supreme Court judge
    148(3)Salary and other service conditions decided by Parliament by law; until then as in Second Schedule
    148(4)Not eligible for further office under Union or State government
    148(6)Administrative expenses of CAG office charged on Consolidated Fund of India
    149Duties and powers of CAG
    150Form of accounts of the Union and of the States
    151Audit reports
    151(1)Union reports → President → laid before each House of Parliament
    151(2)State reports → Governor → laid before State Legislature

    CAG: tenure, salary, service conditions

    • CAG holds office for 6 years or up to age 65 years, whichever is earlier, under the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971.UPPSC
    • Salary and service conditions of CAG are given in the Second Schedule (Part E).
    • CAG's salary = salary of a Judge of the Supreme Court (Second Schedule and Section 3 of the CAG Act, 1971).
    • The power to grant or refuse leave to the CAG vests in the President.
    • After ceasing to hold office, CAG is not eligible for any further office under the Government of India or of any State [Article 148(4)].
    • Administrative expenses of the CAG's office (all salaries, allowances and pensions) are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, not subject to the vote of Parliament [Article 148(6)].

    CAG: removal

    • CAG is removed only in the like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court [Article 148(1)].
    • Grounds: proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
    • Removal is by the President on a resolution (address) passed by both Houses of Parliament with special majority; the President alone cannot remove him.UPPSC
    • Article 124(4): SC judge is removed by President's order after an address by each House, backed by majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting, presented in the same session.

    CAG: duties and audit

    • CAG = guardian of the public purse (public expense).UPPSC
    • CAG acts as the guardian of public finance: custodian and trustee of public money.
    • CAG must see that not a single penny of the Consolidated Fund of India or of any State is spent without proper authorization of the Legislature.
    • CAG audits the whole financial system of the country at both levels: Centre and State.
    • CAG audits all receipts and expenditures of the Government of India and of the State Governments.
    • CAG is the apex authority for external and internal audits of the expenses of the Central and State Governments.
    • The accounts of the States, along with those of the Union, are controlled by the CAG (not by Governor, Chief Minister or State Finance Secretary).UPPSC
    • CAG's duty is to ensure not only legality of expenditure but also its propriety, because he upholds the Constitution and laws of Parliament in financial administration.
    • CAG audits: Ministries and departments of the Government of India and State Governments.
    • CAG audits: Central and State Government Public Sector Undertakings and other autonomous bodies and authorities financed from government funds.
    • CAG audits: receipts of the Union or States (all receipts payable into the Consolidated Fund of India); accounts, stores and stock of any Union or State office or department; companies and corporations.
    • CAG audits and reports on all expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, the Contingency Funds and Public Accounts, and on all trading, manufacturing, profit and loss accounts.
    • CAG does not control the receipt and issue of public money or ensure that public revenue is lodged in the Exchequer.UPPSC
    • Broad aims of audit: legality, regularity, economy, efficiency and effectiveness of financial management and public administration.
    • Financial audit: whether financial statements are properly prepared, complete and presented with adequate disclosures.
    • Compliance audit: whether the Constitution, applicable laws, rules, regulations, orders and instructions of competent authority are complied with.
    • Performance audit: how far an activity, programme or organisation works economically, efficiently and effectively.
    • Public Finance = study of the Government's role in financial activities; a branch of Economics assessing government revenue and expenditure and their adjustment.
    • Public Finance covers public expenditure, public revenue and financial administration; not the functioning of commercial banks.UPPSC

    CAG: Act of 1971 and 1976 amendment

    • The CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act came into effect in 1971.
    • The Act was amended in 1976 to separate accounts from audit; CAG was relieved of preparing accounts and confined to audit.UPPSC ×2
    • The CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Amendment Act, 1976 came into force on 1 March 1976.
    • Earlier the CAG did both tasks; at the State level the CAG still does both accounting and auditing.

    CAG: reports and Public Accounts Committee

    • CAG submits audit reports on Union accounts to the President, who lays them before both Houses of Parliament [Article 151(1)].UPPSC
    • CAG submits audit reports on State accounts to the Governor, who places them before the State Legislature [Article 151(2)].
    • CAG submits three audit reports to the President: on appropriation accounts, on finance accounts, and on public undertakings.
    • After the reports are laid, the Public Accounts Committee examines them and reports its findings to Parliament.
    • Parliament has the ultimate responsibility to take action on CAG's reports; the Public Accounts Committee debates them extensively.UPPSC
    • CAG is the "friend, philosopher and guide" of the Public Accounts Committee (PAC).UPPSC
    • CAG attends the meetings (sittings) of the PAC and assists it in its deliberations.UPPSC
    • Representatives of Ministries appear before the PAC when it examines Accounts and Audit Reports of their Ministries.
    • CAG reports on execution of projects or programmes by ministries are discussed by the PAC; investigating agencies can press charges based on facts from CAG reports.
    • CAG does not exercise exchequer control during emergencies and has no judicial powers to prosecute in government company audits.

    Chapter 20 · Union: executive, Parliament, Supreme Court

    Order of Precedence

    40 facts · 0 repeated by UPPSC

    Meaning

    • Order of precedence = protocol list recording functionaries and authorities by rank in the Central and State Governments, including foreign diplomats and awardees.
    • It is meant for state and ceremonial occasions; it has no application in the day-to-day functioning of the Government.
    • The notification on it was released on 26 July 1979.
    • The President of India is at the highest place in the order of precedence.
    • Sequence: President → Vice-President → Prime Minister → Speaker (Lok Sabha) → Members of Parliament.
    • Sequence: Chief Justice of India → Union Cabinet Ministers → Chief Election Commissioner → Cabinet Secretary.
    • Chief Justice of India and Speaker of Lok Sabha are equal (both rank 6) in the table of precedence.
    • Chairman UPSC, Chief Election Commissioner and CAG are all at 9A; Chief Justice of a High Court is at 14.

    Cabinet Secretary

    • Cabinet Secretary = topmost (highest ranking) civilian officer in the Government of India.
    • Cabinet Secretary is ex-officio head of the Civil Services Board, Cabinet Secretariat and Indian Administrative Service (IAS).
    • Cabinet Secretary is head of all Civil Services under the Rules of Business of the Government of India.

    Chapter 21 · Union: executive, Parliament, Supreme Court

    The Parliament (1)

    200 facts · 9 repeated by UPPSC

    Parliament: basics

    • Parliament = legislative organ of the Union Government.
    • Articles 79 to 122 in Part V deal with the Parliament.
    • Article 79: Parliament = the President + two Houses (House of the People and Council of States).
    • Lok Sabha is also called the "House of the People"; its members are elected by direct election.

    Lok Sabha: strength

    • Maximum strength of Lok Sabha now = 550 (Article 81): 530 from States + 20 from Union Territories.UPPSC
    • Earlier maximum could be 552: 530 States + 20 UTs + 2 Anglo-Indians [Articles 81, 331].
    • Article 81: not more than 530 members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the States.UPPSC
    • Article 81: not more than 20 members to represent Union Territories, chosen in the manner Parliament provides by law.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 81 stands as amended by the 31st Amendment Act, 1973 and the Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act, 1987.
    • At present Lok Sabha has 543 members: States 524 + UTs 19.
    • UT seats in Lok Sabha (19): Delhi 7, Jammu & Kashmir 5, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu 2, Andaman and Nicobar 1, Chandigarh 1, Lakshadweep 1, Puducherry 1, Ladakh 1.
    • UT seats in Rajya Sabha (8): Delhi 3, Puducherry 1, Jammu and Kashmir 4.
    • 7th Amendment Act, 1956 fixed Lok Sabha members at 520; it and the 31st Amendment Act, 1973 raised the number of members elected from States.
    • 31st Amendment Act, 1973: Lok Sabha strength raised from 525 to 545.UPPSC
    • 31st Amendment: members from States raised from 500 to 525; members from Union Territories cut from 25 to 20.

    Anglo-Indian nomination

    • Article 331: President could nominate not more than 2 Anglo-Indian members to Lok Sabha if he felt the community was not adequately represented.
    • The 104th Amendment Act, 2019 [126th Amendment Bill, 2019] did not extend the Anglo-Indian arrangement beyond 25 January 2020; so the nomination has ended.
    • In January 2020 Anglo-Indian reserved seats in Parliament and State Legislatures were discontinued by the 104th Amendment Act, 2019.

    Seat allocation and delimitation

    • Lok Sabha seats are allotted to States on the basis of population.
    • Article 81: each State is divided into territorial constituencies so that the ratio of population to seats is, as far as practicable, the same throughout the State.
    • This allocation procedure does not apply to a State with population up to six million (Article 81).
    • State-wise allocation of Lok Sabha seats (Article 82) is based on the 1971 Census.UPPSC
    • 84th Amendment Act, 2001: allocation frozen till 2026; next assessment after 2026 (first Census after 2026).UPPSC
    • 84th Amendment changed the Article 81(3) proviso: year 2000 replaced by 2026; reference to be read as the 1971 Census.
    • Division of each State into territorial constituencies for Lok Sabha is done by the Delimitation Commission.

    Reserved seats for SC and ST

    1. 1996In 1996 West Bengal and erstwhile Andhra Pradesh had 42 Lok Sabha seats each; SC reserved seats were 8 and 6.
    2. 2008After the 2008 delimitation, SC reserved seats in West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh became 10 and 7.
    3. 2008After the 2008 delimitation: SC seats in Lok Sabha rose from 79 to 84.
    4. 2008Delimitation Commission order 2008: 412 general, 84 SC and 47 ST seats; earlier 79 SC and 41 ST.
    5. 2008Madhya Pradesh has the most ST reserved seats in Lok Sabha: 6 (after Delimitation Commission 2008).UPPSC ×2
    6. 2008Till 2008 no ST reservation in Lok Sabha in: Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Karnataka, Kerala, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Punjab, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh.
    7. 2008After the 2008 delimitation Karnataka and Meghalaya have 2 ST reserved seats each (both Meghalaya seats are ST).
    8. 2008Till 2008 no SC and ST reservation in: Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Goa, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Sikkim.
    9. 2023106th Amendment Act, 2023: reserves one-third of all seats for women in Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and Delhi Assembly, including SC and ST reserved seats.

    330Reservation of seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha

    333Representation of Anglo-Indian community in State Legislative Assemblies
    • Article 330(2): reserved seats in a State/UT bear, as nearly as may be, the same proportion to its total seats as SC/ST population bears to its total population.
    • In 1996 West Bengal and erstwhile Andhra Pradesh had 42 Lok Sabha seats each; SC reserved seats were 8 and 6.
    • After the 2008 delimitation, SC reserved seats in West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh became 10 and 7.
    • After the 2008 delimitation: SC seats in Lok Sabha rose from 79 to 84.
    • Delimitation Commission order 2008: 412 general, 84 SC and 47 ST seats; earlier 79 SC and 41 ST.
    • Reserved-seat members are elected by all voters of the constituency; there is no separate electorate.
    • Madhya Pradesh has the most ST reserved seats in Lok Sabha: 6 (after Delimitation Commission 2008).UPPSC ×2
    • ST seats: Jharkhand 5, Odisha 5, Gujarat 4, Chhattisgarh 4, Maharashtra 4; Uttar Pradesh and Bihar have none.
    • Till 2008 no ST reservation in Lok Sabha in: Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Karnataka, Kerala, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Punjab, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh.
    • After the 2008 delimitation Karnataka and Meghalaya have 2 ST reserved seats each (both Meghalaya seats are ST).
    • At present no ST reservation in Lok Sabha in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.UPPSC
    • Till 2008 no SC and ST reservation in: Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Goa, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Sikkim.
    • At present no SC and ST reservation for Lok Sabha in Arunachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir (UT).UPPSC
    • UTs with no seats reserved for SC and ST: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Puducherry.
    • Rajasthan: 25 Lok Sabha seats; 4 reserved for SCs and 3 for STs.
    • 106th Amendment Act, 2023: reserves one-third of all seats for women in Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and Delhi Assembly, including SC and ST reserved seats.

    Membership and elections

    • Article 84(b): minimum age for Lok Sabha = 25 years; for Council of States = 30 years.
    • Lok Sabha member must: be a citizen of India; be at least 25; make and subscribe an oath; hold other qualifications set by Parliament by law.
    • Article 326: elections to Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies are on the basis of adult suffrage.
    • Article 324: superintendence, direction and control of elections vest in the Election Commission; electoral rolls are prepared under its direction [324(1)], not the President's.UPPSC
    • The Election Commission conducts Lok Sabha elections; on its request the President makes available the staff it needs.
    • Section 4(d), Representation of the People Act, 1951: nomination for Lok Sabha can be filed by any citizen whose name is in the electoral roll of any parliamentary constituency.
    • Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections follow the First Past the Post system: candidate with highest votes wins; a majority (50%) is not needed.
    • A candidate who fails to get more than one-sixth (1/6) of valid votes polled loses the security deposit.
    • Earlier security deposit for Lok Sabha: general Rs. 10,000, SC/ST Rs. 5,000.
    • Since 2010 (raised by the Election Commission): Lok Sabha general Rs. 25,000, SC/ST Rs. 12,500; Legislative Assembly general Rs. 10,000, SC/ST Rs. 5,000.
    • January 2022: ECI raised Lok Sabha candidate expenditure limit from Rs. 70 lakh to Rs. 95 lakh.
    • January 2022: State Assembly expenditure limit raised from Rs. 28 lakh to Rs. 40 lakh.
    • Small States: Lok Sabha limit raised from Rs. 54 lakh to Rs. 75 lakh; Assembly limit from Rs. 20 lakh to Rs. 28 lakh (40 percent higher).

    Tenure, sessions, dissolution

    • Normal tenure of Lok Sabha = 5 years from the date of its first meeting [Article 83(2)], unless sooner dissolved.
    • Article 83(2) proviso: during a Proclamation of Emergency Parliament may by law extend the term by one year at a time.
    • Such extension cannot continue beyond 6 months after the Emergency has ceased to operate.
    • Lok Sabha can be dissolved before its term [Article 85(2)(b)] by the President on the recommendation of the Prime Minister or Council of Ministers.
    • Article 85: sessions, prorogation and dissolution of Parliament.
    • Article 85(1): President summons each House at such time and place as he thinks fit; no minimum number of sitting days is fixed.
    • Gap between last sitting of one session and first sitting of the next cannot exceed six months; so at least two sessions a year are mandatory.
    • The Constitution fixes the maximum gap between two sessions, but no minimum gap; it does not provide for three sessions.
    • Usually three sessions a year: Budget (February–May), Monsoon (July–August), Winter (November–December).
    • A sitting of Lok Sabha may be terminated by adjournment, prorogation or dissolution.UPPSC
    • Adjournment / adjournment sine die is done by the Speaker.
    • Prorogation and dissolution are done by the President [Article 85(2)], not by the leader of the House.UPPSC
    • Summoning of the House means convocation; prorogation ends a session; dissolution terminates a House.
    • Article 100(3): quorum of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha = 1/10th of the total members of the House.UPPSC ×4
    • Quorum = minimum number of members who must be present before the House can transact business.
    • Leader of the Lok Sabha = Prime Minister; he is head of the Council of Ministers and leader of the majority party in Lok Sabha.
    • Article 75(1): the Prime Minister is appointed by the President.
    • If the Prime Minister is not a member of the Lower House, he can nominate another minister as Leader of that House.
    • 14th Lok Sabha: PM Manmohan Singh was a Rajya Sabha member; Leader of the Lok Sabha was Pranab Mukherjee.

    Constituencies and 2024 election

    • Largest Lok Sabha constituencies by area: (1) Ladakh 173266 sq km, (2) Barmer 55074, (3) Kachchh 41414, (4) Arunachal East 39704, (5) Arunachal West 39613.
    • Smallest constituency by area: Chandni Chowk, Delhi (10.59 sq km).
    • In U.P., Unnao is the largest by voters among Amethi, Unnao, Lucknow and Baghpat; the largest in the State by voters is Ghaziabad.UPPSC

    • Malogam is in Hayuliang Assembly Constituency (bordering China) and in the Arunachal East Lok Sabha seat.

    Lok Sabha history

    1. 1951First Lok Sabha elections: 25 October 1951 to 21 February 1952, for 489 seats.
    2. 1952First meeting (first session) of the first Lok Sabha: 13 May 1952.
    3. 19715th Lok Sabha had a tenure of about 6 years: 15 March 1971 to 18 January 1977.
    4. 1977Fewest women in Lok Sabha: 1977 (only 19).
    5. 19807th Lok Sabha election was held in 1980 (not 1982); 9th in 1989, 11th in 1996, 13th in 1999.UPPSC
    6. 19899th Lok Sabha: constituted 2 December 1989, dissolved 13 March 1991.
    7. 199812th Lok Sabha: elections in February–March 1998; constituted 10 March 1998; dissolved 26 April 1999.
    8. 199913th Lok Sabha: constituted 10 October 1999, dissolved 6 February 2004; did not complete its 5-year term.
    9. 1999Around the 1999 General Elections the country's politics faced conflicts and clashes; in this turmoil the 13th Lok Sabha was dissolved early.
    10. 2019Most women reached Lok Sabha in the General Election 2019: 78.
    • First Lok Sabha elections: 25 October 1951 to 21 February 1952, for 489 seats.
    • First meeting (first session) of the first Lok Sabha: 13 May 1952.
    • First Lok Sabha: Indian National Congress won 364 of 489 seats (single largest party); Communist Party of India was second with 16 seats.
    • 5th Lok Sabha had a tenure of about 6 years: 15 March 1971 to 18 January 1977.
    • 7th Lok Sabha election was held in 1980 (not 1982); 9th in 1989, 11th in 1996, 13th in 1999.UPPSC
    • 9th Lok Sabha: constituted 2 December 1989, dissolved 13 March 1991.
    • 12th Lok Sabha: elections in February–March 1998; constituted 10 March 1998; dissolved 26 April 1999.
    • 13th Lok Sabha: constituted 10 October 1999, dissolved 6 February 2004; did not complete its 5-year term.
    • Around the 1999 General Elections the country's politics faced conflicts and clashes; in this turmoil the 13th Lok Sabha was dissolved early.
    • Fewest women in Lok Sabha: 1977 (only 19).
    • Most women reached Lok Sabha in the General Election 2019: 78.
    • 17th Lok Sabha: women were more than 14% of members; 78 women, 41 from BJP and 6 from Congress (INC).
    • 17th Lok Sabha: most women elected from Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal (11 each).

    Speaker and Deputy Speaker: election and oath

    • Article 93: Lok Sabha chooses two of its members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker, as soon as may be; and again whenever the office falls vacant.
    • The Speaker is chosen by all the then members of the Lok Sabha from among themselves.
    • The Speaker must be a member of the House at the time of his election; a non-member cannot be chosen Speaker or Deputy Speaker.
    • By tradition the Speaker's post goes to the majority party and the Deputy Speaker's to the Opposition; the Constitution has no such provision.
    • The Constitution does not require a member elected as Speaker to resign from his political party.
    • The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha do not take an oath of office.
    OfficeOath of office
    PresidentAdministered by the Chief Justice of India (Article 60)
    Vice-PresidentAdministered by the President (Article 69)
    Prime Minister and Council of MinistersAdministered by the President (Article 75(4))
    Judges of the Supreme CourtTake oath under Article 124(6)

    Speaker: Articles

    ArticleSubject
    93Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha

    Speaker: vacation, resignation, removal

    • Speaker or Deputy Speaker vacates office if he ceases to be a member of the House [Article 94(a)].
    • Article 94(b): Speaker resigns in writing to the Deputy Speaker, and the Deputy Speaker to the Speaker.UPPSC
    • Article 94(c): Speaker/Deputy Speaker is removed by a Lok Sabha resolution passed by a majority of all the then members; 14 days' notice is needed.UPPSC ×2
    • The Speaker does not hold office during the pleasure of the President.
    • Article 94 (second proviso): on dissolution the Speaker does not vacate office until immediately before the first meeting of the new Lok Sabha.
    • Article 96(1): while a resolution for his removal is under consideration, the Speaker (or Deputy Speaker) shall not preside though present; Article 95(2) applies as if he were absent.
    • Article 96(2): he can speak and take part in proceedings then, and can vote only in the first instance, not on equality of votes.
    • A Speaker whose position is challenged by a motion stays in office until the motion is disposed of [Article 96(1)].
    • It is also stated that during the debate on a no-confidence motion against him the Speaker is not allowed to vote on that motion.
    • On other matters the Speaker votes only in a tie (casting vote); he may also delegate this casting vote to other members of the House.

    Speaker: powers and voting

    • Article 100(1): questions at any sitting or joint sitting are decided by majority of members present and voting, excluding the Speaker or person acting as Chairman/Speaker.
    • Article 100(1): Speaker/Chairman does not vote in the first instance; he has a casting vote only in case of a tie (equality of votes).UPPSC ×2
    • President summons a joint sitting (Article 108); the Speaker presides over a joint sitting of both Houses [Article 118(4)].
    • Article 110(4): Speaker's signed certificate that it is a Money Bill is endorsed when the Bill goes to the Council of States (Article 109) and to the President for assent (Article 111).
    • Lok Sabha Secretariat works under the direct control and direction of the Speaker.UPPSC
    • The Secretariat has supreme authority over its employees, premises and assets of Parliament, exercised through the Secretary (Article 98 and rules 124 and 124-A).
    • Article 98(3): President makes rules on recruitment of secretarial staff of the House after consulting the Speaker.
    • Individual appointment orders are issued by the Speaker: Rule 6, Lok Sabha Secretariat (Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 1955.

    Pro-tem Speaker

    • The Speaker of the last Lok Sabha vacates office immediately before the first meeting of the new Lok Sabha; so the President appoints a Pro-tem Speaker.
    • Pro-tem Speaker = one of the senior-most members of the newly elected Lok Sabha.UPPSC
    • Process: Legislative section of Parliament lists senior-most members → Minister of Parliamentary Affairs → note to President for approval.
    • Pro-tem Speaker administers the oath to newly elected members and conducts proceedings till a regular Speaker is chosen.UPPSC

    Deputy Speaker

    • Rule 8(1), Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha: election of Deputy Speaker is held on a date fixed by the Speaker; the Secretary conveys it to all members.
    • No mandatory provision that the Deputy Speaker must be from the principal opposition party or the ruling party.
    • Article 95(1): in the Speaker's absence the Deputy Speaker chairs the House with the same power as the Speaker; no appeal lies against his rulings.
    • Rule 8(2): the motion to appoint the Deputy Speaker is moved by one member and seconded by another (not by Speaker and Prime Minister).
    • Article 95: when the Speaker's office is vacant the Deputy Speaker performs its duties; when presiding he can vote only on equality of votes.UPPSC
    • M.A. (M. Ananthasayanam) Ayyangar = first Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha.
    • P.M. Sayeed was Deputy Speaker in 1999.
    • Deputy Speakers: 14th Lok Sabha = Charanjit Singh Atwal; 15th = Karia Munda; 16th = M. Thambidurai.
    • The post of Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha is vacant since May 2019.

    Speakers of Lok Sabha

    • G.V. (Ganesh Vasudev) Mavalankar = first Speaker of Lok Sabha, from 15 May 1952 till his death on 27 February 1956.UPPSC ×2
    • Mavalankar is called the "Father of the Lok Sabha"; the title was given by J.L. Nehru.
    • M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar was Speaker for the rest of the first Lok Sabha.
    • First motion to remove a Speaker (no-confidence) was against G.V. Mavalankar, moved on 15 December 1954; Lok Sabha rejected it on 18 December 1954.UPPSC ×2
    • It was moved by Vigneshwar Missir (Socialist Party M.P. from Bihar) and Acharya J.B. Kripalani with 21 opposition members.
    • Meira Kumar = first woman Speaker of Lok Sabha (15th Lok Sabha, June 2009 to June 2014); chosen unopposed.UPPSC ×3
    • Meira Kumar was an Indian diplomat, politician and government official.
    • P.A. Sangma = first tribal Speaker; became Speaker of the 11th Lok Sabha on 23 May 1996.UPPSC
    • Speakers: 11th Lok Sabha = P.A. Sangma; 12th = G.M.C. Balayogi; 14th = Somnath Chatterjee; 17th = Om Birla.UPPSC
    • Speaker of the present (18th) Lok Sabha = Om Birla (second term).

    Leader of the Opposition

    • A "Leader of the Opposition" was formally recognised in Lok Sabha for the first time in 1969.
    • Before 1969 the leader of the largest opposition party was called leader of the opposition without formal recognition, status or privilege.
    • For recognition by the Speaker, the party needs at least 10% of the total strength of Lok Sabha.
    • 10% of 543 is given as 54.3, i.e. 54 members; elsewhere it is given as 55 seats.
    • In 2014 and 2019 no opposition party got the minimum number; the post stayed vacant in the 16th and 17th Lok Sabha.
    • In the 18th Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi (Indian National Congress) became Leader of the Opposition.

    Chapter 22 · Union: executive, Parliament, Supreme Court

    The Parliament (2)

    101 facts · 7 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha [Articles 64 and 89(1)].×4
    2. The Chairman (Vice-President) is not a member of the Rajya Sabha or of either House; Rajya Sabha is presided over by a non-member.×3
    3. Article 249: if Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by 2/3 of members present and voting, Parliament can make laws on State List subjects in the national interest.×3
    4. Article 312: if Rajya Sabha resolves by 2/3 of members present and voting (not of total membership), Parliament may by law create one or more All India Services.×3
    5. Rajya Sabha is a Permanent House; it is not subject to dissolution [Article 83(1)]; nobody can dissolve it.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 28 UPPSC questions

    Rajya Sabha: composition

    • Rajya Sabha = Upper House of Parliament, also called the Council of States.
    • Article 79: Parliament = the President + House of the People + Council of States (not the two Houses only).
    • Article 80: maximum strength of Rajya Sabha = 250: not more than 238 representatives of States and UTs + 12 nominated.
    • The President nominates 12 members with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service.UPPSC
    • Rajya Sabha has members nominated by the President and members indirectly elected by citizens through their representatives; none is directly elected.
    • Present strength = 245: 233 from States and UTs (225 from State Assemblies + 8 from UT Assemblies) + 12 nominated.
    • Article 80(4): representatives of each State are elected by the elected members of its Legislative Assembly, by proportional representation by single transferable vote.UPPSC
    • Representation of States in Rajya Sabha is in proportion (ratio) to their population.
    • The Fourth Schedule allocates Rajya Sabha seats to States and Union Territories.
    • 7th Schedule: allocation of powers and functions between the Union and the States.
    • 8th Schedule: list of 22 languages recognised by the Constitution.
    • 5th and 6th Schedules: administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Tribes.
    • Union Territories are represented in both Houses of Parliament.UPPSC
    • Only 3 of 8 UTs have Rajya Sabha seats (8 members): Delhi 3, Puducherry 1, Jammu and Kashmir 4.
    • Election disputes are decided by the Judiciary through election petitions, not by the Chief Election Commissioner.
    • The Rajya Sabha was first constituted in 1952 (formed on 3 April 1952).UPPSC
    • The idea of a Second Chamber traces to the Montague-Chelmsford Reform of 1919.
    • The First Amendment Act was enacted in 1951, when the Rajya Sabha did not exist; so its ratification was not taken.

    Rajya Sabha: permanent House and tenure

    • Rajya Sabha is a Permanent House; it is not subject to dissolution [Article 83(1)]; nobody can dissolve it.UPPSC ×2
    • As nearly as possible one-third of its members retire at the end of every second year, as Parliament provides by law; new members replace them.UPPSC ×2
    • Term of a Rajya Sabha member = 6 years.UPPSC

    Rajya Sabha: qualifications and members

    1. 1969Devika Rani Chaudhari: first Indian actress to get the Dada Saheb Phalke Award, in 1969.
    2. 1980Nargis Dutt = first actress nominated to Rajya Sabha, in 1980; tenure 3 April 1980 to 3 May 1981.
    3. 1984Jayalalitha: Rajya Sabha member from 3 April 1984 to 28 January 1989.
    4. 1993Vaijayanthimala Bali: nominated to Rajya Sabha from 27 August 1993 to 26 August 1999.
    5. 2003Before 6 April 2003 a candidate had to be a voter of the State he was elected from; a 2003 amendment to the Representation of the People Act, 1951 removed this.
    6. 20242024: President Droupadi Murmu nominated Satnam Singh Sandhu and Sudha Murty to Rajya Sabha [Article 80(1)(a) and clause (3)].
    7. 2024Satnam Singh Sandhu (educationist, founder of Chandigarh University): nominated on 30 January 2024.
    8. 2024Sudha Murty (philanthropist, former chairperson of Infosys Foundation): nominated on 8 March 2024; became the 12th nominated member.
    • Minimum age for Rajya Sabha = 30 years; member must be a citizen of India.UPPSC
    • A Rajya Sabha member should not hold an office of profit under the State.
    • He must be an elector for a parliamentary constituency anywhere in India.
    • Before 6 April 2003 a candidate had to be a voter of the State he was elected from; a 2003 amendment to the Representation of the People Act, 1951 removed this.
    • Now a person can contest Rajya Sabha from anywhere, even if resident of another State.
    • Nargis Dutt = first actress nominated to Rajya Sabha, in 1980; tenure 3 April 1980 to 3 May 1981.
    • Vaijayanthimala Bali: nominated to Rajya Sabha from 27 August 1993 to 26 August 1999.
    • Jayalalitha: Rajya Sabha member from 3 April 1984 to 28 January 1989.
    • Devika Rani Chaudhari: first Indian actress to get the Dada Saheb Phalke Award, in 1969.
    • 2024: President Droupadi Murmu nominated Satnam Singh Sandhu and Sudha Murty to Rajya Sabha [Article 80(1)(a) and clause (3)].
    • Satnam Singh Sandhu (educationist, founder of Chandigarh University): nominated on 30 January 2024.
    • Sudha Murty (philanthropist, former chairperson of Infosys Foundation): nominated on 8 March 2024; became the 12th nominated member.
    • A Minister who is a Rajya Sabha member can take part in the deliberations of the Lok Sabha.
    • The senior-most minister who is a Rajya Sabha member is appointed Leader of the House by the Prime Minister.
    • The Attorney General of India has the right to speak in both Houses of Parliament.

    Chairman and Deputy Chairman

    • The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha [Articles 64 and 89(1)].UPPSC ×4
    • The Chairman (Vice-President) is not a member of the Rajya Sabha or of either House; Rajya Sabha is presided over by a non-member.UPPSC ×3
    • If an MP is elected Vice-President, his seat in that House is deemed vacant on assuming office.
    • Article 66(1): Vice-President is elected by an electoral college of the members of both Houses of Parliament.
    • Presidential electoral college = elected members of Parliament and State Legislative Assemblies; Vice-Presidential college = all MPs, elected or nominated.
    • When the Vice-President acts as President he gets the President's salary and allowances, not those of the Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
    • Rajya Sabha elects a Deputy Chairman from among its members; the Deputy Chairman is a member of the House.
    • There is also a panel of "Vice Chairmen" in the Rajya Sabha.
    • The Deputy Chairman resigns in writing to the Chairman.
    • Deputy Chairman is removed by a resolution passed by absolute majority of the total members of Rajya Sabha, after at least 14 days' notice.
    • When the Chairman's post is vacant, the Deputy Chairman performs the Chairman's duties.
    • While presiding, the Deputy Chairman cannot vote in general; he has only a casting vote in a tie.
    • The Vice-President does not preside as Chairman while a resolution for his removal is under consideration; likewise the Deputy Chairman.
    • Quorum of Rajya Sabha = one-tenth of its total members.
    • Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (first Vice-President) was Chairman for two consecutive terms, 13 May 1952 to 12 May 1962, but is not the only one.
    • Mohammad Hamid Ansari was also Vice-President/Chairman for two consecutive terms (2007-2017); he was the Chairman in 2010.
    • Presently Vice-President C.P. Radhakrishnan is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
    • Joint sitting (Article 108) has been called for only 3 bills: Dowry Prohibition Bill 1962, Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill 1978, Prevention of Terrorism Bill 2002.

    Special powers of Rajya Sabha

    • Special (exclusive) powers of Rajya Sabha: resolution letting Parliament legislate on the State List (Article 249) and creation of All India Services (Article 312).
    • Article 249: if Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by 2/3 of members present and voting, Parliament can make laws on State List subjects in the national interest.UPPSC ×3
    • Under Article 249 Parliament (not Rajya Sabha alone) makes the law; it may apply to the whole or any part of India.
    • The Article 249 resolution is valid for 1 year; it can be extended by passing another resolution.
    • Article 312: if Rajya Sabha resolves by 2/3 of members present and voting (not of total membership), Parliament may by law create one or more All India Services.UPPSC ×3
    • All India Services are common to the Union and the States, and include an All-India Judicial Service.
    • Article 250: Parliament can legislate on any State List matter while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation; such law expires six months after the Emergency ends.
    • Article 252: Parliament can legislate for two or more States by consent; any other State may adopt such legislation.
    • Article 253: Parliament can make law for the whole or part of India to implement international agreements, conventions or decisions of international conferences.

    Money Bills and Lok Sabha's exclusive powers

    • Article 109: a Money Bill cannot be introduced in Rajya Sabha; only in Lok Sabha, with prior recommendation of the President.UPPSC
    • A Bill other than a Money Bill may be introduced in either House.
    • Article 109(2): Rajya Sabha returns a Money Bill with recommendations within 14 days; Lok Sabha may accept or reject all or any of them.UPPSC
    • Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend a Money Bill, and cannot vote on Demands for Grants.
    • Article 113(2): Demands for Grants go to the Lok Sabha; only it can assent or refuse.
    • Rajya Sabha can discuss the Annual Financial Statement but cannot vote on it.
    • Exclusive powers of Lok Sabha: introduction of Money Bill, its rejection and amendment (Article 109), and accountability of the Council of Ministers.UPPSC
    • Article 75(3): Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; only Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion against it.
    • So if the Government fails in Rajya Sabha, the Prime Minister need not resign, Parliament is not dissolved and there is no President's Rule.
    • Article 352: President can declare National Emergency when security of India or a part is threatened by war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
    • Proclamation of Emergency must be approved by both Houses within one month of issue; not an exclusive power of Lok Sabha.
    • Article 61(1): the charge to impeach the President may be preferred by either House.
    • Rajya Sabha has equal powers with Lok Sabha in amending the Constitution.
    • Article 368(2): amendment Bill may be introduced in either House; passed in each by majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting; then President assents.

    • Earlier Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu both had 18 seats; after Telangana was formed in June 2014, Andhra Pradesh has 11 and Telangana 7.
