    Chapter 23 · Union: executive, Parliament, Supreme Court

    The Parliament (3)

    226 facts · 15 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Article 118 relates to Rules of Procedure; under Article 118(4) the Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over a joint sitting.×8
    2. Article 79 (Part V): Parliament = the President + Council of States + House of the People; these three are its integral parts.×7
    3. Article 109(2): Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill, with or without recommendations, within 14 days of receipt.×6
    4. Article 109(1): a Money Bill is introduced only in the Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation; never in the Rajya Sabha.×5
    5. Article 253: Parliament can make law on State List matters, for the whole or any part of India, to implement international treaties, agreements or conventions, without the consent of any State.×4
    Quick quiz: 10 of 75 UPPSC questions

    Parliament: composition

    • The Parliament of India is the supreme legislative body.
    • India has a parliamentary system of government based on the Westminster model.
    • Article 79 (Part V): Parliament = the President + Council of States + House of the People; these three are its integral parts.UPPSC ×7
    • Article 59(1): the President shall not be a member of either House of Parliament.UPPSC
    • The President does not sit in Parliament or attend its meetings, yet is an integral part of it.
    • The Vice-President is not a part of Parliament.UPPSC
    • Lok Sabha [Article 81(1)(a)]: not more than 530 representatives of States, chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies.
    • Lok Sabha [Article 81(1)(b)]: not more than 20 representatives of Union Territories.
    • Council of States: not more than 250 members = 12 nominated + not more than 238 representatives of States and Union Territories.
    • The President could nominate not more than two Anglo-Indians to Lok Sabha if the community was not adequately represented.
    • 104th Amendment Act, 2019 (amending Article 334): Anglo-Indian nomination in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies not extended beyond 25 January 2020; so it has ended.
    • Earlier both Houses had nominated members: 12 in Rajya Sabha and 2 in Lok Sabha (Anglo-Indian); now only the Rajya Sabha has nominated members.
    • No constitutional bar on a nominated member becoming a Minister; a Minister must be an MP or become one within six months.
    • Article 54: President is elected by an Electoral College of elected members of both Houses and of State Legislative Assemblies; nominated members cannot vote.
    • Elected members of the State Legislative Assembly (Lower House) vote in elections to both Lok Sabha (as citizens) and Rajya Sabha; also for the President.
    • Representation of the People Act, 1951 was amended in 2003: a Rajya Sabha candidate need not be a voter of that State.
    • The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of this amendment in 2006.
    • The Golden Jubilee of the Indian Parliament was celebrated on 13 May 2002; Parliament was constituted on 13 May 1952.UPPSC
    • The new Parliament building was designed by architect Bimal Patel; Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated it on 28 May 2023.
    • The previous Parliament building was designed by British architects Sir Edwin Lutyens and Sir Herbert Baker.
    • In 1925 Vitthalbhai Patel was elected the first Speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly; tenure 24 August 1925 to 28 April 1930.UPPSC

    President's address and sessions

    • Article 87: the President addresses both Houses of Parliament assembled together and informs Parliament of the causes of its summons.
    • Article 87(1), two occasions: start of the first session after each Lok Sabha general election, and start of the first session of each year.UPPSC
    • The President's speech highlights the government's policy priorities and plans for the coming year; it gives a broad framework of its agenda.
    • All executive power is vested in the President; the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister aids and advises him.
    • Article 85(1): the gap between two sessions cannot exceed six months; so Parliament must meet at least twice a year.UPPSC
    • Usually three sessions a year: Budget session, Monsoon session and Winter session.
    • Officers (officials) of Parliament: Speaker, Deputy Speaker and Secretary-General of Lok Sabha; Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 120(1): business in Parliament is transacted in Hindi or English (subject to Article 348, notwithstanding Part XVII).
    • Article 120(1) proviso: Chairman or Speaker may permit a member who cannot express himself in Hindi or English to speak in his mother tongue.

    Membership: vacation and disqualification

    • Article 101 deals with vacation of seats.
    • Article 101(4): if a member is absent from all meetings for 60 days without informing (permission of) the House, the House may declare his seat vacant.UPPSC
    • In counting the 60 days, any period when the House is prorogued or adjourned for more than four consecutive days is excluded.
    • First member disqualified for 60 days' absence: Barjinder Singh Hamdard, Independent member of the Council of States from Punjab, in 2000.UPPSC
    • Article 101(2) (Rule 2, Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950): one cannot be member of Parliament and a State Legislature together.
    • If so elected, his seat in Parliament falls vacant unless he resigns the State Legislature seat within 14 days.
    • Article 102(1)(a): a person holding an office of profit under the Government of India or a State is disqualified from being an MP.
    • Exception: an office declared by Parliament by law not to disqualify its holder.
    • "Office of profit" is not defined in the Constitution or in the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
    • The Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959 lists offices exempted from disqualification; it was amended five times.
    • Office of profit is decided by Parliament for the Union [Article 102(1)(a)] and by State Legislatures for States [Article 191(1)(a)].UPPSC ×2
    • Whether a member is disqualified: President decides on Election Commission's advice [Article 103(1),(2)]; in States the Governor decides on Election Commission's advice [Article 192(1),(2)].

    Note from the book "Who will decide the Office of Profit?" has two keyed answers: Union Parliament (who defines it) and President and Governor (who decide disqualification).

    Privileges

    • Article 105: powers, privileges and immunities of the Houses of Parliament, their members and committees.
    • Article 122: courts shall not inquire into the proceedings of Parliament.UPPSC
    • Parliamentary privileges = special rights of each House collectively and of each member individually, needed to do their work efficiently.
    • Collective privileges: prohibit publication of debates and proceedings; exclude strangers from the House; regulate own procedure and conduct of business.
    • Collective privileges: punish members and outsiders for breach of privilege or contempt of the House.
    • Collective privileges: no arrest or service of legal process within the precincts of the House without permission of Chairman/Speaker.
    • Collective privileges: right to get immediate information of arrest, detention, conviction, imprisonment or release of a member.
    • Freedom from attendance as a witness is an individual privilege, not a collective one.UPPSC
    • A Privilege Motion can be raised against a Minister who withholds facts of a case or gives a distorted version.

    Legislative powers of Parliament

    • The right to amend the Constitution is vested in Parliament under Article 368.
    • Parliament can legislate for the Union of India, the territory of India, and Indian subjects/residents and their property anywhere in the world.UPPSC
    • Article 248: residuary legislative power; Parliament alone makes law on matters not in the State or Concurrent List.UPPSC
    • Parliament can legislate on State List subjects in four cases: Article 253, Article 252, Article 249 and Proclamation of Emergency (given as Article 357).UPPSC
    • Article 252: Parliament legislates for two or more States by their consent (resolutions passed by the States).UPPSC
    • Article 249: in the national interest, after a Council of States resolution passed by 2/3 majority.
    • Article 253: Parliament can make law on State List matters, for the whole or any part of India, to implement international treaties, agreements or conventions, without the consent of any State.UPPSC ×4
    • Article 253 also covers decisions made at any international conference, association or other body.
    • The sovereignty of Parliament is restricted by judicial review; the Supreme Court can check the validity of laws made by Parliament.UPPSC
    • Laws made by the legislature must not infringe the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
    • Article 123: the President may promulgate ordinances at any time except when both Houses are in session, if immediate action is needed.
    • National Development Council is presided over by the Prime Minister; it cannot be constituted without him.
    • 44th Amendment Act, 1978: Right to Property ceased to be a Fundamental Right and became a legal right (Article 300-A).
    • 42nd Amendment Act, 1976: Preamble changed from "Sovereign Democratic Republic" to "Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic"; "Unity of the Nation" became "Unity and Integrity of the Nation".
    • No provision lets the Speaker of Lok Sabha resolve a dispute of Parliament; disagreement between Houses goes to a Joint Session.

    Conduct in the House, Zero Hour

    • Yielding the floor: Speaker/Chairman stops a member from speaking and lets another member speak.
    • Crossing the floor: a member changes party allegiance, leaving one party and joining another or becoming independent.
    • Interpellation: parliamentary procedure of demanding that a government official explain some act or policy.
    • Decorum: every member should enter and leave the chamber so as not to disturb the proceedings.
    • Members should keep a standard of conduct inside and outside the House that enhances the dignity of Parliament.
    • Zero Hour is an Indian innovation in parliamentary procedure; a unique feature of India's Parliament.UPPSC
    • Zero Hour began in the early sixties, when members raised urgent public matters right after Question Hour, with or without the Chairman's prior permission.
    • Zero Hour can be a maximum of one hour; its duration is not fixed in the Rules.UPPSC
    • Zero Hour timing: Lok Sabha 12 noon to 1 pm (after Question Hour); Rajya Sabha 11 am to 12 noon (before Question Hour).UPPSC ×2
    • Question Hour timing: Lok Sabha 11 am to 12 noon; Rajya Sabha (from 2014) 12 noon to 1 pm.
    • In Zero Hour members raise important matters that cannot be delayed; it is described as a question-and-answer session.

    Questions and motions

    • Parliament controls the Council of Ministers through Adjournment Motion, Question Hour and Supplementary Questions.
    • Question Hour = first hour of every sitting, generally kept for asking and answering questions.
    • Starred Question: member wants an oral answer; marked with an asterisk (*); supplementary questions can be asked.
    • Only 20 questions can be listed for oral answer on a day.
    • Unstarred Question: not called for oral answer; no supplementary questions.
    • Short Notice Question: on a matter of urgent public importance; asked with shorter notice than an ordinary question; supplementaries follow.
    • Adjournment Motion: allows discussion on a definite matter of urgent public importance.
    • Adjournment motion draws the government's attention where a starred question, short duration discussion or resolution with notice would be too late.
    • Calling Attention: with the Speaker's prior permission a member calls a Minister's attention to an urgent public matter; the Minister makes a brief statement or asks for time.
    • "Calling Attention" is a concept given by India; it is like an Adjournment Motion but without condemnation, and has restricted its scope.UPPSC
    • Calling Attention is a new concept in modern parliamentary procedure; questions and supplementary questions are asked during it.
    • Censure Motion: expression of strong disapproval or harsh criticism, generally against government policies.
    • Censure Motion differs from a No-confidence Motion in purpose and procedure; reasons must be stated; separate leave of the House is not required.

    Note from the book Censure Motion question: two options were factually correct, so the Bihar Public Service Commission deleted it from evaluation.

    • Rule 184 (Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha): discussion is followed by voting; a ruling party getting fewer votes may lose power.UPPSC ×2
    • Rule 377: matters that are not points of order and cannot be raised under rules on Questions, Short Notice Questions, Calling Attention or Motions.
    • Rule 377 notice is given in writing to the Secretary-General with the text of the matter; the Speaker's consent is needed.
    • In 2015 the number of matters under Rule 377 was raised from 20 to 30 per day (decision of Speaker's meeting with Leaders of Parties).
    • Closure Motion: moved by a member to cut short debate; there are four kinds; Guillotine is one.
    • Guillotine: undiscussed clauses of a bill or resolution are put to vote with the discussed ones when allotted time is over; it stops the debate.

    Bills: stages and lapse

    • An ordinary (legislative) Bill can be introduced in either House of Parliament.
    • A Bill on creation of All-India Services can only be introduced in the Rajya Sabha.
    • Article 107: provisions on introduction and passing of Bills.
    • A Bill passes three stages (readings) in each House.
    • First stage: leave is asked to introduce the Bill; if granted, it is introduced.
    • Second reading: general discussion on the Bill as a whole, then clause-by-clause consideration (as introduced or as reported by Select/Joint Committee).UPPSC
    • Third reading: debate is confined to arguments; then the member in charge moves that the Bill be passed.
    • Private member's Bill = Bill presented by any member other than a Minister; about a dozen have been passed since independence.
    • A private member must give notice and ask leave of the House to introduce a Bill.
    • If a Bill was published in the official gazette before introduction, no motion for leave is needed.
    • Article 107(5): a Bill pending in Lok Sabha, or passed by Lok Sabha and pending in Rajya Sabha, lapses on dissolution of Lok Sabha (subject to Article 108).
    • Article 107(4): a Bill pending in Rajya Sabha and not passed by Lok Sabha does not lapse on dissolution of Lok Sabha.
    • Article 107(3): a Bill pending in Parliament does not lapse by prorogation.
    • Prior sanction of the President is needed for Bills on: formation of a new State, altering State boundaries, taxation in which States are interested, and Money Bills.UPPSC

    Joint sitting

    • Article 108: the President summons both Houses to a joint sitting to resolve a deadlock over a Bill; Article 109 is not the joint-sitting Article.UPPSC ×3
    • Article 118 relates to Rules of Procedure; under Article 118(4) the Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over a joint sitting.UPPSC ×8
    • If the Speaker is absent: Deputy Speaker → Deputy Chairman of the Council of States → a person chosen by the members present.
    • Joint sitting is only for ordinary bills (or non-money financial bills) on which the Houses disagree; not for Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills.UPPSC ×2
    • No joint sitting for a Money Bill: Rajya Sabha cannot block it and must return it within 14 days.
    • A Constitution Amendment Bill (Article 368) must be passed by each House separately by special majority.
    • Quorum for a joint sitting = 1/10th of the total members of both Houses (Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure).
    • Article 108(4): at a joint sitting the Bill is passed by a simple majority of members of both Houses present and voting.
    • No joint sitting can be summoned if the Bill has already lapsed by dissolution of Lok Sabha.
    • Article 108(5): if Lok Sabha is dissolved after the President notified his intention to summon it, the joint sitting is still held; the Bill does not lapse.
    • Only three joint sittings since 26 January 1950: Dowry Prohibition Bill (first, 1961); Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill 1977 (second, 1978); Prevention of Terrorism Bill/POTA (third, March 2002).UPPSC

    Money Bills

    ArticleSubject
    109Special procedure in respect of Money Bills
    110Definition of Money BillUPPSC ×2
    111Assent (permission) on Bills
    112Annual Financial Statement
    113Procedure for estimates; Demands for Grants
    114Appropriation Bills
    115Supplementary grants
    116Votes on account, votes of credit and exceptional grants
    117Special provisions as to Financial Bills
    • Article 110: a Bill is a Money Bill if it contains only provisions on all or any of these matters:
    • (a) imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax.
    • (b) regulation of borrowing or giving of guarantee by the Government of India, or amending the law on its financial obligations.
    • (c) custody of the Consolidated Fund or Contingency Fund of India; payment into or withdrawal from them.
    • (d) appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund of India.
    • (e) declaring any expenditure as charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, or increasing such expenditure.
    • (f) receipt of money on account of the Consolidated Fund or Public Account of India, its custody or issue, or audit of accounts of the Union or a State.
    • (g) any matter incidental to matters in (a) to (f).
    • Provisions for imposition of fines or penalties are not Money Bill provisions.UPPSC
    • Article 110(3): the Speaker of Lok Sabha decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill; his decision is final.UPPSC ×3
    • The Speaker's decision cannot be questioned in any court, in either House or even by the President; he need not consult anyone.
    • The Speaker endorses his certificate that it is a Money Bill when it goes to Rajya Sabha and to the President for assent.
    • Article 109(1): a Money Bill is introduced only in the Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation; never in the Rajya Sabha.UPPSC ×5
    • Article 109(2): Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill, with or without recommendations, within 14 days of receipt.UPPSC ×6
    • Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend a Money Bill; it only recommends, and Lok Sabha may accept or reject all or any recommendations.UPPSC
    • Article 109(3): if Lok Sabha accepts any recommendation, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses with those amendments.
    • Article 109(4): if Lok Sabha accepts none, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form passed by Lok Sabha.
    • Article 109(5): if not returned within 14 days, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form passed by Lok Sabha.
    • A Money Bill cannot be referred to a joint session; the President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration.
    • An ordinary Bill has no time limit in the Rajya Sabha.

    Note from the book Two U.P.P.C.S. questions say "Finance Bill" where Money Bill is meant (presented in Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha delay of 14 days); they are answered as Money Bill.

    Financial Bills

    • Financial bills deal with fiscal matters (revenue or expenditure); three kinds: Money Bills (Article 110), Financial Bills (I) [Article 117(1)], Financial Bills (II) [Article 117(3)].
    • Every Money Bill is a Finance Bill, but every Finance Bill is not a Money Bill.
    • Article 117(1): a Bill with Article 110(1)(a) to (f) matters needs the President's recommendation and cannot be introduced in the Council of States (only in the Lower House).
    • Financial Bill (I) is like a Money Bill in two ways: only in Lok Sabha, only on President's recommendation.
    • Otherwise Financial Bill (I) follows ordinary bill procedure: Rajya Sabha can reject or amend it.
    • For Financial Bills (I) and (II) the President may (not necessarily) summon a joint sitting to resolve a deadlock.
    • The President can return (refuse to sign) a Finance Bill for reconsideration; Rajya Sabha is not limited to 14 days on a Finance Bill that is not a Money Bill.
    • Article 117(3): Bills involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India (Financial Bill II) can be introduced in either House.UPPSC
    • For Article 117(3) Bills the President's recommendation is essential for consideration of the Bill.
    • If a Finance Bill is not a Money Bill, Rajya Sabha can hold it like an ordinary Bill; if it is a Money Bill, only for 14 days.UPPSC

    Funds

    • Article 265: no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.UPPSC
    • Article 266: Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts of India and of the States.
    • Article 300: suits and proceedings. Article 368: procedure for amendment of the Constitution.
    • Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266): all revenues received by the Government of India (taxes and other receipts) are credited to it.
    • It also holds all loans raised by issue of treasury bills, loans or ways and means advances, and all money received in repayment of loans.
    • The Consolidated Fund is under Parliament's control; no money can be withdrawn without Parliament's authorization by appropriation [Article 114(3)].UPPSC
    • To withdraw funds from the Consolidated Fund of India the government must pass Appropriation Bills.
    • Disbursements from the Public Account need no authorization from Parliament; the Executive controls this account.
    • Article 267: Parliament may by law establish a Contingency Fund of India, in the nature of an imprest.UPPSC
    • The Contingency Fund [Article 267(1)] is at the President's disposal; he makes advances for unforeseen expenditure before authorisation by Parliament (pending it under Article 115 or 116).UPPSC

    Charged expenditure

    • Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India [Article 112(3)] is not put to the vote of Parliament; it can only be discussed in either House.
    • Parliament has no role in creating the budget; it cannot impose or increase any tax without the recommendation of the President.
    • Charged: emoluments and allowances of the President and other expenditure of his office.
    • Charged: salaries and allowances of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha and Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha.
    • Charged: debt charges of the Government of India, with interest, sinking fund charges, redemption charges and other expenditure on raising loans and servicing debt.
    • Charged: salaries, allowances and pensions of Supreme Court Judges; pensions of Federal Court Judges; pensions of High Court Judges.
    • Charged: salary, allowances and pension of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.
    • Charged: sums needed to satisfy any judgment, decree or award of any court or arbitral tribunal.
    • Charged: any other expenditure so declared by the Constitution or by Parliament by law.
    • Not charged: salary and pension of members of the Election Commission of India.UPPSC
    • Not charged: salary and allowances of the Vice-President as such.UPPSC
    • The Vice-President gets salary and allowances as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, which are charged on the Consolidated Fund.
    • Not charged: salary and allowances of the Prime Minister.UPPSC

    Budget

    • Article 112: the President causes the Annual Financial Statement to be laid before both Houses for every financial year.
    • Annual Financial Statement = statement of estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for the year; commonly called the Union Budget.
    • Financial year: 1 April to 31 March of the following year.
    • The word "Budget" does not appear in the Constitution; Article 112 uses "Annual Financial Statement".UPPSC
    • The Union Finance Minister lays the Annual Financial Statement on behalf of the President (not the Prime Minister).
    • The Ministry of Finance prepares the Union Budget; within it the Department of Economic Affairs prepares and presents it (not the Department of Revenue).
    • Six stages of the budget: presentation; general discussion; scrutiny by departmental committees; voting on demands for grants; passing of Appropriation Bill; passing of Finance Bill.
    • Stages of normal financial legislation: presentation of Budget, discussion on Budget, passing of Appropriation Bill, passing of Finance Bill.UPPSC ×2
    • Vote on account, vote of credit and exceptional grants (Article 116) are not part of normal financial legislation.
    • Article 113(2): estimates of expenditure are submitted to the Lok Sabha as Demands for Grants; it may pass, reject or reduce a grant.
    • Article 113(3): no demand for a grant can be made except on the recommendation of the President.
    • Usually one demand per ministry or department; large ministries have more than one.
    • Demands for Grants: 102 in Budget 2025-26; 101 in Budget 2021-22.
    • Parliamentary control over public finance: Annual Financial Statement; Appropriation Bill before withdrawal (Article 114); supplementary grants and vote on account (Articles 115, 116); Finance Bill.
    • If the Lok Sabha does not pass the annual Union Budget, the Prime Minister submits the resignation of the Council of Ministers (majority lost).
    • The Economic Survey is presented in Parliament every year before the Budget for the coming year.UPPSC
    • Economic Survey gives the progress, activities and fiscal details of various sectors of the economy for the current year.

    Vote on Account and Cut Motions

    • Article 116: if the Appropriation Bill is not passed, Vote on Account lets the government withdraw money from the Consolidated Fund of India for a fixed period.UPPSC ×2
    • Vote on Account [Article 116(1)(a)] is used when there is no time to pass the full Budget before the new financial year, or elections are near.
    • Vote on Account = the incumbent government draws money from the Consolidated Fund to meet expenses until elections are done; not sanction of all demands for the year.UPPSC
    • Vote on Account covers only expenditure for the next few months; an Interim Budget gives both expenditure and receipts.
    • A vote-on-account is sometimes referred to as an Interim Budget.
    • Cut Motion: Lok Sabha motion to reduce the amount of a demand for grant; it is related to the Union Budget.UPPSC
    • The object of a cut motion is also to draw the House's attention to the matter specified in it.
    • If a cut motion is adopted and the government lacks the numbers, it is obliged to resign.
    Cut motionMeaning
    Policy cut (Disapproval of Policy Cut)Budget demand be reduced to Re. one
    Economy cut (Economic / frugality cut)Budget demand be reduced by a specified amount
    Token cutBudget demand be reduced by rupees one hundred

    Committees, Secretariat, Indian Parliamentary Group

    • Estimates Committee = largest financial committee of Parliament: 30 members, all from Lok Sabha; no Rajya Sabha member.
    • Parliament controls the administration through parliamentary committees.
    • The Secretariat of Parliament is independent of the Government.
    • The idea of a separate Secretariat independent of the Executive was mooted in January 1926 by Vithalbhai J. Patel, President of the Central Legislative Assembly.
    • Article 98(1): each House has a separate secretarial staff; posts common to both Houses may be created.
    • Article 98(2): Parliament may by law regulate recruitment and service conditions of the secretarial staff of either House.UPPSC
    • Indian Parliamentary Group: autonomous body formed in 1949, after a motion adopted by the Constituent Assembly (Legislative) on 16 August 1948.
    • Its membership is open to all MPs and ex-MPs; an MP can become a Life Member by paying a life subscription.
    • A life member who ceases to be an MP is called an "Associate Life Member".
    • Its affairs are managed by the Executive Committee; the Speaker of Lok Sabha is its ex-officio President.
    • The Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha and the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha are its ex-officio Vice-Presidents.
    • Aims: promote personal contacts between MPs; spread information through seminars on issues likely to come before Parliament.
    • It arranges lectures on political, defence, economic, social and educational problems, and visits to foreign countries.
    • It links the Parliament of India with other Parliaments by exchanging delegations, goodwill missions, correspondence and documents.
    • It is the National Group of the Inter-Parliamentary Union and the Main Branch of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association in India.
    ← The Parliament (2)Parliamentary Committees →

    Chapter 24 · Union: executive, Parliament, Supreme Court

    Parliamentary Committees

    98 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. PAC Chairman is appointed by the Speaker of Lok Sabha from amongst its members.×4
    2. PAC submits its report to the Speaker of Lok Sabha, who gets it presented in the Lok Sabha (Parliament); a copy is laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha.×3
    3. It has 30 members, all from Lok Sabha, elected every year by Lok Sabha from among its members; no Rajya Sabha member.×3
    4. Financial Committees (three) = Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee, Committee on Public Undertakings.×2
    5. Estimates Committee is the largest committee of Parliament (among PAC, Public Undertakings and Petitions committees).×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 20 UPPSC questions

    Why committees and their kinds

    • Parliament is assisted by a number of committees in the discharge of its duties.
    • Reason: Parliament's work is varied, complex and voluminous, its time is limited and it is too unwieldy to deliberate closely on every matter; so a good deal of business is done by committees.
    • Parliament exercises control over the administration through Parliamentary Committees (Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee, Standing Committees).
    • Committees are appointed or elected by the Houses, or nominated by the Speaker / Chairman.
    • They work under the direction of the Speaker / Chairman and report to the House or to the Speaker / Chairman.
    • Two main kinds: Standing committees and Ad-hoc committees.
    • Standing committees = permanent (constituted every year or periodically), work on a continuous basis.
    • Ad-hoc committees = temporary; cease to exist when the assigned task is completed.
    • Six classes of Standing Committees: (i) Financial Committees, (ii) Department-related Standing Committees (total 24), (iii) Committees of Enquiry, (iv) Committees to Scrutinise and Control, (v) Committees relating to day-to-day business of the House, (vi) Housekeeping or Service Committees.
    • Financial Committees (three) = Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee, Committee on Public Undertakings.UPPSC ×2
    • These three are also called the three main Standing Committees.
    • Joint Committee on Salaries and Allowances of Members of Parliament is a Housekeeping Committee, not a Financial Committee.
    • Committees of Enquiry include: Committee on Petitions, Committee on Privileges, Ethics Committee.
    • Most standing (joint) committees, leaving some exceptions, take members from Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha in the ratio 2:1.UPPSC
    • The Speaker of Lok Sabha appoints the chairpersons of all parliamentary committees.
    CommitteeType
    Public Accounts CommitteeFinancial CommitteeUPPSC
    Committee on PetitionsFunctional Committee
    Joint Committee on Stock Market ScamAd hoc Committee
    Departmental CommitteesStanding Committee

    Public Accounts Committee (PAC)

    • PAC was first set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919; it has existed since then.
    • PAC is one of the most important committees; it is Parliament's tool for a financial check on the executive and controls public expenditure.
    • PAC has not more than 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha and (not more than) 7 from Rajya Sabha.UPPSC
    • PAC has no eminent persons of industry and trade; only members of the two Houses.
    • The 15 Lok Sabha members are elected every year from its members by proportional representation by single transferable vote; the Rajya Sabha members are nominated by that House and associated with the committee.
    • PAC is constituted every year; its tenure is one year.
    • A minister cannot be elected a member of the PAC.
    • PAC Chairman is appointed by the Speaker of Lok Sabha from amongst its members.UPPSC ×4
    • Till 1966-67 the PAC Chairman belonged to the ruling party.
    • In 1967-68 the Speaker for the first time appointed an opposition member as PAC Chairman; the practice continues since then (Chairman from the opposition in Lok Sabha).
    • Main function of PAC: examine the annual audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) and the financial accounts of the government.UPPSC
    • PAC scrutinises the appropriation and finance accounts of the Government and examines the CAG report (which includes those accounts).
    • Basis of PAC deliberation: Appropriation Accounts of Railways, Defence Services, P&T Department and other Civil Ministries, the CAG reports on them, and CAG reports on revenue receipts.
    • PAC examines various expenditure reports and accounts under the purview of Parliament.
    • CAG reports are laid before Parliament by the President.
    • PAC is assisted by the CAG.
    • PAC ensures public money is spent as Parliament decided; it calls attention to waste, extravagance, loss or nugatory expenditure.
    • PAC highlights misuse and misappropriation of public expenditure before each House and recommends action against public authorities responsible.
    • PAC counterchecks public expenditure on the basis of the CAG report and lays the report before each House of Parliament.
    • PAC submits its report to the Speaker of Lok Sabha, who gets it presented in the Lok Sabha (Parliament); a copy is laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha.UPPSC ×3
    • Ordinarily PAC presents reports to the House; only when the House is not in session it may present to the Speaker and later to the House.

    Estimates Committee

    • Estimates Committee was constituted for the first time in 1950.
    • It has 30 members, all from Lok Sabha, elected every year by Lok Sabha from among its members; no Rajya Sabha member.UPPSC ×3
    • Rajya Sabha members are associated with the PAC and the Committee on Public Undertakings, but not with the Estimates Committee.
    • Estimates Committee is the largest committee of Parliament (among PAC, Public Undertakings and Petitions committees).UPPSC ×2
    • Tenure of Estimates Committee members = one year.UPPSC
    • Its chairman is appointed by the Speaker from amongst its members.
    • Most important function: suggest alternative policies to bring efficiency and economy in administration.
    • It also reports what improvements in organisation, efficiency or administrative reform, consistent with the policy underlying the estimates, may be made.
    • It monitors the examination of estimates, austerity and the expenditure of funds.

    Committee on Public Undertakings

    • Committee on Public Undertakings has 22 members: 15 elected by Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha.
    • A minister is not eligible for election to it; its term is one year.
    • It analyses the accounts and working of state-owned PSUs and checks the disinvestment policies of PSUs.
    • Function (a): examine reports and accounts of public undertakings listed in the Fourth Schedule to the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha.
    • Function (b): examine the reports, if any, of the CAG on public undertakings.
    • Function (c): examine whether public undertakings are managed on sound business principles and prudent commercial practices, in the context of their autonomy and efficiency.
    • Function (d): exercise other functions of the PAC and Estimates Committee about public undertakings not covered above, as allotted by the Speaker.
    • The CAG audit report is examined by the Public Accounts Committee; the Committee on Public Undertakings also examines CAG reports.UPPSC

    Note from the book For the question "CAG audit report is examined by", both Public Undertakings Committee and Public Accounts Committee are given as correct answers.

    • The CAG (Article 148) is not a tool of parliamentary control over public expenditure; PAC, Estimates Committee and Committee on Public Undertakings are.
    • CAG has powers in relation to the accounts of any other authority as prescribed by law made by Parliament.

    Committee on Petitions

    • Committee on Petitions: 15 members in Lok Sabha, 10 members in Rajya Sabha.
    • A minister is not nominated to the Committee on Petitions.
    • Function: consider and report on petitions presented to the House.
    • It also considers representations from individuals and associations on subjects not covered by the petition rules and gives directions for their disposal.

    Department-related Standing Committees

    • In 1993, on the recommendation of the Rules Committee of Lok Sabha, 17 Department-related Standing Committees were set up.
    • In 2004 their number was increased from 17 to 24.
    • Of the 24 DRSCs, 8 are under Rajya Sabha and 16 under Lok Sabha; they have members from both Houses.
    • Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs is given as one of the Departmental Standing Committees.

    Note from the book For "which is not a Standing Committee" (Public Accounts, Estimates, Welfare of SCs and STs, Public Undertakings), no given answer is correct.

    • Under Lok Sabha: Committee on Social Justice and Empowerment, Committee on Urban Development, Committee on Labour.
    • Committee on Health and Family Welfare is under the jurisdiction of Rajya Sabha.
    • DRSCs and ad hoc committees set up by Parliament may review the working of independent regulators (telecom, insurance, electricity).
    • Example: the Joint Parliamentary Committee on 2G spectrum allocation reviewed the policy on spectrum pricing and grant of telecom licences.
    • Finance Commission, NITI Aayog and Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission have no role in reviewing independent regulators.

    Ethics Committee

    • Origin: a resolution at the Presiding Officers Conference, New Delhi, October 1996, asked legislatures to explore constituting an Ethics Committee.
    • Ethics Committee of Rajya Sabha = first such committee of any legislature in India; constituted by the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in 1997.
    • In Lok Sabha the Committee of Privileges recommended an Ethics Committee during the 13th Lok Sabha.
    • First Ethics Committee in Lok Sabha was constituted on 16 May 2000 by Speaker G.M.C. Balayogi (13th Lok Sabha).
    • Lok Sabha Ethics Committee was at first ad-hoc; it became permanent only in 2015, when its rules were put in the Rules of Procedure; it cannot take up a sub-judice matter.
    • Rule 233A(1), Chapter XXA: any person or member may complain about unethical conduct of a Lok Sabha member; a complaint by a person must be forwarded by a member.
    • Rule 233A(10), Chapter XXA: the committee shall not take up a sub-judice matter; its decision on whether a matter is sub-judice is final.

    Other committees

    • Committee on Subordinate Legislation: examines and reports whether the executive properly uses powers to make regulations, rules, sub-rules and bye-laws delegated by Parliament or conferred by the Constitution.
    • Committee on Subordinate Legislation exists in both Houses; 15 members in each; nominated by Speaker (Lok Sabha) or Chairman (Rajya Sabha); ministers cannot be members.
    • Committee on Government Assurances (each House): examines assurances, promises and undertakings given by ministers on the floor of the House and reports how far they are implemented.
    • Rules Committee: considers matters of procedure and conduct of business in the House and recommends amendments or additions to the Rules.
    • Business Advisory Committee: regulates the programme and time-table of the House.
    • No parliamentary committee exists for welfare of minorities; instead a Minority Commission has been set up.UPPSC
    • Parliamentary committees do exist on Public Undertakings, Government Assurances and Estimates.

    Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs

    • The Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs works under the overall direction of the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs.
    • The Minister of Parliamentary Affairs nominates MPs on committees, councils, boards and commissions set up by the Government of India in various ministries.
    • Consultative Committees of MPs for Railway Zones are constituted by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs; MPs of the respective zones are members.

    2G spectrum Joint Parliamentary Committee

    • The proposal for a JPC on the 2G spectrum scam was passed by Lok Sabha on 24 February 2011 and by Rajya Sabha on 1 March 2011.
    • The 2G JPC had 30 members: 20 from Lok Sabha and 10 from Rajya Sabha.UPPSC
    • P.C. Chacko was Chairman of the 2G JPC; he submitted the report to the then Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar.UPPSC

    Committee chairpersons, 18th Lok Sabha (2024-25)

    • In August 2024, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla constituted six new parliamentary committees, including the PAC.

    Public Accounts CommitteeK.C. Venugopal (senior Congress leader)
    Committee on EstimatesSanjay Jaiswal
    Committee on Public UndertakingsBaijayant Panda
    Committee on Welfare of Other Backward ClassesGanesh Singh
    Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled TribesFaggan Singh Kulaste

    Chapter 25 · Union: executive, Parliament, Supreme Court

    The Parliamentary Act

    218 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Right to Information is a legal right; according to the Supreme Court it is also a fundamental right.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 24 UPPSC questions

    Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955

    • The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 prescribes punishment for the preaching and practice of untouchability, for enforcing any disability arising from it, and connected matters.
    • Section 1(2): the Act extends to the whole of India.
    • Section 15(1): notwithstanding the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, all offences punishable under the Act are cognizable and triable summarily; they are also non-compoundable.
    • The Act provides both imprisonment and fine as punishment.

    Note from the book For "all offences under the Act are" (cognizable / triable summarily / non-compoundable) and (cognizable / imprisonment and fine both), two options each are given as correct; M.P.P.S.C. first keyed "compoundable" in the second and then gave bonus marks to all.

    • Offences under the Act are tried by a Judicial Magistrate First Class; in a metropolis by a Metropolitan Magistrate.
    • First-class Judicial Magistrates were empowered to hold special courts for trial of offences under the Act.
    • In Uttar Pradesh, in each district the Courts of Chief Judicial Magistrates / Judicial Magistrates are designated Special Courts for offences under the Act.
    • Section 5: refusing admission to a hospital, dispensary or educational institution (meant for the general public or any section of it) on the ground of untouchability is punishable.
    • Section 5 punishment: imprisonment not less than 1 month and not more than 6 months, and fine not less than Rs. 100 and not more than Rs. 500.
    • Untouchability is not an offence when the accused and the victim belong to the same social group.
    • If a company commits an offence under the Act, the person in charge of its affairs at the time (Director, Manager or Secretary) is deemed guilty and punished.
    • Primary responsibility for implementing the PCR Act / Rules rests in practice with State Governments / Union Territory Administrations.
    • At the Centre, under the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, three ministries handle the PCR Act: Home Affairs, Social Justice and Empowerment, Tribal Affairs.
    • Ministry of Home Affairs: criminal offences against SCs/STs, including offences under the PCR Act.
    • Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment: implementation of the PCR Act for Scheduled Castes (excluding criminal justice for offences under the Act).
    • Ministry of Tribal Affairs: implementation of the PCR Act for Scheduled Tribes (excluding criminal justice for offences under the Act).
    Section (PCR Act, 1955)Provision
    Section 1(2)Extent: whole of India
    Section 5Refusing admission to hospital, dispensary, educational institution
    Section 10Abetment of offence; a public servant who wilfully neglects investigation is deemed to have abetted the offence
    Section 10APower of State Government to impose collective fine
    Section 12Presumption by courts: if the act is against a member of a Scheduled Caste (only SC), court presumes it was on the ground of untouchability unless the contrary is proved
    Section 14Offences by companies (company = any body corporate, includes a firm or other association of individuals; director of a firm = partner)
    Section 14AProtection of action taken in good faith: no suit, prosecution or legal proceeding against Central or State Government for acts or damage done in good faith under the Act
    Section 15Offences cognizable and triable summarily
    Section 16Act to override other laws, customs, usages, instruments, decrees or orders of any court or authority

    SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

    • The President gave assent to the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 on 11 September 1989.
    • The Act of 1989 came into force on 30 January 1990.
    • The Act has 23 sections.
    • The Act is based on the Doctrine of Protective Discrimination; it implements the system under Article 15(4).
    • Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
    • Offences under the Act are committed by a person who is not a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe; prosecution lies only against such a person.
    • Section 23(1): the Central Government may make rules by notification in the Official Gazette to carry out the purposes of the Act.
    • Section 2(bc) defines "economic boycott".
    • "Exclusive Special Court" (set up under Section 14(1) only to try offences under the Act) is defined in Section 2(1)(bd), not Section 2(d).
    • "Victim" is defined in Section 2(ec); "Dependent" in Section 2(bb).
    • A public servant committing an offence under Section 3 gets imprisonment of not less than one year.
    • A non-SC/ST person causing physical harm or mental agony to an SC/ST member on allegation of witchcraft or being a witch: imprisonment not less than 6 months, up to 5 years, with fine.
    • Section 14 provides for a Special Court and an Exclusive Special Court.
    • Under Section 14 the State Government, with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court, by Gazette notification specifies for each district a Court of Session as Special Court.
    • The Special Court is specified for the purpose of speedy trial.
    • Section 15 provides for a Special Public Prosecutor and an Exclusive Public Prosecutor.
    • An appeal from any judgment, sentence or order lies to the High Court both on facts and on law.
    • Section 16: power to impose and realise a collective fine is vested in the State Government.
    • A Special Court cannot impose a collective fine; it can remove a person, forfeit property and take measurements.
    • A Special Court has no power to authorise a person other than police for extra investigation.
    • Special Court powers include: forfeiture of a convict's property, removal of a suspected person from the area, taking measurements and photographs of a suspected person.
    • Section 8: in a prosecution the court may presume abetment, common intention and common object.
    • Section 6 applies Section 34, Chapters 3, 4, 5, 5-A, Section 149 and Chapter 23 of the Indian Penal Code.
    • The Indian Penal Code is replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
    • Section 18 bars anticipatory bail: Section 438 of the Code does not apply to arrest of a person accused under this Act.
    • The accused can plead in defence that he belongs to the same caste as the victim.
    • The accused cannot plead private defence or that the harm was too slight to be a subject of complaint.

    Note from the book For "the accused cannot take the plea that", two options (private defence; slight harm) are correct; M.P.P.S.C. gave bonus marks to all in its revised key.

    SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Rules, 1995

    • The Central Government framed the rules in 1995 to implement the 1989 Act.
    • Rule 7(1): an offence under the Act is investigated by a police officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police.
    • Rule 17: the District Magistrate sets up a District Level Vigilance and Monitoring Committee in each district to review implementation of the Act.
    • Rule 18: "Material for Annual Report".
    • Rules, 1995 (original): investigating officer to complete investigation on top priority within 30 days and report to the Superintendent of Police.
    • Amendment Rules, 2016: SP forwards the report at once to the DGP or Commissioner of Police; the officer in charge of the police station files the charge-sheet in the Special Court within 60 days (investigation plus charge-sheet).

    Note from the book For "in how many days will the investigating officer submit his report", the commission's answer was 30 days, which is wrong as per the Amendment Rules, 2016.

    Right to Information Act, 2005

    • The RTI Act was passed by Lok Sabha on 11 May 2005 and by Rajya Sabha on 12 May 2005; passed in the year 2005.UPPSC
    • It received the assent of President Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam on 15 June 2005.UPPSC
    • It came fully into force after 120 days, on 12 October 2005 (12-13 midnight).
    • Right to Information is a legal right; according to the Supreme Court it is also a fundamental right.UPPSC ×2
    • In many decisions the Supreme Court said freedom of thought and expression includes the right to information; the right is not clearly mentioned in the Constitution.
    • Raj Narain vs State of Uttar Pradesh (1976): Supreme Court ruled the right to information is a fundamental right under Article 19.
    • Objective of the Act: citizens secure access to information under the control of public authorities.
    • Section 2: "right to information" = access to information controlled by public officials; records, documents and works can be inspected and samples of material taken.
    • The Act mandates timely response to citizens' requests for government information.
    • Objects of RTI: empower citizens, promote transparency and accountability in government working, prevent (tackle) corruption, make democracy work for the people in a real sense.
    • "To empower women and weaker sections of society" is not an objective of the RTI Act.
    • An informed citizen can better keep vigil on the instruments of governance and make government more accountable to the governed.
    • The RTI Preamble mentions: transparency of information, revelation of information, informed citizens (citizenry), paramountcy of the democratic ideal.
    • Preamble: democracy needs informed citizens and transparency of information to contain corruption and hold governments accountable; conflicting interests are to be harmonised while preserving the democratic ideal.
    • Section 6(2), Chapter 2: an applicant need not give any reason or personal details for seeking information, except details needed to contact him.
    • A Madras High Court division bench (Justices N. Paul Vasanthakumar and K. Ravichandrababu) said an RTI applicant must disclose the object of seeking information and show it has legal backing.UPPSC
    • No such obligation to give reasons is mentioned in the RTI Act, 2005.
    • Namit Sharma vs Union of India (2012) is related to the RTI Act, 2005.UPPSC
    • Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS): Indian social movement and grassroots organisation best known for its demand for the RTI Act.UPPSC
    • MKSS was founded in 1990 by social activists Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey and Shankar Singh.
    • The people's movement for right to information is taken to have begun in 1990, when MKSS demanded data on famine relief works and workers' wages.
    • The RTI Act has in general increased the sense of responsibility in bureaucracy; it still has miles to go to create the desired impact (both true, second not the explanation of the first).UPPSC
    • The RTI Act, 2005 was amended in 2019.
    • After Article 370 special status of Jammu and Kashmir was abolished (President's notification of 6 August 2019), the RTI Act is in force in the UTs of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.

    Note from the book "Which RTI provision has not been provided" (2006): at that time the Act had all the listed provisions except that an applicant must give reasons; the J&K and tenure provisions have since changed.

    Information Commissions

    • The Central Information Commission was constituted with effect from 12 October 2005 under the RTI Act, 2005.
    • Its jurisdiction extends over all Central Public Authorities.
    • CIC powers and functions are in Sections 18, 19, 20 and 25 of the RTI Act.
    RTI Act sectionSubject
    Section 12Constitution of the Central Information Commission (not about its powers and functions)
    Section 15(3)Appointment of State Chief Information Commissioner and State Information Commissioners
    Section 18Powers and functions of Information Commissions
    Section 19Appeal
    Section 20Penalty: imposed by the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission
    Section 25Central / State Information Commission prepares a report on implementation of the Act
    • The RTI Act provides for a Central Information Commission and a State Information Commission at state level.
    • State Information Commission = one State Chief Information Commissioner and not more than ten State Information Commissioners.
    • Section 15(3): they are appointed by the Governor on the recommendation of a committee: Chief Minister (Chairperson), Leader of Opposition in the Legislative Assembly, a Cabinet Minister nominated by the Chief Minister.
    • The Chief Justice of the High Court is not a member of this committee.
    • Commissioners must be persons of eminence in public life with wide knowledge and experience in law, science and technology, social service, management, journalism, mass media or administration and governance.
    • They must not be a Member of Parliament or Member of the Legislature of any State or Union Territory.
    • Original Act: Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioners (Centre and State) held office for 5 years (or until age 65, whichever earlier).
    • RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 removed the fixed five-year term; the term is as prescribed (notified) by the Central Government.
    • Tenure of CIC and Information Commissioners is now given as 3 years or 65 years of age.
    • The tenure prescribed by the Central Government under the 2019 amendment is also given as 5 years from the date of joining (Central CIC, each Information Commissioner, State CIC).

    Citizen Charter

    • Nine basic elements of the Citizen Charter: set standards of service; be open and provide full information; consult and involve; encourage access and the promotion of choice; treat all fairly; put things right when they go wrong; use resources effectively; innovate and improve; work with other providers.
    • "Provision for inspection of the agency's work" is not a basic element of the Citizen Charter.

    Forest Rights Act, 2006 and PESA

    • Nodal agency for the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 = the Ministry of Tribal Affairs (or an officer or authority authorised by the Central Government).
    • Every authority under Chapter IV of that Act is subject to written general or particular directions of the Central Government.
    • Section 6(1): the Gram Sabha starts the process of determining the nature and extent of individual or community forest rights; then it is enquired at Tehsil and District level.
    • PESA = Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996: Parliament's law ensuring self-governance through traditional gram sabhas for people in Scheduled Areas.

    National Green Tribunal

    • The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 was enacted in line with the right to a healthy environment, read as part of the Right to Life under Article 21.
    • The NGT was established on 18 October 2010 under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.UPPSC
    • Purpose: effective and quick disposal of cases on environmental protection and conservation of forests and other natural resources, enforcement of environmental legal rights, relief and compensation for damage to persons and property.
    • NGT is a specialised body with expertise for environmental disputes involving multi-disciplinary issues.
    • NGT is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908; it is guided by principles of natural justice.
    • NGT can review its own decisions; if this fails, its decision can be challenged in the Supreme Court within 90 days.

    Disaster and epidemic laws

    • The Disaster Management Act was passed by Parliament in 2005 for efficient management of disasters.UPPSC
    • It has 11 chapters and 79 sections; it received the President's assent (was enacted) on 23 December 2005.
    • The Act envisaged the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), headed by the Prime Minister.UPPSC
    • National Disaster Management Division = nodal division in the Ministry of Home Affairs for disaster management.
    • NDMA may have not more than nine members including a Vice-Chairperson; members' tenure is five years.
    • Legal basis of the Government's extraordinary powers during lockdown = Disaster Management Act, 2005 and Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897.UPPSC
    • On 11 March 2020 the Centre advised all States and UTs to invoke Section 2 of the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (a 123-year-old law) to enforce Health Ministry and State advisories on COVID-19.
    • The Disaster Management Act, 2005 was invoked to enforce the 21-day nationwide lockdown that started at midnight on 23 March 2020.

    Environment and biodiversity laws

    • The Forest Conservation Act was enacted in 1980; effective from 25 October 1980.UPPSC
    • The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 was published in the Official Gazette on 3 August 2023, the same day it got the President's assent.
    • It decriminalises violations of the Biological Diversity Act, replacing imprisonment with civil penalties.
    • It gives relief to Indian entities in securing intellectual property rights.
    • It exempts AYUSH practitioners and traditional knowledge holders from paying Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) fees.
    • The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 came into force on 1 October 2003 and 1 July 2004; passed to meet obligations under the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).
    • In a Community Reserve hunting is not allowed and people may collect non-timber forest produce; the Chief Wildlife Warden does not govern it and traditional agriculture is not allowed.
    • Section 36C, Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972: the State Government, not the Central Government, declares a Community Reserve.
    • Section 36D: a Community Reserve is managed by a Community Reserve Management Committee, not the Chief Wildlife Warden.
    • The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 prohibits hunting in protected areas, including Community Reserves.
    • The Act does not explicitly mention non-timber forest produce; sustainable use by local communities is generally allowed under the committee's supervision.
    • Traditional agricultural practices that may alter the habitat are typically restricted in Community Reserves.
    • Community Reserves aim to involve local communities in conservation; the Act stresses protecting flora, fauna and traditional conservation values, which may limit some land uses.
    • The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act was passed in 2001.UPPSC
    • Its aims: an effective system to protect plant varieties and the rights of farmers and plant breeders, and to encourage new plant varieties.

    Aadhaar, IT Act and RTE Act

    • Aadhaar number = 12-digit random number issued by UIDAI to residents of India after verification.
    • Any resident of India, of any age or gender, may voluntarily enrol; enrolment needs minimal demographic and biometric information and is free of cost.
    • Section 9, Aadhaar Act, 2016: Aadhaar is only proof of identity, not proof of citizenship or domicile; Section 23(g): the issuing authority can deactivate or omit an Aadhaar number.
    • Supreme Court: Aadhaar authentication data cannot be kept beyond 6 months (not three months).
    • Supreme Court upheld the Aadhaar Act, 2016 except some provisions on disclosure of personal information, cognizance of offences and use of the Aadhaar ecosystem by private corporations; and held Aadhaar valid for welfare schemes funded from the Consolidated Fund of India.
    • The Court called Aadhaar for welfare schemes a "legitimate" exercise and defined welfare schemes as only those funded directly from the Consolidated Fund of India.
    • Aadhaar is not mandatory for insurance: IRDAI advised insurers not to seek Aadhaar for KYC; it may be accepted only when offered voluntarily.
    Section (IT Act, 2000)e-governance provision
    Section 4Legal recognition of (electronic) records
    Section 5Legal recognition of electronic signatures
    Section 6Use of electronic records and electronic signatures in government and its agencies
    Section 8Publication of rules, regulations in the Electronic Gazette
    • RTE Act: to teach primary classes a candidate must pass a Teacher Eligibility Test held as per National Council of Teacher Education guidelines.
    • Section 23(1), RTE Act, 2009: a teacher needs the minimum qualifications laid down by an academic authority authorised by the Central Government by notification (not by the State Council of Teacher Education).

    Consumer protection and food security

    1. 1986The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 was passed to protect consumer rights.
    2. 1986The 1986 Act gave a 3-tier structure: National Commission, State Commissions and District Forums, to speed up consumer disputes.
    3. 1986Under the 1986 Act the State Government sets up a District Forum in each district; District Forum limit = value and compensation up to Rs. 20 lakh (not Rs. 50 lakh).
    4. 1986Under the 1986 Act the State Commission took claims above Rs. 20 lakh and up to Rs. 1 crore.
    5. 2013State Food Commission is set up under Section 16 of the National Food Security Act, 2013.
    6. 2019The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 got the President's assent on 9 August 2019, came into effect on 20 July 2020 and replaced the 1986 Act, to modernise consumer safety.
    7. 2021Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021: District Commission up to Rs. 50 lakh; State Commission above Rs. 50 lakh up to Rs. 2 crore; National Commission above Rs. 2 crore.
    • The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 was passed to protect consumer rights.
    • Under it, consumers may take samples for food testing, and the legal heir of a dead consumer may file a complaint in the Consumer Forum on his/her behalf.
    • A consumer filing a complaint in the Consumer Forum (for malfunction or failure of a product) has to pay a small fee.
    • The 1986 Act gave a 3-tier structure: National Commission, State Commissions and District Forums, to speed up consumer disputes.
    • Under the 1986 Act the State Government sets up a District Forum in each district; District Forum limit = value and compensation up to Rs. 20 lakh (not Rs. 50 lakh).
    • Under the 1986 Act the State Commission took claims above Rs. 20 lakh and up to Rs. 1 crore.
    • A State Government can file a complaint in a District Forum as a representative of consumers' interest in general.
    • The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 got the President's assent on 9 August 2019, came into effect on 20 July 2020 and replaced the 1986 Act, to modernise consumer safety.
    • Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021: District Commission up to Rs. 50 lakh; State Commission above Rs. 50 lakh up to Rs. 2 crore; National Commission above Rs. 2 crore.
    • Section 28(1): the State Government may set up more than one District Commission in a district if it deems fit.
    • A District Forum is headed by a person who is, has been, or is eligible to be a District Judge; it has two other members, one of whom shall be a woman.
    • A State Commission is headed by a person who is or has been a High Court Judge.
    • State Food Commission is set up under Section 16 of the National Food Security Act, 2013.

    Other Acts and their years

    1. 1871The Criminal Tribes Act was first enacted in 1871 by the British Government; enforced first in northern India, later extended to Bengal.UPPSC
    2. 1894The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was made by British rulers; in effect from 1 March 1894; its purpose was land acquisition for public institutions, organisations and companies, not land reform.
    3. 1923Section 6, Official Secrets Act, 1923: unauthorised use of police or military uniforms, falsification of reports, forgery, personation and false documents.
    4. 1923Section 7, Official Secrets Act, 1923: no one near a prohibited place shall obstruct, knowingly mislead or interfere with a police officer or member of the Armed Forces on guard, sentry, patrol or similar duty (not the Indian Evidence Act, 1872).
    5. 1954The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 was enacted in 1954 and came into force on 1 June 1955; repealed w.e.f. 5 August 2011.UPPSC
    6. 1955Hindu Marriage Act = 1955; Hindu Succession Act = 1956; Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act = enacted 1987, enforced 1988.
    7. 1971MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act): enacted 1971, repealed 1977; for internal security, so not a Social Act.UPPSC
    8. 2005The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 came into force on 26 October 2006.UPPSC
    9. 2013It was replaced by the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013; its implementation had become disputed.
    10. 2019The Code on Wages, 2019 replaces four laws: Payment of Wages Act, 1936; Minimum Wages Act, 1948; Payment of Bonus Act, 1965; Equal Remuneration Act, 1976.UPPSC
    11. 2019The Contract Labour Act is not merged into the Code on Wages, 2019.
    12. 2019The Arms (Amendment) Act, 2019 punishes rash or negligent use of firearms or celebratory gunfire endangering human life or personal safety of others.
    13. 2024The Waqf (Amendment) Bill, 2024 was introduced in Lok Sabha on 8 August 2024; aim: better management of Waqf properties, transparency, governance, accountability, preventing mismanagement.

    • The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 came into force on 26 October 2006.UPPSC
    • The Criminal Tribes Act was first enacted in 1871 by the British Government; enforced first in northern India, later extended to Bengal.UPPSC
    • MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act): enacted 1971, repealed 1977; for internal security, so not a Social Act.UPPSC
    • Anti-Dowry Act, Protection of Civil Rights Act and Prevention of Immoral Traffic Act are Social Acts (against social evils).
    • Hindu Marriage Act = 1955; Hindu Succession Act = 1956; Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act = enacted 1987, enforced 1988.
    • Reservation of seats for women in urban local bodies came by the 74th Amendment, not the 73rd.UPPSC
    • The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was made by British rulers; in effect from 1 March 1894; its purpose was land acquisition for public institutions, organisations and companies, not land reform.
    • It was replaced by the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013; its implementation had become disputed.
    • The Code on Wages, 2019 replaces four laws: Payment of Wages Act, 1936; Minimum Wages Act, 1948; Payment of Bonus Act, 1965; Equal Remuneration Act, 1976.UPPSC
    • The Contract Labour Act is not merged into the Code on Wages, 2019.
    • Section 6, Official Secrets Act, 1923: unauthorised use of police or military uniforms, falsification of reports, forgery, personation and false documents.
    • Section 7, Official Secrets Act, 1923: no one near a prohibited place shall obstruct, knowingly mislead or interfere with a police officer or member of the Armed Forces on guard, sentry, patrol or similar duty (not the Indian Evidence Act, 1872).
    • The Arms (Amendment) Act, 2019 punishes rash or negligent use of firearms or celebratory gunfire endangering human life or personal safety of others.
