    Chapter 26 · Union: executive, Parliament, Supreme Court

    The Supreme Court

    242 facts · 9 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Constitutional cases: Article 132 read with Article 134A gives the appellate jurisdiction.×3
    2. Article 137: the Supreme Court can review (change) any judgment or order made by it, subject to Parliament's law and rules under Article 145.×3
    3. Article 143: the President may seek the Supreme Court's opinion on a question of law or fact of public importance; the Court advises only when he seeks it.×3
    4. Keshavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala (1973): the Supreme Court propounded the Doctrine of Basic Structure; it is not from Indira Sawhney, Shankari Prasad or Rudal Shah cases.×3
    5. A judge resigns by writing under his hand addressed to the President.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 55 UPPSC questions

    Establishment and integrated judiciary

    1. 1935This single judiciary system was adopted from the Government of India Act, 1935.
    2. 1935The Supreme Court was established by the Constitution (Part V, Chapter IV, Article 124); it succeeded the Federal Court of India set up under the Government of India Act, 1935.
    3. 1944The Sapru Committee was appointed by the Non-Party Conference in November 1944 to address minority issues; its report had 21 recommendations on constitutional questions.
    4. 1945The Sapru Committee Report (1945), led by Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru, made recommendations on appointment of Supreme Court and High Court judges.
    5. 1947Its report (21 May 1947) dealt with the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and proposed two alternative methods of appointing its judges.
    6. 1950The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on 28 January 1950.
    • The Constitution sets up an integrated (single) judicial system with the Supreme Court at the top and High Courts below it.
    • This single judiciary system was adopted from the Government of India Act, 1935.
    • The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on 28 January 1950.
    • The Supreme Court was established by the Constitution (Part V, Chapter IV, Article 124); it succeeded the Federal Court of India set up under the Government of India Act, 1935.
    • Articles 124 to 147 (Part V) deal with the Supreme Court: establishment, composition and jurisdiction.
    • The Supreme Court is the highest judicial forum and the final court of appeal.
    • The Sapru Committee Report (1945), led by Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru, made recommendations on appointment of Supreme Court and High Court judges.
    • The Sapru Committee was appointed by the Non-Party Conference in November 1944 to address minority issues; its report had 21 recommendations on constitutional questions.
    • The Constituent Assembly appointed an Ad hoc Committee on the Supreme Court for recommendations on the judiciary.
    • Its members: S. Varadachariar (former Federal Court judge), Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, B.L. Mitter, K.M. Munshi (eminent advocates) and B.N. Rau (Constitutional Adviser, former high-ranking judicial officer).
    • Its report (21 May 1947) dealt with the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and proposed two alternative methods of appointing its judges.

    Number of judges

    • Article 124(1): Supreme Court = Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, not more than 33 other judges (originally 7).
    • The power to increase the number of Supreme Court judges is vested in Parliament.
    • The original Constitution of 1950 provided a Chief Justice and 7 puisne judges.
    • In the early years all the judges sat together to hear cases; the number was raised as work and arrears grew.
    YearTotal judges including Chief Justice
    19508
    195611
    196014
    197818
    198626
    2009 (Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2009)31
    2019 (Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019)34 (33 + 1)
    • Currently the Supreme Court may have up to 34 judges including the Chief Justice.

    Appointment and qualifications

    • Article 124(2): every Supreme Court judge is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.
    • The President appoints after consulting such judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts as he deems necessary; the Chief Justice is appointed after such consultation.
    • For appointing a judge other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of India shall always be consulted.
    • Consultation with the CJI was made obligatory by a decision of 1993.
    • In 1998 the Supreme Court said CJI's consultation means consultation of the collegium = CJI and four other senior-most judges.
    • Article 124(3) qualifications: citizen of India, and High Court judge for at least 5 years (one or more courts in succession), or High Court advocate for at least 10 years, or a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion.
    • No minimum age is prescribed for appointment as a Supreme Court judge.
    • A person appointed as a Supreme Court judge makes and subscribes an oath or affirmation before the President.
    • The Third Schedule has 10 forms of oaths or affirmations: for Union and State Ministers, MPs, members of State Legislatures, judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the CAG.
    • The oath "bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution… uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India… perform the duties of my office… uphold the Constitution and the laws" is for the Chief Justice of India and the CAG.UPPSC

    Collegium and NJAC

    • The Collegium System for appointing judges was adopted by the Supreme Court in 1993.
    • It has its origin in three Supreme Court judgments together called the Three Judges Cases.
    • The Supreme Court Collegium = Chief Justice of India and 4 senior-most judges.UPPSC
    • The Collegium is a five-member body headed by the CJI; judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts are appointed only through the collegium system.
    • The Collegium considers elevation of judges to the Supreme Court and of High Court judges as Chief Justices; in a disagreement the majority opinion prevails.
    • The collegium system of appointment and transfer of judges evolved through Supreme Court judgments, not by an Act of Parliament or a constitutional provision.
    • It arose because the Constitution requires consultation with the CJI before judicial appointments.
    • After the Second Judges Case (1993) the collegium at first had the CJI and the two senior-most judges.
    • Second Judges Case (1993): "consultation" means concurrence, binding the President to the CJI's consultation.
    • The collegium was not introduced by Justice P.N. Bhagwati in the First Judges Case.
    • The National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) was brought by the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014 to replace the collegium system.
    • The Supreme Court struck down the NJAC in 2015 as unconstitutional; the collegium system continues, and India has no NJAC at present.
    • NJAC composition: CJI (ex-officio Chairperson), two senior-most Supreme Court judges, Union Minister of Law and Justice, and two eminent persons.
    • The two eminent persons were to be nominated by a committee of the Prime Minister, the CJI and the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha (or leader of the single largest opposition party).
    • The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended appointing judges of higher courts with participation of the Executive, the Legislature and the Chief Justice of India.UPPSC

    Tenure, resignation and removal

    • A Supreme Court judge holds office until the age of 65 years; High Court judges retire at 62.UPPSC
    • A judge resigns by writing under his hand addressed to the President.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 124(4): a judge is removed only by an order of the President after an address by each House of Parliament.
    • The address needs a special majority in each House: majority of total membership and not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
    • The address must be presented to the President in the same session.
    • Grounds of removal: proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
    • These removals can be declared unconstitutional and illegal in extraordinary conditions.
    • The Constitution gives the grounds of removal but does not define "proved misbehaviour" or "incapacity".
    • The details of the removal process are in the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968; the removal motion needs the special majority in each House.
    • Under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 the Speaker of Lok Sabha can reject the motion to remove a judge.
    • The word "impeachment" is used only for removing the President; for Supreme Court and High Court judges the Constitution uses the word "remove", though the process is impeachment-like.
    • Supreme Court judges are not removed by the Chief Justice of India.

    Salary, independence and after retirement

    • Article 125(1): salaries (and other allowances) of Supreme Court judges are determined by Parliament by law; until then as in the Second Schedule.UPPSC
    • Safeguards of Supreme Court autonomy: the President must consult the CJI in appointing judges, and judges' salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (not voted).
    • Consulting the CJI curtails the absolute discretion of the Executive and keeps political or practical considerations out of judicial appointments.
    • The CJI appoints officers and servants of the Supreme Court without executive interference and can prescribe their conditions of service.
    • Supreme Court administrative expenses (salaries, allowances, pensions of officers and servants) are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India; those of a High Court on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
    • Article 124(7): a person who has been a Supreme Court judge cannot plead or act in any court or before any authority in India.UPPSC
    • Article 220: a former permanent High Court judge cannot plead or act in any court or authority in India except the Supreme Court and the other High Courts.

    Acting, ad hoc and retired judges

    • Article 126: the Acting Chief Justice of India is appointed by the President when the office is vacant or the Chief Justice cannot perform his duties.UPPSC ×2
    • The Constitution provides ad hoc judges in the Supreme Court; there is no provision for additional judges in the Supreme Court.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 127(1): ad hoc judges are appointed when there is no quorum of judges to hold or continue a session of the Court.
    • The CJI, with the previous consent of the President and after consulting the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned, requests in writing a High Court judge qualified to be a Supreme Court judge to sit as ad hoc judge for the needed period.
    • Article 128: the CJI, with the previous consent of the President, may request a retired judge of the Supreme Court or Federal Court, or a retired High Court judge qualified for the Supreme Court, to sit and act as a Supreme Court judge.
    • Article 215: every High Court is a court of record with power to punish for its contempt; as a court of record it can also review and correct its own judgments, orders or decisions.

    Seat, benches and language

    • Article 130: the Supreme Court sits in Delhi or at such other place as the CJI appoints with the approval of the President.UPPSC
    • At least 5 judges must hear a case involving a substantial question of law on interpretation of the Constitution; this is the Constitutional Bench.UPPSC ×2
    • Benches generally have an odd number of judges (3, 5, 7, 9, 11) to avoid a tie of votes or views.
    • Largest bench so far = 13 judges, Keshavananda Bharati (1973).
    • Second largest bench = 11 judges, Golaknath vs State of Punjab (1967).UPPSC
    • Article 348(1)(a): all proceedings in the Supreme Court and every High Court shall be in the English language.UPPSC

    Court of Record and contempt

    • Article 129: the Supreme Court is a Court of Record with all powers of such a court, including power to punish for contempt of itself.
    • Court of Record = its judgments and proceedings are recorded for perpetual memory, have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned in any court.UPPSC

    Note from the book For "Court of Record implies", both evidentiary value and power to punish for contempt are correct; the U.P. Commission took evidentiary value as the answer.

    • Both the Supreme Court (Article 129) and the High Courts (Article 215) are Courts of Record.UPPSC
    • Article 124 = establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court; Court of Record is Article 129, not Article 124.UPPSC
    • The H.N. Sanyal Committee was set up in 1961; on its recommendation the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 was passed.
    • The Constitution does not define "contempt of court" (civil or criminal); it is defined in the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
    • Parliament has the power to make laws on contempt of court.
    • Section 2(b), Contempt of Courts Act, 1971: wilful disobedience of a judgment, decree, direction, order or writ of a court = civil contempt.
    • M.L. Sachdev vs Union of India: wilful non-compliance with court orders held to be contempt of court under Article 32.

    Original jurisdiction

    • The Supreme Court has original, appellate and advisory jurisdiction.UPPSC
    • Collegium system, appellate jurisdiction and original jurisdiction are all concerned with the Supreme Court.
    • Article 131 (original jurisdiction): disputes between the Government of India and one or more States; between the Centre and State(s) on one side and State(s) on the other; between two or more States.
    • This jurisdiction is exclusive, and applies only if the dispute involves a question of law or fact on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends.
    • It does not extend to disputes arising from pre-Constitution treaties, agreements, covenants, engagements or similar instruments that continue in operation or that exclude such jurisdiction.
    • Election disputes of Parliament or State Legislatures and disputes between the Centre and a Union Territory are not in the original jurisdiction.
    • As a federal court, the Supreme Court decides disputes between units of the Indian federation.

    Appellate jurisdiction

    • Articles 132 to 136 deal with the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court; it is the highest court of appeal.
    • All cases on interpretation of the Constitution can be brought to the Supreme Court under its appellate jurisdiction.UPPSC
    • Constitutional cases: Article 132 read with Article 134A gives the appellate jurisdiction.UPPSC ×3

    • Article 136: the Supreme Court can quash the decision of a quasi-judicial tribunal that exceeded its jurisdiction or approached the question in a manner likely to cause injustice.
    • Under the Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007 a court-martial matter can be appealed in the Supreme Court; so the Court can hear appeals from High Courts, tribunals and courts-martial.
    • TDSAT orders: on telecom, broadcasting and airport tariff matters appeal lies to the Supreme Court (only on substantial questions of law); on cyber matters appeal lies to the High Court.UPPSC
    • TDSAT (Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal) was set up when the TRAI Act, 1997 was amended in 2000, to adjudicate disputes and dispose of appeals.

    Review, curative petition and Article 142

    • Article 137: the Supreme Court can review (change) any judgment or order made by it, subject to Parliament's law and rules under Article 145.UPPSC ×3
    • Curative Petition evolved in Rupa Ashok Hurra vs Ashok Hurra (2002); it can be filed in the Supreme Court under Article 142.UPPSC
    • Article 142(1): the Supreme Court may pass any decree or order needed for complete justice in a matter before it, enforceable throughout India as Parliament's law or the President's order prescribes.
    • Limits in ordinary laws cannot limit Article 142 powers = the Supreme Court is not constrained by laws made by Parliament in using these powers.
    • Article 141: law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India.
    • Article 139A: the Supreme Court can transfer any case anywhere in India (send any case to any court).
    • If cases with the same substantial questions of law are pending in the Supreme Court and High Courts, it may withdraw and dispose of them itself, on its own motion or on application by the Attorney-General or a party.
    • Article 138: Parliament, by making a law, can enlarge the jurisdiction and powers of the Supreme Court on any Union List matter.

    Advisory jurisdiction

    • Article 143: the President may seek the Supreme Court's opinion on a question of law or fact of public importance; the Court advises only when he seeks it.UPPSC ×3
    • Second ground: disputes arising from a pre-Constitution treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement or similar instrument.
    • In the first case the Court may give or refuse its opinion; in the second case it is bound to give its opinion.
    • A full bench (5 members) hears a reference; the opinion given is not binding on the Government.
    • Under Article 143(1) the President can refer the process of appointment and transfer of Supreme Court and High Court judges.UPPSC
    • In August 2002 President Dr. Abdul Kalam sought advice under Article 143 on the Election Commission - Government controversy over Gujarat elections.
    • Issues referred: limits of Election Commission powers under Article 324, impact of Article 174 on them, and whether the Commission could recommend President's rule in a State.

    Writs and fundamental rights

    • Article 32 = Right to Constitutional Remedies; the Supreme Court issues directions, orders or writs to enforce Fundamental Rights (Part III).UPPSC
    • Enforcement of Fundamental Rights lies with both the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226).UPPSC ×2
    • Issuing writs is therefore not an exclusive power of the Supreme Court.UPPSC
    • High Court writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is wider: for fundamental rights, other constitutional rights and other purposes.

    Guardian of the Constitution

    • The Supreme Court is the final authority to interpret the Constitution and is the Guardian / Custodian of the Constitution.UPPSC
    • The Supreme Court is the highest court, a federal court, guarantor of citizens' fundamental rights and final interpreter of the Constitution.
    • The Constitution is the supreme law of India and a living document; it sets the political principles, structure, procedures, powers and duties of government institutions, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and duties of citizens.
    • The Supreme Court does not have exclusive jurisdiction on the constitutional validity of central laws; High Courts also have it.UPPSC

    Note from the book On the assertion "Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction on constitutional validity of central laws", UPPSC took both assertion and reason as true with reason explaining it, which is wrong.

    Judicial review

    • Judicial review = power of the judiciary to interpret the Constitution and declare any law or order of the legislature or executive void if it conflicts with the Constitution.UPPSC
    • The doctrine originated and developed in the USA; first propounded in Marbury vs Madison (1803) by Chief Justice John Marshall.
    • In India the power of judicial review is with both the Supreme Court and the High Courts.UPPSC
    • The Supreme Court has declared judicial review a part of the basic structure.
    • Judicial review exists in both India and the USA; in the UK Parliament is supreme and its law cannot be challenged in court.UPPSC
    • Article 13 provides for judicial review: pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with Part III are void, and the State shall not make a law that takes away or abridges Part III rights.
    • Articles establishing judicial review: 13, 32, 136, 137, 226 and 227.
    • Judicial review in India is based on procedure established by law (and supremacy of the Constitution).
    • A Constitution (Amendment) Act can be struck down if it removes the Right of Equality before law from Part III and puts it elsewhere (Article 13(2)).
    • The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 barred High Courts from deciding constitutional validity of central laws; the 43rd Amendment Act, 1977 restored the original position.
    • A High Court can invalidate a central law, and the Supreme Court can question a constitutional amendment that violates the basic structure.
    • The scope of judicial review is limited in India; the Constitution is "a bag of borrowings"; both true but the second does not explain the first.UPPSC
    • Three reasons for limited scope: review mainly when a law affects the basic structure; the Court has outlined the division of sovereign power among legislature, executive and judiciary; the huge size of the Constitution.
    • Due Process of Law in essence = the principle of natural justice; it ensures the law-making procedure is free from arbitrariness and irrationality.
    • Natural justice = fairness, reasonableness, equity and equality; a Common Law concept, like the American procedural due process.
    • Two principles of natural justice: "Nemo judex in causa sua" (no one a judge in his own cause; rule against bias) and "Audi alteram partem" (hear the other party; no one condemned unheard).
    • Natural justice is grounded in Articles 14 and 21; the Supreme Court recognised Due Process of Law in the Maneka Gandhi case.
    • Judicial process in India is based on procedure established by law, the Constitution, conventions and the due process of routine law, all together.
    • Article 14: the State shall not deny equality before law or equal protection of laws; equal protection is from the American Constitution, equality before law from the British Constitution.

    Basic structure

    • Keshavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala (1973): the Supreme Court propounded the Doctrine of Basic Structure; it is not from Indira Sawhney, Shankari Prasad or Rudal Shah cases.UPPSC ×3
    • A 13-judge bench, by 7:6 majority, held Parliament can amend the Constitution under Article 368 only so far as it does not damage or destroy the basic structure.
    • Constitutional amendments are subject to judicial review; a substantive non-legislative check on Parliament's amending power.
    • The source of the Basic Structure doctrine is judicial interpretation; it is not found in the Constitution.UPPSC
    • The Keshavananda view was approved in the Minerva Mills case, 1980.
    • Articles 32, 226 and 227 were declared part of the inviolable basic structure in Keshavananda Bharati.UPPSC
    • Judicial review by High Courts (Article 226) and the Supreme Court (Article 32) is an integral and essential feature; Article 227 = High Court's superintendence over all courts and tribunals in its territory.

    Important cases

    • Zamindari-related cases as given: Kameshwar Singh vs State of Bihar, Ramesh Thaper vs State of Madras, Motilal vs State of Uttar Pradesh, State of West Bengal vs Subodh Gopal.
    • Indra Sawhney: any reservation beyond 50 percent is liable to be struck down; the limit is treated as a constitutional prohibition.
    • Vishakha guidelines were superseded in 2013 by the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.
    • On 13 July 2005 a three-judge bench struck down the Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983 as unconstitutional under Article 355.UPPSC
    • The Court said the large number of illegal migrants from Bangladesh is an aggression on Assam and causes serious internal disturbance.
    • On 23 September 2003 the Supreme Court (Justice M.B. Shah) held that preference to women for Principal of a Government College for Girls does not violate Articles 14, 15 and 16.UPPSC

    Public Interest Litigation and judicial activism

    • PIL = Public Interest Litigation.
    • PIL was introduced by judicial initiative; it is a judicially developed process.UPPSC
    • PIL agrees with Article 39A: prompt social justice with the help of law.
    • Before the 1980s only the aggrieved party could approach courts; after the Emergency the Supreme Court let any member of the public or an NGO seek remedy where public interest is at stake.
    • Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer were among the first judges to admit PILs; they are known for initiating PIL.
    • Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer (15 November 1915 - 4 December 2014) was a Supreme Court judge, never Chief Justice of India; he is a progenitor of PIL.
    • PIL can be filed in both the High Courts and the Supreme Court.
    • First PIL case: Hussainara Khatoon vs State of Bihar (1979), on a petition by Kapila Hingorani, accepted by Justice P.N. Bhagwati; the CJI then was Y.V. Chandrachud.

    Note from the book For "who was CJI when PIL was introduced" none of the given options (Hidayatullah, Ahmadi, Bhagwati, Anand) is appropriate.

    • PIL widened locus standi, giving weaker sections effective access to justice; but PIL is not essential for the rule of law, it only strengthens it.UPPSC
    • Rule of law rests on basic structure, equality (Article 14), Article 32, Article 226 writs and judicial review, which existed before PIL.
    • PIL lets public-minded citizens reach court to seek justice for a person, group or society unable to reach it.UPPSC
    • The term and concept of PIL originated in the United States.UPPSC
    • In the USA public interest law grew from 19th-century movements as part of the legal aid movement; the first legal aid office opened in New York in 1876.
    • Judicial activism in India is related to Public Interest Litigation; it began in the mid-1970s on the Supreme Court's initiative.UPPSC
    • Justice A.S. Anand said judicial activism should not become judicial adventurism.
    • Judicial activism arose mainly from failure of the executive and legislature to act; judicial adventurism is its extreme form.

    Chapter 27 · States and Centre-State relations

    The Governor

    108 facts · 7 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. 155 · Appointment of the Governor by the President by warrant under his hand and seal (not removal)×3
    2. The draft Constitution's plan of an elected Governor was dropped: it meant another election (more expense), an elected Governor might think himself superior to the Chief Minister, and the Governor had to work under the parliamentary system.×3
    3. Article 159: before entering office the Governor takes an oath or affirmation before the Chief Justice of the High Court, or in his absence the senior-most judge available.×2
    4. Article 156(1): the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President (in effect the Union Government); he is responsible to the President.×2
    5. The Governor is appointed by the President, is head of the State's executive power, holds office at the President's pleasure, and normally for five years from the date he enters office [Article 156(3)].×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 27 UPPSC questions

    State executive and the office of Governor

    • The Constitution gives the States the same pattern of government as the Centre: a parliamentary system.
    • Articles 153 to 167 (Part VI) deal with the Government of the State.
    • The Governor is the executive (constitutional) head of the State.
    • All executive work of the State is formally done in the name of the Governor.
    ArticleSubject
    153Office of the Governor: there shall be a Governor for each State
    154Executive authority: executive power of the State vests in the Governor, used directly or through subordinate officers
    155Appointment of the Governor by the President by warrant under his hand and seal (not removal)UPPSC ×3
    156Term of office of the Governor
    157Qualifications for appointment as Governor
    158Conditions of the Governor's office
    159Oath or affirmation by the Governor
    161Pardoning power of the Governor
    163Council of Ministers to aid and advise; Governor's discretion
    164(1)Appointment of Chief Minister and Ministers
    165Advocate General
    200Assent to Bills; reserving a Bill for the President
    201Bills reserved for the President's consideration

    213Ordinance power of the Governor
    361Protection of President and Governors

    Why a nominated Governor

    • The draft Constitution's plan of an elected Governor was dropped: it meant another election (more expense), an elected Governor might think himself superior to the Chief Minister, and the Governor had to work under the parliamentary system.UPPSC ×3
    • In the Constituent Assembly Krishnamachari, B.G. Kher and J.B. Pant favoured election; B.R. Ambedkar and Jawaharlal Nehru favoured a nominated Governor.
    • A nominated Governor was accepted by general consensus.
    • Reasons given: election would raise election expenditure; nomination avoids a clash of political ambitions of Chief Minister and Governor (an election fought on major issues would lead to different policies); otherwise the Centre would lack effective control over the State.

    Appointment, qualifications and oath

    • Article 157: a Governor must be a citizen of India and have completed 35 years of age; the same person may be Governor of two or more States.UPPSC
    • Citizenship by birth is not required; eligibility for Lok Sabha membership is not required.
    • Article 158: the Governor shall not be a member of either House.
    • Generally one person is Governor of one State; the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 added to Article 153 that the same person can be Governor of two or more States.UPPSC
    • Article 159: before entering office the Governor takes an oath or affirmation before the Chief Justice of the High Court, or in his absence the senior-most judge available.UPPSC ×2
    • The Third Schedule does not contain the Governor's oath.
    • Sarkaria Commission (set up 1983, report 1988): Governor should be an eminent person from outside the State, a detached figure without intense political links, not active in politics in recent years.
    • Sarkaria Commission also said: the State Chief Minister should have a say in the appointment; the Governor should not be a member of the ruling party.

    Term and removal

    • Article 156(1): the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President (in effect the Union Government); he is responsible to the President.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 156(2): the Governor may resign by writing addressed to the President.
    • The Governor is appointed by the President, is head of the State's executive power, holds office at the President's pleasure, and normally for five years from the date he enters office [Article 156(3)].UPPSC ×2
    • A Governor continues in office after his term expires until his successor enters office; and he can be removed before five years.
    • The President may remove a Governor any time before five years, on the advice of the Council of Ministers; the State Legislature has no power to remove him.UPPSC ×2
    • The Constitution lays down no procedure for removal of a Governor.
    • The Constitution has no provision for impeachment of a Governor; "impeachment" is used only for the President.UPPSC
    • President: removed by impeachment under Article 61; a President or Vice-President can be removed for violating the Constitution.
    • Vice-President: removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by a majority of all its then members and agreed to by Lok Sabha (Article 67).
    • Chief Justice of India: removed by President's order after an address of each House with special majority, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Article 124(4)).
    • First Governor dismissed from office = Prabhudas Patwari, Governor of Tamil Nadu, October 1980.
    • Raghukul Tilak = first Governor of Rajasthan to be dismissed, August 1981.UPPSC

    Salary and immunities

    • Article 202(3)(a): the Governor's emoluments, allowances and other office expenditure are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
    • Article 158(3A): when one person is Governor of two or more States, emoluments and allowances are shared among the States in the proportion the President decides by order.UPPSC
    • Article 158(4): the Governor's emoluments and allowances cannot be reduced during his term; Article 361: no criminal proceedings against him during his term.
    • Article 361(1): the Governor is not answerable to any court for the exercise of the powers and duties of his office.
    • Article 361(2): no criminal proceedings can be started or continued against the President or a Governor in any court during the term of office.
    • Article 361(4): civil proceedings can be brought against the President or a Governor during the term after two months' written notice; so it is false that they cannot be sued for any act.UPPSC
    • The Governor may be dismissed for unconstitutional acts; the President can be impeached (Article 61).
    • Article 194(2): no member of a State Legislature is liable to court proceedings for anything said or any vote given in the Legislature or its committees; this immunity is absolute.
    • Article 74(2): courts cannot inquire whether any, and what, advice was given by Ministers to the President.UPPSC
    • True statements: President / Governor are immune from legal action for official acts; no court can compel a Governor to perform any duty; two months' written notice is needed for civil proceedings on personal acts.

    Executive powers and appointments

    • Article 164(1): the Governor appoints the Chief Minister, and the other Ministers on the advice of the Chief Minister.
    • Article 165: the Governor appoints as Advocate General a person qualified to be a High Court judge.
    • Members of the State Public Service Commission and the Advocate General are appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister.
    • High Court judges are not appointed by the Governor; they are appointed by the President.
    • Article 217(1): the President appoints High Court judges by warrant under his hand and seal after consulting the Chief Justice of India and the Governor; for other judges the Chief Justice of the High Court is also consulted.
    • The Governor cannot appoint High Court judges, but can nominate some members to the Legislative Council (Article 171(3)(e)).UPPSC
    • The Governor nominates one-sixth of the members of the Legislative Council.
    • The Governor is an integral part of the State Legislature (Governor + Upper House where bicameral + Lower House); he does have judicial powers.
    • He can address and send messages to the Legislature and summon, prorogue and dissolve the Legislative Assembly.
    • Earlier the Governor could nominate one Anglo-Indian member to the Assembly if the community was not adequately represented.
    • The Constitution (104th Amendment) Act, 2019 did not extend this beyond 25 January 2020; nomination of an Anglo-Indian member to Assemblies has ended.
    • The Governor has no emergency powers.

    Discretionary powers

    • Article 163(1): the Governor acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister, except where the Constitution requires him to act in his discretion; so the Constitution explicitly mentions discretion.
    • The President cannot on his own (suo motu) reserve a State Bill without the Governor reserving and sending it.
    • Discretionary powers: sending a report to the President for President's Rule (Article 356) and reserving Bills for the President (Article 200).
    • Not discretionary: appointing Ministers (on Chief Minister's advice, Article 164(1)) and making rules for convenient transaction of government business (Article 166(3)).
    • Governor acts in his discretion: asking the Government to prove majority in the Assembly; terminating a Chief Minister who lost the Assembly's confidence; giving or withholding assent or reserving a Bill; returning a Bill for reconsideration.UPPSC
    • He also uses discretion in imposing President's Rule and dissolving the Assembly; he is not authorised to consult the High Court.

    Bills

    • Article 200: on a Bill passed by the State Legislature the Governor may give assent, withhold assent, return it (if not a Money Bill) for reconsideration, or reserve it for the President.UPPSC
    • If the Legislature passes the Bill again, the Governor may give assent or reserve it for the President.
    • There is no time limit for the Governor to return an ordinary Bill; "as soon as possible" is not defined and is left to his discretion.
    • Article 201: when a Bill is reserved for the President, the President declares whether he assents or not.
    • If a Bill needing the Governor's recommendation was introduced and passed without it, the Act is not invalid once the Governor gives assent.

    Ordinances and pardon

    • Article 213: the Governor can promulgate an ordinance when the State Legislature is not in session and circumstances need immediate action.UPPSC ×2
    • An ordinance has the same force as an Act of the State Legislature; it must be laid before the Legislature (both Houses where there is a Council), so approval of the State Legislature is necessary.UPPSC
    • It ceases to operate six weeks after the Legislature reassembles, or earlier if a disapproving resolution is passed by the Assembly and agreed to by the Council, if any.
    • Article 161: the Governor can grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions, or suspend, remit or commute sentences for offences against laws within the State's executive power.
    • The Governor cannot pardon a death sentence.UPPSC

    Jammu and Kashmir, Union Territories and Rajpramukh

    10. 2025At present the Lt. Governor of Ladakh is Kavinder Gupta, since July 2025.
    • Jammu and Kashmir had special status under Article 370 (Part XXI: Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions).
    • Before 1965 the executive head of Jammu and Kashmir was elected by its Legislative Assembly; later the Governor was appointed by the President of India.
    • In 1965 the 6th Amendment to the State Constitution of J&K changed the name of the executive head from Sadar-e-Riyasat to Governor.UPPSC
    • Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019: UT of Jammu & Kashmir with a legislature and UT of Ladakh without a legislature.
    • Both UTs are administered by the President through a Lieutenant Governor appointed by him.
    • Article 239(1): every Union Territory is administered by the President, through an administrator appointed by him with a designation he specifies.UPPSC
    • In a Union Territory with a legislature the Chief Minister is appointed by the President, not the Lt. Governor; the Chief Minister of NCT of Delhi is appointed by the President (Article 239AA).
    • First Lieutenant Governor of UT of Jammu & Kashmir = Girish Chandra Murmu; Manoj Sinha became the 2nd on 7 August 2020.

    • Rajpramukh was an administrative title in India from 1949 until 1956.
    • On the recommendation of the States Reorganisation Commission, the office of Rajpramukh was abolished by the 7th Constitutional Amendment with effect from 1 November 1956.
    • The States Reorganisation Commission was set up by the Central Government in December 1953: Justice Fazal Ali, K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru.

    Chapter 28 · States and Centre-State relations

    The State Legislature

    157 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Article 169: Parliament may by law abolish or create a Legislative Council in a State, if the State Legislative Assembly passes a resolution to that effect.×5
    2. Madhya Pradesh has no Legislative Council, even though the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956 provides for it.×3
    3. State Legislative Councils cannot be dissolved but can be abolished (Article 169).×2
    4. Article 170(1): subject to Article 333, an Assembly has not more than 500 and not less than 60 members (generally), chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 33 UPPSC questions

    State Legislature: Articles and make-up

    • Articles 168 to 212 in Part VI of the Constitution deal with the State Legislature.
    • Article 168: State Legislature = Governor + Legislative Assembly + Legislative Council (where it exists); in other States = Governor + Legislative Assembly.
    • Article 168(2): where there are two Houses, one is the Legislative Council and the other the Legislative Assembly; where there is one House, it is the Legislative Assembly.
    • With two Houses, Legislative Council = Upper House and Legislative Assembly = Lower House.
    ArticleSubject
    Article 162Extension of executive power of the StateUPPSC
    Article 168Constitution of Legislatures in States
    Article 169Abolition or creation of Legislative Councils in States
    Article 170Composition of the Legislative Assemblies
    Article 171Composition of the Legislative Councils
    Article 173Qualification for membership of the State Legislature
    Article 176Special address by the Governor
    Article 178The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
    Article 179Vacation, resignation and removal of Speaker and Deputy Speaker of an Assembly
    Article 182Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council

    Article 199Definition of 'Money Bills'

    Legislative Council: creation and abolition

    • Article 169: Parliament may by law abolish or create a Legislative Council in a State, if the State Legislative Assembly passes a resolution to that effect.UPPSC ×5
    • The resolution needs a majority of the total membership of the Assembly and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
    • Article 169 applies notwithstanding anything in Article 168.
    • The Assembly's resolution under Article 169 does not impose an obligation on the Union Government to initiate legislation in Parliament.
    • State Legislative Councils cannot be dissolved but can be abolished (Article 169).UPPSC ×2
    • Rajya Sabha can neither be dissolved nor abolished.
    • Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies cannot be abolished but can be dissolved.

    States with Legislative Councils

    • At present only 6 States have Legislative Councils (bicameral legislatures): Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh.
    • Madhya Pradesh has no Legislative Council, even though the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956 provides for it.UPPSC ×3
    • Tamil Nadu has a unicameral legislature (no Legislative Council).
    • Rajasthan has no Legislative Council.UPPSC
    • Kerala, Himachal Pradesh and Delhi do not have Legislative Councils.
    • After the 1956 reorganisation, 7 out of the total 14 States had a bicameral legislature: Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Bombay (Maharashtra), Madras (Tamil Nadu), Mysore (Karnataka), Punjab, West Bengal.
    • Legislative Council abolished: West Bengal in 1969, Punjab in 1970, Tamil Nadu in 1986.
    • The Legislative Council in Jammu and Kashmir was established under the constitution adopted by Jammu and Kashmir in 1957.
    • The Legislative Council of the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir stands abolished since 31 October 2019.

    Legislative Council: size and composition

    • Article 171(1): Council strength must not exceed one-third of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly (so it cannot be larger than half of the Assembly), and must not be less than 40.UPPSC
    • Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council, with 100 members.
    • Article 171(3): nearly 5/6 of the Council members are elected and the remaining are nominated by the Governor.
    • One-third of the Council members are elected by the Legislative Assembly from persons who are not members of the Assembly.
    • One-third are elected by local bodies: Municipalities, District Boards or any other local authority specified by law of Parliament.
    • One-twelfth are elected by graduates of at least three years' standing residing in the State.
    • One-twelfth are elected by teachers of secondary schools with at least three years' teaching experience.
    • Industrialists are not a category that chooses Council members.
    • The remainder are nominated by the Governor from persons with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, the co-operative movement and social service.
    • Article 171(4): elected Council members are chosen by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, and by secret ballot.
    • Article 171(2): until Parliament by law otherwise provides, the composition of the Council is as provided in clause (3).
    • Presently the composition of Legislative Councils is under Section 10 and Schedule 3 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 (as amended), made by Parliament under Article 171(2).
    • Under this Act, only 10 of the 100 members of the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council (1/10) are nominated by the Governor.
    • Governor's nominees: nearly 1/7 in Andhra Pradesh, nearly 1/6 in Bihar, nearly 1/7 in Karnataka, nearly 1/7 in Telangana.
    • So there is no single fixed fraction of nominated members (not 1/3, 1/4 or 1/6 of the total strength).UPPSC

    Legislative Council: tenure and presiding officers

    • The Legislative Council, like the Council of States, is a permanent House; it is not subject to dissolution; one-third of members retire every second year, like the Rajya Sabha.
    • The tenure of a Council member is 6 years.
    • Minimum age for a member of the Legislative Council = 30 years.
    • Article 182: the Legislative Council chooses its Chairman and Deputy Chairman from amongst its members; the Governor does not nominate the Chairman.
    • The Council can remove its Chairman or Deputy Chairman by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council.

    Legislative Assembly: size and seats

    • The Legislative Assembly is composed of members elected by direct election on the basis of Universal Adult Suffrage from territorial constituencies.
    • Article 170(1): subject to Article 333, an Assembly has not more than 500 and not less than 60 members (generally), chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies.UPPSC ×2
    • Sikkim is an exception to the minimum of 60: its Assembly has 32 members, the smallest among States.UPPSC
    • Smallest Assembly among Union Territories = Puducherry (33).
    • Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Assembly, with 403 members.UPPSC
    • Article 170(2): each State is divided into territorial constituencies so that the ratio of population to seats is, as far as practicable, the same throughout the State.
    • 84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001: the number of members in State Assemblies stays the same until the figures of the first census after 2026 are published.
    • Article 332: seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assembly in proportion to their population.
    • Article 333 (earlier): the Governor could nominate one member of the Anglo-Indian community to the Assembly if he felt the community was not adequately represented.
    • The Constitution (104th Amendment) Act, 2019 did not extend Anglo-Indian nomination to State Assemblies beyond 25 January 2020.

    Uttar Pradesh403
    Himachal Pradesh68
    Uttarakhand70
    Arunachal Pradesh60

    Union Territories with Assemblies

    • Only three Union Territories have Legislative Assemblies: Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir.
    • Section 14(3) of the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019: J&K UT Assembly has 90 elected and 5 nominated members, plus 24 vacant constituencies in areas occupied by Pakistan (POK).
    • On 5 August 2019, Jammu and Kashmir became a Union Territory with a legislature and Ladakh a Union Territory without a legislature.
    • J&K and Ladakh have separate Lieutenant Governors.
    • The Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 fixed the tenure of the J&K Legislative Assembly at 5 years.
    • The tenure of the Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir was 6 years earlier; in a way it is not fixed but is deemed to be the tenure of the Legislative Assembly.
    • The leader of the majority party becomes the Chief Minister and holds office as long as he has the majority.

    Elections, qualifications and disqualification

    • Article 324: the Election Commission of India conducts the elections to State Assemblies / State Legislatures.UPPSC
    • Article 173: a member of the State Legislature must be (a) a citizen of India, (b) not less than 25 years for the Assembly and 30 years for the Council, (c) have other qualifications prescribed by or under a law of Parliament.
    • Being eligible to vote does not by itself qualify a person to be made a minister for six months; Article 173 qualifications apply.
    • Representation of the People Act, 1951: a person convicted of any offence and sentenced to imprisonment of not less than two years is disqualified from the date of conviction and for a further six years after release; this is not permanent.
    • Article 191 deals with the disqualification of members of the State Legislature.
    • Article 192: a question on disqualification under Article 191(1) is referred to the Governor, whose decision is final; he must first obtain the Election Commission's opinion and act according to it.UPPSC
    • Disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (defection) is decided by the Speaker in the Assembly and by the Chairman in the Council.
    • The State Legislative Assembly takes part in electing the President of India, members of Rajya Sabha and members of the Legislative Council; it does not take part in electing the Vice-President.

    Speaker of the Legislative Assembly

    • The Speaker is elected by the Assembly itself from amongst its members; usually he remains in office during the life of the Assembly.
    • The Speaker vacates office earlier if he ceases to be a member of the Assembly, resigns in writing to the Deputy Speaker, or is removed by a resolution passed by a majority.
    • Article 179(b): the Speaker gives his resignation to the Deputy Speaker.
    • Article 179: when the Assembly is dissolved, the Speaker does not vacate office until immediately before the first meeting of the Assembly after the dissolution.UPPSC
    • The Speaker exercises a casting vote in case of equality of votes.
    • The Speaker establishes the contact between the House and the Governor.
    • In the absence of the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker works as the Speaker.
    • The rights and functions of the Assembly Speaker are the same as those of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
    • Ramkishore Shukla held the offices of Protem Speaker, Speaker and Deputy Speaker in the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly.
    Newly elected presiding officer of Vidhan SabhaState
    Ramesh TawadkarGoaUPPSC
    Kultar SandhwanPunjab
    T. SatyabratManipur
    Ritu KhandariUttarakhand

    Sessions and procedure

    • Article 174(2): the Governor prorogues the Vidhan Sabha.
    • The Governor addresses the Assembly (both Houses assembled, where there is a Council) at the first session after each general election and the first session of each year, and informs the legislature of the causes of its summons.
    • When a State Legislature has no rule on a particular matter, it follows the Lok Sabha rule.
    • Article 189(3): until the State Legislature by law otherwise provides, quorum = 10 members or one-tenth of the total members of the House, whichever is greater.UPPSC
    • Article 210(1): business in the State Legislature is transacted in the official language(s) of the State, or in Hindi, or in English.
    • The Advocate-General has no right to vote in the proceedings of the State Legislature.
    • The State Legislature cannot discuss the conduct of a Judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court in the discharge of his duties.
    • The validity of proceedings of the State Legislature cannot be questioned on the ground of any alleged irregularity.
    • Order of proceedings in the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly: oath or affirmation → Governor's address → introduction of ministers → mention of death.
    • Rajasthan Assembly adjournment motion on a matter of public importance: needs the Speaker's consent, must be restricted to a specific matter of recent occurrence, and not more than one such motion at the same sitting.
    • An adjournment motion cannot raise a question of privilege and should not be framed in general terms.
    • Rajasthan Assembly: the Speaker does not refer Bills containing delegation of legislative powers to the Committee on Subordinate Legislation.
    • Rule 241 (duties of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation): the Committee selects for scrutiny such orders as it considers appropriate.
    • The Committee on Subordinate Legislation examines all "orders" framed under the Constitution or a statute delegating power to a subordinate authority; it may examine provisions of Bills that seek to delegate powers to make orders; this is done by Rule 240 of the Rajasthan Assembly Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business.
    • Rajasthan Assembly rules: the Home Department's estimates do not come under Estimates Committee 'A'.

    Bills and finance

    • Article 197: a Bill passed by the Assembly is transmitted to the Legislative Council; the Council can withhold it for 3 months the first time.UPPSC
    • When the Assembly passes the Bill a second time, the Council can hold it for up to 1 month; so the Council can detain an ordinary Bill for 4 months in total.UPPSC
    • The Speaker of the Vidhan Sabha decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill in the State.
    • Money Bills are introduced only in the Legislative Assembly.
    • Article 198(2): the Council must return a Money Bill with its recommendations within 14 days; the Assembly may accept or reject all or any of the recommendations.
    • Article 207(1): a Bill or amendment on matters in Article 199(1)(a) to (f) cannot be introduced or moved except on the Governor's recommendation, and cannot be introduced in a Legislative Council.UPPSC
    • The budget is presented by the Finance Minister and officials of the concerned Ministry.
    • If the budget is disclosed before being introduced in the Assembly, the Finance Minister must take individual responsibility and resign; punishment is provided in the Official Secrecy Act, 1923.
    • The State Legislature may by law establish the Contingency Fund of the State, like an imprest, into which sums fixed by such law are paid.UPPSC
    • The State Contingency Fund is placed at the disposal of the Governor, to make advances for unforeseen expenditure pending authorisation by the State Legislature under Article 205 or 206.UPPSC
    • The contingency fund is an account to meet urgent or unforeseen expenditure of the government.
    • Article 162: the State's executive power extends to matters on which the State Legislature can make laws; on matters where both the State Legislature and Parliament can legislate, it is subject to and limited by the executive power expressly given to the Union by the Constitution or a law of Parliament.

    Chief Minister and Council of Ministers

    • Articles 153 to 167 in Part VI deal with the State executive.
    • The State executive consists of the Governor, the Chief Minister, the Council of Ministers and the Advocate General.
    • Article 164(1): the Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor; other Ministers are appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister; Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Governor.
    • The Chief Minister and other Ministers are not selected by the Governor; the Chief Minister is chosen by the members of the majority party in the Assembly and formally appointed by the Governor.UPPSC
    • The Chief Minister generally presides over the Cabinet meetings.
    • Article 163(1): a Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister aids and advises the Governor, except where the Constitution requires him to act in his discretion; so not all his functions are on the Chief Minister's advice.UPPSC
    • Article 163(3): whether any, and what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the Governor cannot be inquired into in any court.
    • Article 164(2): the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the State.
    • Article 164(3): before a Minister enters office, the Governor administers the oaths of office and secrecy as per the forms in the Third Schedule.
    • Article 164(1A), added by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003: total Ministers including the Chief Minister must not exceed 15% of the total members of the Legislative Assembly.
    • The number of Ministers including the Chief Minister must not be less than 12 in any State.UPPSC
    • Article 164(4): a Minister who is not a member of the State Legislature for six consecutive months ceases to be a Minister at the end of that period.
    • Article 164(5): salaries and allowances of Ministers are fixed by the State Legislature by law; until then they are as specified in the Second Schedule.UPPSC
    • Article 167 (duties of the Chief Minister): communicate to the Governor all decisions of the Council of Ministers on State administration and proposals for legislation; furnish such information as the Governor calls for; and, if the Governor requires, submit to the Council a matter decided by a Minister but not considered by the Council.UPPSC
    • The Chief Minister's participation in National Development Council meetings is an administrative duty, not a constitutional duty.

    Chief Ministers: firsts and names

    • Sucheta Kriplani was the first woman Chief Minister of any Indian State; she became Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh in 1963.UPPSC
    • The first Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh was Pt. Ravishankar Shukla; he served from 1 November 1956 to 31 December 1956.
    • Dr. Mohan Yadav is the 19th and current Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh, since 13 December 2023.
    • Govind Narayan Singh, the fifth Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh, did not hold the office of Leader of the House in the MP Legislative Assembly during his tenure.

    State Secretariat and Chief Secretary

    • The State Secretariat is the apex wing of State administration and the centre of the State's political and administrative functions; it is the main force forming the principles of procedure for the State Government's work.
    • The Chief Secretary is chosen by the Chief Minister and appointed by the Governor; there is no fixed tenure of the Chief Secretary.
    • The Chief Secretary is the head of the State's administrative machinery and controls the administrative body of the State.
    • In the State Secretariat, every file is sent to the Cabinet through the Chief Secretary.

    Other State facts

    1. 1867The Goa Civil Code is based on the Portuguese Civil Code (Codigo Civil Portugues) of 1867, introduced in Goa in 1870 with some modifications.
    2. 1992After the Ayodhya incident in 1992, the Vidhan Sabhas of the BJP-ruled States Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan were dissolved; Bihar's was not.
    3. 1995Bihar came under President's rule in 1995.
    4. 2004Andhra Pradesh gave reservation to Muslims in jobs and education in 2004; the Andhra Pradesh High Court cancelled it.UPPSC
    5. 2007In 2007 Andhra Pradesh limited the Muslim reservation to 4 per cent within the 50% limit; the High Court cancelled it again.
    6. 2025Uttarakhand enforced the Uniform Civil Code on 27 January 2025.
    • After the Ayodhya incident in 1992, the Vidhan Sabhas of the BJP-ruled States Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan were dissolved; Bihar's was not.
    • Bihar came under President's rule in 1995.
    • Andhra Pradesh gave reservation to Muslims in jobs and education in 2004; the Andhra Pradesh High Court cancelled it.UPPSC
    • In 2007 Andhra Pradesh limited the Muslim reservation to 4 per cent within the 50% limit; the High Court cancelled it again.
    • The Supreme Court, by an interim decision, accepted the Andhra Pradesh reservation; the final decision is awaited, pending before a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court.
    • Goa was the only State to have the Common Civil Code.UPPSC
    • The Goa Civil Code is based on the Portuguese Civil Code (Codigo Civil Portugues) of 1867, introduced in Goa in 1870 with some modifications.
    • Uttarakhand enforced the Uniform Civil Code on 27 January 2025.

    Chapter 29 · States and Centre-State relations

    The High Court

    125 facts · 0 repeated by UPPSC

    Quick quiz: 10 of 12 UPPSC questions

    High Court: place and Articles

    • The High Court occupies the top position in the judicial administration of the State.
    • The Constitution provides a High Court for each State.
    • The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 authorised Parliament to set up a common High Court for two or more States, or for two or more States and a Union Territory.
    • Articles 214 to 231 in Part VI deal with the organisation, independence, jurisdiction, powers and procedures of the High Courts.
    • High Courts are instituted as constitutional courts under Part VI, Chapter V, Article 214.
    • The institution of the High Court originated in India in 1862; High Courts were set up at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.
    • In 1866 the High Court of Judicature for the North-Western Provinces came into existence at Agra; its seat was shifted from Agra to Allahabad in 1869.
    ArticleProvision
    Article 214Every State will have a High Court
    Article 215Every High Court is a Court of Record
    Article 216High Court = Chief Justice + such other judges as the President deems necessary to appoint
    Article 217(1)Appointment by the President; retirement age 62; resignation; removal
    Article 220Restriction on practice after being a permanent High Court Judge
    Article 222Transfer of a judge from one High Court to another
    Article 223Acting Chief Justice of a High Court
    Article 224Additional and acting Judges
    Article 226Power of High Courts to issue writs
    Article 227Superintendence over all courts and tribunals
    Article 233Appointment of District Judges
    Article 235Control over subordinate courts
    Article 236(a)Meaning of the expression 'district judge'
    • Court of Record: the judgements, proceedings and acts of the High Court are recorded for perpetual memory and testimony.
    • These records have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned when produced before any subordinate court; they are recognised as legal precedents and legal references.
    • A Court of Record also has the power to punish for contempt of itself.

    Judges: number and appointment

    • Article 216: the President decides the number of judges of a High Court; the judges must not exceed the maximum number the President fixes by order for that Court.
    • Article 217(1): every Judge of a High Court is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal; the Governor does not appoint them.UPPSC
    • The President appoints them after consulting the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State and (for judges other than the Chief Justice) the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned.
    • Qualifications of a High Court Judge: citizen of India; and held a judicial office in the territory of India for at least ten years, or been an advocate of a High Court (or High Courts in succession) for at least ten years.
    • Article 223: the President can appoint a High Court Judge as acting Chief Justice when the office of Chief Justice is vacant, or the Chief Justice is temporarily absent or unable to perform his duties.
    • Article 224: additional and acting Judges are appointed in the High Court.UPPSC
    • Article 224(1): on a temporary increase in business or arrears of work, the President may appoint duly qualified persons as Additional Judges for a period not exceeding two years.
    • Article 224(2): when a Judge other than the Chief Justice is absent, unable to perform duties or acting as Chief Justice, a duly qualified person may act as a Judge until the permanent Judge resumes duties.
    • Article 224(3): no additional or acting Judge holds office after attaining 62 years of age.
    • Justice H.R. Khanna, Chairman of the 8th Law Commission, recommended in its 80th Report ('The Method of Appointment of Judges') that at least one-third of the judges of a High Court should be from other States.

    Judges: transfer, tenure, salary and removal

    • Article 222: the President can transfer a judge from one High Court to another after consulting the Chief Justice of India.
    • Third Judges case (1998): for a transfer, the Chief Justice of India must consult the Collegium of the four seniormost Supreme Court judges and the Chief Justices of the two High Courts concerned; his sole opinion is not consultation.
    • A High Court Judge holds office until the age of 62 years; fixed under Article 217(1) by the 15th Constitutional Amendment, 1963; before that it was 60 years.
    • The 114th Amendment Bill (2010) aimed to raise the High Court retirement age from 62 to 65 years; it could not be passed.
    • Article 217(1)(a): a High Court Judge resigns by writing addressed to the President.
    • Article 217(1)(b): a High Court Judge is removed by the President in the manner provided in Article 124(4) for a Supreme Court Judge; the mode of removal is the same.
    • Grounds of removal: proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
    • The President can issue the removal order only after an address by Parliament is presented to him in the same session, passed by a special majority.
    • Special majority = majority of the total membership of each House and not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting in each House.
    • Article 220: a former permanent High Court Judge cannot plead or act in any court or before any authority in India, except the Supreme Court and the other High Courts.
    • Article 202(3)(d): salaries and allowances of High Court Judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.UPPSC
    • Article 112(3)(d): the pension of High Court Judges is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.UPPSC
    • Justice Soumitra Sen, former Judge of the Calcutta High Court, was charged with misappropriation of funds; Rajya Sabha passed an impeachment motion against him in 2011.
    • The motion was to come before Lok Sabha on 5 September 2011, but he resigned on 1 September 2011.
    • Shri Rajeev Gupta became Chief Justice of the Chhattisgarh High Court on 2 February 2008; before that he was Chief Justice of the Uttarakhand High Court.
    • The current Chief Justice of the Chhattisgarh High Court is Justice Ramesh Sinha.

    Number of High Courts and their territory

    • At present there are 25 High Courts; 7 of them have jurisdiction over more than one State / Union Territory.
    • Punjab, Haryana and the Union Territory of Chandigarh have a common High Court; the NCT of Delhi has its own High Court.
    • Delhi, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are the Union Territories with a High Court: Delhi has its own; Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh share a common High Court.
    • The NCT of Delhi is the only Union Territory with a separate High Court.
    • The other Union Territories fall under the jurisdiction of different State High Courts.
    • Parliament can extend the jurisdiction of a High Court.
    • In 2008 there were 21 High Courts; at present there are 25.
    • Excluding Union Territories, three High Courts have jurisdiction over more than one State: Gauhati, Bombay, Punjab and Haryana.
    • Bombay High Court has jurisdiction over more than one State / Union Territory.
    • The High Courts of Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura were established by the Government in January 2013 and started working in March 2013.UPPSC
    • Before March 2013 Manipur had no High Court of its own; it was under the Gauhati High Court.

    Calcutta (Kolkata)West Bengal; Andaman and Nicobar Islands
    Punjab and HaryanaPunjab, Haryana, Chandigarh
    Madras (Chennai)Puducherry also

    • Currently the Bombay and Gauhati High Courts have 3 Benches each, the largest number.UPPSC

    Note from the book Largest number of Benches has two accepted answers: Bombay High Court and Gauhati High Court.

    Jurisdiction and powers

    • Main jurisdictions of a High Court: original, appellate and supervisory.
    • Advisory jurisdiction (Article 143) belongs to the Supreme Court, not to High Courts.UPPSC
    • The second appeal to the High Court is within its appellate jurisdiction.
    • High Courts may accept a petition of Public Interest Litigation.
    • Article 227: every High Court has superintendence over all courts and tribunals in its territory, except those relating to the Armed Forces.
    • Article 235: the High Court has control over all other subordinate courts in the State.
    • The Chief Justice of a High Court acts in a dual capacity: judicial and administrative.
    • In his administrative capacity the Chief Justice of a High Court is subject to the writ jurisdiction of any other Judge of the High Court.
    • The Chief Justice controls, observes, superintends and administers the lower courts.
    • Wilful disobedience or non-compliance of court orders and use of derogatory language about judicial behaviour amount to Contempt of Court.
    • Judicial activism cannot be practised without punitive powers to punish contempt; this is true but does not explain the contempt rule.
    • The Babri Mosque / Ramjanmabhoomi dispute came before the Allahabad High Court as a Title Suit: two communities claimed the same land and property.
    • Allahabad High Court, in Rahmatullah vs State of UP (1994), held that divorce by saying 'Talaq' three times is illegal; it violates Articles 14 and 15.
    • The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019: any pronouncement of talaq by a Muslim husband upon his wife, spoken, written, electronic or in any other manner, is void and illegal.

    Writs

    • Under Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Court), five writs are issued: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto.
    • The Supreme Court's writ power is limited to Part III (Fundamental Rights); a High Court can issue writs for Part III rights and for any other purpose (legal rights).UPPSC
    • So High Courts are in a better position than the Supreme Court to protect the rights of citizens.UPPSC
    • Certiorari: issued by a higher court to a lower court to send up the record of a case, with all files, evidence and documents, for review; usually to overrule the lower court's judgment.UPPSC
    • Certiorari examines the functioning of a subordinate court.UPPSC
    • Certiorari is one of the mechanisms that protect the fundamental rights of citizens.
    • Prohibition means "to prohibit, prevent, forbid or restrain": a superior court orders a lower court or tribunal to stop proceedings beyond its jurisdiction or contrary to natural justice.
    • Prohibition is issued when the procedure is pending in court; when a lower court hears a case outside its jurisdiction, the upper court takes over the case.UPPSC
    • Prohibition applies only to judicial and quasi-judicial bodies; it cannot be enforced against administrative agencies, statutory authorities, or private persons or enterprises.
    • Mandamus will not lie against a private organisation unless it is entrusted with a public duty; it will lie against a government company.
    • Any public-minded person can be a petitioner for the writ of Quo Warranto.

    District Judge and subordinate courts

    • Article 233(1): appointment, posting and promotion of District Judges are made by the Governor in consultation with the High Court having jurisdiction in that State.
    • The District Judge is the highest judicial authority in the district; he has judicial and administrative powers and supervisory powers over all subordinate courts in the district.
    • Article 236(a): 'district judge' includes judge of a city civil court, additional district judge, joint district judge, assistant district judge, chief judge of a small cause court, chief presidency magistrate, additional chief presidency magistrate, sessions judge, additional sessions judge and assistant sessions judge.
    • 'District judge' does not include a Tribunal judge.

    Advocates, prisons and custody

    • The Advocates Act, 1961 aims to create a single class of legal practitioners called 'advocates'.
    • Government law officers, legal firms, corporate lawyers and patent attorneys are all recognised as advocates.
    • The Act provides for autonomous Bar Councils, one for all India and one for each State; the Bar Council of India lays down rules on legal education and recognition of law colleges.
    • 'Prisons / persons detained therein' is a State subject under entry 4 of the State List.
    • Prisons are governed by the Prisons Act, 1894, which gave Provincial Governments (now States) the power to make rules on prisons; so prison management vests solely with State Governments.
    • The Ministry of Home Affairs has finalised a comprehensive 'Model Prisons Act, 2023' as a guiding document for States to adopt.
    • Police custody: police have physical custody of the accused, who is lodged in a police station lock-up.
    • Judicial custody: the accused is in the custody of the concerned Magistrate and is lodged in jail.
    • When police take a person into custody, the Cr.P.C. applies and they must produce him before a Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest.
    • During judicial custody the police officer in charge cannot interrogate the suspect, unless the court allows it as necessary.
    • Cr.P.C. Section 167, Gian Singh vs State (Delhi Administration) 1981: the Magistrate can direct the place and manner of interrogation; interrogation by permission does not change the nature of custody.
    • A person can generally be detained under Preventive Detention for a maximum of 3 months; under certain conditions it may exceed 3 months.

    Lok Adalat, Gram Nyayalaya and mobile courts

    • Lok Adalat (People's Court) is an alternative dispute resolution mechanism; it settles cases pending in court or at the pre-litigation stage.
    • A Lok Adalat can take up civil cases (including marriage and family) and compoundable criminal cases.
    • A Lok Adalat is presided over by a sitting or retired judicial officer as chairman, with two other members, usually a lawyer and a social worker; the composition is not fixed.
    • The consent of both parties is the most important factor; a matter cannot be forced into a Lok Adalat.
    • Once the parties agree to go to the Lok Adalat, neither party can walk away from its decision.
    • Money claims are easier to settle in Lok Adalats, as mostly only the quantum is in dispute.
    • The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 sets up Gram Nyayalayas at the grass-root level to give citizens access to justice at their doorstep.
    • Section 11: a Gram Nyayalaya has both civil and criminal jurisdiction, only for disputes and cases specified in the Act's Schedule.
    • Section 27: the district court, in consultation with the District Magistrate, prepares a panel of village-level social workers (as conciliators).
    • Mobile courts were first imagined by former President Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.
    • The first mobile court of India was set up in August 2007 in Mewat district, Haryana; it was inaugurated by the then Chief Justice K.G. Balakrishnan.
    • Mobile courts aim to take civil and criminal justice closer to people in remote areas, saving them the cost of travelling to distant courts.
