    Chapter 30 · States and Centre-State relations

    The Centre-State Relations

    136 facts · 8 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The Sarkaria Commission was set up to review relations between the Union and the States and suggest ways to strengthen them.×5
    2. Part XI deals with relations between the Union and the States: Legislative Relations (Articles 245–255) and Administrative Relations (Articles 256–263).×2
    3. The Seventh Schedule divides legislative subjects in three lists: List I (Union List), List II (State List), List III (Concurrent List).×2
    4. Article 248: residuary powers of legislation (matters not in the Concurrent or State List) vest exclusively in Parliament / the Union.×2
    5. Article 249(2): a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249(1) remains in force for a period not exceeding one year.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 33 UPPSC questions

    Basis of Centre-State relations

    • The Constitution, being federal in structure, divides all powers (legislative, executive and financial) between the Centre and the States.
    • Part XI deals with relations between the Union and the States: Legislative Relations (Articles 245–255) and Administrative Relations (Articles 256–263).UPPSC ×2
    • Centre-State relations are influenced by: provisions of the Constitution, the planning process, conflict of political interests, and the dominance of desire to dictate.
    • Planning is done by the Union; with different parties in power at the Centre and in a State, conflict of interest and a desire to dominate arise, which hampers the country's growth.
    • Centre-State relations depend upon constitutional provisions, conventions and practices, judicial interpretations and mechanisms for dialogue.UPPSC
    • A federal polity involves relations between Union and States, relations among States, mechanism for cooperation and mechanism for solving disputes.UPPSC
    • The Centre's control over the States in the planning process has been termed 'Municipal Relations'.
    • It promotes relationships and strategic partnerships between levels of government and with non-governmental organisations at all levels.
    • The Central Government is more empowered and has more resources than the States; States lack sufficient resources and depend on the Centre, hence the growing demand to review Centre-State relations.UPPSC
    PartSubject
    Part IIIFundamental Rights
    Part IVDirective Principles of State Policy
    Part VIThe States
    Part XThe Scheduled and Tribal Areas
    Part XIRelations between the Union and the States
    Part XIIFinance, Property, Contracts and SuitsUPPSC
    Part XIIITrade, Commerce and Intercourse within the Territory of India
    • Originally the Constitution had 22 Parts.

    Legislative relations: Articles and lists

    • Articles 245 and 246 regulate the distribution of power through the three lists.UPPSC
    • Article 245: extent of laws made by Parliament and State Legislatures; Parliament can make laws for the whole or any part of India, a State Legislature for the whole or any part of the State.
    • Article 246: subject matter of laws made by Parliament and by State Legislatures.
    • Article 246(1): Parliament has exclusive power to make laws on List I (Union List).
    • Article 246(2): Parliament and, subject to clause (3), the State Legislature also can make laws on List III (Concurrent List).
    • Article 246(3): the State Legislature has exclusive power to make laws for the State on List II (State List), subject to clauses (1) and (2).
    • Article 246(4): Parliament can make laws on any matter for any part of India not included in a State, even if the matter is in the State List.
    • The Seventh Schedule divides legislative subjects in three lists: List I (Union List), List II (State List), List III (Concurrent List).UPPSC ×2
    ListSubjects originallySubjects at present
    Union List9798
    State List6659
    Concurrent List4752
    • Both the Union and the States can make laws on Concurrent List subjects; in a conflict, the Union law prevails.UPPSC
    • 'Economic and social planning' and 'infants and minors' are in the Concurrent List; both Central and State Governments can make laws on them.UPPSC
    • Article 246A (inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016): notwithstanding Articles 246 and 254, Parliament and every State Legislature can make laws on goods and services tax imposed by the Union or by that State.
    • Article 247: Parliament can provide for the establishment of certain additional courts.

    Residuary powers

    • Article 248: residuary powers of legislation (matters not in the Concurrent or State List) vest exclusively in Parliament / the Union.UPPSC ×2
    • Residuary subjects = matters not mentioned in the Union List, State List or Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule.
    • Residuary subjects arise from changing circumstances, advances in technology or new policy needs.
    • Examples of residuary subjects: cyber laws, space research, atomic energy, artificial intelligence regulations, foreign trade policies.
    • In other federal set-ups, such as the USA, residuary powers are often given to the States.
    • The Indian Union is an example of a strong Union, as residuary powers rest with Parliament.

    Parliament's power over State List

    • Article 249: power of Parliament to legislate on GST under Article 246A or on any State List matter in the national interest.UPPSC
    • If the Rajya Sabha resolves that it is necessary in the national interest, Parliament becomes competent to make laws on that State List matter.
    • The resolution must be supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
    • Article 249(2): a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249(1) remains in force for a period not exceeding one year.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 250(1): Parliament can legislate on GST under Article 246A or any State List matter while a proclamation of emergency is in operation.
    • Article 251: if laws made by Parliament under Articles 249 and 250 are inconsistent with State laws, the laws made by Parliament prevail.
    • Article 252: Parliament can legislate for two or more States by consent; any other State may adopt such legislation.
    • Article 253: Parliament can make laws on any State List matter to implement international treaties, agreements and conventions.
    • Article 253 enables the Central Government to fulfil its international obligations and commitments.

    Administrative relations

    • Articles 256 to 263 in Part XI deal with administrative relations between the Centre and the States.
    • Article 256 (obligation of States and the Union): State executive power must ensure compliance with laws of Parliament and existing laws applying in the State; the Union's executive power extends to giving necessary directions to a State for that purpose.UPPSC
    • Article 257 (control of the Union over States in certain cases): State executive power must not impede or prejudice the Union's executive power; the Union may give necessary directions to States.
    • Article 258: power of the Union to confer powers on States; the President may, with the State Government's consent, entrust to it functions relating to any matter of Union executive power.
    • Article 262: adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-State rivers or river valleys (Parliament's power).
    • Inter-State Water Disputes Act = 1956; National Water Policy = 1987.
    • The River Boards Act was enacted and came into force in 1956, not 1970.UPPSC
    • Article 365: effect of failure to comply with, or give effect to, directions given by the Union.
    • Article 360: provisions as to financial emergency.
    • Article 368: provisions for the amendment of the Constitution.

    Inter-State Council

    • Article 263 of the Constitution provides for the Inter-State Council, to investigate and discuss subjects of common interest and co-ordinate relations between the Centre and States and among States.UPPSC ×2
    • The President is empowered to establish the Inter-State Council, by order, whenever he feels it would serve the public interest.UPPSC
    • The Inter-State Council was set up by a Presidential order dated 28 May 1990; the first ISC was established in May 1990 and constituted in December 1990.
    • The Sarkaria Commission recommended a permanent Inter-State Council under Article 263, to be called the Inter-Governmental Council; the Inter-State Council was set up on its recommendation.UPPSC
    • The name Inter-Governmental Council was suggested to distinguish it from other bodies founded under the same Article 263.
    • The Commission wanted it as an independent national forum for consultation with a well-defined mandate under Article 263.
    • The Janata Dal Government headed by V.P. Singh established the Inter-State Council in 1990.
    • Inter-State Council members: Prime Minister (Chairman); Chief Ministers of all States; Chief Ministers of UTs having Legislative Assemblies; Administrators of UTs without Legislative Assemblies; Governors of States under President's rule; six Central Cabinet Ministers, including the Home Minister, nominated by the Prime Minister.
    • The Council is a recommendatory body on inter-State, Centre-State and Centre-Union Territory relations.
    • Of the Inter-State Council, the National Security Council and the Zonal Councils, only the Inter-State Council was established under the provisions of the Constitution.
    • The National Security Council was set up by an executive decision with the Prime Minister's approval, not under any Article.
    • The National Development Council and the Governors' Conference are extra-constitutional and extra-legal devices.

    Zonal Councils and other councils

    • Zonal (regional) Councils are statutory bodies, not constitutional bodies; set up under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, an Act of Parliament.UPPSC ×2
    • They advise on matters of common interest to each of the five zones; they are advisory bodies.
    • Originally five Zonal Councils: Northern, Central, Eastern, Western and Southern.
    • The Union Home Minister is the Chairman of every Zonal Council.
    • The sixth regional council, for the North East, was formed in 1971.
    • Chandigarh, though not a State, is included in a Zonal Council; so are Delhi, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, and Puducherry.
    • The North Eastern States (Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Tripura, Mizoram, Meghalaya, Nagaland) are not in the Zonal Councils; the North Eastern Council looks after their special problems.
    • Regional councils act as 'Sub-Federal Links' of the Indian federal system and pave the way for co-operation and integration among the States.
    • They are a platform to resolve Centre-State and inter-State differences through free and fair discussion and consultation.
    • They are a regional platform for economically, politically and culturally interconnected States, focusing on regional matters while keeping the national perspective.
    • The North Eastern Council (NEC) was established by the North Eastern Council Act, 1971, initially as an apex advisory body for balanced and coordinated development of the seven North Eastern States.
    • NEC is the nodal agency for economic and social development of the North Eastern Region: Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura.
    • NEC Act amendment of December 2002: Sikkim was added as the 8th member State; NEC became a statutory Regional Planning Body.
    • Amended Section 3(1): NEC comprises the Governors and Chief Ministers of the constituent States and three members nominated by the President.
    • Amended Section 3(3): the President nominates the Chairman of the NEC (need not be from the other members) and may nominate a member as Vice-Chairman.
    • At present the Union Home Minister is ex-officio Chairman (notification of 7 July 2018) and the Minister of DoNER is ex-officio member and Vice-Chairman (24 August 2021).
    • The Jharkhand Area Autonomous Council was formed on 8 August 1995; it comprised 18 districts of Santhal Pargana and Chota Nagpur.
    • National integration involves political, economic, social, cultural and psychological dimensions and their inter-relations; the National Integration Council was formed in 1962, not 1961.UPPSC

    Commissions on Centre-State relations

    • The Sarkaria Commission was set up to review relations between the Union and the States and suggest ways to strengthen them.UPPSC ×5
    • It was formed on 9 June 1983 as a three-member commission under Justice R.S. Sarkaria, a retired Supreme Court Judge.
    • The other two members were B. Shivaraman and Dr. S.R. Sen.UPPSC
    • The Sarkaria Commission submitted its final report in January 1988; it had 247 recommendations in 19 chapters.

    Note from the book Year of the Sarkaria report: Bihar Public Service Commission gave 1987 as its answer, which is not correct.

    • The Sarkaria Commission said President's Rule (Article 356) must be used only in rare or exceptional cases, because Article 356 had been misused several times.
    • Often President's Rule was declared without considering other provisions.
    • The Rajamannar Committee and the Punchhi Commission are also associated with Centre-State relations.
    • The Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998) was on state funding of elections, not Union-State relations.UPPSC
    • It recommended state funds only for national and state parties allotted a symbol, not for independent candidates, and in the form of certain facilities.

    Financial relations: Articles

    • Articles 264 to 293 in Part XII deal with Centre-State financial relations.
    • Distribution of revenues between the Union and the States is under Articles 268 to 281: duties and taxes levied by the Union, grants-in-aid, constitution and functions of the Finance Commission.UPPSC
    ArticleProvision
    Article 265No tax shall be levied or collected except by the authority of law
    Article 266(1)Consolidated Fund of India: all revenues, all loans and all money received in repayment of loans by the Union Government
    Article 267(1)Contingency Fund of India
    Article 267(2)State Legislature may by law establish the Contingency Fund of the State, in the nature of an imprest

    Taxes and their sharing

    • Article 270: taxes on income other than agricultural income are levied and collected by the Government of India and distributed between the Union and the States.
    • Presently all taxes and duties in the Union List, except those in Articles 268, 269 and 269A, are levied by the Union and divided between the Union and the States.
    • Stamp duty on financial transactions is imposed by the Union Government but collected and appropriated by the State Government (Article 268).
    • Taxes on transactions in stock exchanges and futures markets belong to the Union List; under Article 270 they are levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the States.UPPSC
    • Land revenue is a tax exclusively imposed and collected by the States; it is entry 45 of the State List.
    • Entry 45 covers land revenue, assessment and collection of revenue, maintenance of land records, survey for revenue purposes and records of rights, and alienation of revenues.
    • Taxes on agricultural income are entry 46 of the State List; so the Constitution itself assigns agricultural income tax to the States.
    • Article 276(2): total tax on professions, trades, callings and employments payable by a person to the State or local bodies cannot exceed Rs. 2,500 per annum; raised from Rs. 250 by the 60th Amendment Act, 1988.UPPSC ×2

    Finance Commission, grants and borrowing

    • Article 280(1): the President constitutes a Finance Commission within 2 years of the commencement of the Constitution and thereafter every fifth year, or earlier if he considers necessary.
    • The Finance Commission is considered a quasi-judicial body, as it has certain powers of a civil court.
    • The Finance Commission recommends to the President the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States (tax sharing); this is its core responsibility.
    • Article 281: the President lays every recommendation of the Finance Commission before both Houses of Parliament, with an explanatory memorandum on action taken.
    • Present means of resource transfer from Centre to States: tax sharing, grants-in-aid and centrally sponsored schemes.
    • Transfer for plan implementation under the Gadgil formula is not a means of resource allocation at present.
    • Article 282: the Union or a State may make grants for any public purpose, even if Parliament or the State Legislature cannot make laws on that purpose.
    • Article 293(1): a State can borrow only within the territory of India, on the security of the Consolidated Fund of the State, within limits fixed by its Legislature by law, and can give guarantees within such limits; so a State cannot take foreign loans directly.UPPSC
    • The Supreme Court is the main agency to resolve fiscal disputes between the Centre and the States, under Article 131.UPPSC

    Trade and suits

    • Article 301: subject to the other provisions of Part XIII, trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free.
    • Article 300: the Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union, and a State Government by the name of the State.
    • They may sue or be sued in like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces or Indian States could have, subject to laws of Parliament or the State Legislature.
    • Pending legal proceedings at the commencement of the Constitution: the Union of India is substituted for the Dominion of India, and the corresponding State for a Province or Indian State.

    Chapter 31 · States and Centre-State relations

    Emergency Provisions

    77 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Grounds: security of India or any part of it is threatened by war, external aggression or armed rebellion.×6
    2. Financial Emergency has never been declared in India; Article 360 has not been used so far.×3
    3. The proclamation is laid before each House and ceases after one month unless approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament.×2
    4. Rights under Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended in any case.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 19 UPPSC questions

    Types of emergency

    • Emergency provisions are in Part XVIII, Articles 352 to 360; they enable the Central Government to meet any abnormal situation effectively.
    • The Constitution envisages three types of emergency.UPPSC
    ArticleEmergency
    Article 352National Emergency: war, external aggression or armed rebellion
    Article 356President's Rule: failure of constitutional machinery in a State
    Article 360Financial Emergency: threat to the financial stability or credit of India
    • The President can declare an emergency for external aggression (Article 352), failure of constitutional machinery in States (Article 356) and financial crisis (Article 360).UPPSC
    • During an emergency the Central Government becomes all-powerful; the Union's executive power extends to directing any State on how its executive power is to be exercised.
    • Article 355: duty of the Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance and to ensure every State Government is carried on as per the Constitution.UPPSC
    • Article 365 deals with the failure of a State to comply with directions given by the Union.
    • K.M. Nambiar, opposing the President's Rule provisions, called the emergency power of the President "a fraud on the Constitution".UPPSC
    • The Indian Constitution is regarded as federal, and as a combination of unitary and federal elements; failure of State constitutional machinery is dealt with by Article 356, not Article 352.

    National Emergency: grounds and proclamation

    • Article 352 deals with the Proclamation of (National) Emergency by the President.
    • Grounds: security of India or any part of it is threatened by war, external aggression or armed rebellion.UPPSC ×6
    • The proclamation may cover the whole of India or the part of the territory specified in it.
    • A proclamation can be made even before the actual occurrence, if the President is satisfied there is imminent danger; an emergency may take place at any time, but that does not explain Article 352.UPPSC
    • The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion'.
    • 'Internal disturbance' was the original third ground; the expression was too vague and had a wider connotation.
    • So a National Emergency can no longer be declared on the ground of internal disturbance, as was done in 1975.
    • Article 352(3): the President cannot issue or vary a proclamation unless the decision of the Union Cabinet is communicated to him in writing.
    • National Emergency has been proclaimed 3 times so far: 1962, 1971 and 1975.
    • On 25 June 1975 President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed declared an emergency under Article 352 on the ground of 'internal disturbance'.
    • That Emergency lasted 21 months, from 25 June 1975 until it was withdrawn on 21 March 1977; Indira Gandhi was Prime Minister.

    National Emergency: approval and duration

    • The proclamation is laid before each House and ceases after one month unless approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament.UPPSC ×2
    • Originally the period was two months; the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 reduced it to one month.
    • Resolutions approving the proclamation or its continuance need a special majority (Article 352(6)): two-thirds of members present and voting; it can be revoked by a simple majority.
    • If Lok Sabha is dissolved when the proclamation is issued, or within the one month without approving it, the proclamation survives until 30 days from the first sitting of the reconstituted Lok Sabha, provided Rajya Sabha has approved it meanwhile.
    • It ceases unless the new Lok Sabha also approves it within those 30 days.
    • Once approved by both Houses, the emergency continues for 6 months from the passing of the second approving resolution.
    • It may be extended for further six-month periods by resolutions of both Houses passed by the special majority.

    National Emergency: effects

    • During a National Emergency, Parliament can make laws on any subject in the State List.
    • Such laws become inoperative six months after the emergency has ceased to operate.
    • The President can also issue ordinances on State subjects if Parliament is not in session.
    • Article 354(1): during a National Emergency the President can modify the distribution of revenues (Articles 268 to 281) between the Centre and the States.
    • This modification lasts only up to the end of the financial year in which the proclamation ceases; every such order is laid before each House of Parliament.
    • Article 83(2): during a National Emergency, the life of Lok Sabha may be extended beyond 5 years by a law of Parliament, one year at a time, any number of times.UPPSC
    • The extension cannot continue beyond six months after the emergency has ceased to operate.
    • Proviso to Article 172(1): Parliament may by law extend the term of a State Legislative Assembly during an emergency, one year at a time, not beyond six months after the proclamation ceases.

    Fundamental Rights during emergency

    • Articles 358 and 359 describe the effect of a National Emergency on Fundamental Rights.
    • Article 358: Article 19 rights are automatically suspended when emergency is declared on the ground of war or external aggression; no separate order is needed.
    • After the 44th Amendment, Article 19 is not automatically suspended in an emergency due to armed rebellion; the President may suspend it under Article 359.
    • Article 359: the President may by order suspend the right to move any court to enforce the other Fundamental Rights (Part III), except Articles 20 and 21.UPPSC
    • Rights under Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended in any case.UPPSC ×2
    • Under Article 359 the President can suspend enforcement of other Fundamental Rights, including Article 21A.

    Note from the book Question on which Fundamental Rights the President can suspend (Article 21A / Article 19): two answers were correct, so the Commission excluded it from evaluation.

    President's Rule (Article 356)

    • Article 356: if the President, on a report from the Governor or otherwise, is satisfied that the State Government cannot be carried on as per the Constitution, he may impose President's Rule.
    • The President can act even without the Governor's report.
    • President's Rule can be proclaimed on two grounds: one in Article 356 itself and the other in Article 365.
    • The President may take over all or any of the powers of the State Government.
    • The President (actually the Governor on his behalf) dismisses the State Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister.
    • The President removes the Council of Ministers and runs the administration with the help of the Chief Secretary of the State.
    • The State Legislature is either suspended or dissolved; the President can dissolve, suspend or prorogue the Assembly; dissolution of the Assembly and of local bodies are not necessary consequences.
    • The powers of the State Legislature become exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament; Parliament passes the State's bills and budget.
    • President's Rule has no effect on the Fundamental Rights of citizens.
    • Parliament can delegate the power to make laws for the State to the President or any authority specified by him.
    • The President can promulgate an ordinance under Article 123, but it is subject to the approval of the House.
    • S.R. Bommai vs Union of India, 1994: a proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review; failure of constitutional machinery must be real, not fictitious.
    • S.R. Bommai: the State Assembly cannot be dissolved with the proclamation until both Houses of Parliament approve it within two months.
    • A proclamation of President's Rule must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within two months of its issue.
    • If approved, President's Rule continues for 6 months.
    • It can be extended, with Parliament's approval every six months, for a maximum of 3 years.UPPSC
    • Resolutions approving President's Rule or its continuance are passed by either House by a simple majority.
    • 44th Amendment Act, 1978 / Article 356(5): extension beyond 1 year needs a National Emergency in operation and an Election Commission certificate that Assembly elections are difficult to hold.
    • President's Rule under Article 356 was first imposed in 1951 in the former Punjab and in 1953 in PEPSU (Patiala and East Punjab States Union).UPPSC
    StateTimes President's Rule imposed till 2019
    Manipur10
    Uttar Pradesh9
    Bihar8
    Odisha6
    • Because of J&K's special status (Article 370), Governor's Rule was also provided under Section 92 of Part 6 of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir, in addition to President's Rule.
    • The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 removed J&K's separate constitutional system; J&K is now a Union Territory.
    • Manipur, Mizoram and Meghalaya have no provision for Governor's Rule.

    Note from the book Question on the State with no provision for Governor's Rule: the U.P. Commission did not evaluate it.

    Financial Emergency (Article 360)

    • Article 360: the President may proclaim a Financial Emergency if the financial stability or credit of India or any part of its territory is threatened.
    • The proclamation ceases after two months unless approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament.
    • Once approved by both Houses, it continues indefinitely till revoked.
    • During a financial emergency the Centre acquires full direction-based control over the States in financial matters.
    • The President can direct States to reduce salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving in connection with the affairs of the State.
    • The President can direct reduction of salaries and allowances of persons serving the Union, including Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts.
    • Money Bills or other financial Bills passed by a State Legislature may be reserved for the President's consideration if he so directs; it is not necessarily required.
    • Financial Emergency has never been declared in India; Article 360 has not been used so far.UPPSC ×3

    The Finance Commission

    35 facts · 5 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The Finance Commission recommends the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States; the federal Finance Commission relates to finances between the Centre and the States.×5
    2. Article 280(1): the President constitutes it within two years of the commencement of the Constitution and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year, or earlier if he considers necessary.×3
    3. The State Finance Commission is a constitutional body, constituted by the Governor under Article 243-I.×3
    4. The Finance Commission consists of a Chairman and four other members (total 5), appointed by the President.×2
    5. It recommends the principles governing grants-in-aid of State revenues out of the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 275); with tax sharing, this is its main function.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 18 UPPSC questions

    Constitution and composition

    • Article 280 provides for the Finance Commission, constituted by the President by order.UPPSC
    • Article 280(1): the President constitutes it within two years of the commencement of the Constitution and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year, or earlier if he considers necessary.UPPSC ×3
    • The Finance Commission consists of a Chairman and four other members (total 5), appointed by the President.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 280(2): Parliament by law determines the qualifications of the members and the manner of their selection; the President only appoints them.UPPSC
    • Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951: the Chairman is selected from persons with experience in public affairs.
    • The four other members are selected from persons who: (a) are, have been or are qualified to be a High Court Judge; or (b) have specialised knowledge of government finance and accounts; or (c) have wide experience in financial matters and administration; or (d) have special knowledge of economics.
    • It is not necessary that at least one member be a Judge of a High Court or the Supreme Court.
    • Section 6 of the Act: the Chairman of the Commission can be reappointed.
    • The Commission makes its recommendations to the President (Article 280(3)); it does not report to NITI Aayog.
    • The recommendations of the Finance Commission are only advisory in nature.
    • Article 281: the President causes every recommendation of the Finance Commission to be laid before each House of Parliament.

    Functions

    • The Finance Commission recommends the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States; the federal Finance Commission relates to finances between the Centre and the States.UPPSC ×5
    • It recommends the allocation among the States of their respective shares of tax proceeds.
    • It recommends the principles governing grants-in-aid of State revenues out of the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 275); with tax sharing, this is its main function.UPPSC ×2
    • It recommends measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities, on the basis of the State Finance Commission's recommendations.
    • It also deals with any other matter referred by the President in the interest of sound finance.
    • Allowing withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund of India is the function of Parliament, not the Finance Commission.
    • Overseeing whether the Union and State Governments collect taxes as per the budget is the task of the Finance Ministry.
    • The Finance Commission does not encourage inflow of foreign capital, distribute finances among Public Sector Undertakings, or ensure transparency in financial administration.
    • The Inter-State Council is for coordination and cooperation among States.
    • The main function of the Planning Commission was to allocate resources between the Centre and the States; it has been replaced by NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India).

    Finance Commissions and chairmen

    • The First Finance Commission was constituted by Presidential order dated 22 November 1951, under K.C. Neogy, on 6 April 1952; he was the first Chairman.
    • Till now 15 Finance Commissions have been constituted (as printed with the 12th Finance Commission answer).
    Finance CommissionChairmanDetails
    FirstK.C. NeogySet up 6 April 1952
    12thDr. C. Rangarajan (former RBI Governor)Recommendations for 2005 to 2010
    13thVijay KelkarReport submitted in 2010UPPSC
    14thDr. Y.V. ReddyFormed January 2013; report 15 December 2014; period 2015-20UPPSC
    15thN.K. SinghConstituted 27 November 2017; recommendations for 2020-21 to 2025-26UPPSC
    16thArvind Panagariya (former Vice-Chairman, NITI Aayog)Constituted 31 December 2023
    • The 14th Finance Commission recommended raising the States' share in the net proceeds of taxes to 42 percent from the then 32 percent.
    • The 15th Finance Commission submitted two reports: the first for the financial year 2020-21 and the final report for 2021-26.

    State Finance Commission

    • The State Finance Commission is a constitutional body, constituted by the Governor under Article 243-I.UPPSC ×3
    • The Governor constitutes it within one year of the commencement of the 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 and thereafter every fifth year.
    • It reviews the financial position of the Panchayats and makes recommendations to the Governor.
    • The Union Finance Commission can recommend for Panchayats under Article 280(3)(bb) and for Municipalities under Article 280(3)(c), on the basis of the State Finance Commission's recommendations.

    Chapter 33 · Bodies, elections, local government and more

    The Planning Commission/NITI Aayog

    45 facts · 4 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. The Planning Commission was neither a constitutional body nor a statutory body; it is not mentioned in the Constitution; it was an extra-constitutional body.×7
    2. The Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission was equivalent in rank to a Cabinet Minister of the Government of India.×2
    3. NITI Aayog is a non-constitutional (extra-constitutional) and non-statutory body.×2
    4. NDC functions: prescribe guidelines for formulating the National Plan (including assessment of resources); consider the Plan made by the Planning Commission; review the working of the Plan and recommend measures to achieve its aims and targets.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 21 UPPSC questions

    Planning Commission

    • The Planning Commission was established on 15 March 1950.
    • It was formed by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet (Government of India), to make planning effective in India.UPPSC
    • It was set up by the first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru to optimise scarce resources in the newly-born nation.
    • It was established on the recommendation of an advisory planning board chaired by K.C. Neogy.
    • The Planning Commission was neither a constitutional body nor a statutory body; it is not mentioned in the Constitution; it was an extra-constitutional body.UPPSC ×7
    • UPSC and State Public Service Commissions (Article 315) and the Finance Commission (Article 280) are provided in the Constitution.
    • The Prime Minister was the ex-officio Chairman of the Planning Commission.UPPSC
    • Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru was the first Chairman of the Planning Commission.
    • Gulzarilal Nanda was the first Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission.
    • The Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission was equivalent in rank to a Cabinet Minister of the Government of India.UPPSC ×2
    • Deputy Chairmen: Dr. Manmohan Singh (1985-1987), Pranab Mukherjee (1991-1996), Montek Singh Ahluwalia (2004-2014); P. Chidambaram was never Deputy Chairman.UPPSC
    • Main function: assess the country's resources and prepare five-year plans for the Central Government for balanced use of those resources; also give suggestions on the annual plans of the States.
    • Almost 70 percent of Central grants to the States were given on the Commission's recommendation.
    • It was called the 'Economic Cabinet' of the Union and the States, because of its extra-constitutional discretionary powers and the comprehensive nature of its terms of reference; it also formulates five-year plans for balanced use of natural resources, but that is not the reason for the name.UPPSC
    • M.V. Mathur suggested merging the Planning Commission and the Finance Commission; he was a member of the 3rd Finance Commission, formed in 1960.

    NITI Aayog

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced from the Red Fort on 15 August 2014 the abolition of the Planning Commission.UPPSC
    • NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.
    • NITI = National Institution for Transforming India.
    • NITI Aayog was formed by a resolution of the Union Cabinet (an executive resolution of the Government of India).UPPSC
    • NITI Aayog is a non-constitutional (extra-constitutional) and non-statutory body.UPPSC ×2
    • NITI Aayog is a policy think-tank of the Government of India; it gives critical directional and strategic input into the development process.
    • NITI Aayog works on the principle of co-operative federalism.
    • The Prime Minister is the ex-officio Chairperson of NITI Aayog; so it has no full-time Chairman, and the Chairperson changes with the Prime Minister's term.UPPSC
    • The current Chairperson of NITI Aayog is Shri Narendra Modi.
    • The Vice-Chairperson of NITI Aayog is appointed by the Prime Minister; his rank and status equal a Cabinet Minister.
    • Dr. Arvind Panagariya was the first Vice-Chairman of NITI Aayog, from January 2015 to August 2017.
    • The current Vice-Chairman is Dr. Suman K. Bery, a former World Bank economist.
    • The Chief Executive Officer of NITI Aayog is B.V.R. Subrahmanyam.
    • Governing Council of NITI Aayog: Prime Minister (Chairperson), Chief Ministers of all States, Chief Ministers of UTs with legislatures (Delhi, Puducherry) and Lieutenant Governors of other UTs; Governors of States are not included.UPPSC

    National Development Council (NDC)

    • The NDC was set up on 6 August 1952 by an executive order of the Government.UPPSC
    • It was set up to ensure the participation of States in the formation of five-year plans.
    • The National Development Council, the Planning Commission and the Zonal Councils are not mentioned in the Constitution.
    • NDC (1952) and Planning Commission (1950) were set up by executive order; Zonal Councils are statutory bodies under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
    • The NDC is a non-constitutional and non-statutory body; it should meet at least twice a year.
    • The NDC, not the Planning Commission, is the apex body for decision-making and deliberation on development matters in India.UPPSC
    • The Prime Minister is the Chairman of the NDC and presides over its meetings.
    • NDC members: Prime Minister (Chairman), Ministers of the Union Cabinet, Chief Ministers of all States, Chief Ministers / Administrators of Union Territories, members of the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog); the Finance Commission Chairman is not a member.
    • The Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog) is also part of the NDC.
    • The Secretary of the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog) is the ex-officio Secretary of the NDC.
    • The NDC finally approves the five-year plans.UPPSC
    • The NDC acts as a coordinator between the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog) and the State Governments.UPPSC
    • NDC functions: prescribe guidelines for formulating the National Plan (including assessment of resources); consider the Plan made by the Planning Commission; review the working of the Plan and recommend measures to achieve its aims and targets.UPPSC ×2
    • The NDC also considers important questions of social and economic policy affecting national development.
    • Suggesting allocation of money for the Plan was the Planning Commission's work, not the NDC's.
    • Main functions of the NDC: activate the means and efforts of States for implementing the plan, develop general policies in all important areas, and ensure balanced development of all areas of the country.

    Chapter 34 · Bodies, elections, local government and more

    Lokpal and Important Commissions

    247 facts · 3 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution was set up by the NDA Government on 22 February 2000 under Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah.×3
    2. NHRC is a statutory (non-constitutional) body, set up on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.×2
    3. Article 323: UPSC presents its annual report to the President.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 36 UPPSC questions

    Ombudsman and origin of Lokpal idea

    • Ombudsman (Scandinavian institution) = earliest democratic institution in the world for redressal of citizens' grievances.
    • Ombudsman first created in Sweden in 1809, as an independent supervisory agency.
    • Indian model of the Ombudsman = Lokpal.UPPSC
    • To deal with corruption complaints against certain public functionaries, India proposed Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayukta at State level.
    • First Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC, 1966-1970) recommended setting up Lokpal and Lokayukta for redressal of citizens' grievances.
    • First ARC gave this recommendation in its interim report dated 20 October 1966.
    • First ARC was set up on 5 January 1966 under the chairmanship of Morarji Desai.UPPSC
    • In 1967 K. Hanumanthaiah became Chairman of the first ARC; its term ended in 1970.
    • Creation of a Local Body Ombudsman was recommended by the First Administrative Reforms Commission.
    • ARC proposal: Lokpal chairperson and members appointed by President on recommendation of a selection committee (PM as chairperson, Lok Sabha Speaker, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, CJI or SC judge nominated by him, one eminent jurist).

    Lokpal Bills

    1. 1968First Lokpal Bill was introduced in Parliament in 1968, in the 4th Lok Sabha.UPPSC
    2. 1969It was passed by the Fourth Lok Sabha on 20 August 1969 (first Jan Lokpal Bill).
    3. 2011Lokpal Bill, 2011 was introduced in Lok Sabha on 4 August 2011 by V. Narayanaswami, then Minister of Parliamentary Affairs (not by Home Minister P. Chidambaram).UPPSC
    4. 2011Lokpal Bill, 2011 was sent to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Public Grievance, Law and Justice.
    5. 2011Civil Society members termed the Lokpal Bill, 2011 'weak'.
    6. 2013Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (Lokpal at Centre, Lokayukta in States) came into force on 16 January 2014.
    7. 2014The Bill relating to Lokpal and Lokayukta took the form of an Act from 1 January 2014.
    • First Lokpal Bill was introduced in Parliament in 1968, in the 4th Lok Sabha.UPPSC
    • It was passed by the Fourth Lok Sabha on 20 August 1969 (first Jan Lokpal Bill).
    • Before Rajya Sabha could pass it, the Lok Sabha was dissolved and the bill lapsed.
    • Lokpal Bill, 2011 was introduced in Lok Sabha on 4 August 2011 by V. Narayanaswami, then Minister of Parliamentary Affairs (not by Home Minister P. Chidambaram).UPPSC
    • Lokpal Bill, 2011 was sent to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Public Grievance, Law and Justice.
    • Civil Society members termed the Lokpal Bill, 2011 'weak'.
    • Five civil society members in the Lokpal Bill drafting panel: Anna Hazare, Arvind Kejriwal, Shanti Bhushan, N. Santosh Hegde, Prashant Bhushan.UPPSC
    • Kiran Bedi and Prashant Joshi were not civil society members of the Lokpal Bill drafting panel.
    • The Bill relating to Lokpal and Lokayukta took the form of an Act from 1 January 2014.
    • Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (Lokpal at Centre, Lokayukta in States) came into force on 16 January 2014.

    Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013

    • Institution of Lokpal was established for the first time in India by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.
    • Lokpal = a chairperson and not more than eight members.
    • Section 4(1): Lokpal chairperson and members are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a selection committee.
    • Lokpal selection committee: PM (Chairperson), Lok Sabha Speaker, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, CJI or SC judge nominated by him, one eminent jurist.UPPSC
    • The eminent jurist is recommended by the other four members and nominated by the President.
    • Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is not in the Lokpal selection committee.
    • Section 1(3): the Act applies to public servants both within India and outside India.
    • Minimum age for Lokpal Chairperson or Member = 45 years on the date of assuming office.
    • Lokpal Chairperson or Member cannot be an MP or a member of the Legislature of any State or Union Territory.
    • Lokpal Chairperson need not be only a CJI: other Supreme Court judges or a qualified 'eminent person' can also be Chairperson.
    • The Prime Minister is within the jurisdiction of the Lokpal.
    • Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose (retired Supreme Court judge) was the first Lokpal of India.
    • Justice Ajay Manikrao Khanwilkar (former Supreme Court judge) was appointed Lokpal Chairperson in 2024; assumed office on 10 March 2024.UPPSC

    Lokayukta in States

    1. 1970Odisha was the first State to pass a Lokayukta Act (1970), but it came into force only in 1983.
    2. 1971Maharashtra Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayuktas Act was enacted on 30 November 1971 and came into effect on 25 October 1972.
    3. 1972Maharashtra was the first State to establish the Lokayukta, in 1972.UPPSC
    4. 1973Rajasthan Lokayukta and Deputy Lokayukta Act, 1973: Section 7 = matters which may be investigated; Section 8 = matters not subject to investigation.
    5. 1975Under the Uttar Pradesh Lokayukta Act, 1975 the Lokayukta submits his report to the Governor.UPPSC
    6. 1993Odisha was also the first State to abolish the Lokayukta, in 1993.
    7. 1995In 1995 the Chief Minister was within the Lokayukta Act in Madhya Pradesh and Orissa.
    8. 2011Uttarakhand was the first State to pass the Lokayukta Bill in 2011, on 1 November 2011.UPPSC
    9. 2014In 2014 Rajasthan set up a high-level committee under Advocate General Narpat Mal Lodha to review the existing Lokayukta Act.
    10. 2017Earlier (when asked in 2017) the tenure of the UP Lokayukta was 8 years.
    11. 2024UP Lokayukta tenure = 5 years or 70 years of age, whichever is earlier, from 26 February 2024 (Act amended February 2024).UPPSC
    • Maharashtra was the first State to establish the Lokayukta, in 1972.UPPSC
    • Maharashtra Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayuktas Act was enacted on 30 November 1971 and came into effect on 25 October 1972.
    • Odisha was the first State to pass a Lokayukta Act (1970), but it came into force only in 1983.
    • Odisha was also the first State to abolish the Lokayukta, in 1993.
    StateLokayukta established
    Maharashtra1972
    Bihar1973
    Uttar Pradesh1975
    Madhya Pradesh1982
    Andhra Pradesh1983
    Karnataka1984
    Assam1986
    • Governor appoints the Lokayukta on the advice of the Chief Minister, for a term of five years.
    • Under the Uttar Pradesh Lokayukta Act, 1975 the Lokayukta submits his report to the Governor.UPPSC
    • The Governor presents the UP Lokayukta's report in both Houses of the State Legislature.
    • UP Lokayukta tenure = 5 years or 70 years of age, whichever is earlier, from 26 February 2024 (Act amended February 2024).UPPSC
    • Earlier (when asked in 2017) the tenure of the UP Lokayukta was 8 years.
    • Uttarakhand was the first State to pass the Lokayukta Bill in 2011, on 1 November 2011.UPPSC
    • In 1995 the Chief Minister was within the Lokayukta Act in Madhya Pradesh and Orissa.
    • At present the Chief Minister is within the Lokayukta Act in Himachal Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha and Punjab.
    • Rajasthan Lokayukta and Deputy Lokayukta Act, 1973: Section 7 = matters which may be investigated; Section 8 = matters not subject to investigation.
    • Rajasthan Lokayukta and Up-Lokayukta mainly investigate corruption and misconduct by ministers and public servants acting in official capacity.
    • Sexual harassment of women, caste discrimination and violence against children are not investigated by the Rajasthan Lokayukta.
    • Those cases fall under criminal laws, the SC/ST Act and the POCSO Act and are investigated by police or other authorities.
    • Rajasthan Lokayukta can investigate: unreasonable harm by public servants, abuse of official position for illegal benefit, corruption or lack of transparency.
    • In 2014 Rajasthan set up a high-level committee under Advocate General Narpat Mal Lodha to review the existing Lokayukta Act.

    Minorities

    • The term 'Minority' is not defined in the Constitution.
    • Minority Commission is a statutory body, not a constitutional body, set up under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992; this does not explain why 'Minority' is undefined.UPPSC
    • National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992 came into force on 17 May 1993; the commission became statutory and was renamed National Commission for Minorities.
    • First statutory National Commission for Minorities was set up on 17 May 1993.
    • Gazette notification of 23 October 1993 (Ministry of Welfare) notified five minority communities: Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Zoroastrians (Parsis).
    • Jains were notified as a minority community on 27 January 2014; so six communities are notified minorities at present.
    • Zoroastrians are not the smallest religious minority; smaller minorities exist that are not notified.
    • The Constitution recognises and protects religious and linguistic minorities.
    • Section 21 of the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 added Articles 350A and 350B (not the 9th Amendment).UPPSC
    • Article 350A = facilities for instruction in mother tongue at primary stage.
    • Article 350B = Special Officer for linguistic minorities, appointed by the President.
    • The Special Officer is for the Union (all India), not one for each State.
    • This officer is named Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities in India.

    Other commissions and committees

    • National Commission for Women Act, 1990 was enforced on 30 August 1990.
    • Section 10 of the National Commission for Women Act, 1990 defines the functions of the Commission.
    • Secondary Education Commission (1952-53) was appointed in 1952 under Dr. A. Laxman Swami Mudaliar, Vice-Chancellor of Madras University.
    • It was also called the Mudaliar Commission; aim: improve the quality of secondary education.
    • Mudaliar Commission stressed science, agriculture and technical education to match national development needs.
    • Planning Commission was set up by a Union Cabinet proposal on 15 March 1950; it no longer exists.
    • NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.
    • NITI Aayog is the main think-tank giving policy inputs and directions; the Prime Minister is its Chairman.
    • NITI Aayog's Administrative Board: Chief Ministers of all States (including Delhi and Puducherry) and Lt. Governors of Union Territories.
    • Ex-officio members of NITI Aayog: Home Minister, Agriculture Minister, Defence Minister, Finance Minister.
    • Vohra Committee (1993) studied criminalisation of politics and the nexus among criminals, politicians and bureaucrats.UPPSC
    • Rajamannar Committee/Commission recommended abolition of the Indian Administrative Service and Indian Police Service.
    • First Law Commission of independent India was constituted in 1955; Chairman = M.C. Setalvad, the then Attorney General.
    • National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution was set up by the NDA Government on 22 February 2000 under Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah.UPPSC ×3
    • Its appointment was not approved by Parliament; its report was recommendatory.
    • Its function: review the working of the Constitution over the last 50 years and assess its present effectiveness.
    • It submitted its last report on 31 March 2002.
    • Central Pollution Control Board Chairman is nominated by the Central Government (not President, PM, Vice-President or Environment Minister).
    • CPCB Chairman = a person with special knowledge or practical experience in environmental protection or in administering such an institution.
    • At present Amandeep Garg (IAS) is the acting chairman of the Central Pollution Control Board.

    Note from the book MPPSC omitted the CPCB chairman question in its provisional key because none of the options was correct.

    • Swaran Singh Committee (1976, set up by the Congress Government) mainly considered priority of Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights.
    • It was called the 'Constitutional Amendment Committee'; the 42nd Amendment resulted from its recommendations.
    • Swaran Singh Committee said the Presidential system is inappropriate for India.
    • Swaran Singh Committee (1976, Congress Party) also made recommendations about fundamental duties, felt necessary during the internal emergency.
    • Kelkar Committee studied and evaluated the public-private partnership (PPP) model in India.
    • Bakshi Tek Chand Committee (1948) enquired into the patent system and recommended reforms.
    BodyYear of establishment
    Inter-State Council1990
    National Development Council1952 (not 1954)UPPSC
    Central Vigilance Commission1964
    National Human Rights Commission1993
    Central Bureau of Investigation1963
    Enforcement Directorate1956 (not 2000)
    Prevention of Corruption Act1988 (not 1985)UPPSC

    Central Vigilance Commission

    • CVC is the main agency for preventing corruption in the Central Government.
    • CVC is an apex body promoting integrity, transparency and accountability in public administration.
    • CVC was set up in February 1964 on the recommendation of the Santhanam Committee on Prevention of Corruption (1962-64).
    • Committee on Prevention of Corruption was appointed in 1962: K. Santhanam (parliamentarian) as Chairman, four other MPs and two senior officers.
    • CVC was set up to advise and guide central government agencies in the field of vigilance.
    • Originally CVC was neither a constitutional nor a statutory body; no Article of the Constitution describes it.UPPSC
    • Parliament gave CVC statutory status by a law passed in September 2003.
    • Article 268 = duties levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States.
    • Article 276 = taxes on professions, trades, callings and employment.

    Mandal Commission and SC/ST report

    • Mandal Commission was set up in 1979 by the Janata Party Government under Prime Minister Morarji Desai.UPPSC
    • Its chairman was Bindeshwari Prasad Mandal (B.P. Mandal), a parliamentarian.
    • Its task: identify socially and educationally backward classes and recommend steps for their advancement.
    • Mandal Commission submitted its report in 1980.UPPSC
    • 1990 report of the National Commission for SCs and STs: main causes of atrocities = land disputes, alienation of tribal lands, bonded labour, indebtedness, non-payment of minimum wages.
    • Religious causes are not among the causes of atrocities on SCs and STs in that report.
    • Article 340 = appointment of a commission to investigate the conditions of backward classes.

    Universal Declaration of Human Rights

    • UDHR was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948.
    • UDHR has 30 Articles.
    • 10 December is observed every year as Human Rights Day.
    • In 1950 the General Assembly passed resolution 423(V) inviting all states to observe 10 December as Human Rights Day.
    • World Health Day = 7 April; UN Day = 24 October; Labour Day = 1 May.
    • Concept of human rights mainly stresses the dignity of man as a human being; UDHR Preamble stresses dignity and justice for every human.UPPSC
    • UDHR includes freedom and equality, right to life and liberty, right to education; it does not include the right to privacy.
    • UDHR is a milestone document but not a legally binding treaty; it first set out fundamental human rights to be universally protected.
    • UDHR Article 3: everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person.
    • UDHR Article 25: right to a standard of living adequate for health and well-being.
    • Right to Universal Basic Income is not included in the UDHR.
    • UDHR principles are reflected in the Preamble, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties, besides Fundamental Rights.
    • UDHR Article 3 is reflected in the Preamble and Fundamental Rights of the Indian Constitution.
    • UDHR Article 26 (right to education; free and compulsory elementary education) is reflected in Article 45 of the Directive Principles.
    • UDHR Article 26 also says technical and professional education be generally available and higher education equally accessible on merit.
    • UDHR Article 29 (everyone has duties to the community) is reflected in the Fundamental Duties.
    • UDHR Articles 3 to 21 = first generation human rights; Articles 22 to 27 = second generation human rights.
    • Right to work (Article 23) and right to education (Article 26) are both second generation human rights.
    • First generation rights deal with liberty and participation in political life; they are civil and political in nature.
    • Eradication of all types of social discrimination comes under the second generation of human rights.
    • Third generation of human rights = community and collective rights.

    Note from the book For the social discrimination question, the Jharkhand PSC held 'third generation' as the correct answer.

    Right to the City

    • 'Right to the City' was proposed by sociologist Henri Lefebvre in 1968; David Harvey developed it in the new millennium.
    • Habitat III (UN-Habitat) policy theme = "Right to the City and Cities for All"; but it is not an agreed agenda.
    • Right to the City gives every occupant the right to reclaim public spaces and public participation in the city; the State cannot deny any public service or facility to unauthorised colonies in the city.

    Note from the book Right to the City and unauthorised colonies: the answer accepts 'the State cannot deny any public service or facility to unauthorised colonies' as correct, yet the same explanation says the right does not mean a guarantee of public services or facilities to unauthorised colonies.

    • Definition: right of all inhabitants, present and future, to occupy, use and produce just, inclusive and sustainable cities as a common good.
    • It implies responsibilities on governments and people to claim, defend and promote this right.
    • Right to the city = spatially just resource distribution + political agency + social, economic and cultural diversity.

    Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993

    • On 28 September 1993 the President promulgated the Protection of Human Rights Ordinance, 1993 under Article 123.
    • The Ordinance provided for a National Human Rights Commission, State Human Rights Commissions and Human Rights Courts.
    • Protection of Human Rights Act came into force on 28 September 1993; it extends to the whole of India.
    • Objectives of the Act: constitute National and State Human Rights Commissions and Human Rights Courts for better protection of human rights.
    • The Act defines human rights as rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity of the individual.
    • These rights are those guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in International Conventions and enforceable by courts in India.

    Note from the book The question on which right is outside NHRC purview was deleted from evaluation by MPPSC.

    • Section 2(M) of the Act defines 'Public Servant'; same meaning as in Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.
    • 'Armed forces' in the Act = naval, military and air forces and other armed forces of the Union; armed forces of the State are not included.
    • Every member and authorised officer of the Commission or State Commission is deemed a public servant (Section 21 IPC).
    • Section 31: for every Human Rights Court the State Government specifies a public prosecutor or appoints an advocate as Special Public Prosecutor.
    • The advocate appointed as Special Public Prosecutor must have at least 7 years of practice.

    National Human Rights Commission

    • NHRC is a statutory (non-constitutional) body, set up on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.UPPSC ×2
    • Constitutional bodies: State Finance Commission (Article 243-I), Secretariat of Parliament (Article 98), Finance Commission (Article 280), Election Commission (Article 324).
    • Article 338B = National Commission for Backward Classes; Article 340 = commission to investigate condition of backward classes.
    • NHRC headquarters are in Delhi; it can set up offices at other places in India.
    • NHRC is a multi-member body: a chairman and four other members.
    • NHRC also has 6 ex-officio members and one special invitee to the statutory full commission.
    • Chairperson of the Law Commission of India is not an ex-officio member of NHRC.
    • Chairpersons of the National Commissions for Minorities, for SCs and STs, and for Women are ex-officio members of NHRC.
    • Section 4: NHRC Chairperson and members are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a 6-member committee.
    • NHRC selection committee: PM (head), Lok Sabha Speaker, Home Minister, Leaders of Opposition in Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
    • Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) is not a member of the NHRC selection committee.
    • Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019 amended the 1993 Act.
    • After 2019: NHRC Chairperson = a former Chief Justice of India or a judge of the Supreme Court; so it need not be headed only by a former CJI, and the term is 3 years, not 5.UPPSC
    • 2019 Amendment: NHRC members with human rights knowledge raised from two to three, of whom at least one must be a woman.
    • 2019 Amendment: term of NHRC and SHRC chairperson and members = 3 years or age 70, whichever is earlier.
    • After their tenure, NHRC Chairman and members cannot take further employment under the Central or State Government.
    • NHRC's function and powers are mainly recommendatory in nature.
    • State Human Rights Commissions are constituted by the States and are not part of NHRC.
    • Section 12 of the Act gives the functions of NHRC.
    • NHRC functions include undertaking and promoting research in human rights and encouraging NGOs and institutions working in the field.
    • NHRC can regulate its own procedure; it has all the powers of a civil court and its proceedings have a judicial character.
    • For human rights violations by armed forces, NHRC's role is limited: it may seek a report from the Central Government and make recommendations.
    • Justice Ranganath Misra was the first Chairman of NHRC (12 October 1993 to 24 November 1996).
    • Justice H.L. Dattu was NHRC Chairman from 29.02.2016 to 02.12.2020.
    • Justice V. Ramasubramanian is NHRC Chairman since 30/12/2024.

    State Human Rights Commission

    • The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 provides for State Human Rights Commissions; currently 25 States have constituted them.
    • After the 2019 Amendment, a Chief Justice or a Judge of a High Court is eligible to be SHRC Chairperson.
    • Section 22: SHRC Chairperson and members are appointed by the Governor on a committee's recommendation.
    • SHRC selection committee is headed by the Chief Minister.
    • Other members: Speaker of Legislative Assembly, State Home Minister, Leader of Opposition in the Legislative Assembly.

    Note from the book Members of the SHRC selection committee: two answers are accepted, Speaker of the Legislative Assembly and Leader of Opposition.

    • Where there is a Legislative Council, its Chairman and its Leader of Opposition are also members.
    • The Governor is not a member of the SHRC selection committee.
    • A sitting High Court judge or sitting District Judge can be appointed to SHRC only after consulting the Chief Justice of the High Court of that State.
    • Governor can appoint a member as acting SHRC chairman when the office is vacant or the chairman cannot function due to absence or other reason.
    • Functions of a Human Rights Commission: suo motu inquiry into violations, visiting any jail, reviewing protection of human rights.
    • The Commission cannot punish for violation of human rights.
    • SHRC submits its annual report to the State Government.
    • The report is laid before the State Legislature with a memorandum of action taken and reasons for not accepting any recommendation.

    State Finance and Information Commissions

    • Chairperson and members of the State Finance Commission are appointed by the Governor.
    • Central Information Commission was set up by Gazette notification under the Right to Information Act, 2005.
    • Under the RTI Act, 2005 the Chief Information Commissioner's term was up to 5 years or 65 years of age.
    • RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019: tenure of Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioners is decided by the Central Government.
    • After 2019, salary, allowances and facilities of Central and State Chief Information Commissioners and Information Commissioners are decided by the Central Government.

    Public Service Commissions: setup

    • Articles 315 to 323 in Part XIV deal with composition, appointment, removal, independence, powers and functions of UPSC and SPSCs.
    • Article 315: a Public Service Commission for the Union and one for each State.
    • UPSC is a constitutional body formed under Article 315; it is the central recruiting agency.UPPSC
    • UPSC has nothing to do with the State Public Service Commission.
    • Article 315(2): two or more States may agree to have one Joint Public Service Commission.
    • If the State legislatures pass a resolution to that effect, Parliament may by law provide for a Joint State Public Service Commission.UPPSC
    • Article 315(4): UPSC may serve the needs of a State on request of the Governor, with approval of the President.UPPSC
    • Article 316(1): Chairman and members of UPSC or a Joint Commission are appointed by the President.
    • Chairman and members of a State Public Service Commission are appointed by the Governor.
    • Government of India Act, 1919 first provided for a Public Service Commission in India.UPPSC
    • First Public Service Commission was set up on 1 October 1926, with a Chairman and four members.
    • It was named Federal Public Service Commission under the Government of India Act, 1935.
    • Madhya Pradesh PSC was constituted by the President under Section 118(3) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
    • Madhya Pradesh PSC has a maximum of five members.
    • Rose Millian Bathew was the first woman Chairman of UPSC (1992 to 1996).

    Public Service Commissions: removal

    • Article 317: removal of the Chairman or a member of a Public Service Commission.
    • Article 317(1): President removes by order for misbehaviour, only after the Supreme Court inquires on his reference and reports for removal.UPPSC
    • The Supreme Court inquiry follows the procedure prescribed under Article 145.
    • SPSC chairman and members are appointed by the Governor but can be removed only by the President.
    • Article 317(3): President may also remove for insolvency, paid employment outside office duties, or infirmity of mind or body.
    • Parliament plays no role in removal of the UPSC Chairman, unlike High Court judges, Supreme Court judges and CAG.UPPSC

    Public Service Commissions: functions, expenses, reports

    • Article 320 = functions of Public Service Commissions (Union and State).
    • UPSC gets functions from the Constitution, parliamentary laws, executive rules and orders, and conventions.UPPSC
    • Article 320(3)(c): PSC must be consulted on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving the government in a civil capacity.
    • This consultation includes memorials or petitions relating to such matters.
    • SPSC is consulted on methods of recruitment, principles of appointment, promotions and transfers from one service to another.
    • SPSC is not consulted on making transfers of civil servants.
    • Article 321: an Act of Parliament or of a State Legislature may give additional functions to UPSC or the SPSC.UPPSC
    • Such functions may also cover services of a local authority, body corporate constituted by law or public institution.
    • Article 318 = power to make regulations on conditions of service of members and staff of the Commission.
    • Article 322 = expenses of Public Service Commissions.
    • UPSC expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India; SPSC expenses on the Consolidated Fund of the State.UPPSC
    • Article 323: UPSC presents its annual report to the President.UPPSC ×2
    • President lays it before each House of Parliament with a memorandum explaining cases where the Commission's advice was not accepted.
    • Article 323(2): each State PSC submits its annual report to the Governor.
    • Article 325 relates to elections and has no clauses.

    Civil services

    • In India, bureaucracy is the agency for the implementation of public policy.
    • Policy implementation by bureaucracy builds the credibility of the political executive among common people.
    • Article 310 = Doctrine of Pleasure.
    • Members of defence services, Union civil services and all-India services hold office during the pleasure of the President.
    • Members of a State civil service hold office during the pleasure of the Governor.
    • UPSC constituted a committee in July 2000 to review the civil services examination, under the chairmanship of Professor Sukhadeo Thorat.
    • P.C. Hota was appointed Chairman of the Committee on Civil Services Reforms in February 2004; report given within six months.UPPSC
    • Civil Services Day = 21 April every year.
    • First Civil Services Day function was held at Vigyan Bhawan on 21 April 2006.
    • Reason for the date: on 21 April 1947 Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel addressed the first batch of civil servants at Metcalf House.

    Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions

    43 facts · 0 repeated by UPPSC

    Quick quiz: 10 of 6 UPPSC questions

    Part XXI

    • Articles 369 to 392 in Part XXI deal with temporary, transitional and special provisions.

    Special provisions for States (Article 371 to 371J)

    • Articles 371 to 371J give special provisions for different States.UPPSC
    ArticleState
    371Maharashtra and GujaratUPPSC
    371ANagaland
    371BAssam (tribal areas of Assam)UPPSC
    371CManipur
    371DAndhra Pradesh / Telangana
    371FSikkim
    371GMizoram
    371HArunachal Pradesh
    371IGoa
    371JKarnataka (Hyderabad-Karnataka region)UPPSC
    • Article 371J was inserted in Part XXI by the Constitution (98th Amendment) Act, 2012.
    • Article 371J empowers the Governor of Karnataka to take steps to develop the Hyderabad-Karnataka region.

    Article 370 and Jammu and Kashmir

    • Article 370 was a temporary provision relating to the State of Jammu and Kashmir.UPPSC
    • Article 370 gave special status to Jammu and Kashmir; currently no special status is granted to it.
    • Jammu and Kashmir had its own separate Constitution; it was the one exception to 'one Constitution for Centre and States'.
    • Its administration and provisions were different from those of other States.
    • J&K was excluded from the definition of 'State' in Article 152 (Chapter 1 of Part VI).
    • Earlier, Article 1 and Article 370 applied on their own to Jammu and Kashmir.
    • Article 1 declared Jammu and Kashmir an integral part of Indian territory.
    • Article 370 was declared inoperative on 6 August 2019 by a Presidential notification on the recommendation of Parliament.
    • Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 split the State into two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.
    • Jammu and Kashmir came into existence as a Union Territory on 31 October 2019.
    • Article 1 = India is a Union of States; Article 360 = Financial Emergency.
    • Article 270 = taxes levied and collected by the Union and distributed between Union and States.

    Jammu and Kashmir timeline

    1. 1947Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947.
    2. 1950The Constitution of India was enforced on 26 November 1950 (date as printed).
    3. 1951J&K Constituent Assembly abolished the Maharaja's hereditary rule and elected Karan Singh as first Sadr-e-Riyasat in 1951.
    4. 1956J&K Constituent Assembly ratified accession to India and adopted the J&K Constitution on 17 November 1956.
    5. 1957Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir came into force on 26 January 1957.
    6. 1965'Sadr-e-Riyasat' was renamed 'Governor' by the Sixth Amendment Act, 1965 of the J&K Constitution.
    • Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947.
    • Order of events: Instrument of Accession → Constitution of India enforced → accession ratified by J&K Constituent Assembly → J&K Constitution in force.UPPSC
    • The Constitution of India was enforced on 26 November 1950 (date as printed).
    • J&K Constituent Assembly ratified accession to India and adopted the J&K Constitution on 17 November 1956.
    • Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir came into force on 26 January 1957.
    • J&K Constituent Assembly abolished the Maharaja's hereditary rule and elected Karan Singh as first Sadr-e-Riyasat in 1951.
    • 'Sadr-e-Riyasat' was renamed 'Governor' by the Sixth Amendment Act, 1965 of the J&K Constitution.

    Special Category Status

    • Special Category Status (SCS) is granted by the Central Government to help States facing geographical and socio-economic challenges.
    • The Constitution does not provide for SCS; it began on the recommendation of the Fifth Finance Commission in 1969.
    • First States to get SCS in 1969: Jammu and Kashmir, Assam, Nagaland.
    • Earlier SCS for plan assistance was granted by the National Development Council of the erstwhile Planning Commission.
    • Eleven States given SCS: Assam, Nagaland, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Sikkim, Tripura, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Uttarakhand, Telangana.
    • Telangana, the newest State, got SCS as it was carved out of Andhra Pradesh.
    • 14th Finance Commission discontinued SCS for States, except Northeastern States and three hill States.
    • SCS parameters (Gadgil Formula): hilly terrain, low population density or significant tribal population, strategic border location, economic and infrastructural backwardness, weak state finances.
    • A sizeable SC and ST population is not an accepted parameter for special status.
    • Bihar was never granted SCS; Sikkim, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir were.
