    Chapter 36 · Bodies, elections, local government and more

    Election Commission

    118 facts · 6 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 reduced voting age from 21 to 18 by amending Article 326; in force from 28 March 1989.×5
    2. Article 324 provides for an Election Commission, a permanent and independent constitutional body.×3
    3. Right to vote and right to be elected in India are legal (statutory) rights, under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.×3
    4. Proportional representation ensures representation of minorities by giving due representation to all sections of society.×3
    5. Article 324(5): CEC can be removed only in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge.×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 29 UPPSC questions

    Constitutional basis

    • Articles 324 to 329 in Part XV deal with elections and the electoral system.
    • Article 324 provides for an Election Commission, a permanent and independent constitutional body.UPPSC ×3
    • Election Commission of India was established in accordance with the Constitution on 25 January 1950 (not 25 January 1952).
    • Article 324(1): superintendence, direction and control of electoral rolls and conduct of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, President and Vice-President vest in the Election Commission.

    Composition and appointment

    • Article 324(2): Election Commission = Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners; their number is fixed by the President from time to time.
    • CEC and other Election Commissioners are appointed by the President, under the law made by Parliament.
    • Till 15 October 1989 there was only a Chief Election Commissioner.
    • On 16 October 1989 two additional Election Commissioners were appointed for the first time; the Commission became a three-member body.UPPSC
    • Those two posts lasted only up to 1 January 1990.
    • On 1 October 1993 two additional Election Commissioners were appointed again; since then the Commission has three members.
    • So the multi-member Commission dates from 1 October 1993, not from 1995.
    • At present: one Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners (three-member body, not five-member).

    Powers, salary, tenure, removal

    • CEC and Election Commissioners have equal powers; their salary and perks equal those of a Supreme Court judge.
    • CEC acts as head, but all issues are decided by majority; differences are not decided by the Law Commission.
    • Tenure of CEC and Election Commissioners = 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier.UPPSC
    • CEC or an Election Commissioner resigns by writing addressed to the President (not to the CEC).
    • Article 324(5): CEC can be removed only in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge.UPPSC ×2
    • Other Election Commissioners or a Regional Commissioner can be removed by the President only on the recommendation of the CEC.UPPSC
    • Article 324 vests the conduct of free and fair elections to Parliament and State Legislatures in an independent Election Commission; the power to remove Election Commissioners lies with the executive (President), but that is not the reason for its independence.UPPSC
    • Table of precedence (mha.nic.in): CEC ranks at 9(A), with the UPSC Chairperson and the Auditor-General of India.
    • Table of precedence: Governor of a State = 4th; Chief Justice of India and Lok Sabha Speaker = 6th; Speaker of a State Assembly = 14th.

    Functions of the Election Commission

    • Functions: supervise, direct and control preparation of electoral rolls; conduct elections to Parliament and State Legislatures; conduct elections of President and Vice-President.
    • Election Commission does not recommend President's Rule when a State cannot hold free and fair elections.UPPSC
    • Making provision with respect to elections to Legislatures is not a function of the Election Commission.UPPSC
    • Elections to local bodies (Panchayats and Municipalities) are conducted by the State Election Commission under Articles 243K and 243ZA.
    • Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha are elected by the members of the House from among themselves.
    • Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
    • Election Commission does not conduct House presiding-officer elections or municipal elections, and does not decide election disputes; the Judiciary resolves election doubts and disputes.UPPSC
    • Election Commission decides the schedule of general elections and bye-elections (not the Home Ministry).
    • Election Commission resolves disputes relating to splits and mergers of recognised political parties.
    • Election Commission distributes election symbols and conducts elections peacefully.
    • Election notification is not issued by the Election Commission: President issues it for Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, Governor for State Assemblies and Councils.UPPSC
    • The President or Governor issues the notification on the recommendation of the Election Commission; then the Commission issues date and time.
    • Elections to President, Vice-President, Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils: indirect, by proportional representation through single transferable vote.
    • Elections to Lok Sabha and State Assemblies: direct, on the basis of adult suffrage.
    • List system and cumulative voting system are not adopted in India.

    Disqualification and Election Commission's advice

    • Election Commission has advisory jurisdiction in post-election disqualification of sitting members: Article 103 (MPs) and Article 192 (State legislators).
    • Article 103: question of an MP's disqualification under Article 102(1) is decided by the President; his decision is final.
    • Before deciding, the President must obtain the opinion of the Election Commission and act according to it.UPPSC ×2
    • Parliament made the decision to disqualify convicted persons from contesting elections.
    • Section 8(3), Representation of the People Act, 1951: conviction with imprisonment of not less than 2 years = disqualified from conviction date and for 6 more years after release.
    • A defeated candidate who fails to get more than one-sixth of valid votes polled loses his security deposit.
    • A winner losing his deposit means a very large number of candidates contested and votes got divided.

    Model Code of Conduct

    • Model Code of Conduct = guidelines for parties and candidates on speeches, polling booths, processions, manifestos and general conduct.
    • It is framed by the Election Commission, not enacted by Parliament; it applies as soon as the election schedule is announced.UPPSC

    Right to vote and voting age

    • Right to vote and right to be elected in India are legal (statutory) rights, under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.UPPSC ×3
    • Kuldip Nayar vs Union of India (2009): right to vote is neither a constitutional nor a fundamental right; merely statutory/legal.
    • Legal right = offshoot of ordinary law made by the Legislature; fundamental rights are of transcendental character and protected against any authority.
    • A fundamental right cannot be waived; an ordinary legal right can be taken away by the State.
    • Fundamental rights are beyond the reach of the State, except as provided by the Constitution.
    • Article 326: elections to Lok Sabha and State Assemblies are based on adult suffrage.UPPSC
    • 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 reduced voting age from 21 to 18 by amending Article 326; in force from 28 March 1989.UPPSC ×5
    • Aim: give unrepresented youth a chance to express their feelings and join the political process; the Representation of the People Act, 1951 was also amended.
    • Youth aged 18 first voted in the Lok Sabha General Election of November 1989.UPPSC
    • Principles of State Legislature elections: adult suffrage; one electoral roll for every territorial constituency; no distinction of religion, race, sex; parties free to set their own norms.UPPSC
    • On 1 March 2024 the Ministry of Law and Justice, after consulting the Election Commission, amended Rule 27A of the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961.
    • Age for senior citizens to vote by postal ballot from home was raised from 80 to 85 years.
    • In the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, citizens aged 85+ and persons with 40% or more certified disability could vote from home by postal ballot for the first time nationally.
    • Voting rights are statutory; there is no legal duty to vote, so non-voters cannot be punished by taking away their voting rights.
    • Lower turnout than the previous election does not bind the Election Commission to order re-election.
    • Awareness campaigns and advertisements are used as tools to increase voter turnout.

    Simultaneous elections, polls and numbers

    • For 'One Nation, One Election', amendment may be needed in Articles 83, 85, 172, 174 and 356.
    • High-Level Committee on Simultaneous Elections was set up on 2 September 2023, chaired by former President Ram Nath Kovind.
    • Members: Amit Shah, Ghulam Nabi Azad, N.K. Singh (former Chairman, 15th Finance Commission), Dr. Subhash C. Kashyap (former Lok Sabha Secretary General), Harish Salve, Sanjay Kothari (former Chief Vigilance Commissioner).
    • Arjun Ram Meghwal (MoS Independent Charge, Law and Justice) was Special Invitee; Dr. Niten Chandra was Secretary of the committee.
    • Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury was named a member but declined to participate.
    • Tushar Mehta was not a member of the High-Level Committee on Simultaneous Elections.
    • Exit Poll = post-election survey of voters about the candidates they voted for.
    • Opinion Poll = survey done by agencies before elections to know public views.
    • Total electors in the 2009 Lok Sabha elections = 714 million.UPPSC

    Representation of the People Act and electoral reforms

    • Section 33, RPA 1951: a person cannot be a candidate from more than two Parliamentary constituencies in a Lok Sabha general election.
    • Same limit for Assembly general elections: not more than two Assembly constituencies in that State.
    • In the 1991 Lok Sabha election Devi Lal contested from three constituencies; in response the RPA was amended in 1996.
    • A leader who wins more than one seat keeps only one, forcing bypolls in the rest.
    • No rule makes a party bear the cost of by-elections for seats vacated by its candidate.
    • Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1996 was based on the Dinesh Goswami Committee recommendations.
    • RPA Amendment 1996: conviction for insulting the National Flag or Constitution = disqualified for six years; security deposit for Lok Sabha increased; no countermanding on a candidate's death.
    • After 1996, on a candidate's death a new candidate of that party contests in his place.
    • Dinesh Goswami Committee was concerned with electoral reforms.
    • Dinesh Goswami Committee recommended government funding of parliamentary elections.
    • Dinesh Goswami was Law Minister in the V.P. Singh Government in 1989.
    Election reformFirst use / year
    Electronic Voting Machine (EVM)19 May 1982, Parur (Kerala) Assembly constituency, experimental use (recorded in A.C. Jose v. Sivan Pillai)UPPSC
    Electors Photo Identity Card (EPIC)Scheme started by Election Commission in 1993
    Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT)4 September 2013, Noksen Assembly by-election, Nagaland
    NOTA (None of the Above)Added in EVMs as per Supreme Court directions of 27 September 2013
    • M3 version of VVPAT machines is used for voting in India.
    • M3 EVMs are third-generation EVMs; can keep data of 384 candidates; have Tamper Detection and Self Diagnostics.

    Delimitation Commission

    • Delimitation = fixing the number of seats and boundaries of territorial constituencies in each State/UT for Lok Sabha and Assemblies.
    • It also fixes the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
    • Delimitation Commission is constituted by the Central Government under a law made by Parliament; not appointed by the Lok Sabha Speaker.
    • Its task: redraw boundaries of Assembly and Lok Sabha constituencies on the basis of the latest census.
    • Its purpose: rationalise constituencies on the principle of "One Vote and One Value".
    • The Delimitation Commission decides which constituency is to be reserved.
    • As per the 2008 Delimitation order: of 543 elected Lok Sabha seats, 84 are reserved for SCs and 47 for STs (not 44).
    • Orders of the Delimitation Commission cannot be challenged in a court of law.
    • Its orders are laid before Lok Sabha or the State Assembly, but they cannot modify them.
    • Delimitation Commissions under the Delimitation Acts were constituted four times.
    Delimitation CommissionUnder Act
    1952Delimitation Commission Act, 1952
    1963Delimitation Commission Act, 1962
    1973Delimitation Act, 1972
    2002Delimitation Act, 2002

    Note from the book Technically 5 Delimitation Commissions (1952, 1963, 1973, 2002 and March 2020 for the UT of Jammu & Kashmir) were constituted till December 2023; the answer 'four' goes by the Delimitation Acts.

    • Chairman of the 2002 Delimitation Commission = Justice Kuldip Singh.
    • Delimitation of Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland and Manipur was deferred for security risks by four presidential orders of 8 February 2008.
    • Those deferment orders were rescinded on 28 February 2020.
    • On 6 March 2020 a Delimitation Commission was set up under Section 3 of the Delimitation Act, 2002 for those four States and UT of Jammu and Kashmir.
    • Its chairperson was Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai.
    • In March 2021 the four north-eastern States were removed from the purview of the reconstituted Commission.

    Proportional representation

    • Proportional representation ensures representation of minorities by giving due representation to all sections of society.UPPSC ×3
    • It gives due representation to all groups based on ethnicity, gender, interests and ideologies.
    • Proportional representation is not necessary where a two-party system has developed.

    Persons and days

    • Sukumar Sen was the first Chief Election Commissioner (21 March 1950 to 19 December 1958).UPPSC
    • Sukumar Sen (2 January 1898 to 13 May 1963) was an Indian civil servant.
    • V.S. Ramadevi was the first and only woman Chief Election Commissioner, in 1990.
    • V.S. Ramadevi was also Governor of Karnataka and Himachal Pradesh.
    • In 2000 M.S. Gill was CEC; T.S. Krishnamurthy and J.M. Lyngdoh were Election Commissioners and later became CECs.
    • N.B. Lohani was not a member of the Election Commission.
    • National Voters' Day = 25 January every year, started on 25 January 2011.UPPSC
    • It marks the Commission's foundation day and encourages young voters to join the political process.

    Chapter 37 · Bodies, elections, local government and more

    Political Parties

    113 facts · 2 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. India has no fixed party system because there are too many political parties.×3
    2. Communist Party of India (CPI) · 17 October 1920 at Tashkent; in India 26 December 1925 at Kanpur×2
    Quick quiz: 10 of 18 UPPSC questions

    Party system

    • Party system is a part of the political system; government in a democracy is formed and run through the party system.
    • In India elections are held on the basis of Universal Adult Franchise.
    • Political parties are free to set their own standards, subject to mandatory legal/registration conditions.
    • Inner-party democracy = periodical elections within a party to elect its office bearers.UPPSC
    • Rajni Kothari described India's party system in the early years of Independence as a one-party dominant system.
    • Rajni Kothari was a political scientist and writer; works: 'Politics in India', 'Caste in Indian Politics', 'Rethinking Democracy'.
    • India has no fixed party system because there are too many political parties.UPPSC ×3
    • Indian democracy is in transition; casteism and regionalism still dominate; regional leaders form parties to meet various interests.
    • Other socio-economic reasons also affect the multi-party system in India.
    • India has a written Constitution; growth of strong regional parties shows regional aspirations; the two facts are unrelated.UPPSC
    • Regional parties raise the region's problems and demand more facilities for it, so the regional public turns to them.
    • Pressure group = organised group that does not put up candidates but seeks to influence government policy or legislation; e.g. a trade union.
    • Pressure groups are also called interest groups or lobby groups: trade unions, farmers' organisations, women's organisations, business organisations.

    Registration and recognition of parties

    • Representation of the People Act, 1951 provides for registration of political parties; the Election Commission registers them.
    • Election Commission recognises parties as National or State parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968.
    • During the 1999 general elections there were six National and 48 State level recognised parties.
    • National party condition 1: 6% of valid votes in four or more States (Lok Sabha or Assembly election) plus at least four Lok Sabha seats from any State or States.
    • National party condition 2: 2% of Lok Sabha seats (11 of 543), elected from at least three different States.
    • National party condition 3: recognised as a State party in at least four States.UPPSC
    • A party needs to fulfil any one of these three conditions to be a National party.
    • State party condition: at least 3 seats or 3% of seats in the State Assembly, whichever is greater.
    • State party condition: at least 1 Lok Sabha seat for every 25 seats (or fraction) allotted to that State.
    • State party condition: 6% of valid votes in the latest Lok Sabha election plus one Lok Sabha seat.
    • State party condition: 6% of valid votes in the latest Assembly election plus 2 Assembly seats.
    • State party condition: at least 8% of total votes in the State, even without winning any Lok Sabha or Assembly seat.UPPSC
    • A party needs to fulfil at least one of these conditions to be a State party.

    Note from the book UPPSC keyed 'None of the above' for the regional-party question; the book calls that key incorrect and takes '8% votes' as correct.

    National and regional parties

    • Presently 6 National parties: INC, BJP, Bahujan Samaj Party, CPI (Marxist), Aam Aadmi Party, National People's Party.
    • Muslim League, Revolutionary Socialist Party, All India Forward Bloc, and Peasants and Workers Party of India are not national parties.
    • Trinamool Congress (All India Trinamool Congress) got national party status on 2 September 2016; at present it is not a national party.
    • Samajwadi Party is not a national party; formed on 4 October 1992 in Lucknow under Mulayam Singh Yadav.
    • Akali Dal (Shiromani Akali Dal) is a regional party of Punjab.UPPSC
    • Telugu Desam Party is a regional party of Andhra Pradesh.UPPSC
    • Aam Aadmi Party was earlier a State-level party and also a registered party (all parties are registered); at present it is a national party.
    • In Kerala, Congress or CPI(M) (both national parties) have formed the government alternately; no regional party in power.
    • Under the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 Jammu and Kashmir is split into two UTs (J&K and Ladakh) and is not a State at present.

    Founding of parties

    1. 1885Indian National Congress was founded in 1885; first president W.C. Banerjee.
    2. 1901Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee (1901-1953) founded the Bharatiya Jana Sangh in 1951 and was its first President; Jagjivan Ram founded Congress for Democracy (CFD) in 1977.
    3. 1925Workers and Peasants Party was founded on 1 November 1925 by Kazi Nazrul Islam, Hemant Sarkar, Shamsuddin Hussain and Qutubuddin Ahmad.
    4. 1925Workers and Peasants Party worked under the Indian National Congress from 1925 to 1929.
    5. 1930Dr. B.R. Ambedkar founded Samata Sainik Dal, Depressed Classes Federation (1930), Independent Labour Party (August 1936) and Scheduled Castes Federation (1942).UPPSC
    6. 1948Peasants and Workers Party of India was founded in 1948 in Maharashtra; a Marxist party, not founded by Ambedkar.
    7. 1964Communist Party of India split into CPI and CPI(M) in 1964, when a faction broke away.
    8. 1980Bharatiya Janata Party was founded in 1980; first president Atal Bihari Vajpayee.
    9. 1982Order of founding: Telugu Desam Party (1982) → Bahujan Samaj Party (1984) → Samajwadi Party (1992) → All India Trinamool Congress (1998).UPPSC
    10. 1999Nationalist Congress Party was formed on 10 June 1999 by Sharad Pawar, P.A. Sangma and Tariq Anwar after a split in the Congress.
    • Indian National Congress was founded in 1885; first president W.C. Banerjee.
    • 'National' in its name reflects its all-India character; the word was influenced by the reaction against British rule.UPPSC
    • Bharatiya Janata Party was founded in 1980; first president Atal Bihari Vajpayee.
    • BJP is the successor party of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh.
    • Nationalist Congress Party was formed on 10 June 1999 by Sharad Pawar, P.A. Sangma and Tariq Anwar after a split in the Congress.
    • They were expelled from the INC after the dispute over Sonia Gandhi's foreign origin.
    • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar founded Samata Sainik Dal, Depressed Classes Federation (1930), Independent Labour Party (August 1936) and Scheduled Castes Federation (1942).UPPSC
    • Peasants and Workers Party of India was founded in 1948 in Maharashtra; a Marxist party, not founded by Ambedkar.
    • Workers and Peasants Party was founded on 1 November 1925 by Kazi Nazrul Islam, Hemant Sarkar, Shamsuddin Hussain and Qutubuddin Ahmad.
    • Workers and Peasants Party worked under the Indian National Congress from 1925 to 1929.
    • Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee (1901-1953) founded the Bharatiya Jana Sangh in 1951 and was its first President; Jagjivan Ram founded Congress for Democracy (CFD) in 1977.
    • Socialist Party's prominent leaders: Jai Prakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Acharya Narendra Dev.
    • C. Rajagopalachari was the founder leader of the Swatantra Party, not the Socialist Party.
    • Communist Party of India split into CPI and CPI(M) in 1964, when a faction broke away.
    • Order of founding: Telugu Desam Party (1982) → Bahujan Samaj Party (1984) → Samajwadi Party (1992) → All India Trinamool Congress (1998).UPPSC

    Elections and governments

    • Bahujan Samaj Party, Samata Party and Haryana Vikas Party were not part of the United Front Government of 1996-97; Asom Gana Parishad was.
    • BJP's Lok Sabha vote share: 7.4% (1984), 11.4% (1989), 22.4% (1991).
    • 2004 General Election (14th Lok Sabha): Congress 145 seats, BJP 138 seats, CPI(M) 43 seats.
    • 13th Lok Sabha seats: CPM 32, TDP 29 (not 30), BSP 14, BJD 10.UPPSC
    • November 1989 election (9th Lok Sabha): Congress was the single largest party with 197 seats but could not form the government.
    • Janata Dal formed a coalition government with outside support of BJP and Left parties; V.P. Singh became Prime Minister.
    • The 1989 elections marked the end of what political scientists called the 'Congress System'.
    • Coalition governments may contain many parties, so the government must respect the feelings of all partner parties.
    • BJP-led coalition's National Agenda had some policy guidance, promises and guiding principles; it also discussed many things in detail (both true, not cause and effect).UPPSC
    • In India governments are formed on majority of seats, not majority of votes; winners are decided by relative majority of votes.
    • First-past-the-post system: candidate with the highest votes wins; percentage of total votes does not matter; causes vote-seat distortion.
    • FPTP is used for the State Legislative Assemblies and the Lok Sabha.
    • Karnataka Assembly election December 1994: Janata Dal 36% votes, 116 seats; Congress 31%, 35 seats; BJP 20.4%, 40 seats.
    • Articles 330 to 334 provide reservation for some special classes in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies; there is no provision for women.
    • 33% reservation for women in Parliament and State Legislatures needs a Constitutional Amendment.
    • Parties can give 33% of the seats they contest to women candidates without any Constitutional amendment.
    • To be recognised as the Opposition Party, a party needs at least 1/10th of Lok Sabha membership (54.3 of 543), i.e. at least 54 seats.

    Anti-defection law

    • 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 gave political parties constitutional status for the first time.UPPSC
    • It added the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law) and amended Articles 101, 102, 190 and 191.
    • Anti-Defection Law was passed by Parliament on 15 February 1985 and came into force on 1 March 1985.UPPSC
    • The law covers en-bloc defection in a party, smaller defection in a single spell, and members voting to topple or support a government.
    • Large defections in a party in various spells are not covered by the law.UPPSC
    • A merger is recognised when at least two-thirds of the members of the legislature party agree to it; members are then not disqualified.
    • Defection disqualification is decided by the Lok Sabha Speaker or Rajya Sabha Chairman, not by the President.
    • The term 'political party' is explicitly mentioned in the Tenth Schedule.
    • A nominated legislator cannot join any political party after six months of being appointed; if he does, he can be disqualified.
    • The law gives no time-frame within which the presiding officer must decide a defection case.
    • An MP or MLA is disqualified if he voluntarily gives up membership of his party.
    • An MP or MLA is also disqualified for being absent from voting in the House on a particular issue.
    • A member is not disqualified if there is a merger of political parties.
    • A presiding officer who voluntarily leaves his party on election to the office is not disqualified, nor if he rejoins it after leaving office.
    • This exemption is given for the dignity and impartiality of the office.
    • But the Lok Sabha Speaker can be disqualified if he becomes a member of another political party.
    • Jammu and Kashmir Assembly passed an Anti-Defection Law as early as 1979.
    • Under the J&K law an MLA who left his party ceased to be a member of the Assembly.

    Movements, plans and party base

    • 'Bhu Poratam' (struggle for land) movement was launched in Andhra Pradesh.
    • It was organised by the Bharatiya Khet Mazdoor Union (BKMU) to demand farm land and house sites for landless agricultural workers.
    • The name 'Bhu-Poratam' was given by the Communist parties.
    • Business class is not part of the social base of the Communist Party; the party opposes capitalism, which business supports.
    • Kamaraj Plan was prepared in 1963 by K. Kamaraj, then Congress President, to make the Indian National Congress vibrant.UPPSC

    Electoral Bond Scheme 2018

    • Electoral Bond Scheme was notified by the Government of India on 2 January 2018.
    • Aim: bring transparency in the funding of political parties.
    • A citizen of India or a body incorporated or established in India may buy bonds; an individual may buy singly or jointly.
    • Eligible parties: registered under Section 29A of RPA 1951 and securing not less than 1% (not 2%) of votes in the last Lok Sabha or Assembly general election.
    • Electoral Bond is valid for 15 days from the date of issue; no payment is made if deposited after validity expires.
    • A bond deposited by an eligible party in its account is credited on the same day.
    • State Bank of India is authorised to issue and encash Electoral Bonds through its 11 Authorised Branches.

    Constitutional Amendments

    156 facts · 9 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. 52nd · 1985 (effective 1.3.1985) · Anti-defection law; Tenth Schedule added×4
    2. Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala (1973): Supreme Court gave the doctrine of 'basic structure' of the Constitution.×4
    3. 69th · 1991 · Delhi given status of National Capital Territory×3

    Quick quiz: 10 of 38 UPPSC questions

    Article 368 and the power to amend

    • Any constitution, however wisely made, needs amendment with time and circumstances.
    • Indian Constitution is a mixture of rigidity and flexibility; it is flexible and adaptable.
    • Article 368 in Part XX gives Parliament's power to amend the Constitution and the procedure for it.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 368(1): Parliament, in its constituent power, may amend any provision by addition, variation or repeal; it is the supreme legislative body elected by the people.UPPSC
    • But Parliament cannot amend provisions forming the 'basic structure' (Kesavananda Bharati case, 1973).
    • India's process of constitutional amendment is taken from the Constitution of South Africa.

    Three ways of amendment

    • The Constitution can be amended in three ways: simple majority; special majority; special majority plus ratification by at least half of the State legislatures.
    • Amendments by simple majority are not treated as amendments under Article 368.
    • Simple majority covers: admission or creation of new States; change of names, areas, boundaries of States; creating or abolishing Legislative Councils; salaries of President, Governors, Supreme Court and High Court judges.
    • Article 368 itself mentions two methods: special majority, and special majority with ratification by half of the States.
    • Special majority (Article 368(2)) = majority of total membership of each House and at least two-thirds of members present and voting.
    • Most Articles of the Constitution can be amended by special majority of Parliament.

    Procedure for an amendment Bill

    • A Constitution Amendment Bill can be introduced in either House of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha), not by State Legislatures or the President.UPPSC ×2
    • A Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed by each House separately by special majority.UPPSC
    • There is no provision for a joint sitting on a Constitution Amendment Bill; if the Rajya Sabha rejects it, the Bill is dropped.UPPSC
    • No prior recommendation of the President is needed; the President must give assent and cannot veto the Bill.
    • After the President's assent the Constitution stands amended as per the Bill.
    • 24th Amendment took away the President's veto over amendment Bills by using the words 'shall give his assent'.
    • Article 368 was amended by the 24th Amendment Act, 1971 and by the 101st Amendment Act, 2016 (to bring in GST).
    • 24th Amendment Act, 1971 (passed 5 November 1971): affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part including fundamental rights; made President's assent compulsory.
    • Article 74: the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

    Ratification by States

    • Proviso to Article 368(2): some amendments also need ratification by legislatures of not less than one-half of the States, before the Bill goes to the President.
    • Matters needing ratification: election of President, executive power of Union and States, Supreme Court and High Courts, federal provisions, Seventh Schedule Lists, representation of States in Parliament, Article 368 itself.UPPSC
    • Articles named in the proviso: 54 (election of President), 55 (manner of election), 73 (executive power of Union), 162 (executive power of State), 241 (High Courts for UTs), 279A (GST Council).
    • Chapters named: Chapter IV of Part V (Union Judiciary), Chapter V of Part VI (High Courts), Chapter I of Part XI (legislative relations between Union and States).
    • Article 279A was added to the proviso after the 101st Amendment in 2016.
    • Ratification is by half of the States, not all States, even for changes in federal character.
    • Formation of new States, change of borders or names, and abolition of a Legislative Council do not need State ratification.
    • Article 158 (conditions of Governor's office) is not in the proviso; no State ratification is needed.
    • Qualification, conditions of office and tenure of the President are not covered by the ratification requirement.
    • A State Assembly can pass or reject the ratification resolution, but cannot propose any amendment to it.
    • Third Amendment, 1954 was the first amendment ratified by State Legislatures under Article 368(2).
    • Third Amendment re-enacted entry 33 of the Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule.

    First Amendment, 1951

    • The first Bill to amend the Constitution was presented in 1951.
    • First Amendment was passed in 1951 by the Provisional Parliament, whose members had just drafted the Constitution in the Constituent Assembly.
    • First Amendment amended Articles 15, 19, 85, 87, 174, 176, 341, 342, 372 and 376.
    • First Amendment added Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule.
    • It was for the protection of agrarian (land) reforms in certain States.UPPSC
    • Object of the Ninth Schedule: protect certain Acts and regulations from being declared void for violating fundamental rights (Part III).
    • First Amendment was widely believed to be enacted to overcome judicial interpretations of the Fundamental Rights.
    • Immediate cause: Supreme Court and High Court rulings holding parts of criminal, press and public safety laws incompatible with free expression.
    • It added clause (4) to Article 15: special provisions for backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
    • It added restrictions in Article 19: 'public order', 'friendly relations with foreign states', 'incitement to an offence'.
    • Constitution as adopted on 26 November 1949 had a Preamble, 395 Articles and 8 Schedules.
    • Sixth Schedule: administration of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
    • Seventh Schedule: three lists (Union, State, Concurrent) fixing legislative authority.

    • The years 1976, 1985, 2002, 2011 for the 42nd, 52nd, 86th, 96th Amendments are years of enactment, not of implementation.
    • By May 2013, 98 Constitutional Amendments had been implemented; by January 2020, the 104th.UPPSC
    • The Constitution (98th Amendment) Bill related to the constitution of the National Judicial Commission; presented by Arun Jaitley, Law Minister in the NDA Government.

    42nd and 44th Amendments

    • 42nd Amendment, 1976 amended the Preamble, 40 Articles and the Seventh Schedule, and added 14 new Articles and two new Parts.
    • Its main objective: overcome difficulties from the Supreme Court's Kesavananda Bharati decision of 1973.
    • It added 10 Fundamental Duties (not eight) in Part IV-A, Article 51A, on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.UPPSC
    • Fundamental duties were 10 earlier and are 11 at present; derived from the Constitution of the Soviet Union.
    • It is not correct that the 42nd Amendment added Articles 39A, 43A and 47 as new Directive Principles.
    • 42nd Amendment gave the President power, in consultation with the Election Commission, to disqualify members of State Legislatures.
    • 42nd Amendment amended Article 74 to state that the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers.
    • 42nd Amendment gave Directive Principles preference over the fundamental rights in Articles 14, 19 and 31.
    • 44th Amendment Act, 1978 was brought by the Janata Party Government (1977-79) to undo several changes of the 42nd Amendment.
    • Under the 44th Amendment the President can return the Council of Ministers' advice for reconsideration only once, then must act on it.
    • 39th Amendment (1975) removed the Supreme Court's authority over election petitions of President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Lok Sabha Speaker.
    • 39th Amendment was nullified by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978; the 44th did not place the PM's election beyond judicial review.
    • Article 31 was repealed by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.

    Anti-defection, education and Council of Ministers

    • Anti-defection law (ban on floor crossing) came by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985 adding the Tenth Schedule; amended by the 91st Amendment Act, 2003.
    • Tenth Schedule: disqualification of MPs and State legislators on the ground of defection.
    • 58th Amendment answered the general demand for an authoritative Hindi text of the Constitution including all later amendments.

    Note from the book The book prints the 61st Amendment Act as 1988 in one place and as 1989 in another.

    • 61st Amendment gave unrepresented youth a chance to express their feelings and join the political process.
    • 104th Amendment Act, 2019: nomination of Anglo-Indians in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies not extended beyond 25 January 2020.
    • 93rd Constitution Amendment Bill = free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14; enacted as the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
    • It added Article 21A (Fundamental Rights), amended Article 45 (Directive Principles) and added Article 51A(k) (Fundamental Duties).
    • Article 21A: State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of 6 to 14 years as the State may by law determine.
    • Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 implements this right.
    • Both the 86th Amendment and the RTE Act came into force on 1 April 2010.
    • Right to Education aims at 'Education for All'; earlier free and compulsory education was in Part IV, Article 45 of the original Constitution.
    • Right to Education became a fundamental right by the 86th Amendment, not the 91st.
    • Till 2003 the Constitution did not fix the number of ministers; it depended on the Prime Minister or Chief Minister.
    • 91st Amendment Act, 2003 amended Articles 75 and 164 and the Tenth Schedule, and inserted new Article 361B.
    • Article 75(1A): ministers including the Prime Minister not to exceed 15% of Lok Sabha strength; in force from 1 January 2004.
    • Article 164(1A): same 15% limit for a State's Council of Ministers including the Chief Minister.
    • Objective of the 91st Amendment: strengthen the anti-defection law.
    • A member disqualified under paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule is also disqualified to be appointed a Minister.

    Co-operatives, land boundary, GST, later amendments

    • 97th Amendment was notified on 12 January 2012 to give constitutional status to co-operatives.
    • It added 'Co-operative Societies' in Article 19(1)(c) (Part III), Article 43B (Part IV) and Part IX-B (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT).
    • These provisions cover voluntary formation, professional management, functioning and operation of co-operative societies.
    • Part IX-B is now operative only for multi-State Co-operative Societies.
    • Article 243ZJ: number of directors of a co-operative society is fixed by the State Legislature, maximum 21.UPPSC
    • 99th Amendment Act, 2014 formed the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC).
    • Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment and NJAC as violating independence of judiciary and separation of powers.
    • A five-judge bench headed by Justice J.S. Khehar declared NJAC and the 99th Amendment void (dates printed: 15 October 2015 and 16 October 2015).
    • 100th Amendment Act, 2015 ratified the 1974 Land Boundary Agreement between India and Bangladesh.
    • India transferred 111 enclaves to Bangladesh; Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India (not the reverse).
    • Under it 6.1 km of undemarcated boundary was demarcated and territories of four States changed.
    • 101st Amendment Act, 2016 introduced a national GST on 1 July 2017.
    • It added Article 246A (legislative power for GST), Article 269A (inter-State GST) and Article 279A (GST Council).
    • 103rd Amendment, 2019: EWS = citizens other than classes in Article 15(4), 15(5) and Article 16(4); 10% reservation in government jobs and education.
    • President Ram Nath Kovind gave assent to the 105th Amendment Act, 2021 on 18 August 2021.
    • 105th Amendment amends clauses 1 and 2 of Article 342A, adds clause 3, and amends Articles 366(26C) and 338B(9).
    • Under it every State or UT may by law keep its own list of socially and educationally backward classes, which may differ from the Central List.

    106th Amendment (women's reservation)

    • Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 = 'Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam'; the latest amendment.
    • It reserves one-third of directly elected seats for women in Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and Delhi Assembly, including seats reserved for SCs and STs.
    • One-third of the seats reserved for SCs and STs are reserved for SC and ST women.
    • It takes effect after delimitation following the first census after the Act's commencement; not from the 18th Lok Sabha.
    • It stays in force for 15 years from commencement; reservation may continue till a date Parliament fixes by law.

    Basic structure and related cases

    • Golaknath vs State of Punjab (1967): Supreme Court limited Parliament's power to amend the Constitution for the first time.UPPSC
    • Order: Golaknath case (27 February 1967) → 24th Amendment (5 November 1971) → Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) → 42nd Amendment (1976).UPPSC
    • Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala (1973): Supreme Court gave the doctrine of 'basic structure' of the Constitution.UPPSC ×4
    • In Kesavananda Bharati the Supreme Court reversed its Golaknath decision and upheld the 24th Amendment.
    • Parliament can amend the Constitution including Fundamental Rights, but not the basic structure, under Article 368.UPPSC
    • A Fundamental Right that is part of the basic structure cannot be restricted or removed by Parliament.
    • Basic structure theory: certain features of the Constitution are so essential that they cannot be abrogated.
    • Basic structure = inviolable features that Parliament cannot amend or alter.
    • Minerva Mills case, 1980: giving all Directive Principles preference (42nd Amendment) is unconstitutional; preference only to Article 39(b) and 39(c) over Articles 14 and 19 is valid.
    • That preference came from the 42nd Amendment, 1976, not the 44th Amendment, 1978.

    Official Language

    61 facts · 1 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. Article 350A: every State and local authority shall try to provide instruction in the mother tongue at primary stage to children of linguistic minorities.×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 11 UPPSC questions

    Part XVII and language of the Union

    • Official language is dealt with in Part XVII, Articles 343 to 351.
    • Part XVII has four heads: Language of the Union; Regional Languages; Language of the Judiciary; Texts of Laws and special directives.
    • The term 'Official Language of India' is nowhere mentioned in the Constitution.
    • Article 343(1): official language of the Union = Hindi in Devanagari script; numerals = international form of Indian numerals.
    • Hindi is the official language of the Union, not the national language of India.
    • Article 343(2): English to continue for all official purposes of the Union for 15 years from the commencement of the Constitution.UPPSC
    • Article 343(3): Parliament may by law make an exception to Article 343(1); under Article 100(1) such a law needs a simple majority.
    • Using this power Parliament enacted the Official Language Act, 1963.
    • Section 3 of that Act: English also to be used, in addition to Hindi, as official language of the Union from 26 January 1965.
    • For some purposes of the Union Government, English is mandatory.
    • The Official Language Act can be amended by Parliament with a simple majority.
    • Articles 343, 344, 346 and 348(1) can be amended only by the special procedure of Article 368(2); no ratification by State legislatures is needed.

    Note from the book The question on how Parliament can amend the official language provision has two answers: 2/3rd majority as per its Hindi version, simple majority as per its English version.

    • Constituent Assembly accepted Hindi as the official language on 14 September 1949; 14 September is Hindi Diwas.

    Official Language Commission and Committee

    • Article 344: President constitutes an Official Language Commission after 5 years and again after 10 years from the commencement of the Constitution.
    • Article 344 deals with the commission and committee of Parliament on official language.
    • First Official Language Commission: appointed by Dr. Rajendra Prasad on 7 June 1955, chairman B.G. Kher.UPPSC
    • Kher Commission gave its report in 1956; recommended steps to replace English with Hindi eventually.
    • Parliamentary Committee on Official Language under Govind Ballabh Pant was set up in 1957 to review the Kher Commission's report.
    • Article 344(4): 30-member Joint Parliamentary Committee on official language: 20 from Lok Sabha, 10 from Rajya Sabha.

    Languages of States, courts and minorities

    • Article 345: a State Legislature may by law adopt one or more languages in use in the State, or Hindi, for its official purposes.
    • Until the State Legislature so provides, English continues for the official purposes it was used for before the Constitution.
    • Article 345 is subject to Articles 346 and 347.
    • Article 346: official language for communication between two States or between a State and the Union.
    • Article 347: special provision for a language spoken by a section of a State's population.
    • Article 348(1)(a): all proceedings in the Supreme Court and every High Court are in English.
    • Article 348(2): Governor, with previous consent of the President, may authorise Hindi or another official language of the State in proceedings of the High Court having its principal seat in that State.
    • Article 350A: every State and local authority shall try to provide instruction in the mother tongue at primary stage to children of linguistic minorities.UPPSC ×3
    • Under Article 350A the President may issue necessary directions to any State; added by the 7th Amendment Act, 1956.
    • A State cannot compel linguistic minorities to take their mother tongue as medium of instruction in primary schools.
    • Article 350B: Special Officer for linguistic minorities, appointed by the President.
    • The Special Officer investigates all matters on safeguards for linguistic minorities and reports directly to the President.

    Eighth Schedule languages

    • Languages recognised by the Constitution are listed in the Eighth Schedule; any language can be added to it.
    • Originally the Eighth Schedule had 14 languages; at present it has 22 languages.UPPSC
    AmendmentLanguages added to Eighth Schedule

    • The 22 languages: Assamese, Bengali, Bodo, Dogri, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Malayalam, Manipuri, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Santhali, Sindhi, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu.

    • 'Angika' is not included in the Eighth Schedule.
    • Uttarakhand gave Sanskrit the status of second official language on 1 January 2010.UPPSC
    • Later former Chief Minister Ramesh Pokhriyal 'Nishank' declared Rishikesh a Sanskrit city.

    Speakers of languages

    • Census 1991 and 2001: among Bengali, Gujarati, Marathi and Telugu, Bengali had the most speakers; Telugu was second.UPPSC

    • Hindi speakers: 41.03% in Census 2001 and 43.63% in Census 2011; Hindi is the most spoken language.
    • Brahui is a language of Baluchistan but belongs to the Dravidian family.

    • On 12 October 2004 the Government created the category 'Classical Languages'; Tamil was the first classical language.
    • Classical status is given to preserve and advance old literary traditions.

    Panchayati Raj and Community Development

    277 facts · 19 repeated by UPPSC

    UPPSC asks these most

    1. It recommended "democratic decentralisation" (Panchayati Raj) with a three-tier system: Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti (block), Zila Parishad (district); Nyaya Panchayat is not a tier.×6
    2. Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated Panchayati Raj on 2 October 1959 at Nagaur, Rajasthan; Rajasthan was the first State to adopt it.×5
    3. Order of committees: Balwant Rai Mehta 1957 → Ashok Mehta 1977 (report 1978) → C.H. Hanumantha Rao 1983 → G.V.K. Rao 1985 → L.M. Singhvi 1986 → P.K. Thungan 1988.×5
    4. The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions as institutions of self-government for rural India.×3
    5. It came into force on 24 April 1993, after ratification by the required number of States.×3
    Quick quiz: 10 of 83 UPPSC questions

    Early ideas and background

    • Sir Charles Metcalfe, acting Governor-General, wrote in 1830 that village communities are "little republics", having nearly everything within themselves and almost independent of foreign relations.
    • Lord Ripon (appointed Viceroy in 1880) is regarded as the Father of local self-government in India.
    • Ripon formulated local self-government and laid the foundations of representative institutions; his scheme developed the municipal institutions.
    • The first Municipal Corporation in India was established in Madras in 1688.
    • Mahatma Gandhi suggested the name "Panchayati Raj" for rural local governments.UPPSC
    • Gandhi wanted each village to be a little republic, self-sufficient in its vital wants and free to decide local affairs.
    • Article 40 (a Directive Principle) directs the State to organise village Panchayats and give them powers to function as units of self-government.UPPSC
    • The Panchayat system has been an integral part of Indian village life through the ages.

    Community development and the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee

    1. 1952The Community Development Programme (CDP) was started in 1952 as a pilot project; first major rural development programme after independence.
    2. 1952NES was formed because CDP (1952) could not be implemented all over India due to shortage of funds.
    3. 1953The National Extension Service (NES), started in 1953, was the first programme of community development.UPPSC
    4. 1953NES was formulated in April 1953 and inaugurated in October 1953.
    5. 1957The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee was set up in January 1957 (by the National Development Council) to examine CDP and NES; it reported in November 1957.
    6. 1959Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated Panchayati Raj on 2 October 1959 at Nagaur, Rajasthan; Rajasthan was the first State to adopt it.UPPSC ×5
    • The Community Development Programme (CDP) was started in 1952 as a pilot project; first major rural development programme after independence.
    • The National Extension Service (NES), started in 1953, was the first programme of community development.UPPSC
    • NES was formulated in April 1953 and inaugurated in October 1953.
    • NES was formed because CDP (1952) could not be implemented all over India due to shortage of funds.
    • Three phases of community development: National Extension Phase, Intensive Community Development Project Phase, Post-Intensive Development Phase.
    • The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee was set up in January 1957 (by the National Development Council) to examine CDP and NES; it reported in November 1957.
    • It recommended "democratic decentralisation" (Panchayati Raj) with a three-tier system: Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti (block), Zila Parishad (district); Nyaya Panchayat is not a tier.UPPSC ×6
    • Balwant Rai Mehta is called the Architect of Panchayati Raj in India.UPPSC ×2
    • Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated Panchayati Raj on 2 October 1959 at Nagaur, Rajasthan; Rajasthan was the first State to adopt it.UPPSC ×5
    • Andhra Pradesh was the second State to establish Panchayati Raj.

    Committees on Panchayati Raj

    CommitteeYearMain recommendation

    K. Santhanam (study team on Panchayati Raj finance)1962Limited revenue powers to Panchayats; Panchayati Raj Finance Corporations
    Ashok Mehta1977 (report August 1978)Two-tier system in place of three-tier
    M.L. Dantwala working group1977Planning at the block level
    C.H. Hanumantha Rao1983Decentralisation of functions, powers and finance; district planning bodies and district planning cells
    G.V.K. Rao1985Improvement in the representative character of Panchayats
    L.M. Singhvi1986Local self-government; more financial resources to village PanchayatsUPPSC
    P.K. Thungan1988Constitutional status for Panchayati Raj Institutions
    • Order of committees: Balwant Rai Mehta 1957 → Ashok Mehta 1977 (report 1978) → C.H. Hanumantha Rao 1983 → G.V.K. Rao 1985 → L.M. Singhvi 1986 → P.K. Thungan 1988.UPPSC ×5

    Note from the book The book's text gives 1983 for the C.H. Hanumantha Rao Committee, but the answer of one matching question pairs it with 1984 (and Ashok Mehta with 1978, the report year).

    • L.M. Singhvi, G.V.K. Rao, Ashok Mehta and Balwant Rai Mehta Committees all looked into Panchayati Raj Institutions.
    • Ashok Mehta Committee two-tier model: Zila Parishad at district level and Mandal Panchayat (group of villages, population 15,000 to 20,000).UPPSC ×2
    • Ashok Mehta: the district (not block) should be the first point of decentralisation below the State; the two-tier idea was not implemented.
    • Ashok Mehta (1977) proposed that some Panchayati Raj provisions could be kept in the Constitution; no central action followed because the Janata Government collapsed.
    • The Ashok Mehta Committee recommended Nyaya Panchayats as separate bodies, not mixed with the elected development Panchayats.
    • It favoured a qualified judge presiding over a bench of separately elected Nyaya Panches.
    • Elected Nyaya Panches cannot seek re-election and should serve in an area other than the one that elected them.
    • The G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985) was set up by the Planning Commission to review administrative arrangements for rural development and poverty alleviation programmes.
    • G.V.K. Rao: strengthen PRIs, hold regular elections, and treat the district as the basic unit of planning and implementation; block-level planning was Dantwala's, not G.V.K. Rao's.UPPSC

    Note from the book UPPCS (Pre) 2024 mismatch question: the Commission gave "Santhanam Committee – Panchayati Raj Finances" as the answer, which the book says is not correct; the wrong pair is "G.V.K. Rao – Planning at the Block Level".

    • The Dantwala Committee of the RBI on Regional Rural Banks reported in 1978: RRBs should be an integral part of the rural credit structure.
    • The L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) recommended that local self-government be constitutionally recognised, protected and preserved.UPPSC
    • Singhvi Committee also recommended non-involvement of political parties in Panchayat elections.
    • First L.M. Singhvi (1986), then P.K. Thungan (1988) recommended constitutional status; their recommendations were clearly accepted.
    • Major recommendations of the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee are also accepted in Part IX.
    • Rationalisation of Panchayat Statistics – V.R. Rao; Working Group on Panchayats and Co-operatives – S.D. Mishra; Administrative Arrangement for Rural Development and Poverty Alleviation – G.V.K. Rao.

    Note from the book In that question the name was printed "G.K.V. Rao"; the book notes it should be G.V.K. Rao, otherwise the question is wrong.

    • The P.V.N. Rao Committee is not concerned with Panchayati Raj.UPPSC
    • The V.K.R.V. Rao Committee is not related to Panchayati Raj; Ashok Mehta, Santhanam and B.R. Mehta Committees are.UPPSC
    • V.K.R.V. Rao was a prominent economist; headed the UN Commission for Economic Development; member of the Committee for National Income.
    • The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) was on electoral reforms, not Panchayati Raj; L.M. Singhvi, Sadiq Ali and Ashok Mehta Committees are related.

    Aims and nature of Panchayati Raj

    • Panchayati Raj = local self-governance, a system of democratic decentralisation (Balwant Rai Mehta's phrase), three-tier governance with bio-relations.UPPSC ×2
    • Its principal aim is to decentralise power to villagers so they make and implement policies for their own needs.
    • Panchayati Raj is called Grass-Root Democracy because it empowers local units by decentralising power.UPPSC
    • Its main objective: people's participation in development and democratic decentralisation; bringing development to the grass-root level.
    • Its main purpose is to enable people to participate in developmental administration.UPPSC
    • Panchayati Raj represents decentralisation of power, community development and participation of the people.
    • It has three tiers, aims at economic development and social justice for villages, and some MPs are representatives in the Zila Parishad.
    • Panchayati Raj needs the full co-operation of the local public to work properly.
    • Attributes of local government: statutory status, participation of the local community, power to raise finances by taxation; central control is not one.UPPSC
    • Decentralisation = delegating decision-making to the lowest possible level; features: autonomy, people's participation, empowering local communities (not non-confidence among them).
    • Under decentralisation the central unit distributes functions, responsibility and accountability to regional and local units; it extends delegation.
    • Decentralisation is the process by which power is divided among many units; local self-government helps manage local affairs.
    • Local bodies have representatives elected by local people, who understand grass-root issues better.
    • Judicial review is a power of the judiciary, not of Panchayati Raj Institutions; implementing land reforms and poverty alleviation programmes are.
    • Under judicial review, legislative and executive actions are subject to review by the Supreme Court.
    • Maintenance of public order is not a concern of local self-government; public health, sanitation, public utility services, roads and bridges, development schemes are.
    • The State Government controls local bodies in legislative, financial and personnel matters, but has no authority over citizens' complaints.
    • There are separate provisions for local governance in the Constitution: Article 40, Part IX and Part IX-A.
    • The 73rd Amendment rejuvenated rural local governance institutions and reduced political interference in their management.UPPSC

    The 73rd Amendment

    • The 64th Amendment Bill (prepared 1989, introduced in Lok Sabha in July 1989) was the first attempt to give constitutional status to PRIs.
    • The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions as institutions of self-government for rural India.UPPSC ×3
    • It came into force on 24 April 1993, after ratification by the required number of States.UPPSC ×3
    • It added Part IX "The Panchayats" (Articles 243 to 243-O, 16 new Articles) and the 11th Schedule.
    • The 73rd and 74th Amendments deal with local governance institutions and added a third tier of governance; they mark a watershed in local self-government.UPPSC
    • The 73rd and 74th Amendments introduced the three-tier governance system in the Constitution; this system is taken as copied from the Constitution of Australia.

    Note from the book The same Chhattisgarh question also treats "74th Amendment gives constitutional recognition to Panchayats" as true, though the book elsewhere links the 73rd to Panchayats and the 74th to Municipalities.

    • Both were made in 1992 when P.V. Narasimha Rao was Prime Minister.
    • The 73rd Amendment lays the foundation of strong and vibrant Panchayati Raj Institutions; the 74th refers to Municipalities.
    • It aims to establish a local self-governance system under Panchayati Raj.
    • The 73rd Amendment gave a practical shape to Article 40.
    • It provides: regular elections (Article 243K), not less than one-third seats for women (243D), transfer of funds recommended by the State Finance Commission (243I), transfer of 11th Schedule subjects.
    • It made Panchayat elections mandatory and set up State Election Commissions, to make them as fair as Lok Sabha and Assembly polls.
    • Regular remuneration to Panchayat members is not a provision of the 73rd Amendment.
    • Its other new provisions: collective responsibilities in agriculture, rural development, primary education and social forestry; mandatory elections for vacant posts; one-third representation of women.
    • After the 73rd Amendment, decision-making powers, administrative powers and the system as a whole are decentralised; judicial power was not.
    • The 73rd and 74th Acts give only a basic framework; giving it practical shape rests with the States.
    • The 73rd Amendment Act was passed in 1992; it let State governments formalise Gram Panchayats and make them work as self-governing bodies.
    • Provisions on Panchayats came by the 73rd Amendment; the 74th Amendment relates to Municipalities.UPPSC
    • 73rd covers Gram Panchayat, Kshetra Panchayat and Zila Parishad; Nagar Panchayat, Nagar Palika Parishad and Nagar Nigam are under the 74th.UPPSC ×2
    • Madhya Pradesh was the first State to implement Panchayati Raj in the true spirit of the 73rd Amendment.
    • National Panchayati Raj Day = 24 April every year; first celebrated in 2010.UPPSC
    • National Panchayati Raj Day 2025 (32nd anniversary) main event: Lohna Uttar Gram Panchayat, Madhubani district, Bihar, on 24 April 2025.
    • Panchayati Raj is a State List subject (entry 5, 7th Schedule).UPPSC ×2
    • The decision to hold Panchayat elections is taken by the State Government, which conducts them through the State Election Commission.UPPSC
    • The State Legislature decides by law the structure of Panchayats and all matters relating to Panchayat elections.
