    Note from the book Articles "243(A), 243(B), 243(C)" as printed in one question do not exist; they should be 243A, 243B, 243C.

    Structure and composition of Panchayats

    • Part IX envisages a three-tier system of Panchayats in every State (Article 243B).UPPSC
    • Three tiers: Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti/Block Panchayat (intermediate/block), Zila Parishad (district).
    • Article 243B(1): Panchayats shall be constituted in every State at village, intermediate and district levels.UPPSC
    • Article 243B(2): intermediate-level Panchayats may not be constituted in a State with population not exceeding 20 lakh; so not every State must have all three.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 243C(1): the State Legislature may by law provide for the composition of Panchayats.UPPSC
    • Article 243C(2): all seats are filled by direct election from territorial constituencies, with the population-to-seat ratio the same throughout the Panchayat area as far as practicable.
    • The territory of a Kshetra Panchayat and all other Panchayats is determined by the State Government.
    • Gram Panchayats are the smallest unit of local self-governance, at the village level.
    • Panchayati Raj is a three-tier, organically linked structure.
    • A Gram Panchayat covers a village or group of villages divided into wards; each ward elects a Panch (ward member).
    • Gram Sabha members elect ward members directly; the Sarpanch is elected by ward members as per the State Act; both serve five years.
    • Panchayat Samiti is constituted at the block (intermediate/tehsil) level.UPPSC
    • Members of the Panchayat Samiti are directly elected by the people.UPPSC
    • Jharkhand's Panchayat Samiti is constituted under Section 32 of the Jharkhand Panchayati Raj Act, 2001.
    • In Uttar Pradesh the Panchayat Samiti is called Kshetra Panchayat.
    • The Panchayat Samiti is an administrative authority; its functions are co-ordination and execution; it links Gram Panchayats and Zila Panchayat.
    • It collects plans prepared by Gram Panchayats, evaluates them and processes them for funding and implementation.
    • Zila Parishad is a supervisory and co-ordinating body, at the apex of the three tiers.
    • Zila Parishad includes district department heads, Panchayat Samiti chairpersons, MPs, MLAs and MLCs of the district, and representatives of SC, ST, women and co-operative societies; so not all members are directly elected.
    Panchayat Samiti nameState
    Janpad PanchayatMadhya Pradesh
    Kshetra PanchayatUttar Pradesh
    Taluka ParishadGujarat
    Anchalik ParishadWest Bengal
    Local body (status of 1999)State
    Zila Parishad at sub-divisional levelAssam
    Mandal Praja ParishadAndhra Pradesh
    Janajati ParishadMeghalaya
    Absence of Gram PanchayatsMizoram
    • At present there is no Panchayati Raj Institution in Mizoram, Nagaland and Meghalaya.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 243M(2): Part IX does not apply to Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and the hill areas of Manipur where district councils exist.

    Gram Sabha

    • Gram Sabha [Article 243(b)] = body of persons registered in the electoral rolls of a village within the Panchayat area at village level; not all persons living there.UPPSC
    • Gram Sabha is the foundation and primary body of Panchayati Raj, by far the largest, and a permanent body.
    • Gram Sabha is a village assembly of all registered voters in the Panchayat area; at village level it has powers like the State Legislature has at State level.
    • Article 243A: Gram Sabha exercises such powers at village level as the State Legislature (not the Central Government) may by law provide.UPPSC
    • Gram Sabha is the Sabha of the electorate; Gram Panchayat, Block Panchayat and Zilla Parishad consist of elected representatives.
    • A Gram Sabha decision cannot be annulled by any other body; only the Gram Sabha itself can annul it.
    • A Gram Panchayat can have more than one village; Gram Sabha can meet in each village by rotation; Gram Panchayat meets at its headquarters.

    Powers and the Eleventh Schedule

    • Article 243G: the State Legislature may by law give Panchayats powers to function as institutions of self-government; it adds to their importance.
    • Such law may devolve powers for preparing plans and implementing schemes for economic development and social justice, including Eleventh Schedule matters.
    • The 11th Schedule (added by the 73rd Amendment) lists 29 subjects for Panchayats.UPPSC ×2
    • Rural Sports is not among the 29 matters of the 11th Schedule; libraries, fuel and fodder, and technical training are.

    Duration and elections

    • Article 243E: every Panchayat continues for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting, unless sooner dissolved.UPPSC ×2
    • If dissolved early, elections must be completed within six months of dissolution.UPPSC
    • No election is needed if the remaining period of the dissolved Panchayat is less than six months.
    • A Panchayat formed after early dissolution continues only for the remainder of the dissolved Panchayat's term.
    • Example: first meeting 10 February 2014, dissolved 2016; the new Panchayat lasts only up to 10 February 2019.
    • The minimum age to be a member of a Panchayat (all three levels) is 21 years [Article 243F(1)].
    • Articles 243K(1) and 243ZA(1): the State Election Commission superintends, directs and controls electoral rolls and all elections to Panchayats and Municipalities.UPPSC ×3
    • The State Election Commission consists of a State Election Commissioner; detailed provisions are in Article 243K itself.
    • The State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor.UPPSC
    • The State Election Commission is a constitutional authority for each State/UT; the Election Commission of India has no role in local body elections.UPPSC
    • SECs conduct elections to corporations, municipalities, Zilla Parishads, District Panchayats, Panchayat Samitis, Gram Panchayats and other local bodies.

    Note from the book MPPCS (Pre) 2021 asked who appoints the "State Chief Election Commissioner"; the Commission deleted the question because of that wording (the State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor).

    • Constitutional authorities: State Election Commission (243K), State Finance Commission (243I), District Panchayat (243B); State Electoral Officer/Chief Electoral Officer is not.UPPSC ×2
    • The Rajasthan State Election Commission was constituted in July 1994 under Article 243K; single-member body headed by the State Election Commissioner; its secretary is also the State's Chief Electoral Officer.
    • It prepares electoral rolls and holds elections for Panchayati Raj Institutions and municipal bodies.
    • The Madhya Pradesh State Election Commission was constituted on 1 February 1994, under Articles 243K and 243ZA.

    Reservation of seats

    • Article 243D(2): not less than one-third of the seats reserved for SCs/STs are reserved for SC/ST women (not one-fourth or fifty percent).
    • Article 243D(3): not less than one-third of directly elected seats in every Panchayat (including SC/ST women's seats) are reserved for women; added by the 73rd Amendment.UPPSC ×2
    • Such seats may be allotted by rotation to different constituencies in a Panchayat.
    • Article 243D(4): one-third of Chairpersons' offices at all levels are reserved for women.
    • Article 334 deals with reservation in the House of the People and Legislative Assemblies, not Panchayati Raj.
    • Women's reservation in village local bodies was not the result of any demand; it did change the working of Panchayats.UPPSC ×2

    Note from the book IAS (Pre) 1997 and UPPCS (Mains) 2016: women's reservation is one-third, not 30 percent; and no two-child disqualification was proposed by the 73rd Amendment, so two options fit / no option fits.

    • Earlier, seats were reserved for women only in Panchayati Raj Institutions.
    • The 106th Amendment Act, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, also called the Women's Reservation Bill) reserves one-third seats for women in Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly, including SC/ST seats.
    • It takes effect after the first delimitation based on the first census after the Act's commencement.
    • In 2011, 50% seats for women in Panchayats existed in Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Himachal Pradesh.
    • At present 50% women's reservation in Panchayats: Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Tripura, Bihar, Uttarakhand, Madhya Pradesh, Assam, Gujarat, Karnataka, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, West Bengal, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh.
    • The U.P. Panchayat Laws (Amendment) Act, 1994 (in force 22 April 1994) reserves one-third of total seats for women.UPPSC
    • SC reservation in Panchayat elections does not apply to Arunachal Pradesh, which has no Scheduled Caste population (Census 2011).UPPSC

    Finance

    • Article 243I: the Governor constitutes a Finance Commission within one year of the 73rd Amendment and then every fifth year, to review the financial position of Panchayats.UPPSC
    • It makes recommendations to the Governor (printed once as "to the President") for Panchayats at all levels, not only the intermediate level.
    • The State Finance Commission recommends the principles for distributing net proceeds of taxes between State and Panchayats, and the taxes, duties, tolls and fees assignable to Panchayats.UPPSC
    • The Union Finance Commission (Article 280) also recommends measures to augment a State's Consolidated Fund to supplement Panchayats and Municipalities, based on SFC recommendations.UPPSC
    • Local government remains a State subject in the Seventh Schedule despite the 73rd and 74th Amendments.

    PESA Act

    • The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act (PESA) was passed by Parliament in 1996.UPPSC
    • PESA was enacted on the recommendations of the Bhuria Committee.
    • PESA applies in ten Fifth Schedule States: Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Telangana; not Assam, Meghalaya, Tamil Nadu.
    • PESA aims at self-governance, recognising tribals' traditional rights and freeing them from exploitation; it has no provision for creating autonomous regions.
    • Under PESA the Gram Sabha owns minor forest produce and can ban transfer of land.
    • Gram Sabha consent is needed for licences/mining leases for minor minerals only; not for other minerals.
    • PESA rules: a Scheduled Tribe member is chosen by consensus to chair Gram Sabha meetings for one year.
    • If there is no consensus, the oldest Scheduled Tribe lady among the members present is the Chairperson.

    State-specific Panchayat rules

    • Chhattisgarh Panchayati Raj Act, 1993: a Gram Panchayat has 10 to 20 wards, each electing one Panch, plus a Sarpanch as head; all are elected, none nominated.
    • In Chhattisgarh a tie (equal votes) in the election of a Panch is decided by lot.
    • Chhattisgarh (Act as amended in 2004): Gram Sabha meets once every three months; quorum = 1/10th of members, of whom 1/3rd must be women.
    • Sarpanch and Panchs are responsible for the quorum; removal of Sarpanch is initiated if quorum is absent in five consecutive meetings.
    • Annual working plan, beneficiary selection, annual budget, audit report, annual accounts and administrative report must be passed in a meeting with quorum.
    • A Gram Sabha meeting can be adjourned for want of quorum; an adjourned meeting needs no quorum, but the budget and audit report cannot be passed without quorum.
    • Chhattisgarh Panchayat Raj Act, 1993 gives Zila Panchayats: planning minor water bodies, control over institutions in all social sectors, control of tribal sub-plans, other functions conferred by the State Government.
    • Section 127 of the Chhattisgarh Act: the Governor may by notification change a Block's headquarters or alter its limits.
    • Section 39(3), Chhattisgarh Act: if a Sarpanch or Janpad/Zila Panchayat President is suspended, members elect one of themselves to hold the office temporarily.
    • For this the secretary/Chief Executive Officer calls a special meeting immediately, within fifteen days of receiving the information.
    • The officiating Sarpanch or President does all duties and uses all powers of the office while the suspension lasts.
    • A woman Sarpanch cannot nominate her husband to attend Gram Panchayat or Janpad Panchayat meetings; MLA/MP ex-officio members can nominate representatives.
    • Section 46, Chhattisgarh Panchayat Nirvachan Niyam, 1995: if a candidate dies before polling, poll is postponed only if just one candidate remains; not if more than one remains.
    • Chhattisgarh Panchayat election: one district election officer; one or more returning officers, appointed by the State Election Commission or, with its consent, by the District Election Officer.
    • A Naib Tehsildar may be returning officer for Janpad Panchayat and Gram Panchayat.
    • M.P. Panchayati Raj Avam Gram Swaraj Adhiniyam, 1993: if Sarpanch and Up-Sarpanch are absent, a Panch elected by members present presides over the Gram Sabha.
    • Standing Committees of Zila Panchayat in Madhya Pradesh include General Administration, Agriculture and Education Committees.
    • Others are Communication and Works, and Co-operation and Industries Committees; Zila Panchayat may create more committees beyond the five.
    • Section 89 of the Rajasthan Panchayati Raj Act, 1994 was amended to use "Gram Vikas Adhikari" in place of "Gram Sevak".
    • Section 19, U.P. Kshetra Panchayats and Zila Panchayats Act, 1961: the Zila Panchayat Chairman is elected by its elected members from among themselves.UPPSC
    • Section 19-A of that Act reserves the Chairman's office for SCs, STs and Backward Classes.
    • Bihar Panchayati Raj Acts of 1947 and 1993 let the village court (Nyaya Panchayat) award imprisonment.
    • In 1996 the Patna High Court declared Part VI (village court) of the Bihar Act, 1993 illegal.
    • Under the Bihar Panchayati Raj Act, 2006 no bench of a village court may sentence any imprisonment.

    The 74th Amendment and Municipalities

    • The 74th Amendment Act, 1992 gave constitutional status to urban local self-government (Municipalities).UPPSC
    • It added Part IX-A "The Municipalities" (Articles 243P to 243ZG), relating to urban areas only; in force from 1 June 1993.UPPSC ×2
    • It added the 12th Schedule with 18 functional items, restructured Municipalities, reserves seats for women, and applies to all States.UPPSC
    • Article 243Q: three types of Municipalities — Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council (smaller urban area), Municipal Corporation (larger urban area).
    • Municipal corporations are formed in big cities with definite area and population, because urban administration of big cities is very complex.
    • Eight types of urban local government: Municipal Corporation, Municipality, Notified Area Committee, Town Area Committee, Cantonment Board, Township, Port Authority (earlier Port Trust), Special Purpose Agencies.
    • All members of a Municipality are directly elected by the people of the area; additional representation may be given under Article 243R(2).
    • Article 243P(d): the municipal area is the territorial area notified by the Governor.UPPSC
    • A Municipality's term is 5 years from the date of its first meeting; it can be dissolved earlier.
    • Article 243T(1) provides reservation of seats for Scheduled Tribes (and SCs) in Municipalities.
    • Article 243T(3): not less than one-third of directly elected seats in every Municipality (including SC/ST women) are reserved for women; many States have raised it to 50%.UPPSC
    • Article 243V proviso: a person who has attained 21 years is not disqualified from Municipality membership for being under 25.
    • A person can be elected to a Municipal Council only if his name is in its electoral roll.
    • The Mayor is the highest-ranking official of a city's municipal government; tenure 5 years (Article 243U).UPPSC
    • In Delhi and Bengaluru the Mayor's tenure is one year; in Mumbai 2.5 years.
    • Article 243S: wards committees for one or more wards in Municipalities with population of three lakh or more.
    • Wards committee: made of some wards; ward councillors are members; two residents of the area are nominated (by the Mayor).
    • Each ward has one seat in the wards committee; members are elected by adult franchise for five years.
    • Census of India urban area: municipality/corporation/cantonment/notified town area committee; minimum population 5000; at least 75% of working males in non-agricultural work (not 60%); density at least 400 per sq km.UPPSC

    State-specific municipal rules

    • Rajasthan: security deposit for Mayor's election = Rs. 30,000 for general candidates.
    • It is Rs. 15,000 for women, SC, ST and Backward Class candidates.
    • Rajasthan Municipal Act, 2009: State Government may nominate up to 8 persons to a Municipal Council.
    • The limit is 6 for a municipal board and 12 for a municipal corporation.
    • Section 79(2), Chhattisgarh Municipalities Act, 1961: a Panchayat–Cantonment Board dispute is decided by the State Government, subject to the Central Government's concurrence.
    • Section 34, Chhattisgarh Municipalities Act: enrolled voter may contest; President needs age 25, Councillor 21; one may contest President and Councillor together.
    • A candidate for one ward cannot be a candidate for another ward.
    • A person elected both President and Councillor must resign one office within seven days of being declared elected.
    • Chhattisgarh municipal body: 5 years from the first meeting; one formed after dissolution serves only the remainder (dissolved at two years → new one for three years).
    • Its election must be completed before expiry of term or within six months of dissolution; not needed if the remainder is under six months.
    • Section 47, Chhattisgarh Municipalities Act: recall of Council President needs a proposal signed by 3/4 of elected Councillors, a majority of voters by secret ballot, and can be initiated only once in the term.
    • Recall needs more than half of the total voters casting votes; the proposal is presented to the Collector.
    • Recall cannot start within two years of the President entering office, or before half the tenure of a President elected in a by-election.
    • The Collector verifies the signatures and sends the proposal to the State Government, which refers it to the State Election Commission to arrange voting.
    • Chhattisgarh: a Councillor who acts as a legal practitioner for another person against the Municipal Council is removed by the Collector.
    • In U.P. the chairman of a Municipality is elected by the voters on the electoral list of the municipal area, including ward electors.UPPSC
    • Ghaziabad has a Nagar Nigam (Municipal Corporation), not a Nagarpalika Parishad.UPPSC
    • Lucknow has a Municipal Corporation and a Cantonment Board; Kanpur has a Nagar Nigam; Kakori is a Nagar Panchayat in Lucknow.

    Planning committees

    • 73rd and 74th Amendments created: State Election Commission (243K; 243ZA), State Finance Commission (243I; 243Y), District Planning Committee (243ZD); not the State Property Tax Valuation Board.UPPSC
    • District Planning Committees came by the 74th Amendment (Part IX-A); the 73rd provided State Election Commissions and State Finance Commissions.
    • Article 243ZD(1): the District Planning Committee consolidates plans of Panchayats and Municipalities and prepares a draft development plan for the whole district.
    • The 74th Amendment provides ward committees, Metropolitan Planning Committee (243ZE) and District Planning Committee (243ZD).
    • Article 243ZE: a Metropolitan Planning Committee in every metropolitan area prepares a draft development plan for it; it only sends the draft to the State Government.
    • Rajasthan District Planning Committee: 20 elected and 5 ex-officio members.
    • Other nominated persons there: Collector, ADM and two nominations from MLA, MP or CSO.
    • DPC size differs by State: 34 members in Bihar, 20 in Chhattisgarh.
    • Section 121(6), Rajasthan Panchayati Raj Act, 1994: the Zila Pramukh chairs the District Planning Committee.
    • The Planning Commission issued its first district planning guidelines in 1969; this led several States to formulate District Plans.
    • In U.P. the District Plan includes Nagar Panchayat, Gram Panchayat and Kshetra (Block) Panchayat, along with the District Panchayat.UPPSC

    MGNREGA

    • The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 was passed in August 2005 and came into force on 2 February 2006.
    • It was renamed MNREGA on 2 October 2009; the programme started in Anantpur district, Andhra Pradesh.
    • Adult members of any household are eligible for at least 100 days of guaranteed employment.
    • Under MNREGA the Gram Panchayat, after considering Gram Sabha recommendations, prepares the scheme and is responsible for execution of works.
    • The VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin)) got the President's assent on 20 December 2025.
    • It comes into effect on a date notified by the Central Government; it replaces MGNREGA with a new statutory framework aligned with Viksit Bharat 2047.
    • It raises the employment guarantee to 125 days per rural household annually and strengthens income security.

    • Part XVI also includes Articles 330A, 332A and 334A, inserted by the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023.

    Reservation of seats for SC and ST

    • Under Article 332, reserved seats are fixed by the proportion of SC or ST population to the State's total population.
    • Article 332 thus keeps SC/ST representation in the Assembly roughly proportional to the total number of seats.
    • Article 332 also extends to the autonomous districts in Assam's Legislative Assembly.
    • SC/ST reservation exists only for Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies; there is no reservation for any caste in Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Councils.UPPSC
    • After the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, the Union Territory has no Legislative Council.
    • Under the 2019 Act, seats are reserved for SCs and STs in the Legislative Assembly of the UT of Jammu and Kashmir.
    • The 104th Amendment Act, 2019 amended Article 334 and extended SC/ST seat reservation in Lok Sabha and Assemblies for 10 more years (80 years from the commencement of the Constitution).

    Anglo-Indian representation

    • Article 331: despite Article 81, the President could nominate two Anglo-Indian members to Lok Sabha if the community was not adequately represented.
    • Under Article 334 this provision was first for 10 years; later it was extended for 10 years each time.
    • The 104th Amendment Act, 2019 did not extend Anglo-Indian nomination in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies beyond 25 January 2020; so the arrangement has ended.
    • The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 was enacted by Parliament in 2020 (as printed).

    Reservation of seats for women (106th Amendment, 2023)

    • Article 330A: as nearly as may be, one-third of the directly elected seats of the House of the People are reserved for women.
    • This one-third includes the seats reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
    • Article 332A: as nearly as may be, one-third of the directly elected seats of every State Legislative Assembly are reserved for women (including SC and ST women's seats).
    • Article 334A: women's reservation takes effect after a delimitation based on the first Census taken after the commencement of the 106th Amendment Act, 2023.
    • This reservation ceases on the expiry of 15 years from such commencement.

    Lists of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes

    • Article 341(1): the President specifies, by public notification, the castes, races, tribes or parts/groups to be Scheduled Castes for a State/UT; for a State, after consulting its Governor.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 342(1): the President (not the Governor) specifies tribes, tribal communities or parts/groups as Scheduled Tribes for a State/UT; for a State, after consulting its Governor.
    • The ST list is State/UT specific: a community declared a Scheduled Tribe in one State need not be so in another State.
    • A tribe can be declared a Scheduled Tribe for only a part of a State.
    • The SC and ST lists were made by an order of the President issued in 1950 for each State after consulting its Governor.
    • Only Parliament, by law, can include in or exclude from the SC list (Article 341) and the ST list [Article 342(2)]; State Governments cannot prepare or amend them.
    • Once the President issues a notification under Article 342, it cannot be altered by any subsequent notification.
    • Bihar's 2015 notification moved the Tanti-Tantwa community from Extremely Backward Class to Scheduled Caste; the Supreme Court quashed it in July 2024.
    • The Supreme Court ruled that States cannot change the SC list published under Article 341.
    • Scheduled Tribe status is religiously neutral under the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950: a follower of any religion can be included.
    • Para 3 of the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950: only Hindus (including Buddhists and Sikhs) can be included in the Scheduled Castes.
    • The National Commission for Religious and Linguistic Minorities, headed by Rangnath Mishra, recommended repealing this para.
    • Criteria for specifying a Scheduled Tribe: indications of primitive traits, distinctive culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact with the community at large, and backwardness.
    • These criteria are not spelt out in the Constitution but have become well established.
    • After Parliament's amendment of 2007 (14 August 2007), there were 1206 Scheduled Castes in India.
    • As per the Constitution (Scheduled Castes Amendment) Act, 2017, the total number of Scheduled Castes in India is 1261.
    • Census 2011: Scheduled Castes form 16.6 percent of the total population.
    • Madhya Pradesh has the maximum Scheduled Tribe population.UPPSC
    • Descending order of ST population among four States: Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar.

    National Commissions for SC and ST

    • Original Article 338 provided a Special Officer for SCs and STs to look into constitutional safeguards and report to the President.
    • The 65th Amendment Act, 1990 replaced the single Special Officer with a high-level multi-member National Commission for SCs and STs.
    • The 89th Amendment Act, 2003 split the combined commission into two: NCSC (Article 338) and NCST (new Article 338A).
    • At present, Kishor Makwana is the chairman of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes.
    • NCST was set up on 19 February 2004.
    • Objective of NCST: oversee the implementation of safeguards for STs under the Constitution or any government order, and evaluate their working.
    • The commissions under Articles 338 and 338A each have a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson and three other members; NCST's three full-time members include one female member.

    • Dattatreya Balkrushna Kalelkar (1 Dec 1885 – 21 Aug 1981), popularly Kaka Kalelkar, was an independence activist, social reformer and journalist.

    United Nations: founding and membership

    • The United Nations is an international organization founded in 1945.
    • The draft UN Charter was finalized at the San Francisco conference held from April to June 1945.
    • On 26 June 1945, 50 nations signed the Charter.
    • Poland's representative was absent at San Francisco; Poland ratified the Charter on 16 October 1945 as the 51st member.
    • The UN came into being on 24 October 1945; this date is observed as United Nations Day.
    • Switzerland became a UN member on 10 September 2002; it was not a member in 1996.
    • UN membership years: Iraq 1945, Libya 1955, Namibia 1990.
    • South Sudan was created on 9 July 2011 as the newest and 193rd country of the world; its current capital is Juba.UPPSC
    • General Assembly, International Court of Justice and Trusteeship Council are three of the six principal organs of the UN.
    • Antonio Guterres (a Portuguese politician and diplomat) is the present UN Secretary-General.

    UN Security Council

    • UNSC is one of the six principal organs of the UN; it is charged with maintaining peace and security.
    • UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent (USA, France, China, UK, Russia) and 10 non-permanent; Germany is not a permanent member.
    • The 10 non-permanent members are elected on a regional basis for a term of 2 years.
    • Only the five permanent members have veto power to stop a resolution being passed with a majority; not every member has it.
    • The veto rests on Article 27 of the UN Charter: a Council decision needs 9 affirmative votes including the votes of the five permanent members, so any permanent member can withhold a decision.
    • The demand for democratisation of the UN mainly relates to the Security Council, as it has only five permanent members.
    • India, Brazil and South Africa are among the countries demanding democratisation of the Security Council.
    • India began a two-year term as non-permanent UNSC member on 1 January 2021 (2021-22 term).
    • Others elected for the 2021-22 term: Ireland, Kenya, Mexico and Norway; Canada was not elected.UPPSC
    • April 2024: UNSC rejected the proposal for Palestine's full UN membership; USA vetoed it, Switzerland and UK abstained = three members.

    UN peacekeeping, committees and observers

    • UN peacekeepers can use force in self-defence and also in defence of the mandate.
    • Peacekeeping operations can be withdrawn only by a UN Security Council resolution; USA is the largest budget contributor (around 28% in 2020-21).
    • The UN Credentials Committee is appointed at the beginning of each regular session of the General Assembly (not set up by the Security Council).
    • It has nine members, appointed by the General Assembly on the proposal of the President; it usually meets in November.
    • It assesses the credentials of all UN members before submitting a report to the General Assembly for approval.
    • The General Assembly can grant observer status to non-member States; inter-governmental organisations can seek it; Permanent Observers can maintain missions at UN headquarters.
    • Permanent observer status is based purely on practice; the UN Charter has no provision for it.
    • The practice dates from 1946, when the Secretary-General accepted the Swiss Government as a permanent observer.

    Good governance (UN)

    • UN lists 8 characteristics of good governance: Participation, Rule of law, Transparency, Responsiveness, Consensus Oriented, Equity and Inclusiveness, Effectiveness and Efficiency, Accountability.
    • "Government legitimacy" and "religiosity and emotionality" are not among them.

    UN Secretaries-General

    • Boutros-Boutros Ghali (Egyptian politician and diplomat) was the first African UN Secretary-General; he was the 6th, from 1 January 1992 to 31 December 1996.
    • Kofi Annan was the second African Secretary-General.
    • U Thant, the third Secretary-General, served for the longest period (1961-1971).

    • Riksdag = Sweden; Cortez = Spain; Sejim = Poland.
    • China's Parliament = National People's Congress (NPC).
    • NPC has 2977 members presently and is the biggest Parliament in the world.
    • In practice NPC is a rubber-stamp legislature approving the decisions of the Communist Party of China.
    • Princelings (the Party's crown princes) = descendants of prominent senior communist officials in China.
    • Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Sri Lanka was the first woman Prime Minister of any country, in 1960.UPPSC
    • She was sworn in as Prime Minister of Sri Lanka three times: 1960–65, 1970–77 and 1994–2000.

    Commonwealth

    • The Commonwealth has no charter, treaty or constitution.
    • Former British Empire territories did not join automatically; a willing country has to make a declaration.
    • Burma, Egypt, Kuwait and UAE never became members of the Commonwealth.
    • Nehru's words "an agreement by free will to be terminated by free will" refer to India's association with the Commonwealth of Nations.UPPSC

    India's foreign policy

    1. 1959Jawaharlal Nehru was the first Indian Prime Minister to visit Afghanistan, in September 1959.UPPSC
    2. 1966Tashkent Agreement (Pakistan) 10 January 1966 → Indo-Soviet Treaty of friendship and cooperation 9 August 1971 → Shimla Agreement (Pakistan) 2 July 1972 → Farakka Accord (Bangladesh) 1977.UPPSC
    3. 1971On 3 December 1971 India intervened on behalf of Bangladeshi refugees who had fled oppression in East Pakistan after Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's arrest.
    4. 1971On 16 December 1971 the Pakistani Army surrendered unconditionally; East Pakistan became Bangladesh (December 1971).
    5. 1976Indira Gandhi visited Afghanistan in 1976; Narendra Modi visited on 4 June 2016.
    6. 1977The Farakka Accord was signed temporarily in 1977 and finally on 12 December 1996.
    7. 1982The first Festival of India outside India was organised in Britain in 1982.UPPSC

    • Jawaharlal Nehru was the first Indian Prime Minister to visit Afghanistan, in September 1959.UPPSC
    • Indira Gandhi visited Afghanistan in 1976; Narendra Modi visited on 4 June 2016.
    • Nehru, after taking over as interim Prime Minister, announced a foreign policy based on non-alignment.UPPSC
    • Non-alignment = staying away from international power groups and developing an independent policy.
    • Panchsheel = five rules of conduct: mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty; mutual non-aggression; non-interference in internal matters; mutual benefit and equality; peaceful co-existence.
    • Non-alignment is not a principle of Panchsheel; the policy of non-alignment is itself based on Panchsheel.
    • Atal Bihari Vajpayee was Prime Minister when India's nuclear doctrine of No First Use was adopted.
    • India enunciated No First Use after the 1998 nuclear test; the doctrine was formally adopted in January 2003.
    • India's Six Points Formula proposal for the South Asian region was presented by Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee.UPPSC
    • Tashkent Agreement (Pakistan) 10 January 1966 → Indo-Soviet Treaty of friendship and cooperation 9 August 1971 → Shimla Agreement (Pakistan) 2 July 1972 → Farakka Accord (Bangladesh) 1977.UPPSC
    • The Farakka Accord was signed temporarily in 1977 and finally on 12 December 1996.
    • On 3 December 1971 India intervened on behalf of Bangladeshi refugees who had fled oppression in East Pakistan after Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's arrest.
    • On 16 December 1971 the Pakistani Army surrendered unconditionally; East Pakistan became Bangladesh (December 1971).
    • Sheikh Mujibur Rahman became the first Prime Minister of Bangladesh.
    • India–Sri Lanka Accord, 1987: keeping the integrity of Sri Lanka was part of it; complete freedom for a Tamil State was not mentioned.UPPSC
    • The first Festival of India outside India was organised in Britain in 1982.UPPSC

    Terrorist and extremist groups, operations

    • Lashkar-e-Taiba was founded by Hafiz Muhammad Saeed, Zafar Iqbal and Mahmoud Mohammad Bahaziq in 1990 in Kunar Province, Afghanistan.UPPSC
    • Lashkar-e-Taiba is an active terrorist organization in South Asia.
    • India, Sri Lanka, the United States and many other countries have banned the LTTE.UPPSC
    • In 2009 the Sri Lankan Army launched a massive operation against LTTE; its chief B. Prabhakaran was killed.
    • Djibouti Code of Conduct = international maritime grouping against piracy.UPPSC
    • It is the code on repression of piracy and armed robbery against ships in the Western Indian Ocean and the Gulf of Aden; adopted on 29 January 2009.
    • ULFA (United Liberation Front of Assam) is a separatist outfit operating in Assam.UPPSC
    • ULFA was founded on 7 April 1979; seeks a sovereign Assam via armed struggle; banned by the Government in 1990.
    • People's War Group was established by Kondapalli Seetharamaiah on 22 April 1980 in Andhra Pradesh.

    Assorted polity facts

    • Extra-constitutional right/power = one that finds no mention in the provisions of the Constitution.UPPSC ×2
    • Example: the Planning Commission had no constitutional provision; it was formed by a Cabinet resolution, yet exercised power over the Centre and States.
    • Air India nationalised (1953) → Imperial Bank of India renamed State Bank of India (July 1955) → first elected communist government in a State (April 1957) → Goa part of India (1962, 12th Amendment).
    • E.M.S. Namboodiripad (EMS) became the first non-Congress Chief Minister in the Indian Republic.
    • District Collector as District Magistrate: maintains law and order, controls the district police, recommends passport and visa cases and watches foreigners' movement.
    • Control of land revenue is exercised by him as Collector, not as District Magistrate.
    • Rajni Kothari, in his book "Politics in India", called the District Collector an "Institutional Charisma".
    • "Politics in India" is the pioneering research study of Rajni Kothari.
    • The total number of Articles in the Constitution is 395; the Finance Commission is constituted under Article 280.
    • Annie Besant (not Madam Cama) was the first woman President of the Indian National Congress; she chaired the 32nd session, 1917, Kolkata.UPPSC
    • Madam Cama hoisted the National Flag of India on 22 August 1907 at the International Socialist Conference in Stuttgart, Germany.
    • The right to protection of life and personal liberty cannot be suspended during Emergency; the Vice-President is removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution agreed to by Lok Sabha.UPPSC
    • In 2010 Montek Singh Ahluwalia was Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission; the Prime Minister used to be its Chairman.
    • NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.
    • In 2010 Arun Jaitley was Leader of the Opposition in Rajya Sabha; currently it is Mallikarjun Kharge.
    • The 92nd Amendment, 2003 added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali to the 8th Schedule; total languages became 22.
    • The 8th Schedule had 14 languages when the Constitution was enforced in 1950.
    • Queen Victoria's proclamation of 1 November 1858 (not the Charter Act of 1813) is called the "Magna Carta" of Indian liberties.
    • The Supreme Court is the highest court of appeal in India.
    • Article 35 read with Article 17 gives Parliament the power to make a law prescribing punishment for practising untouchability.

    Note from the book UP Lower Sub. (Pre) 2013 "not correct" question: two statements are incorrect (18 regional languages; Charter Act 1813 as Magna Carta), so no single answer.

    • High Court judge holds office till 62 (Article 217(1)); a party recognised in at least 4 States is a national party; Speaker decides Money Bill (Article 110(3)); cognizable offence = arrest without warrant.UPPSC
    • Suicide: once done the doer cannot be punished; its attempt was earlier punishable under Section 309 of the IPC.
    • The Law Commission's 210th report recommended deleting Section 309 IPC; 18 States and 4 Union Territories supported it.
    • A record nine coalition governments were formed in Bihar between 1967 and 1971.UPPSC
    • Joyita Mondal (West Bengal) is the first transgender judge of a Lok Adalat; also a social worker.UPPSC
    • At 29 she sat as a Lok Adalat judge at Islampur in North Dinajpur.
    • Causes of regionalism in India: unbalanced development of regions, fear of losing cultural identity, greed for political prominence.UPPSC
    • The National Water Development Agency (NWDA) was set up in July 1982 as an autonomous society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860.UPPSC
    • NWDA carries out water balance and other scientific studies for optimum use of water resources.
    • The Government of India constituted the National Water Board in September 1990.
    • Castes are being politicized in India and casteism is increasing in politics: both true, but the second does not explain the first.
    • Castes are emerging as pressure groups.
    • In 2003 Uttarakhand gave OBC status to the Gurkhas and two other communities, Ghrit Chahang and Uthalia Vora.UPPSC
    • Silent Valley Movement is linked with Dr. Salim Ali, not Baba Amte; Baba Amte was associated with wildlife conservation and Narmada Bachao.UPPSC
    • Appiko Andolan – P. Hegde; Chipko Andolan – S.L. Bahuguna; Narmada Bachao Andolan – Medha Patkar.

    1. 1923Gita Press, established in 1923, is one of the world's largest publishers: 41.7 crore books in 14 languages.
    2. 1950Param Vir Chakra = India's highest military decoration; instituted on 26 January 1950.
    3. 1954Padma Awards (instituted 1954) are announced every Republic Day, except breaks during 1978 to 1979 and 1993 to 1997 (two interruptions).
    4. 1954Bharat Ratna is the highest civilian award of India; instituted in 1954 along with Padma Vibhushan.

    6. 1987Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (Pakistan), 1987 = first non-Indian Bharat Ratna awardee; Nelson Mandela (South Africa), 1990 = second of two non-Indians.

    8. 1995The Outstanding Parliamentarian Award is given by the Indian Parliamentary Group to an outstanding sitting MP for overall contribution; instituted in 1995.
    9. 2009Awardees: Murli Manohar Joshi 2009, Arun Jaitley 2010, Karan Singh 2011, Sharad Yadav 2012.
    10. 2019Pranab Mukherjee got Bharat Ratna in 2019; he was India's 13th President.

    12. 2024Bharat Ratna 2024: five people — Karpuri Thakur, L.K. Advani, P.V. Narasimha Rao, Chaudhary Charan Singh and M.S. Swaminathan; four posthumous (all except Advani).
    13. 2024Announcement dates in 2024: Karpuri Thakur 23 January; L.K. Advani 3 February (PM Modi's tweet); Rao, Charan Singh and Swaminathan 9 February.
    14. 2024L.K. Advani was awarded at his residence on 31 March 2024; the other four at Rashtrapati Bhawan on 30 March 2024.
    15. 2025Till 31 December 2025, only 21 people have been awarded the Param Vir Chakra.
    • Param Vir Chakra = India's highest military decoration; instituted on 26 January 1950.
    • Four replicas of "Indra Vajra" are embossed on the Param Vir Chakra medal.
    • It can be given to a person once or more than once in a lifetime.
    • Till 31 December 2025, only 21 people have been awarded the Param Vir Chakra.
    • Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles barred by Article 18; they only denote State recognition of good work by citizens.
    • Padma Awards (instituted 1954) are announced every Republic Day, except breaks during 1978 to 1979 and 1993 to 1997 (two interruptions).
    • The number of Bharat Ratna awards is restricted to a maximum of three in a year (not five).
    • Bharat Ratna is the highest civilian award of India; instituted in 1954 along with Padma Vibhushan.
    • Bharat Ratna is given for exceptional service/performance of the highest order in any field of human endeavour; it is treated differently from Padma Awards.
    • The Prime Minister recommends Bharat Ratna to the President; no formal recommendations are necessary.
    • First Bharat Ratna awardees (1954): C. Rajagopalachari, Dr. S. Radhakrishnan and C.V. Raman.UPPSC
    • Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (Pakistan), 1987 = first non-Indian Bharat Ratna awardee; Nelson Mandela (South Africa), 1990 = second of two non-Indians.
    • Pranab Mukherjee got Bharat Ratna in 2019; he was India's 13th President.
    • Bharat Ratna 2024: five people — Karpuri Thakur, L.K. Advani, P.V. Narasimha Rao, Chaudhary Charan Singh and M.S. Swaminathan; four posthumous (all except Advani).
    • Announcement dates in 2024: Karpuri Thakur 23 January; L.K. Advani 3 February (PM Modi's tweet); Rao, Charan Singh and Swaminathan 9 February.
    • L.K. Advani was awarded at his residence on 31 March 2024; the other four at Rashtrapati Bhawan on 30 March 2024.
    • Gandhi Peace Prize = annual international award instituted by the Government of India in 1995, on Mahatma Gandhi's 125th birth anniversary.
    • Its jury has five members: Prime Minister (Chairperson, ex officio), Chief Justice of India, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, and two other eminent persons.
    • If the Leader of Opposition post is vacant, the leader of the single largest opposition party in Lok Sabha is the member.
    • One of the two nominated eminent persons may be the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
    • The President is not a jury member; the President confers the award as constitutional head.
    • Gandhi Peace Prize 2021 was conferred on Gita Press, Gorakhpur.
    • The prize is open to all persons regardless of nationality, race, language, caste, creed or gender.
    • It carries Rs. 1 crore, a citation, a plaque and an exquisite traditional handicraft/handloom item.
    • Gita Press, established in 1923, is one of the world's largest publishers: 41.7 crore books in 14 languages.
    • The Outstanding Parliamentarian Award is given by the Indian Parliamentary Group to an outstanding sitting MP for overall contribution; instituted in 1995.
    • Awardees: Murli Manohar Joshi 2009, Arun Jaitley 2010, Karan Singh 2011, Sharad Yadav 2012.

    Defence and security forces

    • The Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) is the Principal Military Advisor to the Defence Minister on all tri-service matters.
    • First CDS: General Bipin Rawat, took office on 1 January 2020; incumbent CDS: General Anil Chauhan.
    • Maximum age limit for the CDS post is 65 years; he is a member of the Defence Planning Committee.
    • The Defence Minister (not the CDS) chairs the Defence Acquisition Council; the National Security Advisor chairs the Defence Planning Committee.
    • CDS heads the Department of Military Affairs in the Ministry of Defence and functions as its Secretary.
    • CDS is Permanent Chairman of the Chiefs of Staff Committee but does not exercise military command over the three Service Chiefs.
    • Each Service Chief retains operational command over his own Service.
    • CDS administers tri-service organizations/agencies/commands and brings jointness in operation, logistics, transport, training, support services, communications, repairs and maintenance.
    • Armoured Corps Centre and School is in Ahmednagar, Maharashtra, not Jabalpur.
    • Southern Air Command – Thiruvananthapuram; Eastern Naval Command – Visakhapatnam; Army Medical Centre and School – Lucknow.
    • Operational commands of the Indian Army: 5 as of June 1999, 6 at present.

    • Operation Sadbhavana = Army operations for upliftment of local people in remote areas, including meeting their basic needs.
    • Its core concept: human security is the key element of national security, ensured through human resource and infrastructure development.
    • Its focus: infrastructure development, quality education, women empowerment, health care, community development, integration tours and sports.
    • Under it the Army runs welfare activities in remote areas of Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and Sikkim.
    • The Border Security Force was raised on 1 December 1965; headquarters in Delhi.
    • BSF is a specialized, centrally controlled force armed and trained to man the international border with Pakistan.
    • Central Armed Police Forces (paramilitary forces) guard six different international borders.

    • Home Guards = voluntary force to assist the police in controlling civil disturbance and communal riots.
    • Home Guards are raised by State governments under State Acts, not by the Central Government; they are an auxiliary to the police, and Border Wing battalions exist.
    • Home Guards also help the community in emergencies: air raids, fires, cyclones, earthquakes and epidemics.
    • Border Wing Home Guards battalions (Punjab, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Meghalaya, Tripura, West Bengal) are auxiliary to the BSF to prevent infiltration on international border/coastal areas.
    • The Internal Security Academy is at Mount Abu (Aravali Range, Rajasthan), under the Ministry of Home Affairs.UPPSC

    Law universities, thinkers and books

    • India's first law university, the National Law School of India, was established in August 1987 in Bangalore.UPPSC
    • National Law University is in New Delhi; National University of Advanced Legal Studies is in Kochi; Trivandrum has no law university.
    • Scientific socialism is attributed to Karl Marx, who gave socialism a scientific foundation.
    • Karl Marx is also regarded as the father of communism.
    • Morstein Marx gave four types of bureaucracy: Guardian, Caste, Patronage and Merit.
    • "Gandhian Constitution for Free India" (1946) was drafted by Shriman Narayan Agarwal, a Gandhian economist, on Gandhi's ideas; Gandhi did not write it.

    Countries and regions in the news

    • Argentina: worst economic crisis; Sudan: war between regular army and paramilitary forces; Turkey has not left NATO.
    • Argentina: among the world's highest inflation rates, over a decade of stagnation and rising poverty; cause = persistent public overspending financed by money creation.
    • Javier Milei assumed office as President of Argentina on 10 December 2023, with a mandate to end inflation and revive growth.
    • Sudan civil war began on 15 April 2023 (during Ramadan): Sudanese Armed Forces under Abdel Fattah al-Burhan vs Rapid Support Forces under Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo "Hemedti".
    • RSF and its allies are together called the Janjaweed coalition; thousands of civilians were killed and millions displaced.
    • The conflict traces to April 2019, when Sudan's President Omar al-Bashir was overthrown by military generals after a nationwide uprising.
    • NATO was established in 1949; Turkey joined in 1952; all NATO members must approve new applicants.
    • Turkey objected when Sweden and Finland asked to join in 2022; in January 2024 it finally backed Sweden's bid.
    • Chechnya is in the North Caucasus of the Russian Federation, in the most southern part of Eastern Europe, 100 km from the Caspian Sea.
    • Darfur is a region in Western Sudan (not Mali).
    • Swat is a river valley and district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan (not Iraq); the Swat River rises in the Hindu Kush.
    • The Berber-speaking community (Amazigh) lives in North African countries like Morocco and Algeria.
    • Berbers speak a language completely different from Arabic; they are the original inhabitants of the region.
    • Arctic Council was established by the Ottawa Declaration in 1996; it is the pre-eminent intergovernmental forum on Arctic issues.
    • Its eight members: Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, the Russian Federation and the United States; Japan and the United Kingdom are not members.
    • It promotes cooperation among Arctic States, with Arctic indigenous communities, on sustainable development and environmental protection.
    • India and Japan are among its 12 permanent observers.
    • Its chairmanship changes every two years: Iceland 2019–2021; Kingdom of Denmark 2025–2027.
